#1. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#2. Cheesy Vegan Enchilada Skillet (30 Minutes!)

Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!

Everything you love about enchiladas, minus the fuss! This super flavorful, cheesy vegan enchilada skillet comes together in about 30 minutes with simple methods, minimal dishes, and no need to fill or roll tortillas.

This easy, nourishing dish features tender cubed sweet potato or winter squash, fiber- & protein-rich black beans, and a rich red enchilada sauce. Everything gets simmered in 1 pan and topped with a melty cashew “cheese” that makes it SUPER satisfying and delicious!

It’s believed that enchiladas may have originated from a similar Mayan dish called papadzules. But the first written recipe for enchiladas was in an 1831 cookbook called El Cocinero mexicano. Typically, enchiladas are made with meat, seafood, beans, cheese, potatoes, or vegetables stuffed in corn tortillas and topped with enchilada sauce.

Our “inspired-by” enchilada skillet has all the flavors of classic enchiladas, but it’s vegan, and instead of rolling the filling in tortillas, we slice the tortillas and cook everything together in one pan on the stovetop!

This 1-pan, 30-minute vegan enchilada skillet begins with a base of sautéed vegetables — onion, garlic, sweet potato, and poblano pepper. The veggies are flexible here, so feel free to experiment! We love kabocha squash for a fall variation and have found green bell peppers work well when poblanos aren’t available. We also think butternut squash would be nice, as would greens such as kale or spinach.

Once the onions are very tender and the squash and peppers are just beginning to soften, we stir in black beans + corn tortillas that have been sliced into strips.

Next comes the final ingredient in the skillet portion of this dish (hello, simple + flavorful!): red enchilada sauce. We love the bold flavor of our homemade enchilada sauce (and usually have it stocked in the freezer), but this recipe also works well with store-bought enchilada sauce.

And lastly, it just wouldn’t be enchiladas without: the CHEESE! More specifically, a flavorful cashew “cheese” sauce inspired by our fan favorite Cheesy Vegan Pizza Beans. It’s made by blending up cashews, water, lime juice, garlic, tapioca starch, and sea salt. When poured over the enchilada skillet and covered with a lid, the heat and tapioca starch do their magic, creating a melty, cheesy layer! Total swoon!

We highly recommend trying the cashew “cheese” sauce, even if you’re not vegan or dairy-free! It’s super easy and takes this dish to a whole new level. However, this enchilada skillet is also delicious with shredded vegan or dairy cheese (such as pepper jack).

We think you’ll LOVE this recipe! It’s:SmokySpicySuper flavorfulSatisfyingVersatileQuick & easy to make& SO delicious!

This dish is hearty and amazing as a standalone quick meal for weeknights! It would also pair well with our Smoky Shredded Tofu Taco “Meat” or 1-Pan Mexican Shredded Chicken for a higher-protein option. Or, for more veggies, try it with our Crunchy Jicama Slaw or Quick Citrusy Cabbage Slaw.

#4. 29 Best Pumpkin Desserts to Bake This Fall

Among our favorite pumpkin desserts, you’ll find chewy pumpkin mochi crumb cake, lush pumpkin tiramisu, and a Basque cheesecake with a burnished umber top. Most start with canned pumpkin purée, so you don’t have to wrestle with a whole squash. Whether you’re plotting your Thanksgiving dessert spread or just looking for an excuse to turn on the oven, there’s plenty here to keep you baking all season long.

Fresh ginger gives this sweet pumpkin bread a little kick, while pumpkin seeds add crunch. Don’t skip the salted maple butter for slathering on each and every slice.

A sweetened cream cheese center, pepita streusel, and plenty of pumpkin spice. These muffins make a strong case for eating cake for breakfast.

She’s the queen of pumpkin desserts: silky filling, flaky crust, a whisper of spice. This is pumpkin pie done right.

Classic crumb cake meets chewy, bouncy mochi in this pumpkin-spiced mash-up. A buttery pecan streusel makes it a delightful cacophony of textures.

With dramatic chocolate swirls and a glossy ganache topping, this austere pumpkin Bundt cake looks like a project. Good news: You don’t even need a mixer.

With its deeply browned top and custardy, pumpkin-spiced center, this Basque cheesecake looks impressive and skips the fussy water bath. No crust required.

Everything you love about classic tiramisu, with the warming spices of a pumpkin spice latte. There’s bourbon in there too, so it’s decidedly not your morning coffee order.

Pumpkin sheet cake, tangy maple cream cheese frosting, and a little extra maple syrup drizzled over the top. What’s not to love?

A chocolate crust, bourbon-spiked pumpkin filling, and crackly brûléed top. It’s a lot, in the best possible way. Watch Claire make it here →

This pumpkin-spiced take on Puerto Rican flan de queso gets its luscious texture from cream cheese. And that glossy caramel topping? We’d happily eat it by the spoonful.

With nearly as much buttery streusel as fluffy pumpkin cake, this is one crumb cake that takes its topping seriously.

Bourbon adds depth to the spiced pumpkin filling, while a tangy sour cream topping balances the richness. Even the graham cracker crust gets an upgrade with chopped pecans.

Tahini gives this cloudlike pumpkin mousse pie a little nutty depth, while whipped cream keeps the filling light and airy.

Can’t choose between pumpkin pie and cheesecake? These tangy, maple-sweetened bars make a pretty convincing argument for having both.

From Yossy Arefi's Snacking Cakes, this chocolate loaf cake gets a generous dose of pumpkin and spices inspired by Mexican chocolate. Add the optional pinch of cayenne for a little heat.

A press-in hazelnut crust, rich pumpkin filling, and caramel topping make this tart holiday-table-worthy. Even better, you can get most of the work done ahead.

Maple syrup sweetens the classically spiced pumpkin filling, while a toasty oat-flour crust means no one misses out on pie.

Combine tiramisu, a pumpkin spice latte, and an icebox cake and you get this make-ahead dessert. Graham crackers soften into tender, cake-like layers as it chills.

Imagine pumpkin pie with pecan pie’s best feature: that crunchy, candied nut topping. A nutty rye crust makes the whole thing even better.

Who needs regular pie dough when you can press cinnamon-sugar-coated snickerdoodle dough into the pan instead? Flood it with the creamy pumpkin filling and chill.

Tender layers of pumpkin spice cake, tangy cream cheese frosting, and homemade caramel. It’s the kind of cake that doesn’t necessarily need a special occasion, but sure does do well at one.

Not your usual dramatically puffed Dutch baby, this pumpkin version is creamy and custardy in the center, with airy edges. Serve it with pumpkin butter for breakfast or a scoop of ice cream for dessert.

It’s giving classic American diner-style carrot cake—but make it pumpkin. Chinese five-spice adds unexpected warmth, while orange zest gives the frosting a little zip.

Cream puffs filled with pumpkin custard and drizzled with bourbon-spiked maple caramel? Yes, please. There’s whipped cream and toasted pecans involved too.

The only thing more satisfying than cracking through that caramelized sugar topping? Finding a luscious, pumpkin-spiced custard underneath.

Dress these mini pumpkin cupcakes up for Halloween, or down for fall bake sales and birthday parties. Set out the frosting and candy, and let everyone decorate their own.

Part pineapple upside-down cake, part pumpkin loaf, part gingerbread. Three desserts in one, with a sticky, buttery topping to seal the deal.

#6. Fall Freezer Meals #2

These Fall Freezer Meals have been SO helpful for us. The prep is shockingly easy!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 14, 2026

A few months ago, I discovered what feels like a little life hack.

I started spending an hour each month getting a few meals prepped for the month ahead. We’re talking just assembling stuff for my favorite recipes into bags and freezing it!

And I can’t tell you how much this system makes me feel like I have my life together! It’s the best.

The recipes this month are absolute family favorites for fall!

And they all have cook times for Crockpot, Instant Pot, and stovetop methods. 🙂

Hope these help make your life easier this month like they have for us!

Everything you need is right on them. I print the cards out and attach them to the bags so I don’t have to use my phone at all for the prep or cooking.

For the streusel: mix 4 tablespoons melted butter, 1/3 cup brown sugar, and 3/4 cup flour into small crumbles.

Spray a muffin tin with avocado oil. Fill tins two-thirds of the way full with batter; top with streusel.

Store muffins in an airtight container or bag in the freezer (or fridge). To reheat from frozen, microwave 45-60 seconds.

Remove chicken from the sauce and shred. Blend sauce until smooth. Add chicken back in. Serve in tortillas with all the taco fixings you want!

Add 2 cups heavy cream and 2 1/2 cups chicken broth. To thicken: whisk 1 1/2 tbsp. cornstarch with 1 1/2 tbsp. cold water; add and simmer.

Whisk 1 1/2 tbsp. cornstarch in 1 1/2 tbsp. cold water; add to bubbling pot and let simmer until slightly thickened.

Stir in 2 cups of fresh spinach and fresh cilantro just before serving.

Serve with rice and chili crisp. I also love this with cucumber salad (thinly sliced cucumber and red onion, tossed with vinegar, avocado oil, salt, and sugar).

#7. The ‘Tavern-Style’ Pizza Takeover

It’s the year of the tavern — and that means pizza style, too

In the suburbs of Chicago where they both grew up, it was just pizza, according to Brittany and Brennan Grosvenor, the couple behind Proof in Portland, Oregon. Ordering came down to the question of “thin-crust, deep-dish, or double-dough,” Brittany recalls of her family’s Friday night tradition. The Grosvernors sell the former at Proof, though the language of “thin crust” has given way to the more nationally familiar phrasing of “tavern-style,” the pizza trend that has swept from coast to coast in recent years.

Outsiders might associate Chicago with its famous, tourist-beckoning deep-dish pizza, but Brittany says that’s just not reflective of reality, citing deep dish as a much less frequent treat than the Midwestern, thin-crust style that’s gaining popularity. “The pizza you get every week, or if you go to a kid’s birthday party, it’s always tavern-style,” she says.

“Tavern-style” pizza — which is prevalent across the Midwest, with Chicago, Milwaukee, Minnesota, and St. Louis touting similar pies — is known for its thin, cracker-like crust, cut into a lattice instead of triangular slices. Depending on the region and the pizza shop where one’s nostalgia lies, the sauce might lean sweet or spicy. Lightness and crispness, though, is the style’s unique sell. Writing for Esquire in 2023, Omar Mamoon called the variant, which was then still on the rise, “a foil” to famously thick Detroit-style pizza, which had its big moment in the late 2010s.

The beauty of the tavern-style pie is its shareability. A pizza yields more slices when cut into a grid than into triangles, explains Bradley Shorten, who’s behind both Kim’s Uncle Pizza in his hometown Chicago suburb of Westmont, Illinois, and the recently opened La Merna in Washington, D.C. Pizza cut into little squares makes for great drinking food, especially since it fits on a cocktail napkin. What makes a good pie, according to Shorten, is that every square has a little of every ingredient; the toppings go to the edge. And while the four, small corner slices might not be the “best” ones, Shorten says, they’re the ones “everybody goes for,” especially if they’re from Chicago.

Over the past few years, as “taverns” have become growing fixations for a cadre of restaurateurs, the “party cut” pizza and tavern-style pizza spots have also become ubiquitous, with openings like Keepers in New York city; One Trick Pony in Forth Worth, Texas; Tillie’s Tavern Pizza in Wheat Ridge, Colorado; and Zarella and Dimmi Dimmi Corner Italian in Chicago, where the style has always been abundant. For some Chicagoans, these openings across the country are an opportunity to correct the record about their city’s pizza culture, and for other Midwesterners to claim their stake in the region’s pizza, too.

When Mike Fadem opened the second location of his popular NYC pizzeria Ops — known for its wood-fired Neapolitan-esque pies with leopard-spotted crusts and pliant dough — he wanted to offer something new. Fadem is from St. Louis, where the city’s namesake pizza is super-thin. Despite his love for it, “it’s maybe not the best version of tavern pizza,” Fadem admits, noting the iteration’s many critics, some of whom take issue with its use of the gooey processed cheese called provel. The trajectory of tavern-style pizza has been like a game of telephone, he explains: St. Louis pizza is derived from thin-crust Chicago pizza, which itself came from Neapolitan pizza. Divergence has accompanied each jump.

One of Fadem’s employees at Ops, meanwhile, is from New Jersey, which claims its own thin-crust, tavern- or bar-style pizza tradition. (The bar pies of the Boston area also have their own devoted following.) Accordingly, “I had this interest in ‘can we make an Ops version of this?’” Fadem says. With Ops known for sourdough, Fadem also wanted to highlight the rich flavor of whole grains. And he wanted it to be really crispy, a quality he says draws in New Yorkers. Fadem’s take is on the menu as the regionally agnostic “tavernetta.” Though St. Louis and New Jersey served as initial inspiration, the best pizza from his research was actually in Milwaukee. The Tavernetta hasn’t displaced the other pies at the restaurant; it’s ordered in addition to them, with most groups getting at least one.

In June, Los Angeles cocktail spot Bar Next Door celebrated its third anniversary by adding food to its menu. Previously, the bar had allowed customers to bring in pies from Prince Street Pizza next door since Prince Street co-owner Lawrence Longo is a partner in it. “But, you know, after having a slice, sometimes you get a little full and you’re like, I want to go to bed,” says owner and bar director Brynn Smith. “That’s the whole goal for us: for people to stay a little longer, drink more. We thought the tavern-style pizza would be perfect.” The fact that the pizzas — they’re technically listed on the menu as “bar pies,” to better go with the establishment’s name — are made exclusively for the bar by Prince Street just adds another reason for people to go out, Smith says.

The idea of the tavern as a social and convivial space is inseparable from the tavern-style pizza. Shorten’s goal with La Merna — which he runs with his wife Meg Schmitt, who grew up in St. Louis — was the feel of a Chicago dive bar or a Wisconsin supper club: a place with wood-paneled walls and checkered floors, where people could slide into a red leather booth for pitchers of beer and pizza and hang out for a while. As my colleague Francky Knapp wrote last year, the rising appeal of the “tavern” vibe across restaurants nationwide is rooted in the sense of providing somewhere homey and lived-in. At taverns, diners are beckoned to sprawl out and stay awhile; to free themselves of pretense and to tap into something welcoming in its familiarity. This, for so many people, is exemplified by the archetype of hometown pizza shop, which is forever tethered in our cultural imaginations to the trappings of a previous, simpler era.

It’s for this reason that, in Oregon, the Grosvenors have started serving their take on Bosco sticks, the stuffed breadsticks of Midwestern cafeterias, and Italian beef with giardiniera. While they could find certain Midwestern hits around Portland, it sometimes frustrated them that they couldn’t find everything in one place. According to Brennan Grosvenor, “We’re just trying to embody the feeling: If you went into a tavern in Chicago, what could you order there?”

#8. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#12. Pumpkin Bread

Pumpkin bread is a fall classic, and for good reason. It’s an easy recipe to have up your sleeve that’ll come in handy for every meal: Maybe as a quick bite before you run out the door in the morning, a perfect mid-morning snack, or even a scrumptious dessert to end a weeknight dinner. Easy to whip together, this quick bread is super-moist and tender, with just the right amount of pumpkin flavor. The best part? It’s totally adaptable—once you have the recipe down, you can experiment with it as you please.

What People Are Saying:“This turned out amazing and was so easy to bake!” - Cami.wood.wa

“This pumpkin bread is easy to bake and turned out delicious. I highly recommend trying!” - harbergabri7415

Preheat your oven (350°, please) and prep your pan. You'll need an 8" loaf pan, nonstick spray, and some parchment paper. The first task is to line the pan with a parchment sling to help lift the baked bread out of the pan without doing it any harm. Spray the inside of the loaf pan to anchor the parchment. Trim a sheet of parchment so it's a little shorter than the length of the pan; you don't have to be too precise. Line the pan with the parchment and trim the overhanging edges to 1" to 2"; these will serve as handles. Spray the parchment with nonstick spray and set the pan aside while you make the batter.

Mix the dry ingredients first. Flour, baking soda, salt, and spices all go into a medium bowl. Whisk them well so they are evenly combined.

Now for the wet ingredients. A handheld electric mixer is the tool for this job. Combine the eggs, granulated sugar, pumpkin, butter, sour cream, and vanilla in a large bowl and mix, starting on low speed (to avoid a mess) and gradually increasing to medium-high, until the mixture is visibly light and fluffy.

Time to bring the wet and dry together. With the mixer on low speed, gradually add the flour mixture to the wet ingredients and beat until just combined. It's important to keep the mixing to a minimum to avoid developing gluten, which can turn the quick bread tough and dry. Pour the batter into the prepared pan and spread it into an even layer with a rubber spatula. Sprinkle the top with demerara sugar and cinnamon sugar.

Bake the pumpkin bread for 50 to 60 minutes, until a toothpick or cake tester inserted in the center comes out clean. Using the parchment sling, remove the bread to a wire rack and let it cool completely.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

If your perfect loaf just isn’t complete without some chocolate or a nutty addition, feel free to add it! Fold in 1 cup of extra stuff, like chocolate chips, nuts, dried cranberries, or pepitas, into the batter and bake as directed.

First off, if you do have any leftovers, we recommend keeping the loaf whole and not in slices. The loaf can be left on your counter, covered with a towel or plastic wrap, for up to 4 days. Want it for longer? Wrap it thoroughly in plastic wrap, give it a once-over with foil, and freeze for up to 3 months.

#13. Is Pumpkin Good for You?

Pumpkin is one of our favorite fall flavors, but its nutritional benefits are worth celebrating year-round. Packed with fiber and antioxidants, this colorful squash deserves a place on your plate beyond pie.

Pumpkin isn’t just for pie! Sure, its subtly sweet flavor makes it a natural fit for pumpkin desserts, but the winter squash can be used for so much more. Whether I’m stirring it into a jar of pumpkin chia pudding or blending it into a PSL-inspired smoothie, pumpkin is an easy, tasty way to work more nutrients into my day.

As a dietitian, I reach for this fall favorite for its flavor, beautiful color and impressive health benefits. This low-calorie squash is packed with beta-carotene, which your body converts to vitamin A to support vision and your immune system. It also provides fiber to help make meals feel more satisfying and keep digestion moving, plus antioxidants that help protect your cells from damage.

I incorporate it into everything from warming soups and oatmeal to muffins and smoothies. And thanks to the convenience of canned pumpkin, it’s a pantry staple I can keep around long after Halloween to work more veggies into everyday recipes.

Pumpkin is loaded with vitamin A, with 1 cup of canned pumpkin providing about 200% of an adult’s daily need. This essential nutrient helps you see clearly, especially in low light, and keeps the surface of your eyes healthy. Much of pumpkin’s vitamin A comes from beta-carotene, the pigment that creates that bright orange color. Pumpkin also contains lutein and zeaxanthin, two antioxidants that help protect the cells in your eyes from damage.

Cooking with pumpkin can help get more fiber into your day. High-fiber foods feed the beneficial bacteria in your gut, keep your digestive system moving and support regular bowel movements. Fiber also helps you feel fuller for longer, which can make it easier to manage hunger between meals—whether you’re working toward a weight goal or simply trying to eat more satisfying meals and snacks.

The vitamin A in pumpkin does more than keep your vision sharp! It also helps keep your skin and other tissues healthy, making it harder for germs to get into your body. Pumpkin also contains vitamin C and vitamin E, which play important roles in keeping your immune system working properly. Eating more pumpkin won’t keep every sniffle away, but it’s a tasty way to get more of these important nutrients.

Pumpkin is rich in carotenoids like beta-carotene. These antioxidants help protect your cells from the kind of damage that can contribute to inflammation and chronic disease over time. That’s one of the many reasons it’s worth eating a rainbow of fruits and veggies, as each color brings its own mix of protective plant compounds to the table.

Pumpkin has a few things going for it when it comes to heart health. It provides potassium, a mineral that helps keep blood pressure in a healthy range, along with fiber that can help support healthy cholesterol levels. Pumpkin is also naturally low in saturated fat, making it an easy choice for heart-healthy meals.

When it comes to pumpkin’s health benefits, it doesn’t matter if you eat fresh or canned pumpkin. It really comes down to time and convenience. I lean on fresh pumpkin when I’m making recipes like salad, roasted veggies or soup, where it contributes a vibrant color that really pops. It might be tempting to use one of the large orange pumpkins used for carving, but a sugar pumpkin or pie pumpkin is actually the best pumpkin for soups. These varieties have sweeter, smoother flesh and less water than carving pumpkins.

Canned pumpkin is already cooked and pureed, so it’s a convenient shortcut when you’re short on time or want to enjoy pumpkin outside of fall. It’s especially handy when a recipe calls for just a little puree, since you can measure out what you need instead of cooking a whole pumpkin. Just be sure to grab 100% canned pumpkin, not pumpkin pie filling, which has added sugar and spices.

If you’re starting with a whole pumpkin, tackle it the same way you’d cook any other winter squash. Cut the pumpkin in half, scoop out the seeds and stringy bits with a spoon, then roast the halves cut-side down at 400°F for about 45 minutes, or until the flesh is fork-tender. Once it’s cool enough to handle, scoop out the flesh and cube, mash or puree it.

Once you have your pumpkin puree, there are plenty of ways to put it to work! Use it to make pumpkin overnight oats, stir it into cozy pumpkin soups or turn it into something a little unexpected like pumpkin hummus. The puree adds color, flavor and a little extra nutrition to sweet or savory dishes.

To get the most nutritional bang for your buck, make sure your pumpkin recipes contain a little healthy fat. The beta-carotene in pumpkin is fat-soluble, so your body absorbs it better when you eat it with fat. #14. George Lucas's Skywalker Grill Reminds Me of Applebee's in the Best Way

Skywalker Grill sits on the top floor of the new Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, a project that cost over $1 billion to build. With its plush interior and sweeping views of the Los Angeles skyline, it seems like the kind of place that would serve fussy little plates with foams, sauce squiggles, and $500 tasting menus. Instead of any special effects, the restaurant features a menu of crowd-pleasers.

Among the undulating walls (there are zero right angles), soaring ceilings, and completely custom furniture, diners dig into familiar favorites like spinach and artichoke dip and grilled salmon. Of course, the ruffled potato chips that arrive with the dip are made in-house, and the fish is lacquered with a honey miso glaze. Imagine Applebee’s had a cousin that grew up in Bel-Air and insisted on only the best ingredients.

Legendary filmmaker George Lucas and business executive Mellody Hobson, his wife, founded the museum with the ethos that everyone should feel welcome. It’s why many spaces at the Lucas Museum are open to the public without needing a ticket. Entry to the museum is free for people under 17 and anyone who lives in the same zip code, and the lobby cafe has a $2 grilled cheese. The dress code on Skywalker Grill’s Resy page says it all: “Come as you are. Stay for the experience.”

Diego Cardoso, the culinary director for the museum, developed a menu that nails the balance of high-low. Chicken tenders are served with a generous ramekin of caviar-topped ranch. The pigs in a blanket are the best I've ever had—snappy Wagyu beef hot dogs wrapped in the most buttery puff pastry, sprinkled with everything-bagel seasoning, and served with a truly exceptional grainy mustard—also made on-site.

Wagyu beef pigs in a blanket show off Skywalker Grill's approach to homey hors d’oeuvres.

Every leaf of the Caesar salad is perfectly coated in a garlicky dressing. The sizable chicken milanese is crispy and golden. And the mac and cheese (made with shells, the ideal pasta shape) is so creamy it deserves to be promoted from a side to a main. A chicken and wild mushroom crepe is an ode to a Lucas favorite from a long-shuttered chain called the Magic Pan.

Not every dish is a hit: a vegetarian pasta that featured patty pan squash and zucchini was reminiscent of plane food, and a side of brussels sprouts arrived limp and soggy.

Those looking for something spendier can order a $35 blue crab cake, a $52 lobster salad, and a $38 Wagyu burger made with grass-fed beef raised on Lucas’s Skywalker Ranch. Most items still manage to feel like a value given the generous portion sizes for the price point and many tables around me had leftovers boxed up to take home.

Shells go into a standout mac and cheese.

Since it opened in late September, Skywalker Grill has remained a tough table to get. The highly anticipated museum is already popular among locals and tourists, and the restaurant is no exception. According to its Resy page, there are zero tables for two available for the rest of the year.

Skywalker Grill is part of a growing trend of museum restaurants that are as much of a draw as the institutions that house them. In LA alone, the Hammer Museum is home to Lulu from David Tanis and Alice Waters. Fanny’s, in the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures, is a scene-y 10,000 square feet. LACMA has a café from Erewhon.

In its mission to be one of the most welcoming restaurants, Skywalker Grill is definitely one of the most comfortable. Velvet chairs feature sturdy back support and plush cushions, and sleek black marble tables are spaced out so that it’s nearly impossible to hear another party’s conversation. The wave-like architecture of the banquets means each nook of the restaurant feels private. The extensive use of cherrywood, renowned for its durable patina, speaks to Lucas’s desire to build a place that will outlive him.

The ruffled potato chips are made on-site.

The restaurant has been busy, but it doesn’t feel packed. Thanks to felt under the tables and the liberal use of an acoustic plaster that absorbs sound, it’s easy to forget that there’s a rambunctious toddler two tables over treating the space as his personal jungle gym.

While Skywalker Grill isn’t Star Wars themed, there are subtle nods to the franchise throughout. The curved bar, constructed from cast-glass beams covered in silver leaf, takes on an intergalactic glow when illuminated at night. In the private dining room, the chandelier is modeled after a specific dust cloud in space. The more obvious tributes come from diners who proudly show up in their most prized Star Wars shirts.

For all the cosmic flourishes, the restaurant’s greatest trick is unpretentious cooking: the room may transport you to another galaxy, but the food is down-to-earth.

#17. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#18. Where Chef Eric Sze Eats on His Day Off in NYC

Award-winning Taiwanese chef Eric Sze takes Eater on a food tour of NYC

Chef Eric Sze, the owner of NYC’s Wenwen, shows us the bakeries, pizzerias, and restaurants he visits weekly for everything from simple baguette sandwiches to oversized wontons.

Sze starts his day off with a sandwich at Bakeri; his go-to order is honey, apple, and brie layered on a crunchy baguette. Then he heads to The Meat Hook, Wenwen’s meat supplier, to get a specialty cut of steak and dry-aged short ribs for dinner. Next, he grabs a whole, crispy, NY-style pie at Chrissy’s Pizza (chef Chris Hansell has been perfecting this pie for years). The jalapeño and garlic pie has perfect proportions of each ingredient, all on a doughy, yeasted crust.

For his final stop, Sze goes to Maxi’s Noodle 2 in Flushing for the nostalgic Chinese food he’s craved since leaving Taiwan. Owner Maxi Lau-O’Keefe teaches him how to make her iconic wontons, filled with shrimp and pork before being expertly folded. After being humbled by the complex folding process, Sze settles in for a soup full of thin noodles made with duck eggs and those classic wontons, alongside beef soup.

#19. Easy Eggplant Bolognese (1 Pot!)

Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!

When we add another bolognese to the blog (Yes, we already have versions 1, 2, 3, and 4), you know it’s something special! This newest version is made with EGGPLANT, meaning it’s the perfect bolognese for late summer. It’s light yet satisfying, creamy yet bright, and full of bold Italian-inspired flavor — everyone will be asking for seconds!

Even better? It’s a breeze to make — just 1 pot required! What are you waiting for? Get that pasta water boiling!

Bolognese is an Italian sauce that gets its name from the Italian city of Bologna. It’s typically made with meat, soffrito (onions, celery, and carrots), white wine, milk, and tomato paste or sauce, all simmered to create a rich, flavorful sauce.

Our eggplant version strays from the traditional as it excludes meat (and includes eggplant) and incorporates dairy alternatives. But the rest of the dish is very similar to traditional bolognese and feels so hearty it might convert even the most adamant veggie skeptics!

This 1-pot eggplant bolognese is everything you want for a cozy pasta night, minus the fuss! It starts with sautéing onion and carrots to create a simple, savory-sweet base. Next, we add eggplant (cut into very small cubes) and let it sauté until it has softened and browned (hello, flavor!).

Build the flavor even further with garlic and red pepper flakes and by deglazing the pan with wine. Crushed tomatoes and tomato paste ensure a bright, tomato-forward sauce, and a small amount of dairy-free milk (we like homemade cashew milk) gives it a gentle creaminess and richness. The final flavor touches include dried Italian herbs (basil + oregano), sea salt, and maple syrup to balance the acidity of the tomatoes.

Once all the ingredients are in your pan, it’s time to let the heat do its magic. Simmering for at least 20-30 minutes allows the sauce to thicken and concentrates the flavors as liquid evaporates away. If you have the time, you can let it continue simmering for up to an hour for even more flavor!

When it’s done simmering, you’ll be left with an oh-so delicious, plant-powered sauce perfect for serving with your favorite pasta! It would also be lovely over polenta and is elevated by garnishing with fresh basil and our homemade vegan parmesan cheese.

We think you’ll LOVE this eggplant bolognese! It’s:RichSavoryCreamy yet brightLight yet satisfyingEasy to make& SO delicious!

It’s the perfect dish for a late summer pasta night! While quick enough for a weeknight, it’s also impressive enough to serve to dinner guests, especially paired with our Simple Vegan Meatballs, Pesto Turkey Meatballs, or Chickpea Caesar Salad (30 Minutes!).

#22. This Is What Halloween Candy Looked like in the 1960s

We've lost some excellent Halloween candy since the '60s, yet somehow, we've kept the raisins.

Halloween in the 1960s was a little less elaborate than the theatrical holiday we know today. There was no popping into Target for a complete costume in a plastic bag. Costumes were often assembled from whatever was already in the house, and the treats waiting at the neighbors’ doors weren’t necessarily wrapped in plastic either. My mom was a teenager in the ’60s, and when I asked her what she remembered, she told me about going as a cowgirl one Halloween, likely outfitted with my grandpa’s bandana and her older brother’s hat and boots. A little ingenuity could get you through the evening, preferably with a good haul of candy to show for it.

The contents of kids’ Halloween bags at the time offer a fascinating glimpse of the era. Familiar chocolate bars shared space with forgotten confections, homemade sweets and the occasional box of raisins that probably disappointed children then just as much as it would now.

A chocolate bar called Chicken Dinner sounds like a joke, but Milwaukee’s Sperry Candy Company was entirely serious when it introduced the candy in 1923. Despite the name, it contained no poultry, just a chocolate-covered nut roll. The name borrowed from the old promise of a chicken in every pot, and Sperry took the bit well beyond the packaging.

The wrappers featured roasted chickens, and the company even sent enormous chicken-shaped promotional trucks onto the streets to advertise the candy. I can’t decide if seeing one drive past would have made me more or less inclined to try a Chicken Dinner bar, but I’d certainly have wanted a closer look.

Sadly, the chickens came home to roost in 1962, when Pearson’s acquired Sperry and discontinued the bar.

Butterfinger turned 40 years old in 1963, and its crisp, flaky peanut butter center was as distinctive then as it is now. The bar was among those advertised for Halloween that decade, and its appeal was easy to understand. Unlike the smooth fillings and chewy centers of most other chocolate bars, Butterfinger offered a delicate crunch that shattered into little peanut buttery flakes beneath its chocolate coating.

It’s a texture that still sets Butterfinger apart from nearly everything else in the candy aisle.

A Snickers bar in your Halloween bag in the ’60s was a particularly good find, especially in 1968, when the Fun Size version first appeared. Now, we almost take the handful of minis we grab from the bowl for granted!

The bar itself was familiar territory: milk chocolate, peanuts, caramel and nougat, just as it had been since its introduction in 1930. And while smaller candy bars certainly existed, finding a full-sized one would have been a welcome improvement over a handful of pennies or a stale piece of hard candy.

The Seven Up Bar is one of those discontinued candy bars that makes me question the judgment of everyone involved in its disappearance. The bar had nothing to do with the lemon-lime soda, although the two companies did eventually find themselves negotiating over the Seven Up name. Made by Pearson’s, the candy bar contained seven individually filled sections beneath a chocolate coating. Depending on the period, the fillings included flavors like caramel, coconut, fudge, buttercream, cherry cream, orange jelly and Brazil nut.

It was essentially an assorted box of chocolates in bar form, with none of the uncertainty of biting into a mystery piece. I can’t help thinking it was an excellent idea abandoned too soon.

If you found a 100 Grand in your Halloween bag in the ’60s, you’d have known it by a different name. Nestlé introduced the $100,000 Bar in 1964, filling it with chewy caramel and crisped rice beneath a milk chocolate coating. It was a rather ambitious name for a candy bar that originally cost a dime.

The original wrapper promised “A Fortune in Flavor,” and the candy quickly caught on. By the end of the decade, miniature versions had appeared too. The name eventually changed to 100 Grand, but the combination of gooey caramel and crunchy rice has stuck around. Apparently, it’s the one fortune that hasn’t suffered much from inflation.

Tootsie Rolls were practically antiques by 1960, having been introduced in 1896, but the individually wrapped chocolate chews were perfect for trick-or-treating, and miniature versions appeared in Halloween advertisements that October. Tootsie Pops were available, too, although the famous television commercial featuring the owl wouldn’t arrive until 1970.

The candy itself has changed remarkably little. It still occupies that curious territory between chocolate and caramel, requiring more chewing than its modest size would suggest. And for anyone who has ever bitten into a Tootsie Pop rather than patiently licking their way to the center, the appeal of the combination needs no explanation.

By Halloween in the 1960s, candy corn had long since traded its agricultural roots for a permanent place among the seasonal sweets. The little tricolored kernels originated in the late 1800s, when candy makers were marketing the treat as Chicken Feed. Seems a questionable way to persuade people to eat something.

Whatever your feelings about candy corn, its unusually waxy texture and honeyed flavor have proved remarkably resistant to change. Set a handful of candy corn from the ’60s next to today’s version, and you’d have a difficult time telling them apart.

Of all the things a child might find in a Halloween bag in the ’60s, candy cigarettes may be the most revealing of the time. The chalky white sugar sticks came in miniature cigarette packs, sometimes designed to resemble actual tobacco brands. Kids could even pretend to smoke them, because nothing says childhood innocence quite like a pack-a-day habit.

The 1964 Surgeon General’s report would formally establish smoking as a major health hazard, helping change public attitudes toward cigarettes. But in the early ’60s, handing a child a tiny pack of candy smokes was still considered an adorable treat. It’s hard to imagine a better illustration of how much Halloween—and the world around it—has changed.

Bazooka offered something the chocolate bars couldn’t: reading material. Each piece of bright pink bubble gum came wrapped with a Bazooka Joe comic, a feature introduced in 1953 that gave kids something to enjoy long after the gum had lost its flavor.

The gum itself was famously firm, particularly when first unwrapped, but once you managed to soften it, there was the prospect of blowing an enormous pink bubble.

Cracker Jack had a persuasive argument for its place in a trick-or-treat bag: It was two treats in one. The caramel-coated popcorn and peanuts were only half the attraction; every box also contained a surprise. By the early 1960s, the company was promoting Cracker Jack for Halloween, and I suspect the possibility of finding a miniature toy inside the box was enough to make it a welcome addition to the evening’s haul.

The prizes weren’t particularly valuable, but that was hardly the point. Half the fun was digging through the popcorn to discover what you’d gotten. Cracker Jack retired its physical prizes in 2016, replacing them with digital experiences. I can’t imagine anyone feeling quite the same anticipation about scanning a QR code.

A candy apple was a rather extravagant addition to a Halloween haul in the 1960s. Instead of a few bites of factory-made chocolate, you got an entire apple encased in a glossy red shell of hardened sugar, often with a wooden stick for a handle. It was probably inconvenient to carry around while trick-or-treating, but I doubt many children objected to receiving something that looked as though it had come straight from a carnival.

Pixie Stix made their debut in 1959, just in time to give the children of the 1960s a remarkably efficient way to eat sugar. The colorful paper straws were filled with sweet-and-sour powdered candy, which you poured directly into your mouth. No chocolate, no caramel, no pretense of nutritional value. Just sugar with an easy delivery system.

The candy actually began as a powdered drink mix until someone noticed that children were skipping the water and eating the powder instead. Rather than discourage them, the company leaned into the idea. The kids had spoken, and they wanted their sugar straight.

Before individually wrapped candy became the default Halloween handout, plenty of neighbors made their own treats, and popcorn balls were a classic. Making them was a somewhat sticky undertaking: Freshly popped corn was coated in hot sugar syrup, then shaped into balls while the mixture was still pliable. Wrapped in waxed paper or cellophane, they were ready for the trick-or-treaters who came knocking.

And then there were raisins. In October 1962, the Chicago Daily Tribune recommended miniature boxes of Sun-Maid raisins for Halloween. The writer seemed confident that trick-or-treaters would be delighted, which suggests a rather optimistic understanding of what children hope to find in their Halloween bags.

Of course, the miniature Sun-Maid boxes are still with us, and so, I suspect, is the disappointment of discovering one at the bottom of a bag full of chocolate. Some traditions survive without the benefit of popular demand.

Do you remember your favorite candy from the ’60s? Let us know in the comments below!

#23. Easy Homemade Cranberry Sauce

This easy cranberry sauce recipe has been a fixture on my family’s Thanksgiving table for years, served alongside my mother’s elaborate Indian-inspired holiday dishes. With just 10 minutes on the stove and a handful of ingredients—fresh or frozen cranberries, sugar, orange zest, and water—it delivers the bright, tangy flavor that cuts through all the richness of the holiday meal.

My mom started making cranberry sauce after tasting a homemade version at a friend’s house. Over time, she made it her own, dialing back the sugar for extra tang and adding orange zest for brightness. We’ve tried fancier versions with maple syrup, chiles, and warm spices, but always come back to this stripped-down sauce. Anything more dulls the sharp cranberry bite we love.

A splash of orange liqueur is entirely optional, and you can swap some or all of the white sugar for light brown sugar. Best of all, you can make the sauce up to five days ahead, leaving one less thing to think about on Thanksgiving Day.

Can I use frozen cranberries to make cranberry sauce?

Absolutely. Fresh and frozen cranberries both work, and there's no need to thaw frozen berries before cooking. They may take a little longer to burst and become jammy.

Yes. The liqueur adds another layer of citrus flavor, but it's entirely optional. Brandy-based Grand Marnier brings warm, vanilla-like notes, while Cointreau offers a cleaner, brighter orange flavor. You can also simply leave it out; the orange zest provides fruity brightness on its own.

Cranberries contain natural pectin, which helps the sauce thicken as it cools. If yours still seems thin once cooled, return it to a simmer and cook until it coats the back of a spoon and holds a line when you run your finger through it.

What can I do with leftover cranberry sauce?

Cook 1 (12-oz.) bag fresh or frozen cranberries, ¾ cup granulated sugar, 1–2 Tbsp. Grand Marnier, Cointreau, or other orange liqueur (if using), 1 Tbsp. finely grated orange zest, a pinch of kosher salt, and 1 cup water in a medium saucepan over medium heat, stirring often to prevent scorching, until cranberries burst and sauce becomes jammy and coats a spoon, about 10 minutes.Let cool before serving.

Do ahead: Cranberry sauce can be made 5 days ahead. Transfer to an airtight container; cover and refrigerate until well chilled.

#24. Burger King Launched A Hello Kitty Kids’ Meal With A Rare Golden Toy: ‘NEED IT!!!’

Fans already know exactly which Sanrio character they’re hunting for.

Hello Kitty lovers, it's time to beeline to Burger King. Starting today, the fast food chain is launching the Hello Kitty and Friends King Jr. Kids’ Meal nationwide for a limited time. And personally, my inner child has never been more excited.

The meal includes the same year-round options: four- or six-piece chicken nuggets, a hamburger or cheeseburger, a drink, and your choice of fries or applesauce. But the Sanrio spirit really comes through with the extras. Each order also includes a limited-edition Hello Kitty Burger King Crown and a mystery toy.

Each blind box contains one of six exclusive collectibles inspired by some of the most popular characters in the Sanrio universe. The collection features Hello Kitty, My Melody, Kuromi, Cinnamoroll, and Keroppi, all wearing Burger King crowns. Some are even holding miniature versions of BK menu items!

A lucky few may also find the ultra-rare golden Hello Kitty toy. Is it a golden ticket to BK HQ? No. But it is really cute, and sometimes that’s all that matters.

This isn’t the first time Hello Kitty has graced a fast food menu. McDonald’s has rolled out several Happy Meals over the years featuring the character and her friends, including versions that came with watches in the late 2000s.

Fans are clearly excited about the new collection. “See you on 10/20, 10/21, 10/22, and every day after that until I get them all,” one Instagram user wrote. Another added, “NEED IT!!!”

And plenty of people already have favorites in mind. “Gotta get Hello Kitty because she my GOAT but i really want Keroppi because of the nuggets lol,” one commenter said. “I just want Cinnamoroll my boy,” another wrote.

Whether you’re hoping for one specific toy or want to collect them all, make your Burger King run before the limited-edition meals disappear.

#25. Pastina Soup (Italian Penicillin)

This soup is my new go-to when my family is sick. The broth here is AMAZING – light, flavorful, and nourishing. Absolute comfort food.

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 1, 2026

Like, slurp that savory broth and go back for a third bowl kind of good.

My daughter got sick last week, which means that our whole family got sick last week. And when I get sick, I lose two things: 1) my appetite, and 2) my interest in cooking.

This pastina soup truly SAVED us last week. It is:

I can’t say enough about how much I loved this last week. I sat down at the table with a steamy bowl with extra parm on top, and found myself repeatedly going back for “just one more scoop” of the broth over those tiny stars, even though I swore I hadn’t been feeling hungry just a moment earlier.

My girls were pretty excited about eating tiny star pasta with olive oil + Parmesan, while Bjork and I ladled the luscious broth over our bowls and finally tucked into some nurturing food for the first time in several days.

Pastina refers to the tiny star shaped pasta, which I found at Target, and the nickname Italian Penicillin refers to the healing nature of the savory broth – almost like a chicken noodle soup, but simpler. (And if I’m being honest, I prefer this to chicken noodle.)

I hope you are healthy and well, physically and emotionally. But if you’re not, this is comfort meal that has been serving our family so well lately!

I keep them real chunky, and I give them a quick sauté with olive oil before adding all the liquid just to get things extra fragrant.

I use water and Better Than Bouillon broth base.

Transfer to a bowl to cool down for a moment.

And then add them right back to the broth pot.

Source Notes: “Italian penicillin” is a nickname for pastina soup, or pastina (small pasta) in broth. It is playfully compared to medicine because of its healing vibe, being that it is a warm, nostalgic, nourishing comfort food. It originated with generations of Italian grandmothers and it has moved into the spotlight after becoming a popular trend on TikTok over the last few years. 🙂

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

This soup has become my go-to recipe when my family is sick. The broth is amazing – simple, light, flavorful, and nourishing! It’s absolute comfort food.

#27. The Best Gifts for Martini Lovers (Besides an Ice-Cold Martini)

From a martini lover to my brethren: 27 gifts that hit that brisk, briny spot, whether you like gin or vodka, shaken or stirred, twist or olives

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Ah, a perfectly made martini. When in the right mood, is there anything better than its bracing crispness? Then there’s the saline hit of the brine, should you take yours dirty, and the yield of an olive’s flesh between one’s teeth while your dining or drinking companion commiserates, flirts, or reveals gossip as juicy as your vodka- or gin-soaked Castelvetrano. (If you’re a twist person, respect, but we’re different.)

Sipping on an icy martini really conveys a feeling of glamour and mystery— there’s really no other cocktail that quite embodies elegance and timelessness that same way, nor that hits quite the same (did I mention they’re very strong?). No wonder a martini is the drink of choice for everyone from James Bond to Jay Gatsby to Brian Griffin from Family Guy (yeah, the dog). In fact, the martini is the second most popular drink in America after the margarita, with some bars in New York making more than 1,000 martinis each night.

Once considered an old man drink by Gen Xers and millennials, the martini’s popularity has been majorly revived in recent years, and being a martini-lover has become something of a personality trait. In my early 20s, when I discovered the appeal of the dirty martini, it quickly became my go-to drink at the San Francisco dive bars that occupied that time of my life in the late aughts — I was fine with well vodka as long as the martini was extra, extra dirty (some drinkers, as you’ve likely noticed, revel in saying “filthy” to their bartender). Nowadays, my taste is a bit more dignified and I’ll call my spirit (Tito’s, Belvedere, or Ketel One, depending on my mood) and ask for my drink with only a whisper of brine and, instead, a couple of extra olives. This is the thing about becoming a martini person: This simple drink suddenly becomes a blank slate for your micro-preferences, in the same way espresso does for coffee snobs.

Martinis are having a reawakening, no doubt, and there’s an unprecedented array of martini-centric bar gear, accoutrements, and even merch out there, from jewelry to martini-specific insulated tumblers to high-end olive brine. If you’re hunting for the best gifts for martini lovers, look no further — I’ve skipped the corny stuff and reached straight for the top shelf.

The gear you need to make a perfect homemade martini depends on that (frankly worn out) adage: shaken or stirred? The truth is that most bartenders will recommend stirred, but most people in casual bar settings are fine with shaken, and may even prefer it if they like each sip icy. If you’re making martinis at home (or know someone who likes to), a great cocktail kit sets the stage for a better drink.

This classic Williams Sonoma set is top of the line; yes, it includes everything you need for a Ritz-caliber martini, but will also come in handy for any other cocktail your recipient wishes to whip up.

For something a bit more affordable but still luxe-feeling, this stirred martini cocktail kit from Barfly comes with an etched 24-ounce mixing glass as well as copper tools that make handsome additions to a bar cart.

On the more whimsical side, this best-selling set from Mark & Graham nests into a cute boat, so it’s ornamental even when not in use. If you know anyone with a yacht, well, perfect gift for them.. and we’re not jealous at all, but maybe they should extend an invitation for us to all drink martinis on the deck.

There is an argument to be (convincingly) made that “soggy, splintered, deflated” “bottom-shelf bulk olives”actually make the best brine — the cheapo Manzanilla and Queen olives that culturally preceded the now ubiquitously trendy Castelvetrano. To be real with you, I adore all olives — the fancy newcomers and artisanal beauties but also the Mezzettas that have been living in the door of my parents’ fridge for my entire life. That being said, this is a story about gifts, and the thing about gifts is that a good one should feel a little bit special, curated, lesser-seen, harder-to-acquire, thoughtful, more premium than what you’d typically buy for yourself.

I recently became a big fan of Quincy olives; the olive-to-brine ratio is specifically formulated to make 14 dirty martinis with no waste (of fruit or liquid). The brine itself is just the right level of salty and umami; I’ve made a few friends dirty martinis with it recently and they all commented on how excellent their drinks came out. The recipe is right on the label, so it’s foolproof.

Another great brand for both brine and olives is Filthy; a friend of mine who works at a high-end Hollywood cocktail bar said that Filthy brine is the fave of both staff and customers. Filthy also makes standalone brine as well as a variety of stuffed olives; some dirty-martini-drinkers really love a blue-cheese-stuffed olive for a more creamy, complex experience, and they are a smart offering for a host gift or housewarming present.

Cocktail glasses have never been more personality-forward than in the present, with elegance, eccentricity, and whimsy all equally playing into the current renaissance of Very Interesting Glassware. Half the fun of drinking a martini is doing so from a smart, snazzy glass, whether minimalist or over-the-top decorative. I am addicted to collecting cocktail glasses and so have a half-dozen different options at home, should a guest arrive or the need for a martini strike. In recent years, restaurants and bars have begun thinking outside the box in terms of how to serve a martini; the only hard rule in my book (and that of many others) is that the glass should have a stem or at least a foot to help it stay cool as long as possible.

Here are a few special-looking martini glasses that have caught my eye recently…

Cocktail napkins and picks are truly underrated gifts — they’re small, easy to transport and store, and in that category of home goods that feels a little frivolous to buy for yourself but that is well-appreciated in ownership. I like these jeweled Joanna Buchanan cocktail picks for the martini-sipping diva in your life or the Archer stainless steel picks for a more Don Draper type.

Plutonia Blue is a New York City-based artist and jewelry designer whose sterling silver cocktail picks are dripping with iridescent keshi pearls. According to the designer, the string of pearls was first envisioned as the “the tresses of a woman dining alone (one of my favorite pastimes, how scandalous!).”

Founded by New York-based caterer Stephanie Nass, the brand Chefanie is behind these entertaining-ready olive napkins.

Another cocktail napkin I’m a bit obsessed with right now: this set of Polo Bear napkins from Ralph Lauren Home — they’re preppy (which I am decidedly not) but I appreciate that they seem self-aware. No, they aren’t emblazoned with any martini-specific imagery, but something about them does feel perfect for being the resting surface for an ice-cold Belvedere martini.

Being a martini drinker is now akin to being a huge fan of the Philadelphia Eagles or something; it no longer seems to be enough to just really like martinis. One must make it known that martinis are one’s thing. The market is abundant with ways to do so, from jewelry to hats to phone cases to sweaters.

Attention: true martini lunatics only! This section is for you.

Brümate is known for its functional, colorful water bottles, coolers, and other vessels — and for a martini-lover who needs to take one on the go (perhaps to the beach, a picnic, or the upcoming Wicker movie) and keep it chilled, there’s the MargTini, a tumbler made specifically for transporting cocktails. It has a splash-proof lid and slip-proof base, is made of double-walled steel so it doesn’t get condensation on the outside, and it keeps your drink cold for 12 hours. As one gin-drinking reviewer notes, “It even fits in the cupholder on the golf cart.”

I did a double take at the sight of this wildly lifelike handcrafted candle that uses gel wax for its doppelgänger of a frosty ‘tini, complete with extra olives. A fun accent piece that you’ll probably want to keep around instead of burn — but should you want to light it, its made with premium unscented wax.

I’m not advocating spending $565 on what’s essentially jewelry for your handbag, but I will note that if you’re, as noted above, a true martini freak, you should probably be made aware of the popular Loewe olive bag charm.

A slightly more reasonably priced option would be Chloe’s martini bag charm, although purists like myself may raise an eyebrow at the lime wheel on the side of the glass. Not a classic martini garnish; just saying!

If the trompe l’oeil candle above didn’t do it for ya because it’s unscented, I present this alternative: a candle from Rewined that “captures [a dirty martini’s] essence with the crisp, briny hint of olive and the fresh, piney aroma of juniper pays homage to the gin at the heart of this storied drink — rounded out with a touch of amber, evoking the luxurious ambiance of a high-end cocktail lounge.” Alluring! It has an 80-hour burn time for many evenings spent in the aura of a dirty martini right in your very living room.

For the martini-drinker who has it all — the cocktail picks, the carefully selected olive — we must ask: Do they have their very own signature cocktail? If not, another great gift option remains. Wonderbly will customize and print a cocktail book for your recipient of choice that includes 29 recipes for both classic and newfangled cocktails, but most importantly, its main attraction is a drink named for your friend and formulated specifically with their tastes in mind. Might we suggested a drink that includes gin or vodka, a touch of vermouth, and perhaps some olive juice? Just an idea.

#28. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#31. I Went to Epcot’s 30th International Food and Wine Festival and Wish I Could Eat the Paella Every Day

I ate my way through Disney's Epcot theme park, where even torrential rain couldn't hold me back from diving into a delicious sampling of international food and wine.

“A dream is a wish your heart makes” might be one of the most iconic song lyrics in the entire Disney canon. Sung by everyone’s favorite rags-to-riches princess, Cinderella, it’s become synonymous with fairy-tale magic. Considering that my ultimate dream is to travel around the world, eat delicious food and write about it, I felt like Disney was answering my heart’s greatest wishes with the Epcot International Food and Wine Festival.

The festival is celebrating its 30th anniversary now through Nov. 21, 2026, and I was lucky enough to make my way down to Orlando for the occasion. But the trip wouldn’t be complete unless I brought one of the people responsible for making a lot of my own dreams come true: my mom, Gayle.

Gayle and I checked into our room at Disney’s Coronado Springs Resort and excitedly planned out how we would navigate the festival. Through heatwaves and rainstorms, we persisted. And after two days at Epcot, we both had the same favorite food and wine.

Epcot is one of the theme parks at Walt Disney World in Orlando, Florida. In my opinion, one of the best features of Epcot is the World Showcase. Here, 11 countries have immersive pavilions of food, culture and shopping experiences. Each location is staffed by cast members from those countries, so you can practice your Japanese in Japan and your French in France if you so desire.

The 11 World Showcase countries (Mexico, Norway, China, Germany, Italy, the United States, Japan, Morocco, France, the United Kingdom and Canada) have permanent year-round food offerings. The Food and Wine Festival adds even more food from more countries with pop-up booths placed along the World Showcase. It began in 1996 and has since become an annual tradition running from August to November. Australia, Belgium, Greece, India and Spain are just a few of the additional countries with booths at the fest.

And of course, no trip around the world is complete without a passport. The Food and Wine Festival passport became an incredibly handy asset for my mom and me. The passport listed the locations of the additional booths and their food and drink offerings. It made it really easy to plan our day.

Every country had a special menu for the festival, including a couple of food options and a variety of alcoholic beverages to choose from. Wherever possible, my mom and I opted to get a “flight” of beer or wine so we could sample as many different drinks as possible. We also chose one food option to split because we knew we would be eating a lot throughout the day.

My mom and I thought splitting up the festival over two days would be plenty of time to try out everything. Dear reader: it was not! We had to make a lot of hard decisions during our “travels,” because there was such an abundance of offerings.

And despite my best efforts to get a cocktail in every country, I had to slow my roll by the time I got to Italy.

The fact is, we could have easily spent half a day at every booth. The quality and quantity of offerings were that good. But of everything we tried, we agreed that the Paella Caldoso from Spain and the Mimosa Flight from the Shimmering Sips kiosk were the highlights.

The paella was incredibly flavorful, a combination of chicken, chorizo and saffron rice. This was a 30th-anniversary legacy item, meaning it premiered at the very first festival in 1996. It cost $7.99 and was such a big portion that splitting it was absolutely the right way to go. But it tasted so good that we both joked about getting another plate even though we were totally stuffed.

The mimosa flight was how we started our second day at the festival, and it was incredibly delicious. Each mimosa had a different flavor profile: blood orange, berry and tropical. The ratio of juice to sparkling wine was perfection, and the trio of drinks was $15. We even saved the little glasses from this flight so we could recreate it on our own once we got back home.

I was overwhelmed in the best way possible by this festival. In some ways, I felt like a kid again. I was constantly being distracted by a new, shiny toy—although the “toys” in question were risotto, shrimp, egg rolls and beer. My mom and I are already planning on a return trip for next year’s festival. This list of advice is as much for you as it is for me:

#32. Easy Jalapeño Corn Fritters (Vegan)

Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!

Just when we thought summer’s most perfect veggie couldn’t get any more delicious, corn FRITTERS graced our palettes. These crispy-on-the-outside, tender-on-the-inside, lightly spiced fritters are a must-try appetizer or side!

Not only are they incredibly delicious, but these fritters are vegan, optionally gluten-free, and SO easy to make! Grab your mixing bowl and 10 basic ingredients, and you’ll be enjoying fritters in 30 minutes or less. What are you waiting for? Let’s do this, friends!

Giving traditional corn fritters a vegan spin requires a couple adjustments. First, instead of eggs for binding, we rely on flaxseed meal. And instead of milk, we rely on a neutral-flavored, unsweetened dairy-free milk (homemade cashew being our favorite). The rest of the ingredients are pretty classic, but we gave these fritters our own flavor spin and also made them gluten-free!

Besides flaxseed meal and dairy-free milk, the ingredients for the batter include baking powder for fluffiness; salt, garlic powder, and nutritional yeast for flavor; and all-purpose flour or gluten-free blend to thicken it.

You’re looking for a thick, fluffy batter, which can be achieved by adding more flour or dairy-free milk as needed. With the batter ready, we’re just 3 ingredients away from fritter time!

Next up, fresh corn gets nestled into the chunky batter, along with finely chopped jalapeño for a subtle heat. While we love using fresh ingredients when it’s summertime, this recipe also works with frozen corn — just let it thaw at room temperature, then pat dry with paper towels to remove extra moisture. And if you don’t have fresh jalapeño, a pinch of cayenne would likely work as well!

Now for the frying! Instead of deep frying, we go with a shallow fry, cooking for 2-3 minutes per side in avocado oil in a cast iron skillet. Not only do we find shallow frying less daunting, but it minimizes the amount of oil needed and maximizes the health benefits. Win, win, win! And still, major YUM!

When the fritters are golden on both sides, it’s time to enjoy! They’re incredibly flavorful on their own (we were snacking right off the cooling rack), but they’re also amazing paired with a sauce. Try our Go-To Guacamole, Creamy Cashew Jalapeño Sauce, or Easy Vegan Ranch Dressing.

We hope you LOVE these corn fritters, friends! They’re:SavoryCrispyNaturally a little sweetJust a little spicyQuick & easy& SO delicious!

This is the perfect appetizer or side to make during peak summer, when fresh corn and jalapeños are in season! However, they’re so delicious you may find yourself craving them year-round (in which case, using frozen corn is also a great option).

These fritters are flavorful without being heavily seasoned, making them a good fit for pairing with a variety of other sides and mains, especially grilled proteins, side salads, and anything BBQ seasoned (hello, summertime!). Here are several delicious pairings:

If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!

#33. A Torchy’s Tacos Customer Says She Found A Cow Tooth In Her Taco

There are some things you expect to find in a taco: shredded lettuce, a zesty salsa, fresh veggies. A cow tooth is definitely not one of them.

A Texas woman is suing Torchy’s Tacos after she says she found what turned out to be a cow tooth in a takeout order from the chain’s South Congress location in Austin. According to her attorney, Scott Vasquez, she ordered a Democrat taco—which includes beef barbacoa, avocado, cotija cheese, cilantro, and diced onions—when she made the discovery, he told News Channel 10.

Vasquez said his client’s first reaction was basically what you’d expect: “Her reaction was disgust. ‘What is this?’ Looking at it, she thought it was a tooth.”

Torchy’s later confirmed that the item was, in fact, a cow tooth.

According to the lawsuit filed Tuesday, the plaintiff alleges that Torchy’s knew or should have known something like this could end up in its food and that it was negligent in its safety standards. Vasquez argued that someone should have caught the tooth somewhere along the supply or preparation process before the food reached the customer.

Torchy’s Tacos said in a statement that it was aware of the complaint and takes food safety concerns seriously. The company also explained that the barbacoa used in the taco is made with natural beef cheek sourced from a supplier. After reviewing the complaint, Torchy’s said it identified the item as a cow tooth and that this can occasionally happen. The company said it has since worked with the supplier to reinforce procedures to prevent it from happening again.

The woman’s attorney also raised a safety concern, saying an object like that could potentially be a choking hazard. The lawsuit seeks $250,000 or less, with a jury to determine the final amount.

It is worth noting that the negligence claims are allegations in the lawsuit, not established findings. Torchy’s has acknowledged the incident itself and confirmed that the object was a cow tooth. Still, this may be one of those stories that makes you inspect your next taco just a little more closely.
