#34. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#39. Apple Crisp

My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 29, 2026

I jotted this apple crisp recipe into the notes app in my phone several years ago, and I return to it every fall.

Jammy, cinnamon-scented apples baked under a heavy (and I do mean heavy) blanket of buttery crumble.

I remember first making this in our old kitchen for a late-October dinner party – I made wild rice soup and apple cider old fashioneds (unreal), and someone pulled out the guitar just as the smell of apple crisp was floating from the oven. Absolutely charmed. I obviously bonded with this specific apple crisp that night and it has been with me ever since.

Why it’s good, if you ask me: the caramely apple layer underneath gets properly jammy, the topping gets properly crisp – just enough to provide contrast, AND, and, and, where the two layers melt together in the middle is just pure fall magic. Soft, buttery, and delicious.

Apple crisp in general is very simple, and this one feels rustic, almost, especially if you make it in a cast iron pan, which I usually do. Is she making apple crisp or is she living out her dreams from Little House on the Prairie on a chilly fall night? We’ll never know.

Toss apples with sugar, cinnamon, and flour. This photo shows apples that have been thinly sliced on a mandoline. You can also dice them! Both delicious.

I stir it up with a spoon or fork, and then bring it together into crumbles with my hands.

It’ll turn into a beautiful golden crumble with a layer of jammy apples underneath.

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!

This can work with or without peeling the apples. Personally, I don’t peel the apples – I am lazy, and I just can’t be bothered to mess with what is already a perfectly good fruit. The peels cook down the same way the apples do, so they become soft and unobtrusive in the apple crisp.

#41. The Best Trader Joe’s Products to Buy If It’s Your First Visit

I asked our editors what they'd recommend to someone shopping at Trader Joe's for the very first time. They had opinions, and so do I.

When I lived in San Francisco, I had a Trader Joe’s within walking distance of my apartment and visited regularly. I just never bought much in the way of groceries. I went for the wine. (And in my defense, Trader Joe’s has an excellent wine selection.) I was completely unaware of what I was missing in the rest of the store though!

One afternoon, on a whim, I picked up a tub of hummus and a bag of pita chips to pair with my sauvignon blanc. When I got home and started snacking, I realized that for years I’d been walking past an entire store full of things I might love. I went back the next day to fill my cart with things I’d never noticed before. That trip made a convert out of me.

These days, I live on the Oregon coast, two hours away from my nearest Trader Joe’s. My visits require quite a bit more planning, usually involving a long shopping list and a cooler or two, but I still make the trip whenever I can. The wine remains a staple, though I’ve since developed strong opinions about everything from the hashbrowns to the blueberry goat cheese.

Of course, Trader Joe’s has so many interesting products that a first visit can be a little overwhelming. Between the cult-favorite frozen foods, inventive snacks, excellent cheeses and affordable pantry staples, it’s difficult to know where to begin. So I asked some of my Taste of Home colleagues to share their favorites. Here are the products we’d recommend putting in your cart first.

There’s a reason Trader Joe’s Mandarin Orange Chicken has such a devoted following. The breaded chicken cooks up crisp, and the accompanying sauce delivers the sweet, tangy flavors you’d expect from a takeout favorite. It’s an excellent introduction to the store’s freezer aisle, particularly for anyone who appreciates having easy weeknight dinners on hand. Taste of Home editor Lesley Balla has a useful tip: Don’t use all the sauce provided. Start with less and add more to taste.

The Trader Joe’s cheese selection deserves a visit of its own, and this blueberry vanilla chevre is one of my longtime favorites. The soft, tangy goat cheese is coated with a sweet blueberry mixture, with vanilla rounding out the flavors. I love it with crackers, although it’s equally wonderful spread over a toasted bagel or on a charcuterie board. It’s an easy way to make an ordinary afternoon snack feel a little more special.

Senior editor Lindsay Mattison credits this salsa with helping turn her into a Trader Joe’s regular, and it’s an excellent place to begin exploring the store’s condiments. Salsa Autentica is a smooth, tomato-based salsa with a little heat, making it especially appealing to anyone who prefers a pourable salsa over a chunky one. It’s great with tortilla chips, spooned over tacos or added to scrambled eggs. Lindsay discovered it around the same time as another favorite, Trader Joe’s corn taco shells, and the two paired together make an excellent introduction to the store.

Trader Joe’s frozen hashbrowns have a permanent place in my freezer. My kids will eat them just about any way I serve them, but they’re most fond of loading them like loaded baked potatoes with sour cream, shredded cheese and crispy bacon. Lesley is a fan, too, and likes topping hers with scrambled eggs and salsa. Between the two approaches, there’s a strong case for keeping more than one package on hand.

An acai bowl is an excellent excuse to eat something that looks like dessert for breakfast, especially when you’re generous with the toppings. Rosie keeps Trader Joe’s Unsweetened Organic Acai Puree Packets on hand for exactly that reason. She tops her bowls with strawberries, blueberries, sliced banana, coconut, sunflower kernels and honey. The acai itself has an earthy, slightly tart flavor, which makes a lovely contrast to the sweet fruit and honey. And since the puree comes in individual frozen packets, there’s no need to commit to making a whole blender’s worth.

When someone buys a product 10 bags at a time, I’m inclined to pay attention. That’s exactly what editor Lauren Pahmeier does with Trader Joe’s Spicy Alfredo Fusilloni. The oversized, spiral-shaped pasta comes in a creamy sauce with a little heat, making it a particularly appealing freezer find for pasta lovers. Lauren says the enormous pasta shapes are half the fun, and I can certainly respect that.

French butter has a way of making ordinary butter seem like it isn’t trying very hard. Trader Joe’s Cultured Salted Butter has a rich flavor and subtle tang that comes from culturing the cream, making it a wonderful spread on good bread. Lesley is an enthusiastic supporter, and this is an excellent purchase for anyone who believes butter should be more than just a background ingredient.

Hummus was my gateway into Trader Joe’s groceries, and it’s still one of the first things I look for when I visit. Associate community editor Ivis Estrada shares my enthusiasm, particularly for the Mediterranean Style Hummus, which is rich, creamy and generously seasoned. It’s wonderful with fresh vegetables, spread onto sandwiches or served alongside warm pita bread. If you’re new to Trader Joe’s, I recommend making the hummus selection one of your first stops.

You could make a compelling argument that this seasoning blend helped launch an entire grocery-store obsession. A combination of sesame seeds, poppy seeds, dried garlic, diced onion and salt, this blend brings the familiar flavors of an everything bagel to practically anything you sprinkle it over. Try it on avocado toast, eggs, roasted vegetables or homemade crackers. Lesley counts Trader Joe’s spice blends among her favorites, and this one is a perfect starting point.

Sometimes nostalgia is all the encouragement you need to try something. Lindsay spotted Trader Joe’s corn taco shells on the shelf and realized she hadn’t eaten a crunchy taco in years. The shells have that familiar crisp texture that makes an old-fashioned taco night so satisfying. Fill them with seasoned ground beef, shredded lettuce, cheese and a generous spoonful of Salsa Autentica.

Salsa is one of those things Trader Joe’s does exceptionally well, and Lauren’s recommendation is the Pepita Salsa. Made with pumpkin seeds and roasted red peppers, it has a rich, savory flavor that goes well beyond the usual tomatoes and chiles. Lauren likes stirring it into scrambled eggs, although it’s equally delicious with tortilla chips, tacos or grilled meats. This one is a great alternative for anyone looking to mix up their salsa game.

Some grocery store sweets are perfectly pleasant. Others inspire people to hide the container from themselves. Trader Joe’s Dark Chocolate Peanut Butter Cups fall firmly into the second category. The combination of dark chocolate and creamy, salty peanut butter has earned them a devoted following, including editors Lesley and Rosie. Rosie even ventures that they’re better than Reese’s, which is a bold statement about a peanut butter cup. Lesley, meanwhile, warns against buying them if you have any intention of exercising restraint.

A frozen pizza with a deep-fried crust is already an intriguing proposition, but add roasted garlic and pesto, and you’ve got something considerably more interesting than the usual freezer-aisle offering. Ivis calls this one of the best frozen pizzas she’s ever had. It’s a good reminder that a frozen pizza from Trader Joe’s can be every bit as exciting as something you’d order from your local pizzeria.

Hot honey has found its way onto everything from pizza to ice cream, so popcorn was probably inevitable. Trader Joe’s hot honey popcorn coats the kernels in a thin, crunchy layer of honey sweetness with enough cayenne to make its presence known. Editor Caroline Stanko was so taken with the caramel corn-like crunch that she gave it a Taste of Home Award. She even used the popcorn as a cocktail garnish, proving that some snacks have ambitions beyond the bowl.

Fiocchetti are little pasta parcels, and Trader Joe’s version comes filled with cheese and coated in a creamy tomato-based pink sauce. Ivis makes a point of picking up at least one package whenever she shops there. It’s another excellent example of the store’s knack for turning frozen pasta into something that feels a little more special than a last-minute dinner.

Not everything worth buying at Trader Joe’s comes in an inventive flavor or colorful package. Lindsay recently discovered how affordable the store’s nuts and seeds can be and now stocks up on slivered almonds, sunflower seeds and cashew pieces for homemade granola. It’s a practical recommendation if you bake regularly or like making your own trail mix. Nuts can be expensive at conventional grocery stores, so it’s worth comparing prices while you’re there. Sometimes the best grocery store discovery is simply finding a better place to buy something you already use.

This sweet, savory corn salsa is one of Ivis’s favorites for making copycat Chipotle bowls at home. The combination of corn, peppers and spices make it equally useful for tacos, burritos and grilled chicken, and its chunky texture adds a welcome contrast to rice and beans. It also makes an excellent topping for grilled fish. Just add a squeeze of fresh lime!

Trader Joe’s wine section was my introduction to the store, and it remains one of my favorite reasons to visit. Corvelia Cabernet Sauvignon is one of the bottles I regularly bring home, often in embarrassingly large quantities. It’s a true California Cab with dark fruit notes and a little oak, without the price tag that sometimes accompanies wines in this style. It’s lovely alongside a grilled ribeye, where the richness of the beef gives the wine’s tannins a beautiful balance.

Our head of editorial, Ellie Martin Cliffe, nominated Trader Joe’s fresh flowers, a recommendation I wholeheartedly second. The floral section is one of my favorite parts of the store, with seasonal offerings that range from plush peonies and colorful tulips to hydrangeas, roses and fresh eucalyptus, sold in generous bunches. They’re definitely worth one last stop before you head for the checkout.

Between the new foods you’ll be bringing home and the flowers to arrange alongside them, your first Trader Joe’s trip should give you plenty to look forward to once you’ve unpacked the grocery bags.

#42. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#43. Spooky Ravioli

Unfortunately, you can’t rely on candy alone to get you through Halloween night. When you need to fuel up before your trick-or-treating, spooky ravioli is the scary-good dinner you can count on. The cheesy ravioli “ghosts” swim in a rich and creamy sauce, which will keep you fueled up and ready for whatever All Hallows’ Eve brings your way. The best part? They are relatively easy to make, which means everyone can get in on the frightfully fun dinner.

The ravioli:I wanted to make these approachable and tasty, so I kept things simple. The filling consists of ricotta, Parmesan, and finely chopped pear (trust me, it adds a welcome sweetness and texture). The recipe also calls for wonton wrappers, which take a huge step out of the process of making homemade dough.

Can you make these ahead of time?You sure can! These are frozen before cooking anyway. You can freeze for up to 2 weeks for the best quality. Do not cook these ahead of time, however; they should be made and eaten right away!

#44. 11 Types of Vinegar: A Guide to Cooking With Them and More

There are an awful lot of vinegars in the world—which ones you cook with depends entirely on your favorite flavors and what you’re making. Maybe you favor red wine vinegar for the punchy tang it brings to salad dressing. Or you can’t imagine a bowl of white rice without the gentle acidity of seasoned rice vinegar running through it. Perhaps you fall asleep at night dreaming of bowls of vanilla ice cream covered in ripe summer strawberries dripping with balsamic vinegar.

Whether you’re the kind of cook who has a favorite vinegar for every occasion or simply grabs whichever bottle is closest to the stove, it pays to know what you’re working with. You can often substitute one vinegar for another, but it's worth being strategic. “Each vinegar contributes its own flavor and character rather than just adding acidity,” says Sathish Kumar, the head chef of Indienne in New York and Chicago.

So which bottles deserve a spot in your pantry? We’re breaking down 11 types of vinegar, what to use them for, and substitutions that work in a pinch.

Vinegar starts with alcohol, which bacteria convert into acetic acid. The starting ingredient—wine, apples, rice, malted barley, or sugarcane, for example—helps determine the flavor, as do the fermentation and aging processes. That’s how you get everything from the crisp, fruity tang of apple cider vinegar to the rich, savory complexity of Chinese black vinegar.

There are countless varieties of vinegar; these are just the ones we reach for most often.

Apple cider vinegar starts with—you guessed it—apples. The fruit is fermented first into hard cider and then into vinegar. The result is bright, fruity, and pleasantly tart with enough character to stand up to bold ingredients. It’s also the subject of some debatable health claims.

We like it in salad dressings, quick-pickled onions, and anything that could use a little fruitiness. It’s a natural partner for pork and chicken, particularly in apple cider braises, and its acidity cuts through the richness of cheeseburger fried rice or braised collard greens. And not for nothing, it makes a heck of a pie.

White wine vinegar is the closest everyday substitute, though Champagne vinegar or unseasoned rice vinegar can also work when you want a lighter touch.

Clear, inexpensive, and unapologetically sharp, distilled white vinegar is the pantry's most straightforward source of acidity. Made by fermenting distilled alcohol, often derived from grains, it has a relatively neutral flavor that lets other ingredients shine.

Tom Carlin, the chef of Burl in Evanston, Illinois, likes adding a dash to braises at the end of cooking. It brightens them “without changing the flavor at all,” he says. That same clean tang makes distilled white vinegar a natural choice for classic dill pickles. It’s also a great base for homemade flavored vinegars, especially those infused with chiles, herbs, or spices.

In many cooked dishes and dressings, you can substitute rice, apple cider, or white wine vinegar. Each will bring its own flavor to the party, so taste as you go.

Red wine vinegar is bold, fruity, and assertive. You can’t dress a classic Greek salad or splash oysters with mignonette without it. Like white wine vinegar, it begins with wine that undergoes a second fermentation, but the red wine base gives it a more robust fruit flavor.

Red wine vinegar brings welcome acidity to BA’s Best Gazpacho, coq au vin, a pot of hearty lentils, and rich meat marinades. If you’re making a vinaigrette for a salad loaded with tomatoes, olives, or cheese, this is a good bottle to reach for.

You can use white wine or apple cider vinegar in its place, but Chicago-based Sifr culinary director Sahil Sethi favors sherry vinegar. He says its nutty, aged character gives it a depth that mirrors red wine vinegar’s body and acidity.

Find out which bottle won Epicurious’s red wine vinegar taste test →

Fermented from white wine, white wine vinegar has a lighter, more delicate flavor than red wine vinegar. Its gently fruity acidity makes it particularly useful when you want to brighten a dish without overpowering it.

Reach for it to use in salad dressings, seafood marinades, braised chicken, brothy steamed mussels, or a buttery pan sauce like beurre blanc. Conor Dalton, head chef at Smyth in Chicago, calls white wine vinegar “the most versatile” option and likes infusing it with herbs, such as lemon verbena, to sharpen creamy sauces for shrimp and balance richer preparations.

Champagne vinegar is an especially good substitute. Sherry, apple cider, and unseasoned rice vinegars can also stand in, depending on the dish.

Light, fruity, and delicately tangy, Champagne vinegar is typically made from wines produced using the same grape varieties as Champagne, such as Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. That doesn’t mean it’s necessarily made from Champagne wine, nor does it enjoy the same strict regional protections. Its subtle fruit and floral notes give it a gentler flavor than many white wine vinegars, though it isn’t necessarily less acidic. Some producers age Champagne vinegar in barrels to develop a rounder, more complex flavor. It’s a particularly good choice when a more assertive vinegar might steal the show.

Sethi calls Champagne vinegar his favorite for salad dressing thanks to its subtle fruitiness. Try it in a vinaigrette for tender greens, drizzled over seafood, or in a dressing for spring vegetables. It can bring a little lift to richer dishes, too, without contributing much competing flavor.

White wine vinegar, though slightly more assertive, is the most straightforward substitute. Unseasoned rice vinegar also works when a mild flavor is the primary goal.

If red wine vinegar is bright and brash, sherry vinegar is its smoother, more nuanced cousin. Made from sherry wine and aged in wood barrels, this amber-hued vinegar develops a rounded acidity with nutty, sometimes caramel-like notes.

That complexity makes sherry vinegar especially good at finishing sauces, dressing roasted vegetables, and brightening stews. Try it in a classic leeks vinaigrette, braised chicken escabèche, or a glaze for rib eye. Dalton also likes using it to deglaze a pan or brighten a sauce at the end of cooking.

Vinagre de Jerez comes from the area around Jerez, Spain, and must age in wood barrels for at least six months. It’s worth keeping a bottle around if you like a vinegar with a little more depth, but red or white wine vinegar works in many of the same applications. Malt vinegar has a more robust flavor, but it can contribute some of the same woody, caramel undertones.

Dark, rich, and sweet-tart, balsamic vinegar can be a finishing touch or an essential ingredient, depending on the bottle. Traditional balsamic vinegar, made in Modena or Reggio Emilia, Italy, starts with cooked grape must (freshly crushed grape juice) and ages in wood barrels for at least 12 years. The result is intensely concentrated, syrupy, and complex.

The balsamic vinegar you’re more likely to find at the supermarket is different. Commonly made by combining grape must with wine vinegar, it’s generally thinner, tangier, and far less expensive than traditional balsamic. That’s not a bad thing: It’s the kind we reach for when making balsamic dressing, roasting brussels sprouts with honey and garlic, or adding sweet-tart depth to Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta.

For a thicker finishing sauce, you can also simmer everyday balsamic into a balsamic reduction, concentrating its sweetness and acidity. Save especially good aged balsamic for drizzling over Parmesan, ripe tomatoes, or even strawberries and vanilla ice cream.

Made with grape must processed to minimize browning, white balsamic is paler, lighter, and fruitier than traditional dark balsamic. Use it to brighten a melon salad, dress roasted peppers, bring a little sweetness to a pan sauce without turning everything brown, or to make a sweet-and-tangy custard for a fruit tart.

Both varieties of balsamic are tricky to substitute because their sweetness is as important as their acidity. For dressings or cooked sauces, try sherry or apple cider vinegar with a little honey or brown sugar. It won’t have the same depth, but it’ll get you closer to the sweet-tart balance.

Mild, gently sweet, and endlessly versatile, rice vinegar is a staple in Japanese, Korean, Chinese, and Vietnamese cooking among other cuisines. It’s made by fermenting rice into alcohol and then vinegar, though its flavor and production vary by region.

At the grocery store, you’ll usually encounter two kinds: seasoned and unseasoned.

“Unseasoned rice vinegar has a clean, mild acidity with a subtle sweetness,” says Jae Seong Ha, head chef at Jeong Yuk Jeom restaurant in New York. That makes it a natural fit for Korean dressings, marinades, and pickled vegetables. We also like it in this Crispy Rice Salad with Spicy Tahini Dressing, tomato-basil salad, Salt and Pepper Fish, and miso-caramel glazed salmon.

Seasoned rice vinegar contains added sugar and salt, making it especially convenient for sushi rice and certain dressings.

Wondering about rice wine vinegar? “The terms rice vinegar and rice wine vinegar are used interchangeably,” Ha says. “When shopping, I pay more attention to the ingredient list and whether the vinegar is seasoned or unseasoned.”

To substitute unseasoned rice vinegar, try Champagne or white wine vinegar. If you need seasoned rice vinegar, start with unseasoned and add a little sugar and salt to taste. You can do the same with another mild vinegar in a pinch.

Dark, earthy, and deeply savory, black vinegar brings considerably more than acidity to a dish. There are several styles, including Chinkiang vinegar from China, but they’re generally made from fermented grains, such as rice, wheat, or sorghum.

“It has a little sweetness, a malty character, and more fermentation flavor” than milder rice vinegar, says Cheng Lin, chef-owner of Shota Omakase in Brooklyn. He likes it with dumplings, noodles, “and other dishes where you want the vinegar to have a stronger presence.”

Try black vinegar in dipping sauces for scallion pancakes, splashed into a cabbage stir-fry or Black Vinegar Chicken With Radishes, or whisked into a punchy dressing. A little goes a long way.

There’s no substitute for black vinegar’s complex, distinctive flavor. If you’re in a pinch, Lin suggests combining balsamic and unseasoned rice vinegar. “It won’t be exactly the same, but it gives you some of that darker, sweeter, aged character.”

If you’ve eaten fish and chips, you’ve probably tasted malt vinegar. Made from malted barley, it can range from amber to dark brown, and it has a sweet, nutty tang with a toasted flavor.

It’s hard to beat on french fries, but we’d happily splash it over roasted or steamed potatoes, or stir it into mayonnaise for dipping sweet potato wedges too. Malt vinegar can also lend depth to Sweet-and-Sour Tomato Chutney and other sauces. Reduce it with chiles and molasses for a sticky glaze for roast chicken or use it in a tangy lamb chop marinade.

For fried foods, a squeeze of lemon will provide a similar bright finish, though not malt vinegar’s toasty flavor. Apple cider or sherry vinegar is a reasonable stand-in for sauces and glazes.

Made from fermented sugarcane juice, cane vinegar is a staple in many Filipino kitchens—and important in many other cuisines, too, but the category is broad. Sukang maasim is an all-purpose white (clear) cane vinegar, while sukang Iloko is a darker variety hailing from the country’s north, often made from clay-aged sugarcane wine (basi).

Its flavor varies by producer and region, but it generally offers a clean, sometimes subtly sweet acidity. It’s a key ingredient in Philippine adobo, often balanced with soy sauce and aromatics like black pepper and bay leaf. Kumar also points to cane vinegar’s importance in Northern Indian pickling traditions, including sirka pyaaz, tangy onions commonly served alongside kebabs. It also works well in dipping sauces or infused with chiles for a spicy, tangy condiment.

If you can’t find cane vinegar, try unseasoned rice vinegar or apple cider vinegar, depending on the dish. Neither is an exact match, but both can provide the acidity you need. Coconut vinegar is another popular option in regions that favor cane vinegar, and can also work well in similar applications.

The world of vinegars is vast. Other varieties include honey vinegar, made from mead and vaguely similar to white balsamic; akazu, a beautifully layered red vinegar that comes from aged sake lees; and roasty-toasty beer vinegar, a good swap for malt vinegar.

Coconut vinegar, made from fermented coconut sap, is another versatile option, especially in Filipino and South Asian cooking. Kumar says its flavor is “distinctive and slightly funky” and that it works well in dipping sauces, marinades, and rich, savory dishes.

Ume-su (Japanese plum vinegar) isn’t technically vinegar at all. This intensely tart, salty seasoning is the tangy brine left over from making umeboshi (salt-preserved plums). It’s terrific in salad dressings or splashed over cooked vegetables.

Unseasoned rice vinegar and Champagne vinegar are good choices when you want acidity without an overpowering flavor. White wine vinegar is another versatile option. Distilled white vinegar has a neutral flavor, but a sharpness that can make it aggressive in some dishes.

Can you substitute one type of vinegar for another?

Usually, yes. Red and white wine vinegars can often stand in for each other, though red wine vinegar has a bolder flavor. Apple cider vinegar works well in place of white wine vinegar, while unseasoned rice vinegar is a good choice when you want something milder. Balsamic and black vinegars have more distinctive flavors and are harder to replace. For home canning and shelf-stable pickling, follow a tested recipe and use vinegar with the specified acidity rather than making substitutions based on taste alone.

Which vinegar is best for salad dressing?

You know that old saying: The limit does not exist. And a simple vinaigrette is a great way to taste the nuances of a new-to-you vinegar.

That said, red wine, white wine, Champagne, and sherry vinegars are all commonly used in Western-style salad dressings. Red wine vinegar works particularly well with bold ingredients like tomatoes and olives, while Champagne and white wine vinegars complement delicate greens. Reach for sherry vinegar when you want something a little richer and nuttier.

Most commercially produced vinegars don’t need refrigeration. “Vinegar is actually very easy to take care of,” Lin says. He recommends storing bottles tightly closed in a cool, dark cabinet away from sunlight and heat. Some vinegars may become cloudy or develop harmless sediment over time, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they’ve spoiled. Homemade infused vinegars may require refrigeration.

Read more about vinegar storage at Epicurious →

What are the essential vinegars to keep in your pantry?

The answer depends on what you cook. One way to cover your bases is with something mild and versatile, like unseasoned rice vinegar; something fruity, like red wine or apple cider vinegar; and something distinctive, like sherry or balsamic.

But if chicken adobo is in heavy rotation, you’re going to want a steady supply of cane vinegar. Love fish and chips? Don’t skip the malt. Whatever your pleasure, there’s no wrong way to take an acid trip.

#47. The Best Culinary Resorts in the United States

Where to go to rest, relax, recharge, and eat well while doing it

At some hotels, food is an afterthought: Breakfast buffets are bland, in-room mini bars are stocked with generic snacks, and lobby bars are lackluster. But other resorts understand that we don’t simply factor food into an itinerary; many people plan their entire trip around eating, hoping to get to the heart of local cuisine and dine at the area’s best restaurants without ever leaving the property.

These culinary resorts will help you build an entire vacation around great meals. If you want to get your hands dirty, resorts on working farms have guests harvesting produce that will end up on their dinner plates that night, and some properties send visitors off on fishing and foraging expeditions to find their own meals. Other spots keep it more low-key with award-winning restaurants, special wine tastings, and wellness-minded retreats serving homegrown juices. No matter how you want to engage with the food that will power your trip, these 10 culinary resorts are the best places in the U.S. to have a truly delicious stay.

Acura has always done things its own way. We believe the best experiences are created through intentional choices, thoughtful craftsmanship, and the confidence to pursue a different approach. This spirit is reflected in our philosophy of Precision Crafted Performance. Learn more.

Made up of 65 freestanding cottages, Wildflower Farms gives guests a taste of farm life — albeit an incredibly chic version. Guests can start the day with a complimentary tour of the 6-acre farm and a visit to feed the resort’s Icelandic sheep and chicken, then pick up a few eggs to bring over to the on-site restaurant Clay for an incredibly fresh breakfast. Other food-focused activities include suiting up in beekeeping gear to learn how to make honey, taking a guided foraging walk, or stirring up a cocktail using ingredients grown on-site in a class hosted in the resort’s cooking school barn.

Clay serves breakfast, lunch, and dinner in a cozy dining room that centers a massive wood-burning fireplace. The menu changes seasonally to feature lamb and pork raised just steps from the kitchen, plus a selection of the 14,000 pounds of fruit, vegetables, and herbs that the farm produces annually. The beverage program also has local roots: Wine director Vanessa Price has built a 7,000-bottle cellar that shines a light on New York’s often-overlooked Finger Lakes and North Fork wine regions, and ingredients like carrot eau de vie show up in martinis.

With just four cabins situated on 3,800 acres of working ranch, Quercus is a small culinary resort that punches well above its weight. Chiara Visconti di Modrone and her husband Angelos Pervanas originally launched Quercus as a regenerative farming project an hour outside Atlanta before teaming up with acclaimed Atlanta restaurateurs to morph it into a full-scale culinary escape. Now the all-inclusive experience features private saunas and cold plunge pools, holistic wellness consultations, and activities like horse training or kayaking in the Flint River.

Guests are encouraged to kick off their visit with a garden tour so they understand the property’s commitment to biodynamic farming principles and recognize the rare varieties of turmeric and uncommon peppers that will later appear on their plates. The resort offers three meals per day, along with snacks like beef jerky and gochujang okra chips stocked in each room. Each meal can be enjoyed in the restaurant spaces on the property or delivered in a wicker picnic basket through the resort’s charming take on room service. Uberto is the pinnacle of Quercus’s culinary experiences, a 10-plus course tasting menu helmed by chef Ryan Smith, whose Atlanta restaurant Staplehouse earned a Michelin star. The menu changes with the seasons, but mainstays like clarified curry made with lemongrass and galangal from the farm’s tropical greenhouse showcase an essential truth: Chefs spend all week in the kitchen and fermentation lab crafting each dish, but the garden has been working on dinner all year.

Mii Amo is an adults-only wellness resort tucked into the red rocks of Sedona’s Boynton Canyon vortex, which is supposedly one of the most powerful hubs for spiritual and healing energy in the area. It has everything one would expect at a luxury wellness retreat: lodging in one of 23 cozy casitas, a daily credit to book treatments at the 40,000-square-foot spa, an array of sound baths and meditations, and guided hikes and mountain bike rides through the canyon.

But unlike some other wellness resorts, Mii Amo has a top-notch culinary program as well. During all-inclusive stays ranging from three to 10 nights, guests get three meals per day at the on-site restaurant, Hummingbird, along with unlimited juice bar visits to pick up protein-packed smoothies, ginger shots, and sleep tonics. While menus are rooted in seasonal produce from the chef’s garden, the resort doesn’t believe in total restriction so sweet treats, alcohol, and caviar are available to add a little indulgence to your stay. Book one of the weekly nutrition classes or juicing demonstrations to learn how to recreate the nourishing fare served at Mii Amo after returning home.

On a hillside in the Catskills, Susan Manning and Doug Doetsch built a cidery, farm-to-table restaurant, and hotel on the same land that Doetsch’s family has farmed for five generations. Eight Shaker-inspired, apartment-style accommodations are built into two 19th-century historic buildings located just down the hill from the cidery on which the resort is centered.

The 12-acre orchard features rows upon rows of trees bearing 60 different varieties of apples and pears. The resort offers weekend tours of the orchard, plus cider tastings. Cider-maker Joshua Hinchman turns the fruit into an ever-expanding portfolio of traditional cider, while also experimenting with other beverages like fortified apple wines and cyser, a type of mead. All tastings are hosted in a barn that was built into the hillside using reclaimed wood that once supported the original Tappan Zee Bridge, and the structure is also passive house-certified, making it the world’s first cidery to receive that energy efficiency designation. Apples find their way onto executive chef and culinary director Edwyn Ferrari’s menu as well, so digging into custardy cider posset at the end of a meal in the resort’s restaurant feels full circle.

This Healdsburg hotel is the flagship property from Appellation, a hotel collection co-founded by chef Charlie Palmer and Christopher Hunsberger, who spent more than 35 years working for Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts. As a self-described culinary hotel, the 108-room resort set lofty expectations for itself, but Appellation Healdsburg delivers with three restaurants, a packed schedule of food-focused activities, and a premier location in the heart of Sonoma County.

Folia Bar & Kitchen is the resort’s premium restaurant, and it offers a three-course menu of local ingredients from purveyors like Hog Island Oyster Co. and Sonoma Bee Company. For guests who want to try their hand in the kitchen, the resort offers a variety of hands-on cooking classes, some of which are taught by Palmer himself. Since the hotel counts hundreds of wineries as neighbors, it invites a different winemaker to the property every Friday to host a guided tasting. But when it’s time to venture off the property, guests can also book with the concierge to get special access to Sonoma County producers like Knights Bridge Winery, Bricoleur Vineyards, and Dry Creek Vineyard for behind-the-scenes tours and tastings.

Los Poblanos is a historic inn dating back to 1932 where lavender grows in wide, fragrant rows and fruit trees line the paths between buildings. The property was designed by seminal architect John Gaw Meem in classic Santa Fe style with pitched tin roofs that nod to the site’s history as a dairy farm and the original 1934 hand-painted grain silos still stand on site.

Though it no longer produces dairy or serves as the headquarters of a larger ranch, a 25-acre organic farm is the heart of the property. Guests can take a formal tour of the greenhouses or wander the resort’s gardens, orchards, and cottonwood trees, which are fed by community-managed irrigation systems called acequias that are older than the state itself. All that benefits Campo, the property’s signature restaurant, where the flavors of the Rio Grande Valley appear on every plate. In addition to homegrown produce, the restaurant sources meat and other ingredients from local purveyors including Native American Beef, a program that supports Indigenous cattle producers who faced hurdles competing in the commercial meat industry. Don’t miss the Farm Shop with lavender-scented products, hot sauce from the garden’s peppers, and the estate’s handcrafted gin, which is produced in the resort’s distillery just down the road in downtown Albuquerque.

The Ojai Valley Inn has long been lauded as a wellness escape thanks to its 31,000-square-foot spa and location at the center of the hippie enclave of Ojai, but the resort is also a culinary destination in its own right. With six restaurants and bars on the property, options range from a casual pub serving quintessential burgers and local beer to a renowned four-course tasting menu at Olivella, where guests will eat dessert drizzled in honey from the resort’s apiary and order wine from the 10,000-bottle cellar.

In addition to the restaurants and bars, the resort recently poured $20 million into an epicurean center called the Farmhouse, where culinary ambassador and beloved California chef and restaurateur Nancy Silverton curates a slate of cookbook talks, cooking classes, and special tasting menu dinners with visiting chefs and buzzy winemakers. It’s also the site of the annual Ojai Food & Wine festival, held in March, which brings renowned chefs from around the world to the peaceful valley.

For travelers looking to be spoiled for choice, look no further than the Grand Hotel. Abundance is wrapped into every aspect of the resort, from its 660-foot porch that offers views of the idyllic car-free island to 388 Victorian-style guest rooms dressed up in maximalist candy-colored decor.

The property is not lacking in options on the food front either: It has 13 different bars and restaurants. The elegant main dining room serves breakfast, lunch, and dinner, but the peak time to visit is for nightly live entertainment from the Grand Hotel Orchestra and a five-course menu that rotates every three days to highlight a different type of cuisine. Other restaurants are just as grand; the Woods Restaurant serves cozy Bavarian dishes in a dining room that feels like a lodge with a roaring fireplace, while the Jockey Club serves seafood towers and steakhouse classics in a room outfitted in saddle leather. More casual picks are also available like Detroit-style pies at Mackinac Island Pizza Company or old-school sundaes made with scoops of Guernsey Farms Dairy ice cream at Sadie’s Ice Cream Parlor.

When visitors check into one of the rustic cabins at Windy Hill Farm and Preserve, a retreat and upland preserve in the foothills of the Great Smoky Mountains, there are plenty of ways to get involved in cultivating the food that will eventually end up on their plates. The all-inclusive experience features activities like beekeeping demonstrations, bourbon tastings, and cooking classes hosted by executive chef Ben Warwick, and every evening ends with an opportunity to make s’mores around a campfire. The resort has also recently launched themed dinners that offer built-in lessons on the surrounding Appalachian region. The first in the series is called Watershed, which tells the story of how water flows from the highlands surrounding the resort to the Gulf in 10 delicious courses.

But some of the most popular ways to spend a day on the 650 acres of rolling hills are more hands-on. Guests who opt to go crappie fishing on the Tennessee River will cast their reels in search of the native fish, and those who get lucky can have their catch cleaned and cooked at Wilder, the hotel’s restaurant. Quail hunting is also popular. Each hunt begins with a hearty breakfast at Wilder before guests head out with professional guides and sporting dogs. Proceeds from the hunting operation are used to fund large-scale land conservation and native habitat restoration.

Hidden Pond is a retreat where the quintessential clapboard cottages are as beloved as the property’s farm-to-table restaurant. Many of the accommodations were recently redesigned, and part of the revamp included outfitting the in-unit kitchens with top-of-the-line Breville appliances. However, you may not even bother firing up the appliances once you try the fresh-baked pastries delivered to each room by picnic basket, and dig into the menu at the on-site restaurant Earth.

The restaurant is popular with locals as well as hotel guests, and the menu is built around produce pulled from the resort’s organic garden. Summer brings heirloom tomatoes and micro basil while cooler months stock pumpkins and root vegetables like celeriac. It’s all paired with fresh-caught lobster and other local seafood, so you’ll also get a taste of the Atlantic that inspired the trip to Maine in the first place.

#51. 36 Healthy Fall Dinners With All The Cozy

Healthy and nourishing fall dinners that are super cozy, too! Some of my favorite bowls, salads, soups, and more!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 18, 2026

Fall dinners are here, and honestly, this is the kind of food I wait for all year. Steamy bowls, creamy sauces, roasted veggies, cozy spices, and meals that make the whole house smell amazing. These healthy fall recipes bring all the sweater-weather comfort while still being nourishing enough for an everyday weeknight!

To call out a few of my all-time favorites from this list:

Nourishing food should still feel generous, cozy, and completely delicious, and these dinners are it!

Roasted sweet potatoes topped with creamy chipotle sauce, spicy ground chicken, avocado, cilantro, and pickled onion. My family loves them!

I love this Kale Apple Salad! Kale, brussels sprouts, rosemary cashews, apples, fried bread cheese, crispy shallots, and crisp apple maple dressing!

Silky carrot soup topped with spiced ground beef and toasty pine nuts! Bright, savory, warming, all the best things!

Amazingly creamy, saucy chickpea curry served over rice with a dollop of chili crisp and a side of cucumber salad. Ready in 20 minutes!

One of my family’s favorite easy dinners that works SO well for meal prep! Sweet potatoes and ground beef get dolloped with a creamy high protein street corn style dip that is bonkers delicious.

Detox Crockpot Lentil Soup – a clean and simple soup made with onions, garlic, carrots, olive oil, squash, and LENTILS! Super healthy and easy to make.

The BEST Grain Bowl! Roasted root vegetables, earthy grains, dried fruit, dark leafy greens, buttery goat cheese, and lusciously creamy balsamic dressing.

Coconut Curry Salmon! Broiled salmon with a salty-sweet spice rub, creamy coconut curry sauce, and steamy rice to soak it all up.

These tempeh bowls are a true fall favorite! Massaged kale, sweet potatoes, roasty marinated maple-mustard tempeh, crunchy apple, and an unexpected pile of briney sauerkraut.

Lemongrass, ginger, shallot, and the brightness of lime! These broth bowls have got it all – luscious broth, fluffy rice, protein, and fresh herbs.

Saucy shredded chicken, yellow rice, pickled onions, greens, and cilantro pesto on top. It’s a flavor and color delight!

We are living our best bowl life this week. Seasoned sweet potato wedges and chicken meatballs or rotisserie chicken all piled onto a plate with a little puddle of punchy green avocado mojo sauce. Yes, wow, repeat.

This 7-Layer Beet Salad is a stunner! Studded with cooked beets, supremed oranges, chopped pistachios, creamy truffle ricotta, and a bit of fresh mint. So fresh, so good!

These House Favorite Brussels Sprouts are the best side veg and are speckled with bright bursts of cranberries and nutty walnuts. The perfect addition to any meal!

These Spicy Peanut Tofu Bowls are a meal prep / weeknight dinner life-saver! Crispy tofu, roasted veggies, fluffy rice, and a spicy sweet peanut sauce all over top.

These beauties need to be on your table! Deeply roasted rainbow carrots, swizzles of tangy garlicky yogurt sauce, a golden drizzle of honey, and festive pistachio crunches on top.

Healing Chicken and Rice Soup that is limey, salty, and so fresh! Garlic-ginger-infused broth, shredded chicken thighs, tender jasmine rice, fresh herbs, and peanuts. YUM.

Brussels & Kale Caesar! Papery-thin shreds of brussels sprouts and chopped lacinato kale, tossed with a creamy, garlicky, avocado-based vegan caesar dressing, topped off with the most addicting cheezy garlic croutons.

Autumn Glow Salad with Lemon Dressing – a MUST for healthy, glowy eating! Roasted cauliflower, sweet potato, grains, and apples.

Healthy and versatile bowls that come together under a generous drizzle of addictingly creamy vegan chipotle tahini sauce.

A savory coconut creamy broth, swirls of chili oil floating on top, beautiful veg and cubes of flavor-soaked tofu, and a pile of steamy rice at your service.

A cozy, hearty, humble bowl of this Country Chicken Stew is waiting for you! Chicken, thick-cut bacon, navy beans, veggies, and fresh herbs all simmering in one big pot. It’s a good one, friends!

This Hot Honey Salmon is giving off major fancy-to-eat-but-not-fancy-to-make vibes. Spicy-sweet salmon coated in fresh garlic, stone ground mustard, sweet honey, and flecks of red peppers flakes. It’s a magical little number!

Harissa Chickpeas with Whipped Feta! Perfectly spicy/saucy/tomato-y chickpeas smothered in creamy, garlicky whipped feta and served with naan, lemons, and cucumbers. Your next weeknight wonder!

Easy Veggie Enchiladas! Saucy, cheese, filling, cozy, and packed with any roasted veggies you want. Super versatile and easy to make!

Guess what’s for dinner? Creamy, spicy, delicious red curry lentils, made in the Instant Pot.

Amazing Mushroom Bowls with Kale Pesto! Smoky, sweet, salt mushrooms (or tempeh!), caramelized pineapple, peppers, and dollop of kale pesto, all served over rice.

Sesame Beef and Broccoli! Full of protein, green broccoli goodness, and sticky-sweet garlic and ginger flavor. Perfect at-home takeout!

Creamy Thai Sweet Potato Curry – packed with nutrition! Our favorite easy, healthy, winter comfort food recipe.

These Roasted Cauliflower Hummus Bowls are LIFE-CHANGING. A bed of garlicky creamy hummus, piled high with spiced roasted cauliflower, and a speckling of fresh lemony tomatoes and herbs.

Spicy Shrimp with Cauliflower Mash and Garlic Kale – tender-sweet shrimp and smoky garlic kale over creamy cauliflower mash. The most DELICIOUS fake-fancy weeknight dinner!

Roasted Vegetable Bowls! Crispy tender roasted veggies, buttery avocado, all together in a bowl with a drizzle of green tahini sauce.

15 Minute Meal Prep Cilantro Lime Chicken and Lentils! The BEST easy protein powerhouse meal prep. Just 15 mins of prep and totally hands-off cooking!

Instant Pot Sweet Potato Tortilla Soup! A smoky, limey, tomato-rich broth with onion, garlic, jalapeño, crispy tortilla strips, and tender chunks of sweet potato.

These healthy chipotle sweet potato skins are stuffed with a chipotle-sweet potato filling, black beans, corn, and topped with cheese. SO GOOD.

Healing Bowls: turmeric sweet potatoes, brown rice, red quinoa, arugula, poached egg, lemon dressing.

Fall is for snacking, too! Here are some of my favorite healthy snacks – for myself, or for my kids’ lunchboxes!

#52. These are the Best Hybrid Pans for Home Cooks, Tested for Performance and Durability

Tested by Katie Bandurski, Nicole Doster and Marisa Hillman

We tested all the combo clad pans we could get our hands on to find the best hybrid cookware for every home chef.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Stainless steel, nonstick, ceramic, cast iron—these days, you can find dozens of different materials by simply walking down the cookware aisle. But the best hybrid cookware is something entirely different. Instead of settling for a single material, this type combines the best traits of all these options into a single pan.

According to cookware expert Alycia Johnson, Vice President of Merchandising at Sur La Table, this Frankenstein-ed result is the main reason hybrid cookware is so popular. She likens hybrid cookware to a cronut, in that it combines two things to create something even better.

“Hybrid cookware combines the benefits of multiple cookware materials and technologies in a single pan,” says Alycia. “It most often combines the durability and cooking performance of stainless steel with the convenience of a nonstick cooking surface. The result is cookware designed to offer the versatility of stainless steel while making everyday cooking and cleanup easier.”

While hybrid cookware is relatively new to the cookware scene, its usefulness is undeniable. From Gordon Ramsey’s recommendations to budget-friendly finds, our team at Taste of Home just had to see which options make up the best hybrid cookware. After trying eight popular brands, here’s what we found.

As the original hybrid cookware brand, it’s no surprise that our pick for the overall best hybrid pan is none other than HexClad. This Gordon Ramsay-backed cookware claims to combine the best parts of stainless steel, cast iron and nonstick pans all in one. And, according to testing data from three different editors, it delivers on this promise—and has been for years.

While we love the orignal HexClad pan, that’s not all the brand has to offer. In fact, Deputy Editor Katie Bandurski has spent the past two years reviewing HexClad gear ranging from pans to pots to knives. “I first tried the Dutch oven and was instantly hooked,” she explains. “Then I ordered a three-piece skillet set, which is now my go-to cookware. I love that I can pull out my stainless steel turner and not have to worry about nicking the coating like I do with ceramic.”

While pricey, we find that it’s worth the splurge—especially with HexClad’s generous lifetime warranty. It’s also the most heat-resistant option we’ve tried with a temperature rating of up to 900ºF. HexClad pans heat evenly, remain nonstick through years of use and can perform almost any cooking task you throw at them.

In our full HexClad cookware review, Katie details her experience using the pans over the course of several years. As of June 2026, she notes that most of her skillets have held up like a dream, with only the small one developing a noticeable scratch in the coating.

“They still perform beautifully for nonstick searing and high-heat cooking. Maintenance has been pretty simple, too. Occasionally, I need to scrub off some burnt-on marks with coarse salt, but it lifts away very easily,” she raves. “I’m still so pleased with this purchase and the pans’ longevity. I tell all my friends/family who are getting married to add HexClad to their registry!”

Size(s) Available: 7, 8, 10, 12 and 14 inches| Lid Included: No | Oven Safe: Up to 900ºF | Metal Utensil-Friendly: Yes | Features: Aluminum core, diamond dust-infused nonstick coating, patented

GreenPan is one of our favorite kitchenware brands. Over the years, we’ve tried several top sellers from the brand’s myriad cookware and appliance categories. While some of our favorite picks include a handsome  ice cream maker and a hosting-friendly raclette grill, GreenPan’s Spectra hybrid cookware line might just be our favorite of all the brand’s offerings.

In our full review, we cover the ins and outs of these hybrid pans. Much like HexClad kitchenware, they are resistant to high heat and come with a slick, PFAS-free nonstick coating. The rivetless interior is also a huge bonus, as it prevents gunky buildup. Where these pans really shine in comparison to the rest, though, is their luxe look. The polished stainless steel exterior and raised star-shaped pattern looks ultra-professional.

“So far, I’ve been impressed with how quickly the pans heat up and how effortlessly food slides off,” says tester Nicole Doster. “Cleanup is quick and easy, too. Plus, the stainless steel finish looks luxe on my stovetop.”

While we haven’t yet put GreenPan’s Spectra line through the same paces as HexClad, we’ve tested the brand’s ceramic cookware extensively at Taste of Home. In fact, after testing over 17 brands, we rated the GreenPan Valencia pan as our top pick for the best ceramic cookware. So far, we’re just as impressed with this set, especially given that it uses the same Thermolon 9G nonstick technology as GreenPan’s ceramic cookware.

Size(s) Available: 8 and 10 inch | Lid Included: No | Oven Safe: Up to 850ºF | Metal Utensil-Friendly: Yes | Features: Thermolon 9G nonstick ceramic technology, 3-ply stainless steel, aluminum core

Made with non-toxic ceramic covered by a stainless steel grid, the OXO hybrid frying pan is ideal for searing, braising and sauteing. While HexClad is still our top pick for longevity seeing as we have yet to test this version longterm, the early results indicate a similarly impressive performance.

Like similar options, it features a hybrid construction with a nonstick surface and a stainless steel grid pattern. The exterior is composed of a solid stainless steel layer, which helps the pan heat evenly. While OXO uses non-toxic ceramic as its nonstick layer, this particular coating is diamond-infused and safe for use with metal utensils.

In our review, I detail its performance as I work my way through a breakfast plate. My egg cooked quickly and efficiently, even getting a layer of crispy lacy goodness on the edges. Flipping it was surprisingly simple, too. A quick turn with my nylon spatula was all it took to release the egg. There was nary a speck of egg white stuck anywhere. It also produced some of the crispiest hash browns I’ve ever enjoyed!

While it’s still a bit pricey, it’s also nearly half the price of our top pick, making it a solid mid-price option for folks who want to try out their first hybrid pan. Plus, unlike our budget option, this one is oven-safe up to 850ºF!

Size(s) Available: 8, 10 and 12 inch | Lid Included: No | Oven Safe: Up to 850ºF | Metal Utensil-Friendly: Yes | Features: Pouring rim, aluminum core, dishwasher safe

Folks on the hunt of a budget hybrid pan should look no further than Walmart. The Beautiful by Drew Barrymore hybrid pan offers comparable performance to the pricier pans on this list, but at less than $30. For those wanting to try out their first hybrid pan, that’s a total steal. Plus, it comes with a lid!

“I was surprised by how well this pan worked given its low price point,” says tester Marisa Hillman. “If I were to stock a rental home, I’d buy a set of Beautiful by Drew cookware. It’s incredibly affordable and I’m really impressed by the quality. It heats up quickly, cooks evenly and is very easy to clean.”

While we were overall impressed by this inexpensive pan’s performance, it’s worth noting that it offers the lowest heat resistance of all the options we tested. While most of the combo clad pans we tried were oven-safe up to at least 850ºF, this one can’t handle more than 500ºF (or 350ºF if you’re using the lid).

Additionally, this is one of the smaller options we tested at only 10 inches. Unfortunately, the brand has yet to release any additional sizes, though we’re hoping that changes. That said, for the price point, we’re willing to overlook these marks against it thanks to its overall performance.

“When I cook, I’m generally cooking for six people in a much larger pan,” says Marisa. “This was perfect for eggs and pancakes for one. If I was just cooking for myself or myself plus one, I’d definitely break it out on a regular basis!”

Hunting down a new set of pans, but don’t want to fuss with stainless steel or nonstick? This pair of Circulon hybrid pans offers the best of both worlds: a solid sear and easy cleanup, no sticking or questionable coatings required!

“As someone who struggles cooking on stainless steel, this hybrid pan is a great way to get the best of both worlds: tough and long-lasting like stainless but easy to cook on like nonstick,” says tester Amanda Oliver. While we wish this pair of pans offered a higher temperature resistance—they’re only oven-friendly up to 500ºF—we still found the performance impressive at such a low price point.

Amanda also notes that this might be her new favorite set of pans. Both perform better than the T-Fal nonstick pans she’s used to. So far, everything she has made has cooked evenly and easily with little to no sticking. As someone who wishes she could use stainless but finds it difficult, this pair of pans made a big impression!

“I thoroughly enjoyed cooking with this pan. Even with scrambled eggs—which I usually have issues with egg pieces sticking to pans or uneven browning—the food cooked evenly and quickly,” raves Amanda. “It required little effort on my part to get good results.”

For the price, we’re incredibly happy with the pans’ performance. Plus, you get two for the price of one, making this a good option for a full kitchen upgrade. While we love that our top budget pick comes with a lid, it also has a few drawbacks that come hand-in-hand with a lower price point. That’s why we advise anyone who wants to grab something comparable—albeit a bit more robust—to snag the Zwilling Peak hybrid frying pan. Not only does this top-tier pick come with a clear lid for added versatility, but it’s also impressively heat-resistant and slick.

While the nonstick properties are the main attraction, the included lid is the true star of the show. It fits securely, and the glass makes it easy to check progress without opening the pan. Size(s) Available: 8, 9.5, 10, 12 inches | Lid Included: Yes | Oven Safe: Up to 500ºF | Metal Utensil-Friendly: Yes | Features: Deep sides, clear tempered glass lid

According to cookware expert Alycia Johnson, Vice President of Merchandising at Sur La Table, hybrid cookware makes up a unique category of cookware in that the materials differ from pan to pan. Typically, hybrid pans combine a nonstick material such as ceramic with stainless steel ridges. This offers many of the benefits of both stainless steel and nonstick cookware in one singular pan.

“Hybrid cookware gets its performance from a combination of materials and surface design,” says Alycia. “Many pans feature a textured cooking surface with raised stainless steel elements and recessed areas containing a nonstick coating. The stainless-steel helps create a durable cooking surface, while the nonstick components help release food more easily.”

She notes that depending on the pan’s construction, additional layers of conductive materials such as aluminum help distribute heat evenly.

“Together, these features allow home cooks to tackle a variety of techniques, from browning proteins and sautéing vegetables to preparing delicate foods that might stick to traditional stainless steel,” she says. “It brings together the best of two worlds so you can sear your proteins to a beautiful golden brown and slide a delicate omelet right onto the plate without a hitch. No compromise required.”

Overall, the biggest benefit of a hybrid pan is versatility. Alycia explains that hybrid cookware bridges the gap between traditional stainless steel and nonstick. It offers a more forgiving cooking surface without sacrificing the ability to achieve a good sear. As a bonus, a single hybrid pan can often handle a wide range of everyday tasks.

“Depending on the construction and coating, durability and easier cleanup can be added advantages,” she says. “For home cooks who want cookware that performs well across daily cooking needs, hybrid cookware can be a smart investment that delivers both searing power and nonstick performance.”

To find the right cookware for you, Alycia advises that you consider what you cook most often. If you frequently sear meats, look for cookware designed to withstand higher-heat cooking and provide higher heat retention. For folks who cook a lot of eggs, fish, or other delicate foods, the type and quality of the nonstick surface is extra important.

“Shoppers should also consider compatibility with your stovetop, whether it is oven-safe, and what temperatures it can withstand. Understanding how to clean and maintain the pan will help extend its performance and lifespan,” she explains. “Look for hybrid cookware with sturdy construction, high-quality materials and a trusted nonstick coating. A good pan should feel solid but not too heavy, heat evenly and have a comfortable, secure handle.”

Ultimately, the best hybrid cookware should strike a balance. It should offer the durability and performance of stainless steel, plus the ease and convenience of nonstick.

Alycia notes that hybrid cookware is a versatile addition to your kitchen rather than a replacement for every pan. Therefore, we chose to focus testing on hybrid cookware’s purported strengths. To do this, we created a testing criteria based closely on our tests for nonstick, ceramic and stainless steel cookware.

Tests centered on several cooking tasks, including browning, searing, deglazing, tossing stir fries and, of course, making eggs. Our testers used the pans over the course of two months in their day-to-day cooking tasks. We also consulted cookware expert Alycia Johnson to get her take on the most important features to look for.

“While [hybrid cookware] offers benefits from both stainless steel and nonstick cookware, understanding its capabilities and limitations is key to getting the most out of it,” says Alycia.

She also notes that the best way to use hybrid pans is to first read your cookware manual. To ensure we gathered accurate data, we treated the pans based on each manufacturer’s included instructions. This is especially important when it comes to heat levels, utensils, and cleaning methods.

Hybrid cookware usually combines a nonstick material like ceramic with raised stainless steel ridges. This creates a pan that is durable, nonstick, typically safe for metal utensils and offers amazing searing power.

Unlike other types of cookware, “hybrid cookware” is a term that encompasses several different materials and constructions. cookware expert Alycia Johnson notes that the term “hybrid cookware” covers a lot of different options. When shopping, it’s important to look beyond the term “hybrid.” Instead, pay attention to the specific materials, construction and coating used. This will be different from pan-to-pan.

Some hybrid pans will have you lightly season the pan with olive oil or another type of fat. This will depend on the materials used, so be sure to read your product manual prior to use. Some, like HexClad pans, suggest seasoning the pan once when you receive it. You’ll also want to do this anytime you do a deep clean.

Our cookware experience spans everything from new releases to reputable ceramic cookware brands like Caraway, GreenPan, Alva and more. To find the best hybrid pans for every home cook, we tried out nine different options in our own homes. We put them through the paces by searing, steaming and sautéing over the course of several months. After all that testing, only seven of them stood up to our rigorous standards.

#55. Why You Should Always Read the Label on Your Cleaning Spray

Until I started reviewing kitchen gear five years ago, I rarely read product manuals or user guides. I’m sure that’s due in large part to my ADHD, as my brain tends to move more quickly than step-by-step instructions allow. Plus, I like to figure things out on my own, thank you very much!

But my rogue, DIY, quick-start method hasn’t always worked out in my favor. I inadvertently killed my first Dyson stick vacuum (that I saved for months to buy) because I failed to educate myself on proper filter maintenance. And I’ve owned my car for a decade and still have no clue what a couple of the buttons actually do.

While user error can make for a funny punchline, it can also get expensive. For example, it might seem silly to read the manual for a nonstick frying pan or enameled cast-iron Dutch oven, but that’s where you’d learn that putting it in the dishwasher or using metal utensils can destroy or degrade the cooking surface.

In the case of cleaning products, the stakes can be even higher—especially in this era of, er, less restrictive food safety regulations.

Before you get to the instructions on the back of a cleaning spray bottle, you need to pay close attention to what’s on the front, because not all kitchen cleaning sprays (no, not even all all-purpose cleaning sprays) are created equally.

Though they might have some very minimal, naturally occurring disinfecting properties from ingredients like vinegar or essential oils, basic cleaning sprays like Mrs. Meyer’s and Aunt Fannie’s have one job—and that is to clean the surfaces in your kitchen. And by “clean,” I mean they contain surfactants, which help to dislodge grease and gunk so you can more easily wipe away a mess.

Mrs. Meyer’s Clean Day All-Purpose Cleaner Spray

Aunt Fannie’s All-Purpose Cleaning Vinegar Spray

But simply removing discernible debris won’t leave you with a germ-free countertop, which is why you also need a disinfectant to kill bacteria and viruses (not to be confused with a sanitizer, which only kills bacteria). And if you want to ensure your counters are so clean you could eat off of them, I recommend using both. If you spray a disinfecting solution on top of a spill, it’s not disinfecting the counter underneath the spill—it’s sanitizing the surface of whatever is stuck to your counter.

Here’s the real kicker, and the reason it’s important to read the instructions on the back of your disinfecting (or sanitizing) spray: In order for the product to kill the number of germs the label claims, it needs to sit on the surface in question for anywhere from about two to 10 minutes. This period is called the “dwell time” or “contact time,” and the product needs to remain visibly wet for however long it takes to be truly effective.

For example, Lysol's All-Purpose Cleaner (which is truly all-purpose when used properly), is a sanitizer at 10 seconds, but it only "kills 99.9% of viruses and bacteria" as the front of the label claims, if it’s left to sit for 10 minutes. The little asterisks after that claim lead you to the back label, which details the dwell time along with the common bacteria and viruses it kills.

All-Purpose Cleaner Spray, Lemon Breeze Scent, 32 oz.

“Use as directed” shows up four times in the online product description for Clorox’s Multi-Surface Disinfecting Mist, which also claims to kill 99.9% of viruses and bacteria. It even has a specific instruction for kitchens (to rinse off of any food-prep surfaces after a 10-minute dwell time).

The moral of the story? Use your cleaning products as directed, which unfortunately does require reading the fine print on the label. While you’re at it, you might want to consider replacing your microfiber cleaning cloths after a 2010 study found that microfiber becomes less effective at removing contaminants from surfaces the more it gets used.

#56. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.
