#60. These Resorts Offer a Real Taste of American Regional Cuisine

No more generic resort food. These culinary-savvy properties bring a distinct sense of place to the all-inclusive experience.

American resorts are once again having a moment — and it’s not pickleball partisans driving the trend. A new generation of travelers, beset with decision fatigue in their daily lives, are embracing the all-inclusive stay where activities, amenities, and dining are all on the menu and usually just a short walk from their rooms.

Fortunately, stress-free no longer needs to mean bland or generic when it comes to cuisine and culture. Resorts have begun forging deep culinary connections to their surroundings, far beyond merely offering a few regionally specific cocktails or themed burger toppings.

Onsite farms, creameries, and distilleries provide fresh ingredients with true terroir, as well as a new category of resort activity: food-and-drink-focused tours and workshops to fill the time between morning yoga and an afternoon poolside nap.

Some resort restaurants, like Clay at Wildflower Farms in New York’s Hudson Valley and Sierra Mar at the Post Ranch Inn in Big Sur, California, have become destinations in themselves, where star chefs take diners deep into a region’s foodways.

These resorts leave visitors not just relaxed but also satisfied, having truly experienced — and tasted — a particular place.

Acura has always done things its own way. We believe the best experiences are created through intentional choices, thoughtful craftsmanship, and the confidence to pursue a different approach. This spirit is reflected in our philosophy of Precision Crafted Performance. Learn more.

By the time you get to Hawks Cay Resort in the middle of the Florida Keys, the blue vistas of the Overseas Highway will have made mainland worries seem very far away. The 60-acre resort on Duck Key offers a spa, five pools (including a saltwater lagoon), and soon a full water park. Also making a splash is Salt + Ash, the resort’s flagship live-fire restaurant from Florida native, Top Chef winner, and former Eater Miami Chef of the Year Jeremy Ford. Of course, fish and seafood from the surrounding waters feature prominently. But Florida flavors shine through in other ways too: Much of the produce on the menu comes from Ford’s Farm, strategically located between Miami Beach and the Keys. That might mean homegrown lychees in a uniquely local take on conch salad, or heirloom tomatoes just hours off the vine accompanying crisp-fried spear-caught fish.

Many resorts lay claim to a signature dish or cocktail. But the Tides Inn, situated on a quiet tributary of the Chesapeake Bay about 3 hours’ drive from Washington, D.C., has something few resorts, if any, can boast: its own oyster. Cultivated near the property by resident ecologist Will Smiley and served exclusively at the resort’s Salt & Meadow restaurant, the Widgeon oyster provides guests with an intimate connection to the estuary it calls home. To taste it is to taste the tides and the weather. “Our oyster changes salinity as the season changes, and as the weather changes,” says executive chef Kyle Perkins. He further notes that the freshwater influx with a heavy rainfall can quickly, if temporarily, change how much of a salty punch a Widgeon possesses. Beyond bivalves, Perkins sources everything from beef to blackberries from the region. Along with activities from lawn games and pickleball to kayaking, guests can even help themselves to the harvest: Those blackberries, a thornless variety, grow in abundance on the property, giving many children a first foraging experience.

Though it’s only about a 90-minute drive from the concrete canyons of Manhattan, Auberge Collection’s Wildflower Farms feels a world away. The Hudson Valley property’s 65 cabins, cottages, and suites feature floor-to-ceiling windows framing arcadian views. Thistle, an Auberge Spa, makes use of local botanicals and blooms in its treatments, while the on-site farm provides more than 14,000 pounds of produce annually for the restaurant, Clay. “The Hudson Valley is unique in the array of locally grown ingredients available,” says farm director Will Conway, noting that the resort’s culinary reach extends beyond its 140 acres. The menu is resolutely seasonal; even a dish like ricotta meatballs provides a changing taste of what is coming from nearby producers, with the protein shifting from pork to lamb depending on the time of year.

The Kohler name is, for most people, synonymous with kitchen and bath fixtures. But the company is also a serious player in hospitality, most notably with Kohler, Wisconsin, its sprawling resort in the town where the company is headquartered, two and a half hours from Chicago. Along with golf, a legendary spa, and outdoor activities like canoeing, hiking, hunting, and fishing, Kohler, Wisconsin, puts a strong emphasis on dining with Midwestern ingredients and hospitality. Among the on-site options is River Wildlife, a log cabin restaurant offering regional specialties like walleye, pheasant, and duck. The Wisconsin Room, meanwhile, combines steakhouse fare with Wisconsin supper club favorites like a “Not So Lazy” Susan, which includes deviled eggs, chicken liver mousse, and pickled vegetables in a nod to the classic relish tray. Regional cocktails like a brandy Old Fashioned and a grasshopper (de rigeur after dinner) leave no doubt where you are.

This resort three and a half hours northwest of Denver is big — about twice the size of Manhattan big. That leaves plenty of room for culinary operations that include a distillery, a bakery, and a greenhouse. Brush Creek Ranch’s herd of American wagyu cattle is raised using Japanese methods, which minimize stress in the name of producing superior marbling for added tenderness. You may not run into a steer getting a facial in one of the resort’s two spas, but rest assured, these animals are living their best lives. The ranch’s goats, meanwhile, don’t just assist with yoga classes: Some provide milk for the property’s Medicine Bow Creamery and its range of excellent cheeses. It all comes together at the Cheyenne Club restaurant, where meals and most beverages — like many of the resort’s activities, ranging from horseback riding and hiking to fly-fishing and standup paddleboard yoga — are included in the room rate.

At Castle Hot Springs, everything comes back to the water. The 130-year-old resort in the Bradshaw Mountains, about an hour north of Phoenix, was Arizona’s first spa retreat; families like the Rockefellers and Astors would come to soak in the spring-fed pools first discovered by Native American people thousands of years before. Along with a full roster of wellness and outdoor activities, the resort grows 35 types of citrus and features a 3-acre farm, irrigated by the same mineral-rich water that fills the pools. “Everything tastes a little bit better because it’s already pre-seasoned for me,” said executive chef Chris Knouse. To get a taste of “the farm on a plate,” Knouse recommends the lunchtime “farmer’s hummus,” which comes with that day’s harvest as a crudités assortment. At dinner, Harvest restaurant offers a tasting menu where dishes like cavatelli with corn, zucchini, tatsoi, and cherry tomatoes offer a deeper dive into what the Sonoran Desert can produce.

Arguably the only thing more beautiful than Post Ranch Inn is the drive there. It is, after all, located along what might be the most picturesque stretch of road in the entire country: Highway 1 in Big Sur. On a cliff overlooking the Pacific Ocean, the resort offers guests access to a spa and three pools, as well as activities like forest meditation and stargazing. Of Post Ranch Inn’s 100 acres, 90 are kept wild, and just over one is dedicated to a chef’s garden, which supplies the resort’s restaurant Sierra Mar. On this patch of land, chef Reylon Agustin and his team grow everything from apples and tomatoes to herbs and specialty ingredients like celtuce. From the surrounding forests come wild mushrooms, while nearby waters provide treasured ingredients like abalone for Sierra Mar, which is housed in a glass and wood pavilion that feels like it’s hovering over the cliff’s edge. Augustin knows well enough not to try to compete with the view. Instead, dishes like abalone congee and Grimaud Farms guinea hen with sunchokes and stone fruit highlight local ingredients to “complement the experience” of being in such a singular place.

#63. Chicken with Cajun Cream Sauce

Pan-fried chicken in a luscious Cajun cream sauce, served with mashed potatoes and green beans – SO cozy! I love this meal!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 17, 2026

That tomatoey, creamy, shallot-infused gravy is something I haven’t been able to stop thinking about.

I made this dinner for my family on the first barely chilly day a few weeks ago. I think my body had just been waiting for permission to go fall cooking mode, and I just unleashed.

Pan-fried chicken. Luscious, savory Cajun cream sauce. Homemade mashed potatoes. Green beans. Apple crisp for dessert.

I served it in deep bowls and we let the girls eat on the living room floor, using the coffee table as their table, while we watched American Ninja Warrior together with the windows open – which, frankly, is the move of two parents who are feeling extra generous and a little out of their mind with the joys of early fall weather. But that meal will be a top 5 meal for me this year, for sure. We all devoured in silence and then cozied up with full bellies to watch some ridiculous TV together.

Here’s an idea I keep coming back to: shrimp. Like what if you just made the sauce, and then threw a pound of uncooked jumbo shrimp in there? It would poach right in the sauce! I haven’t been able to pull myself away from the chicken and mashed potatoes combination, but I feel shrimp should at least be considered.

Hope this recipe gives you all same cozy fall feelings it gave me.

Also a big fan of using the air fryer here, if you’re not feeling the pan-frying.

This picture shows the shallots minced; I also really love to do this with a thinly sliced shallot, sliced on a mandoline. The shape will give you these little ribbons through the sauce.

Add cream and broth, and simmer till it’s GLORIOUS.

I mean, showstopper material right there.

My favorite combo for serving is mashed potatoes and green beans. LIGHTS OUT. So good.

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

Pan-fried chicken in a luscious Cajun cream sauce, served with mashed potatoes and green beans – loving this easy, cozy weeknight dinner!

To air fry the chicken: Air fry at 375 for 10-12 minutes, or until at least 165 degrees internal temperature.

Roasted Potatoes and Broccoli (Oven): Toss 3-4 cups halved baby potatoes with avocado oil and salt on a sheet pan. Roast the potatoes at 425 for 15 minutes. Scoot the potatoes over, add 3-4 cups broccoli and ¼ cup water to the same sheet pan, and roast for another 15 minutes.

Roasted Potatoes and Broccoli (Air Fryer): Toss 2 cups halved baby potatoes with avocado oil and salt. Air fry at 375 for 12 minutes. Add 2 cups frozen or fresh broccoli; air fry at 400 for another 10-12 minutes.

Keywords: cajun chicken, chicken dinner, mashed potatoes

#64. Chili’s Just Put Its Fried Mozzarella On A Chicken Parm Sandwich—Here’s My Review

Bring an appetite and maybe a plan for a nap.

As a longtime Chili’s lover, I treat every new menu addition like a sacred holiday. So yes, when I heard the chain was combining its Big Crispy chicken sandwich with Fried Mozzarella and marinara sauce, I took time out of my day to try it for myself.

The new Chicken Parm Big Crispy launches nationwide on October 20, following an early release at Chili’s locations in Florence, Kentucky; Rome, Georgia; and Venice, Florida. It starts with the chain’s Big Crispy chicken sandwich, then adds its Fried Mozzarella and marinara sauce to turn it into Chili’s very literal interpretation of chicken Parm.

And considering I’m already a huge fan of the original Big Crispy, adding one of Chili’s massive pieces of fried mozzarella on top felt like a pretty safe bet.

As soon as the sandwich hit the table, I knew this would be a heavy bite. There’s a giant piece of crispy chicken, an equally substantial piece of fried mozzarella, and marinara covering the whole thing. There was really no universe in which this was going to be a light lunch.

Thankfully, the flavor made the commitment worth it.

After my first bite, the first thing out of my mouth was, “This literally tastes like a chicken Parm.” And I mean a genuinely good chicken Parm.

The chicken was crispy on the outside while staying tender and juicy inside, which is exactly why I already liked the Big Crispy. But the Fried Mozzarella is what takes the sandwich somewhere else entirely. Mine arrived steaming hot, with a crisp exterior surrounding soft, molten cheese. The cheese pull felt like it could have stretched across the restaurant if I had given it the chance.

I was actually most nervous about the marinara. Chain-restaurant tomato sauce can go many ways, and mediocre sauce can easily overpower everything else on the sandwich. But Chili’s version was surprisingly solid. It added enough tangy tomato flavor to cut through all that fried chicken and cheese without drowning them out either.

Then there’s the bun, which deserves some credit simply for knowing its role. With this much happening between the bread, the last thing the sandwich needed was a dense or overly buttery bun making every bite feel even heavier. Instead, it was light and soft enough to hold everything together without competing with the chicken, mozzarella, and sauce.

Chili’s serves the sandwich with fries, white cheddar mac and cheese, plus sides of marinara and its house-made ranch.

This is absolutely not the sandwich I’d order before doing anything remotely athletic. But if the goal was to take chicken Parm and turn it into something unmistakably Chili’s, they nailed it.

You get the crunchy chicken that made the Big Crispy so good in the first place, a ridiculous amount of hot fried mozzarella, and enough marinara to make the whole thing taste like the dish it’s inspired by, not just a chicken sandwich with red sauce slapped on it.

Would I order it again? Easily, but I just might need a minute afterward.

“I've always wanted to go to a state fair,” Shilpa tells cohost and fellow Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk. “I only know that there's a lot of fried food, and there's sometimes butter sculptures…. Oh my God, what a magical place this sounds like!”

In her latest BA Bake Club drop, Shilpa makes at least a part of this dream a reality in the form of her Glazed Apple Pie Fritters. They’re studded with tender chunks of apple, and spiced with nutmeg and cinnamon, and yes, deep fried.

Food journalist and podcaster Mark Bittman and his cohost and daughter Kate Bittman from the podcast Food with Mark Bittman stopped by to help coach Kate in the fine art of frying. “Frying dough is kind of benign, right?” assures Mark. “And once it's browned, it's done…so start with that [cue for beginners].” It’s as easy as apple…fritters.

We’d love to hear from you! Send your questions to BA Bake Club on Substack or send a voice memo or email to [email protected].

Shilpa Uskokovic: And I'm Shilpa Uskokovic.

JS: We're both senior test kitchen editors at Bon Appétit.

SU: We're creating the nerdiest and most wholesome corner of the baking internet.

SU: And I've always wanted to go, and it's just... I only know that there's a lot of fried food at the state fair. And there's sometimes butter sculptures. Oh, my God, what a magical place this sounds like.

SU: I mean, we have been running Bake Club for almost two years, or more than two years now.

SU: Almost two years. Yeah, all of our Bake Clubs are pros now, Jesse. We got to step up our game.

JS: Okay, okay. So, the fritters. And before we get too far, can you walk us through the recipe? And for that we'll need what else but our jaunty Bake Club music. Yes, there it is. Shilpa, where do we start?

SU: I think Jesse, that this might be one of our easiest Bake Club recipes. It's certainly one of our quickest. To make the fritters, you cook a bunch of apples down with sugar and spice, and everything nice, I guess. And then separately you make a batter with ricotta, eggs, flour, and leavener. And then you combine both of these mixtures. You flop the cooled cooked apples into the ricotta batter and you fold them together, and you fry those things up. And then, to finish, we have a very simple 10X powdered sugar glaze that's spiked with a little bit of cinnamon.

JS: 10X Shilpa. Do you want to tell the people what a 10X is?

SU: Yes. I'm sorry, I'm sorry. 10X is just the kitchen term, I guess, for powdered sugar. And the reason it's called 10X is because it's 10 times finer than regular sugar. And it's also 20X, which I never used personally.

SU: Yeah. But it's just, I don't know, kitchen speak for powdered sugar.

JS: Okay. So we talked about your inspiration at the state fair, but you've never been to a state fair.

SU: It was just the concept. The idea that a state fair is filled with fried foods, like the deep-fried Mars bars and the deep-fried-

SU: And this was actually inspired, or rather stolen, from my husband, Miro, who when he was pastry chef at Gramercy, he made these ricotta beignets. And then he would often serve them with custard and a huckleberry or other sort of berry jam, and they were so good. And I've been trying to pitch ricotta beignets.

SU: No one was biting. So, then I morphed the pitch into yeast free cake donuts. I was like, "Let's do this." There was a lot of back and forth, I remember. JS: Thank you for your transparency here.

SU: See, sometimes it's just the way the fritter is fried.

SU: Okay. So, I think the unifying factor... I know you asked about the differences, but I think the unifying factor is obviously that-

SU: Yeah. Those are cute molds. For me, I think of a donut as being typically yeasted, whereas a cake donut is usually made with a chemical leavener such as baking soda and/or baking powder.

I wanted those chunks of fruit in the batter, so when you bite in you hit those juicy pockets of fruit.

SU: It is a lie. And then we discovered that an apple such as Honey Crisp is actually the best one for baking because it softens, but it still holds its texture without collapsing into an applesauce.

SU: Okay. The ricotta, I was actually very inspired by Eastern European, Central European baking traditions of adding fresh cheese to doughs and batters. You see it a lot in German and Austrian and Balkan baking. And I like ricotta because it adds moisture to the dough, which translates into a more moist fritter in this case. And it also adds this nice acidity, which just lifts all of the flavors up. It's like when you season food and you put a squeeze of lemon juice in the end-

SU: It just tastes better, exactly. So, ricotta brings that natural acidity. And also, the acidity tenderizes the batter and it reacts with any of your leaveners and creates a much more fluffy, tender product.

JS: And the batter, what is the consistency?

SU: What is the consistency of the batter? Okay. So, before you add the apples, the batter is actually very thick, and there will be larger streaks of flour. It will look a little bit dry and clumpy almost. So the batter is a little bit unusual. It is very thick. It can be dry and it can be clumpy.

SU: Damn. You really make me reach far back. Thicker than pancake batter.

SU: Yeah. And when you add the apples, like the cooked down apples and their syrup, at first it'll be very difficult to incorporate. The batter looks like it's almost breaking-

SU: ... because that moisture is trying to be added to this fat. And then you keep folding it in and everything comes together into what I would describe as a pancake-like batter.

JS: Sure. Okay. Now you have your batter.

JS: I think it's time to address the elephant of the room, deep-frying. This is maybe the part where people have anxiety, hot oil is scary.

JS: So, what is the key to a good deep-fried fritter and moving past the sphere?

SU: I actually think the secret to better deep-frying, or more streamlined, less anxious deep-frying, is to just use a smaller pot.

SU: I almost never use a Dutch oven for frying. I just think it's-

SU: Yeah, it's a lot of oil. And I think that's what... At least to me, that's what builds up my anxiety when I see a huge pot of oil, because I think things can go south very fast with such a large volume of oil because it can hold onto a lot of heat.

SU: Yes. So I prefer to use a smaller pot. I usually fry in a wok at home. But over here, I remember I was using a skillet. I was using a straight sided skillet, which is about nine to 10 inches. And then I filled it with maybe three-ish cups of oil, and I think that affords you a certain sense of control. And then the second point, I would say, is also get a pan with high enough sides. Make sure that the oil comes no more than halfway up the sides of the pan.

SU: Because when you add things into the oil, the hot oil is reacting with... The moisture in there evaporates, essentially, and things do bubble up.

JS: Yeah, it's a little violent at first.

SU: It is. And sometimes that can cause the oil to rise up in the pan. So allowing yourself enough margin will sort of relieve that anxiety.

SU: I hate the deep-frying thermometer. I hate one. I don't know if I can say this though.

SU: So old-fashioned. I find them useless. I can never get them to clip on. They're always falling over because I never use-

SU: ... because I never use a Dutch oven. I suppose if you're using a Dutch oven [inaudible 00:13:10] I think it's nice and convenient to clip on. But I'm almost always frying in a wok, which has a curved side. Or I'm using a skillet, which has short side, so this thing never stays on. I just use a chopstick. People have been using that technique for centuries. Nothing has happened. We're good.

SU: Okay. So, you can use a chopstick to test the temperature of your oil, and you do this by using a wooden chopstick, obviously, not a metal one. You take a wooden chopstick, which is not polished or sealed or lacquered in any way.

SU: Like a takeout one. And then when you feel your oil is hot enough, you plunge the tip of the chopstick into the oil, and then you watch the part that's submerged.

SU: Yeah. You watch the part of the chopstick that's submerged, and you should see, right where it meets the oil, you should see little bubbles forming. And that is an indication of how hot your oil is. If there are no bubbles or just very few small lazy bubbles, that means your oil is not hot enough. If there's a stream of bubbles that immediately rises and they lazily, blub, blub, blub, blub, that means your oil is kind of at the right temperature. And then if you have very rapid boiling and they're violently hissing against the side of the chopstick, that means your oil is a bit too hot.

JS: And this is just the moisture from the wood coming out, essentially?

SU: Yes, I think so. So that's the part about frying. And when you're ready to fry also, I think part of it is setting yourself up for the post-fry part.

SU: Exactly. That's a good point, Jesse, it does go so fast. And I think having that setup really helps. So, I almost always use a wire rack that's set inside a rimmed baking sheet, like a half sheet tray. And I have something, either it's tongs or a spider, or a slotted spoon so I can fish out my fried food and move it to the wire rack. I never place it on paper towels.

SU: Because I think it just steams up, because-

SU: It gets soggy. You're putting this paper towel on a platter or a plate, and when the fried food makes contact, yes, the oil tends to get absorbed, but then it's steaming up beneath the surface because there's no air circulating. So I almost never put fried food on a plate with a paper towel.

JS: Sure, sure, sure. I've seen people put paper towels under the wire rack.

JS: I don't really know what that's about.

SU: ... but it's not sucking the oil out of that fried food because it's now suspended over the wire rack.

JS: It's just depleting Earth's resources.

JS: Okay, okay. So we're set up for frying.

JS: How do you scoop the batter in? How do you avoid sploshing hot oil everywhere? What is your technique?

SU: I know it's scary to get your hand close to the pot of oil, but actually the closer you can possibly get to the pan and the surface of the oil, the less dangerous it is. If you plop your, in this case, the fritters from up high, let's say chest height into the oil, that's going to fall and splash. Think of somebody diving into a pool, it's going to splash oil on you. Whereas, if you think of instead of a, I don't know, like a hippo entering the water. And you just gently glide the fritter into the oil, it's less likely to splash and splatter. So, I use an ice cream scoop to portion the batter, because I think that leads to consistent fritters and they all fry evenly. I've also made it with measuring cup, like a quarter or one third measuring cup, and it's worked perfectly fine. But I like the scoop because the spring-loaded action lets you drop the batter in quicker.

SU: And then I hold the batter as close to the surface of the oil as I feel comfortable and I just let it go gently.

JS: And what about overloading the pan? I know this is a big thing people preach about frying is don't overload the fryer.

SU: Yes. I think that's a valid concern. I think it's overloading or not is a matter of how big your pan is, obviously. The larger your pan and the more oil you have, the more you can fit in there. I would say think about deep-frying the same way as you would when you're sauteing something. You're looking for something to get color. You're looking to give these things enough space to float around, be surrounded with the oil and have the moisture evaporate. Same as you would in a skillet when you're sauteing chicken breast, for instance. You don't want to crowd things to the point where they don't have space to move and there's too much steam builds up. I would say have the pan about three-quarters full. That's a good gauge.

JS: Sure. Okay. So you have your fritters frying.

SU: This one, these fritters in general, because they have a lot of sugar. They have the sugar from the apples, they have the sugar from the syrup, so they will brown quite rapidly.

SU: They are quite dark. And in shaping the fritters, I also found it very helpful to... After I put the oil, I found it very helpful to go in with the back of the scoop that I use, for instance, and just squish the batter down a little bit because then that flattens the fritter.

SU: And it helps things cook a bit more evenly.

SU: Think of it like when you're grilling a burger, and you know how when you grill or cook the burger and the center tends to rise?

SU: Yes. And then to prevent that you dimple the middle.

SU: So think of that as the same way. By pressing down on the center of the fritter, you even everything out and things fry quicker and more evenly. This one, I would say push it a little past golden brown to a deep golden. And this rule applies, what I'm about to say next applies to anything that you're frying. I always use the bubbles around the fried food as an indication to know when to take things out. Because the more bubbles there are around the food that's in the oil, the more moisture there is. And when you're frying, you're really trying to drive away that surface moisture. And when the bubbles start to slow down or become really lazy, that's when you know that enough moisture has been driven off of the surface of whatever you dropped in to be crispy.

SU: So when there's less bubbles, pull that thing out.

JS: And then the dreaded question, what do you do with the oil? When you're done, can I reuse it?

SU: This one you can. I would wait for it to cool, and then you strain it. I often just put a fine mesh strainer over a large mouth mason jar, and then I pour the oil in. I get rid of whatever's in the sieve, little bits and bobs and apple pieces sometimes. And then you can reuse the oil once, for sure. You might have to top it off with fresh oil, and then after that I would get rid of it. Whatever you do, don't put oil down your sink or in the toilet.

SU: That's true. Don't do that. The best way to dispose cold oil is to put it in something else, like a clean used milk jug, for instance, or a bottle.

SU: Yes, or it's original container. And then seal it tightly and put it in the trash. Never pour oil down your sink.

SU: Yes, it's like a shellac. But I would prefer, if the fritter is cool, I do a thinner glaze. And if the fritter is warm to hot, I do a thicker glaze.

#69. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#70. Enjoy Fishing, Foraging, and Focaccia-Making at These U.S. Resorts

Guests today expect more than a Michelin-starred restaurant. They want to get into the kitchen and out in the field.

Plenty of resorts across the country have excellent restaurants, but travelers seeking more should explore the hands-on side of culinary resort experiences. From New York’s Hudson Valley to the South Texas Coast, adventurous food lovers can partake in workshops and experiences that get them out of the dining room and into the kitchen, garden, farm, or ocean. Whether you’re looking to forage or fish, these excursions will introduce you to local people, ingredients, and techniques, and ultimately offer a true taste of the destination.

At these properties, it’s less about what’s on your plate and more about how it got there. Big Sur is the perfect place to forage for edible botanicals and aromatics, and on Chesapeake Bay, harvesting and shucking oysters is woven into the community’s cultural fabric. Those wanting to escape the hustle and bustle of New York City can head up to the Hudson Valley for focaccia-making, while a desert oasis on the outskirts of Scottsdale, Arizona, teaches you how to craft pasta like a pro.

No matter your level of expertise, these resort experiences are designed to connect curious travelers with an impressive network of chefs, farmers, ecologists, mixologists, and bakers. For a vacation that will also quench your thirst for knowledge, head to these exciting culinary resorts.

Acura has always done things its own way. We believe the best experiences are created through intentional choices, thoughtful craftsmanship, and the confidence to pursue a different approach. This spirit is reflected in our philosophy of Precision Crafted Performance. Learn more.

Head down to the South Texas Coast for a true catch-to-table culinary experience. Local guides at La Pesca Lodge take guests to prime spots throughout Baffin Bay, offering everything from fly-fishing and wading to drifting and sight casting. Though you’re welcome to bring your own gear, the lodge provides spinning rods, lures, and live bait if needed.

Expect to reel in an array of speckled trout, redfish, flounder, and black drum. Your catch will be cleaned and bagged for you to take back to the lodge, where chefs transform your bounty into ceviche, grilled fillets, and more. Just remember that you’ll need to purchase your own Texas fishing license in advance. Those more interested in old-fashioned hunting can partake in dove, duck, or nilgai shoots.

The Andaz Scottsdale Resort & Bungalows is a retro, palm-tree-lined oasis with a premier spa, unique art collection, and the on-site restaurant Weft & Warp. Every Thursday, guests can beat the desert heat with a hands-on pasta class in the restaurant for $65.

You’ll learn a variety of techniques while crafting a few different pasta shapes. You might make agnolotti filled with a chive and shrimp paste; and you will also learn simpler pastas, like classic linguine or fettuccine. Once you’re done, enjoy your finished product with an optional wine pairing on the patio. If you’ve got dessert on the brain, book the Sweet Escape truffle-making workshop (hosted every Friday) and elevate your pastry skills by learning the basics of chocolate tempering.

Virginia’s Tides Inn gives travelers the chance to live like a Chesapeake waterman for the day. This signature activity pairs guests with a resident ecologist who takes you out to oyster cages via boat for an educational experience that’s all about shellfish. You’ll haul up your own oyster cages and sort through the very best bivalves, all while learning about the region’s longstanding history with oystering and the positive impact it has on the local ecosystem. Oysters harvested during the excursion need to be refrigerated for at least 24 hours, so when you return to the inn, enjoy a shucking how-to with the previous day’s haul while sipping on local wine and beer. The Chesapeake Gold experience is a similar outing, but includes a visit to one of the inn’s very own oyster farms, meaning you get to consume the same ones you collect. Once back at the inn, enjoy them both raw, grilled, and topped with your favorite seasonings.

Located in the foothills of Tennessee’s Great Smoky Mountains, Blackberry Farm is a working estate that maintains a strong connection to Appalachian agriculture. A twice-daily farmstead tour is available all year long, giving guests an in-depth look at the heirloom gardens, heritage livestock pasture, and dairy barn. These manicured, bright green gardens create a scenic backdrop to your itinerary, which includes sampling of farmstead cheeses, cured meats, preserves, and a rotating seasonal beverage. Those wanting a more formal culinary experience can book a three-hour artisan cooking demo with a three-course educational lunch and a glass of wine to pair.

Located about an hour and 20 minutes away from Phoenix, Castle Hot Springs is a picturesque desert resort with a thriving agricultural operation. The 3-acre garden yields more than 150 seasonal fruits, veggies, herbs, and flowers, supporting a dynamic farm-to-table ethos across the resort’s Relais & Châteaux-approved restaurant, Harvest.

Start your day with a one-hour farm tour, tasting your way through a variety of crops as you learn about the fertile soils supported by the area’s natural geothermal hot springs. In the afternoon, test your skills with a hands-on mixology class using produce and botanicals straight from the property grounds.

Ready to hard-launch your sourdough baking era? Learn the basics with Ashley Napoli, also known as the Focaccia Flourist, at the Hudson Valley’s Wildflower Farms. This Auberge Collection property is about 90 miles away from New York City, which makes it an easy escape for city dwellers needing to touch some grass.

The focaccia workshop costs $168 per person and starts by teaching you how to care for and maintain a living sourdough starter. You then knead, arrange, and shape your loaf, topping it with herbs, onions, florals, olives, and anything you’d like before baking. This particular workshop is being offered every Sunday and Tuesday through the end of October, but the resort typically hosts some version of a focaccia class throughout the year.

In Big Sur, towering redwood forest meets dramatic, bluff-lined coast, creating a diverse ecosystem brimming with unique plant life. The serene 54-room Alila Ventana Big Sur is a wellness-focused resort that spans 160 acres of lush, open meadows, tree-lined trails, and shaded ravines, creating the ideal conditions for a plethora of fungi and botanicals.

Every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, the hotel hosts a complimentary foragers hike for guests, who will learn all about wild-food harvesting and spotting secret ingredients hidden within the local terrain. There’s also a year-round Foragers Cocktail class ($99), a more in-depth experience that begins with an outdoor search for various herbs and aromatics, and culminates in a mixology lesson where you craft small-batch bitters for a custom cocktail.

#71. Brown Butter Banana Bread

If there's anything better than freshly baked banana bread, it's this toasty, nutty brown butter banana bread. Browning the butter gives the classic loaf an extra layer of flavor—and the scent is irresistible.

Brown butter gives our back-pocket banana bread a little more oomph in this new-fashioned recipe. Although brown butter isn’t exactly new (the French have used beurre noisette for centuries), it’s picked up within the past decade in the States. When butter melts down and cooks further, the milk solids toast and turn golden brown, deepening the flavor into something wonderfully nutty. You’ll smell it in the air as the brown butter banana bread bakes in the oven—it’s so good, you’ll want to turn it into a candle.

Baked with bananas and toasted walnuts, this version is pure heaven and totally steps up the classic banana bread recipe.

Place the cubed butter in a small heavy saucepan. Cook the butter over medium heat until it’s golden brown, 5 to 7 minutes, stirring constantly to evenly cook the milk solids. Immediately pour the butter into a bowl to stop the cooking process and to let it cool slightly.

Editor’s Tip: If you’ve never browned butter before, know that it feels like it takes forever to turn. Then when it does, it happens instantly. It’s going to foam up at some point, too, but keep stirring and scraping the bottom so you can keep an eye on the milk solids.

Preheat the oven to 350°F. In a large bowl, whisk together the all-purpose flour, sugar, baking soda and salt. In another bowl, stir together the eggs, mashed bananas, cooled brown butter, buttermilk and vanilla extract. Add the banana mixture to the flour mixture, stirring just until they’re combined. If you’re using walnuts, fold them in now.

Pour the batter into a greased or parchment-lined 9×5-inch loaf pan. Bake until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean, about 1 hour. Cool the loaf in the pan for 15 minutes so it can finish setting up its crumb structure, then remove it from the pan and onto a wire rack.

Editor’s Tip: If your banana bread’s top is browning too much while the inside is still raw, lower the oven’s temperature to 325° and cover the pan with aluminum foil.

Allow the brown butter banana bread to cool completely to room temperature, then transfer it to an airtight container or wrap it tightly in a few layers of storage wrap. Keep the loaf at room temperature for up to three days or in the fridge for up to five days.

Yes, you can freeze brown butter banana bread. Allow the loaf to cool completely to room temperature, then wrap it tightly in two layers of storage wrap followed by a layer of aluminum foil. It feels excessive, but this keeps the moisture locked in and prevents freezer burn. Freeze for up to two months, then thaw the loaf at room temperature for a few hours.

You can quickly ripen bananas using your oven. It’s my favorite trick when I need ripe bananas like, now—not in two days! Place the unpeeled bananas on a baking sheet and into a 250ºF oven until the skin turns brown and the flesh becomes soft and super sweet, about 15 minutes. Let them cool before using.

If your banana bread is gummy, there may be a few culprits at play. The first is whether you used two bananas instead of measuring out 1 cup of mashed bananas. Since bananas vary in size, you might have added too much to the batter, and too much moisture will make your banana bread gummy. Always follow the exact measurement rather than the suggested number of bananas.

Also, make sure you’re mixing enough, but not too much. Undermixing won’t develop the gluten and create a strong crumb structure for your loaf. Overmixing will lead to excessive gluten development, causing your bread to sink after baking. Mix the batter just until no flour streaks remain.

Lastly, let your banana bread cool completely before cutting into it. I know, this is the hardest part! But the cool-off period is important because the loaf is still developing its crumb structure, even after coming out of the oven. Let the loaf cool in its pan for 10 minutes, then remove it to a wire rack to cool off completely. Leaving the loaf in its pan will trap moisture and make it gummy.

Yes, you can bake brown butter banana bread in a different-sized pan. Instead of a 9×5-inch loaf, divide the batter evenly between three greased 5-3/4 x 3-inch mini loaf pans, or one 8-inch square pan. Start checking for doneness around the 40-minute mark.

#73. Watergate Salad

If you’re looking to take a nostalgic trip to a bygone era, you can’t beat a big bowl of Watergate salad. Made with canned pineapple, pistachio pudding, and Cool Whip, this retro crowd-pleasing dessert “salad” will take you straight back to the ’70s with just one bite. Watergate salad has just five ingredients and can be assembled in a single bowl, so it’s the perfect recipe to throw together if you don’t have a ton of time, but you need to take something to that potluck or family gathering.

In a large bowl, combine the drained crushed pineapple, reserved pineapple liquid, and pistachio pudding mix. Whisk everything together until thickened—this shouldn’t take more than a minute.

Next, add the marshmallows and Cool Whip to the bowl. Fold them into the pudding mixture, using a flexible rubber spatula to scoop around the sides of the bowl and down through the middle, until everything is combined and no streaks of Cool Whip are left.

Dollop the Watergate salad into a serving bowl and cover loosely with plastic wrap, then refrigerate until the marshmallows have softened and the salad is set; this will take at least 4 hours, but overnight is better.

When you’re ready to serve, uncover the bowl and top with pistachios. If you’re feeling especially retro, you can add a few cherries too!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Watergate salad is best eaten 4 to 24 hours after it’s first made and refrigerated. As time goes on, the salad will get looser as the marshmallows get softer and eventually dissolve completely. Texture aside, it’ll still taste good (and be completely safe to eat) for 3 days.

#75. Our Best Thanksgiving Yet

If you listen in on Test Kitchen conversations, you’ll hear the editors say that Thanksgiving is our Super Bowl, our World Cup, and our Fashion Week. For food people, it’s the culmination of a year’s worth of prep, planning, brainstorming, and, as my colleague Hana Asbrink describes, Post-it Note–filled recipe scrums. But I wouldn’t call it stressful.

We look forward to basking in the day’s many gravy-soaked superlatives. We delight in stories that showcase celebrating family, friendship, and community while giving guidance for making the most of the holiday season. Of course, it’s a busy time, but it also brings so much joy.

I revel in the little tasks that make the day feel even more special, like sorting my china patterns and silverware, checking napkins for grease stains, and sending table linens to the cleaners for some extra TLC.

I’ve never really bought into Thanksgiving Day angst. I find the shopping stress and pressure-packed meal planning to be exaggerated myths perpetuated by pop culture. After all, the mac and cheese, potatoes, pies, and pound cakes are similar to the celebratory dishes that punctuate the year’s other holidays.

Of course, traditions vary between cultures and communities. What makes a classic Thanksgiving recipe is a matter of heritage, geography, and nostalgia. But even tradition can use a little zhuzh. New recipes, such as our Cranberry Meringue Pie and A Beautiful Cabbage Galette can add excitement—and practicality—to the holiday.

The Bon Appétit Test Kitchen has created 18 dishes, including breakfasts and variations for sides and salads to complement your family staples. We even asked five sommeliers for their recommendations for the best wines to pour on the big day.

These all add up to the best Thanksgiving ever.

#77. Steal my Food Itinerary: A SoCal Beach Dive Bar Crawl

In my opinion, this is the best way to celebrate your birthday.

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Do birthdays matter? Not really. But they are, at the very least, an excuse to do something you might not usually do as a middle-aged father of two. On this most recent occasion, my birthday was a reason to drag an assortment of friendship flotsam across the Los Angeles coastline, working our way down through a selection of Southern California beach dive bars. (It also marks the second time I’ve used my assignments for Eater and Punch to rationalize, or maybe subsidize, a birthday bar crawl.) I truly believe that these old, salt-crusted pubs are an essential, last-remaining stronghold of our regional culture, and that they demand both our respect and our money.

This crawl took place on a Saturday in September, filled with drinks and snacks (but mostly bites of bar burgers), working our way from Santa Monica to Manhattan Beach before wandering inland for dinner in Torrance, home to some of the best Japanese food in the United States.

The plan was to start relatively early, enjoying as much sunlit ocean breeze as we could, while also allowing me to get a normal amount of sleep at the end of the night before waking up at traditional dad hours. The great thing about a bar crawl is that it allows people to jump on and off as they see fit. I’m also a sucker for a brisk itinerary, moving quickly from place to place: the key is to not care who shows up when and where, simply telling someone to add the necessary ETAs to the group chat as applicable.

Opened in 1959, and a roughly 8-minute walk from the beach, Chez Jay has remained a staple and a refuge in a city that has been rapidly pricing out old neighborhood bars and restaurants. It is a place to drink a martini or a beer, where the only rules are that you “take no pictures, and throw your peanut shells on the floor.” (I broke one of the rules.) The kitchen was not open yet, but the peanuts were plentiful and the pours were heavy. The red booths and red checkerboard tablecloths evoke an old Italian restaurant, though it is certainly more of a steak-and-seafood kind of place to have dinner. It started strong, with six people showing up, including my dad and stepmom.

Hinano Cafe has been operating on a busy stretch of Venice Beach since 1962. This perpetually packed place has become an iconic surfer hang serving beer and burgers (no full liquor license here) — and like a true surfer bar, it serves breakfast from 8 a.m. until noon. Our group swelled with more friends at our second location, where pitchers of beer were poured in a standing-room-only setting, alongside board-short-wearing day drinkers who were far too young and attractive for us to stay any longer than it took for this gaggle of graying dads to order and split a hamburger. At $12.50, this perfectly acceptable bar burger on a sesame seed bun was a pleasant enough edible intermezzo. I’d prefer to come back again at another time, like maybe 1975.

We had now crossed to the other side of the marina — something of a traffic dividing line in Los Angeles County — and settled into a perfect little three-bar-crawl that exists on a 0.2-mile stretch of this hidden, working-class LA beach community. The sun was starting to drop and the ocean breeze was relaxing our shoulders (although that also may have just been the drinks). We sauntered into Prince O’ Whales, which has been serving drinks under this name for over five decades, with another 18 years before under a different one (“The Bowsprit”). There are two indoor bars, though one was closed for the afternoon. Our bartender was the kind of grumpy you look for in a sailor’s saloon, and the room was crowded with some rather loud folks watching college football. (It turns out I’m getting old.) We took our drinks to the back patio, a serene little patch of cement, brick, faded paint and sun-withered wood. There was also a ping-pong table, and this round was highlighted by exactly the kind of late-summer weather that makes people live by the beach in Southern California.

After walking for about 90 seconds, we made it to a place known as “the smallest dive bar in Los Angeles.” It would feel like a California-themed yokocho in Tokyo if it weren’t so perfectly lived in, lined with old wood that feels like you’re drinking in the bowels of a turn-of-the-century vessel crossing the Atlantic. A drunk, nonthreatening stranger joined our group and asked a lot of questions. I ordered a vodka-soda and they gave me a gin and tonic, so I ordered a gin martini. It came with a “sidecar” that was, incredibly, just a rocks glass with a splash of rapidly warming gin in it. I curiously wandered into the adjoining Italian restaurant and was convinced by some very friendly women to order some food. I told them to pick their favorite dish and near the end of my martini, a foil container of steaming hot ravioli was dropped at our table. If my wife divorces me, I could see myself paying rent on one of these barstools, living out my twilight years and wondering where it all went wrong.

Looking back at my iPhone photo timestamps, I am incredibly impressed that we were able to have a round of martinis and a plate of ravioli in 26 minutes. We soldiered on, with an even shorter walk to our next location: the classic old surf bar and restaurant, The Shack. It feels almost set-decorated, with the perfect amount of wear and tear. This place was significantly more spacious and we found room at the bar, where we ordered the Shack Burger for all to try, as well as some wings. The signature burger comes, miraculously, with a butterflied Louisiana hot link on it, operating like juicier, snappier, spicier bacon. I, meanwhile, remained impressed with my ability to have five drinks (or was it six?) — a skill that rarely gets tested anymore.

Nearing its 100th year of operation (though not always as a bar — it opened during Prohibition), this could easily have been the last stop of the tour, the flagship bar you build a crawl around. Known among my friends as “the best dive bar burger in LA County,” this proud, defiant establishment has stood the test of time, surviving rapidly escalating real estate prices to remain the great neighborhood dive it has always been. It feels like a sacred escape from the rest of this wealthy beach community. The whole place seems to be made of wood and beer signs; there is one line for ordering and another for the bathroom; and every single patron — whether gray-haired in Hawaiian shirts or tatted-up bikers — seems to know how lucky they are to be there. There is a small grill behind the bar in the corner, under a yellow sign proudly proclaiming “no fries.” The cheeseburger is an exercise in simple chargrilled perfection, its meat sourced from the butcher shop next door, all served in a basket with a bag of potato chips. The menu also claims to have a teriyaki chicken sandwich, though I’ve never seen one there. I wished we could have stayed longer, or to have eaten a whole burger instead of just two bites, but such is the nature of a crawl. We quickly made our way out, calling our next restaurant to let them know we were running about 20 minutes late for our reservation.

Stop 7: Torihei — Torrance – sometime not long after 8 p.m.

We did a decent job of snacking rather than eating on our beach dive crawl, so after we settled into a long table adorned with sake and beer, there was perhaps no more comforting bite of food in the world than Torihei’s simmered slab of daikon radish, served in dashi and blanketed in katsuobushi (smoked, dried skipjack tuna flakes). It warmed my chest. This classic standby izakaya specializes in yakitori (grilled chicken skewers) and oden (simmered ingredients in broth). We sipped beers and crunched tender chicken cartilage alongside grilled chicken meatballs before finishing the night with some soborodon (a ground chicken and rice bowl).

I was home, showered, and in bed before 11:15. I think we nailed it.

#79. More Than 1.5 Million Pounds of Meat Recalled—Here’s What You Need to Throw Out

Time to check your refrigerator for recalled meats like hot dogs, chicken sausage, bacon and deli products sold under several brand names.

A package of chicken sausage can settle the question of what to make for dinner in a hurry. But before you put one to work this week, check the label. A nationwide recall includes chicken sausage, hot dogs, bacon, deli meats and other refrigerator staples sold under several brand names.

Kayem Foods, based in Chelsea, Massachusetts, is recalling approximately 1,584,361 pounds of ready-to-eat meat and poultry products, according to an October 17 USDA announcement. The products were shipped to retailers and foodservice locations nationwide and in Hong Kong.

Here’s what to check before you make your next meal.

The products may have been stored at improper temperatures. According to the USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), Kayem received a customer complaint on Oct. 1 about products arriving warm. The company investigated and found that a warehouse cooler had not consistently kept the products at a safe temperature.

In Kayem’s announcement, the company attributed the problem to a cooling system malfunction at one of its warehouses. Kayem says it has now corrected the issue.

As of the USDA’s October 17 announcement, there were no confirmed reports of illness linked to the recalled products.

The products went to stores and foodservice locations across the country, but the USDA notice does not name specific locations. It says retail distribution lists will be posted on the agency’s recall website when available.

Kayem’s consumer product list includes items sold under these brands:

Examples include Kayem Fenway Franks, Al Fresco fully cooked chicken sausages and chicken meatballs, McKenzie bacon and turkey breast and Triple M ham. Check the product details carefully. A brand name alone does not establish whether a package is recalled.

The USDA says the recalled products were produced approximately March 31 through Oct. 7, 2026. That’s the production window, not a range of best-by dates to look for on your package.

Start by checking for one of these establishment numbers inside the USDA inspection mark:

Then match your product’s brand, description, UPC and applicable date or lot information against the USDA’s complete product list. Package sizes and identifying details vary, so there isn’t one date or code that covers everything.

The USDA also provides product label images to help you identify recalled packages. If you bought meat slices at a deli counter and no longer have the original label information, ask the store whether your purchase was included.

Do not eat the recalled products. The USDA advises throwing them away or returning them to the store.

For help identifying a product or questions about the recall, contact Kayem Foods Customer Service at 800-426-6100, Monday through Friday, 7:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern, or email [email protected].

If you’re concerned about an illness after eating one of the recalled products, contact a healthcare provider.

#80. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#81. Heavy cream vs. whipping cream: What's the difference?: Understanding the right cream for your baking.

If you’re baking a recipe that calls for heavy cream, or picking up a carton to turn into whipped cream to finish a dessert, you may be confused when you hit the dairy aisle. There’s “heavy cream” — but also “heavy whipping cream” or, in some cases, just “whipping cream.”

So when it comes to heavy cream versus whipping cream, is there truly a difference?

Aside from being delicious, there are very specific definitions and standards that must be met in order for something to be labeled as heavy cream. It is made by separating the fatty top layer from the base milk layer during processing. The FDA states that heavy cream is cream that contains no less than 36% milk fat.  Comparatively, milk has 0% to around 3% milk fat, as well as a higher water concentration. Because of its fat content, heavy cream retains a rich taste and, when whipped, it excels at creating stiff peaks that hold their shape for a long time.

Whipping cream — sometimes called “heavy whipping cream” — is made using a similar process as heavy cream and is also the milk fat removed before milk is homogenized. However, heavy cream can contain somewhere between 30% and 35% milk fat content, according to FDA regulations. Because of its slightly lower fat content, it whips into a softer, more billowy cream, and it will deflate more quickly than whipped cream made with heavy cream.

Luckily, the difference in taste and performance between the two types of cream are not very discernible. This means you can use them interchangeably in recipes — and it's okay if you accidentally buy the "wrong" one. Both can yield a delicious bowl of homemade whipped cream. (Can’t justify buying a whole carton of either one? We’ve got you covered with an easy homemade heavy cream substitute.)

A note on King Arthur recipes: The King Arthur Test Kitchen prefers heavy cream in most instances, particularly when making whipped cream, because of the higher fat content. That said, you can substitute heavy whipping cream 1:1 in any King Arthur recipe that calls specifically for heavy cream without any issue.

As a general rule of thumb, use heavy cream for making stable whipped cream for topping pies, layered desserts like tiramisu or banana pudding, and any sweet where the structural integrity hinges on the cream really holding its shape. Heavy cream can also be handy for making cream scones and drop biscuits, where the richness of the dairy can shine through. For more heavy cream baking inspiration, check out these 12 recipes that call on heavy cream.

#85. Make-Ahead Mashed Potatoes

Thanksgiving dinner can feel like a game of Tetris, but this make-ahead mashed potato recipe gives you one less thing to juggle. It lets you prepare the potatoes up to two days in advance, then reheat them just before serving without sacrificing their rich flavor or velvety texture.

The secret is in the technique: Simmer whole, skin-on Yukon Gold potatoes to keep them from absorbing excess water, then pass them through a potato ricer with plenty of butter. Adding the butter before the warm milk and cream coats the potato starches in fat, helping the mash stay smooth and creamy even after refrigeration. A little sour cream adds a welcome tang.

For extra flavor, try adding roasted garlic, finely grated Parmesan, or infusing the milk and cream, as we do in BA’s Best Mashed Potatoes, with bay leaves, thyme, or rosemary.

How far in advance can you make mashed potatoes?

Up to two days. Let the finished mashed potatoes cool slightly, then cover and refrigerate promptly. Need a longer head start? Learn how to freeze mashed potatoes.

How do you reheat mashed potatoes without making them gummy?

Gently warm them in a saucepan over medium-low heat with the additional milk and cream to restore the proper consistency. Stir often but gently to prevent scorching without overworking the potatoes, which can turn them gluey.

The potatoes may have absorbed too much water during cooking. For this recipe, simmer them whole, with the skins on, until very tender but not falling apart. Drain well and let them dry in the warm pot before ricing. Add the warm milk and cream gradually, stopping when the potatoes reach your desired consistency.

No. Leaving the skins on while boiling helps prevent waterlogging, and most of the peels will stay behind in the ricer. Clear out the collected skins between batches to prevent clogging. If you prefer to peel the potatoes yourself, do so after cooking, while they’re still warm.

Can you make mashed potatoes without a ricer?

A food mill fitted with a fine disk is your best alternative. A potato masher will produce a less uniform texture and requires peeling the potatoes first. Avoid a food processor or blender, which can overwork the starches and make the potatoes gluey.

OXO Good Grips Stainless Steel Potato Ricer

Rubbermaid Brilliance Glass Food Storage Containers

Place 4 lb. medium Yukon Gold potatoes, scrubbed, in a large pot and pour in cold water to cover by 1". Add a large handful of kosher salt (water should taste briny, like the ocean) and bring to a boil. Reduce heat and simmer until potatoes are very tender but not crumbly, 30–40 minutes. Drain and return potatoes to warm pot to dry (off heat).

Meanwhile, heat ⅔ cup heavy cream and ⅔ cup whole milk in a small saucepan over medium until just about to simmer. Reduce heat to low and keep warm until ready to add to potatoes.

Pass hot potatoes and 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, through ricer into a large bowl (this will help combine them quickly; most of the skins should stay behind, but pick out any small pieces that get through if you want); season generously with salt. Mix with a potato masher until butter is melted and combined.

Gradually add half of the warm cream mixture to mashed potatoes, folding with a spatula until combined, followed by ½ cup sour cream. Gradually add remaining cream mixture until you reach your desired consistency (the potatoes will thicken slightly as they sit). Taste and season with salt and freshly ground black pepper as desired.

Transfer mashed potatoes to a baking dish or other shallow container, let them cool until the potatoes stop steaming, then cover and chill up to 2 days.

To serve, transfer refrigerated potatoes to a small pot and add ⅓ cup heavy cream and ⅓ cup whole milk; reheat over medium-low, stirring often (but gently) to prevent scorching.

#86. Chicago’s Most Exciting New Restaurant Is Cooking From 900-Year-Old Recipes

An interview with the chef behind Muhājir

Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants. Throughout the year, we’ll check in with teams in Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C., to hear what it’s really like behind the scenes of a buzzy opening. Then, we’ll host exclusive meals at these restaurants as part of Dinner Party, presented by Capital One. Read along for challenges, candid reflections, and advice from the proprietors behind some of the country’s hottest new openings.

Zubair Mohajir is one of Chicago’s most prolific new chefs and restaurateurs, behind such openings as Lilac Tiger, Mariela, Mirra, Sarima, and most recently, Muhājir, a restaurant that traces historical spice routes to tell the story of global migration. I talked to Mohajir about how the opening is going, how he thinks about collaboration across his different projects, and why Muhājir is finally the restaurant that feels like home.

Zubair Mohajir: Muhājir is such a personal story for me, because my last name is Mohajir, and the meaning of “muhājir” in Arabic and Urdu is “one who migrates.” When the partition [of India and Pakistan] happened, the Muslims that were moved from India to Pakistan were named Muhājirs because they were migrated. In my family, we always wondered why that was our last name. When I started cooking [after working in finance], it really started to settle in. Our late maternal grandfather was obsessed with mapping where this family name came from. It comes from Southern Basra, Iraq, and that was so mind-blowing for me because it’s one of the biggest spice roads.

At Coach House for the past five years, I’ve been exploring ancient recipes in southern Spain and southern Portugal. [They] bring in pre-Crusade Muslim, Christian, Jewish [influences] that are also affected by the Southeast Asian traders coming on the spice road that shoots through the Mediterranean and hits North Africa and the Iberian Peninsula. I’m just obsessed with history and it started to become very evident for me that I really wanted to feed people, but with the context of where the food came from.

At Muhājir, it’s all about riding the spice road that runs from Portugal through the Mediterranean, through the Levantine [region], and then hits out of Basra, Iraq, into the Persian Gulf, and the first landmass it comes across is southern India, where I’m from. We’re all muhājirs — you know, all of our families came from somewhere, and that really has been the driving force for me.

I’d never cooked on live fire, but we’re cooks, and it was going back to core things. I remember growing up in my grandmother’s house back home in India, and it’s not like there were gas stoves everywhere. When I decided that I was going to do Muhājir, it became so obvious to me that it couldn’t just be a sauté pan on a stove. The story that we wanted to tell had to be told through wood fire.

We do a duck that is inspired by a 927-year-old recipe we found from southern Spain that is influenced by Roman garums, Muslim origins, and Jewish origins. We do this duck “experience,” where we take a whole duck, butcher it, and have the crown dry-aging for seven days. We take the wings and make a jus [and] take the legs and make a confit. We blast that duck crown over the fire when we start service every day, and then it gets finished in the brasa. If you’re sitting in the restaurant, you can see the ducks hanging over the fire.

When we present it, we have this beautiful ornate Turkish platter. There’s black raspberry achaar, the duck jus in a saucier, the duck rice next to it, the duck skin cut in these beautiful medallions on top almost like duck chicharrón, and then we’re also presenting the duck breast itself that has a very crispy skin. The top of that duck breast is the spice mix from that exact recipe that’s more than 900 years old, with cumin, coriander, cardamom, toasted pine nuts, red wine vinegar, and fish sauce. It’s a story of cross-cultural collaboration.

Bobo’s really inspired by Jacob Dela Cruz, who’s my partner here. We built Sarima together, and it became very important to me to highlight his upbringing and his background as well. He was one who said, “You should name the restaurant Muhājir.” His point was that we’re all immigrants. I was like, “That’s such a simple statement, but such a profound statement.” It was kind of vice versa when we were talking about the bar: Jacob’s father is an amazing person and his name is Bho, and “bobo” in Tagalog means “silly” or “stupid,” as a term of endearment. We always say that as Spice Road-driven and transformative the food experience at Muhājir is, we still like to have fun.

If people are early for their reservation, we take them back to Bobo, or they stop by after dinner. You can’t get to Bobo without walking through the restaurant, so the spaces contribute to each other. If you came to Bobo, you might be like, “I want to eat there.” And if you come straight to Muhājir and see people walking back constantly, you might be like, “What’s happening back there?”

I wouldn’t say it’s easier [than my other restaurants], but now I don’t freak out. I’ve created a methodical way of approaching issues or problems head-on and figuring it out as a group or with the people that support us. We don’t have investors who are private equity firms; our investors are our guests. When it comes to managing expectations and navigating obstacles, you get better with repetition.

I’m living a dream. Sometimes, when you’re building restaurants with others, you’re not necessarily in the kitchen. [At Mirra, I] was like, “I’m helping create and build this concept, but that’s [chef Rishi Kumar’s] kitchen to run.” Here, it’s the home that I’ve been yearning for and working toward my whole career. I plan to be old in this place. Things have been so crazy and wild and amazing, but slowly, every day, I sit more and more in that moment where I’m like, “This is home.”

#89. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.

#90. Schmaltzy Chicken and Stuffing Skillet

While you might think of instant stuffing as a once-a-year darling that makes an annual appearance like Punxsutawney Phil, this recipe is a case study of why this product should be put to use throughout the year. (Boxes of the dried mix can be found near the breadcrumbs any month.) Here, it’s called into action to prop up skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs in a bed of savory stuffing that’s bolstered by aromatics and sweet-tart dried cranberries. Starting with a cold pan ensures even rendering of the chicken fat and crispy skin. The lot gets baked together, allowing the savory drippings from the chicken to soak into the stuffing. Serve with a side of cranberry sauce, a fresh salad, or all by itself for a one-pan dinner that recalls Thanksgiving any night of the week.

More delicious skillet dinners this way: Chicken Thighs With Spiced Couscous and Carrots; Ruffled Mushroom Pot Pie; and One-Skillet Chicken Pot Pie.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Season 2 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (about 4 medium) on both sides with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Pour 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil into a cold large stainless-steel skillet and swirl to coat bottom of pan. Arrange chicken, skin side down, in pan and place over medium-high heat. Cook undisturbed, rotating pan around on burner often to promote even browning, until skin is browned and chicken releases easily from pan, 7–10 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet or large plate and arrange skin side up.

Combine 1 large onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan and cook over medium-high heat, stirring often, until onion is softened and just starting to turn golden, 8–12 minutes. Add one 6-oz. box instant stuffing mix, ½ cup unsweetened dried cranberries, and 1¼ cups water, then finely grate in zest from 1 lemon and set lemon aside. Mix until stuffing is hydrated. Remove pan from heat and push stuffing to sides to create wells for chicken to rest in. Nestle thighs, skin side up, into stuffing. Transfer pan to oven and bake until chicken is cooked through and top of stuffing is golden brown and crisp, 45–55 minutes.

Top chicken and stuffing with more dried cranberries and reserved celery leaves. Cut reserved lemon into wedges and serve alongside for squeezing over.
