#92. Hasan Minhaj Thinks America’s Greatest Accomplishment Is Cereal

This is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people. This interview series dives deep into their food routines, including dinner party strategies, cherished cookbooks, and the memorable bites they’d hop on a flight for.

Comedian and actor Hasan Minhaj is known for quippy questions, biting comebacks, and colorful commentary, but his most delightful soundbites are about food. During a recent  hour-long chat, he named a wide range of favorites, including bananas and oranges (“they come prepackaged and are great for traveling”); macaroni and cheese (“I love every category and version of it, from the box of Kraft to anyone’s Thanksgiving mac ’n’ cheese”); and dal chawal (specifically his mom’s version of the lentils and rice dish, “pure comfort food and my love language”).

These are the best-of-the-best bites for Minhaj, which is coincidentally the name of his new movie—Best of the Best, streaming now on Netflix—that he cowrote and produced with Prashanth Venkataramanujam and stars in as a professor and former dancer. The film pays homage to real-life Bollywood competitions, following collegiate dancers Maya and Anjali (played by Maitreyi Ramakrishnan and Priyanka Kedia, respectively), whose characters were inspired by “deeply passionate college kids in the biggest world that a lot of people have never heard of.”

Fiery passion is at the center of Minhaj’s life, especially when it comes to actual spice. “Some people want to drive at 85, some like a nice even 65, and some take it five miles below the limit,” he explains in a speedy analogy. “My spice level? I want to feel things in all caps. Life is to be lived. So I’m like, ‘Give it to me!’ Give me the full robustness of flavor that’s possible. I am a maximalist and love it all!”

His other spice of life is chai, “a form of commiseration, community, and love in Indian households—and an entry point to gossiping.” He loves that everyone does chai differently (he and his wife, Beena, prefer a more ginger-forward profile, while his parents like it sweeter). That’s why he became an investor and partner in the New York City-based Kolkata Chai in 2024, working with brothers Ani and Ayan Sanyal to expand the reach of a drink so engrained in their lives and culture. “It’s a welcome change to a lot of people’s only chai experience being at Starbucks in Middle America. It’s really amazing how you can change the complete perspective of an entire culture because of a drink that people can explore and make their own.”

Read on for Minhaj’s answers to our Amused Bouche questionnaire—it’s no surprise they’re chock-full of equally heartwarming and appetizing soundbites.

If you could only eat one thing 24/7/365, what would it be?

America is celebrating its 250th-year anniversary, and I think as a country, America’s greatest accomplishment is what we brought to cereal. I have been caught many a time red-handed with my full paw inside of some Golden Grahams, going to town. I will kill half a box, straight up, no milk. It is a snacking cereal. I’ll be watching a prestige drama and stress-eating Golden Grahams. Sometimes I’ll even drizzle honey over a bowl. I’ll also do the same with Honey Bunches of Oats. There’s a Montagues-and-Capulets debate here of blue box or orange box. I’m a blue box guy, because I love the almonds, extra crunch, and sweetness. It was my granola mix before I started eating granola, and it’s like trail mix without dastardly raisins coming in and f—ing shit up!

What’s the first thing you learned how to cook?

A strawberry Toaster Strudel, one of my all-time favorites. I popped it in the toaster as a kid, and it was an eye-opening experience. When I came home from elementary school, it felt like I was a master chef making myself this crisp little strudel cake and frosting it. I felt like a confectionery master. It was incredible. I toasted it on a level three and would sometimes pop it up and flip it midway through.

I actually didn’t hit my growth spurt until much later in high school, so I was quite undersized and malnourished-looking when I was younger. I was bullied a lot. My mother would make me eat three hard-boiled eggs on the way to school. And I hated hard-boiled eggs. Now that I’m a parent of small children, I understand the efficacy of hard-boiled eggs. But now I will pan-fry hard-boiled eggs, because really my hatred of them came from texture and temperature issues. But if you cut them in half and fry them yolk side down, there’s a crispness that makes it turn into a crunchy, almost taco-like topping that you can put on top of bread and butter.

It’s a really delicious, warm-and-gooey snack that I started making when I tried to give my daughter a hard-boiled egg and she immediately spit it out. I’m like, “Yeah, the cycle of torture continues! There needs to be a better way! Let me figure out a way to make this delicious.” The secret was making a quesadilla as the on-ramp she needs to get eggs in her. It was an experiment I worked backward from, kind of like writing a joke, telling a story, or working on a screenplay. My daughter loves quesadillas but hates eggs, so by making it into crunchiness that would blend right in, it wouldn’t feel like a squishy thing that I’m force-feeding her.

Growing up, we were never allowed to order dessert from restaurants. It is my greatest joy to order dessert from restaurants. I’ll tell the missus to order whatever she wants. Sometimes she’ll be indecisive. She always wants the chocolate lava cake, but she’ll be eyeing a berry tart. It’s a distant second, but I’ll take the bullet and order both for us to share. Sometimes when I do it, I’ll look over my shoulder to be like, “Are mom and dad going to find out?” But now I’m dad. We’re mom and dad!

I do not cook from cookbooks, but I will cook from YouTube Shorts. There’s just something about the looping nature of it breaking down the recipe. It’s tickling something in my mind and letting me know, “Hey, it’s not that hard. You can totally do it! You’ll get to completion, and it’s going to look pretty good.” And then as soon as doubt kicks in, the video starts playing again and snaps me out of it. It’s like the feeling of playing a song that you love over and over again, like “This Is How We Do It” by Montell Jordan. Play it again! “Men in Black”—play it again! I want to listen to it again, and that’s the feeling I get when I search “chicken tinga recipe” on YouTube Shorts.

Is there a cooking disaster that made you swear off a dish forever?

My wife does most of the cooking, but I want to put on the record that I try. I do cook, but a lot of the reaction is like, “Oh, you tried. I appreciate the effort. And that’s great for you. Why don’t you enjoy the omelet that you’ve made?” But I think I make a great soft-scramble, and what I bring to the breakfast table is pretty solid. I used to burn all of my food because I got impatient and cranked up the heat too fast. I learned you can’t bring microwave energy to a stove. Once I understood that foundational element in not burning your eggs, it was a huge unlock. Then I got to experience the full variety of eggs that aren’t charred.

Which nostalgic foods from childhood bring you the most comfort?

Dal chalwal: just lentils and rice. It has always been the first thing my mom makes for me when I get home to Sacramento, from college until now. It’s this beautiful gesture of love that I’m eating dal chawal with my mother, and her grandchildren are eating it with her at the same time. It’s pure comfort food and my love language.

When you’re playing dinner-party DJ, what’s spinning?

It’s a seasonal thing. Beena is really the entertainer and has been an incredible host since we met. For a holiday party, she’ll queue up a Pentatonix holiday playlist. Thematic, but a little left of center and unexpected.

What is your biggest entertaining flex to impress guests?

Beena loves a theme. We host Halloween on our block every year and call it Boo Bash. We go all out with a Halloween-themed live band, fog machines on the dance floor—aka the driveway—children’s face painting, bounce house, fake blood as drinks in IV bags. Her level of joy and imagination is unparalleled. She’s incredible. I add pizzazz, but I’m like, “Go off, queen!” She is the show. She’s the show creator, and I’m the showrunner.

Tell me about a meal so good you would hop on a flight to relive it.

My grandparents on both sides of my family have passed away, but I’m lucky enough that I was raised by my grandmother on my mother’s side from third to fifth grade. There’s a specific memory of when my grandmother made biryani. When the lid came off the pot and the steam and aroma of all the flavors escaped for the first time, she would put a ladle in and scoop it out for me, with meat that is so tender because it’s been cooking for so long. That’s the feeling that I would chase and book a flight immediately for, but it’s just a feeling. A feeling of love from it taking all day to make biriyani and that she loved me enough to put in that time and energy. Goat biriyani especially was a special-occasion dish, like when a cousin was getting married, and I associate it with being with family and something happy happening. In Hindi you call it ghar kha khana, the food from home. Biryani is the crème de la crème and the chef’s kiss of Indian cuisine for me. Especially my grandmother’s.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#95. Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake

In my opinion, a Basque cheesecake is the best kind of cheesecake to make. No water bath, no worrying about the top cracking, and no waiting to let the whole thing cool means that you get all of the lovely cheesecake rewards without any of the stress. It embraces all of the imperfections that can happen with cheesecake, but promises an ultra-silky interior with a crust that adds an extra caramelized flavor. This pumpkin version packs in warm spices and an extra drizzle of caramel on top, creating a stunning dessert for any fall holiday or potluck. The best part? You can make it ahead of time—basically, it’s about as stress-free as an impressive dessert like this can get.

Line your springform pan with parchment paper. Scrunch the parchment up into a ball and then straighten it back out. This helps the parchment hold its shape and stay in the pan better. Place the parchment paper overlapping in opposite directions so that all of the sides are well covered with a bit of overhang.

In the large bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the paddle attachment, beat cream cheese and sugar on medium speed until creamy and no lumps remain, about 2 minutes. Add pumpkin and beat until combined. You want to make sure you aren’t seeing any bits of cream cheese in the now orange mixture. Keep beating until everything is smooth. Make sure to scrape down the sides and bottom of the bowl as well.

Add eggs and beat until incorporated, then scrape down the bowl and add egg yolks and vanilla, beating until incorporated, 1 minute more. Add flour, pumpkin pie spice, and salt and beat on medium-low speed until just combined. Add cream and beat until incorporated, about 2 minutes. The mixture should be smooth and pretty loose at this point.

Pour the batter into the lined pan. It will be very full, and that’s okay. The parchment helps hold it in. It will puff up while baking, but should overflow.

Bake the cheesecake until the top is very dark and puffed, the edges are slightly set, and the center is still quite jiggly. This should take about 60 to 70 minutes. Then you’re ready to top with caramel and serve!

The cheesecake keeps well in the refrigerator. It can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 5 days.

#96. How This Snack Brand Gained 929k Followers by Mocking Influencers

In Person of Interest we talk to the people catching our eye right now about their projects past and present. Next up, we chat with Jay, who cofounded popcorn brand Daadi Snacks with his family but has become internet-famous for his anti-influencer videos.

There’s a standard playbook that most consumer product good (CPG) companies use when launching their company into the marketplace. They might make a few cute reels or TikToks showing the behind-the-scenes process, maybe host an in-person pop-up or two, but most importantly, they send thousands of dollars of product to influencers to help get the word out.

Jay (who prefers to keep his last name off the internet), the 30-something cofounder of Daadi Snacks, decided to burn that playbook to the ground when launching his family’s popcorn company.

Instead of sucking up to influencers, he started calling them out for their over-the-top and ridiculous antics. Parodying their annoying parlance, by opening each video with an “OHMYGODYOUGUYS” or a nasally “Come with me…” before skewering his latest victim, such as the American tourist upset that baristas in Italy refuse to mimic her Dunkin’ coffee order.

With this strategy, Daadi Snacks has amassed 929,000 followers and counting, which has turned Jay into the very thing he spends his time making fun of: an influencer. Or is he a content creator? Surprising for someone who never even had an Instagram account until 2022.

But unlike the folks he skewers, Jay likes to use his powers for good, aiming to be “the Keith Lee of New York City” and shining a light on spots that don’t tend to get attention. We called him up to speak about how his family started Daadi Snacks, the impact of his anti-influencer reels, and if it really has helped him sell any popcorn at the end of the day.

How did your family get into the snack business?

My grandma made this popcorn for our family growing up for as long as I can remember. We had floated the idea of commercializing it and turning it into an actual product, but it was more just like an idea than anything else. When COVID hit, I was working remotely, and we were just looking for ways to stay in touch with my grandparents, my mom, my uncles. I brought it up to them. “Why don't we use this time inside to actually start working on this?” My family worked on the recipe. I thought about marketing, branding, and promotion. When things started to normalize in 2021 and 2022, we spent two years iterating on what we wanted our first two flavors to be.

There's no denying that social media is an important part of growing brands, especially CPG brands. Did you think you'd need to work with influencers to get the brand out there?

I didn't get on Instagram until 2022! I never had one before then. There was one specific well-known food influencer—I've made a video about them—and I think I had a pretty terrible interaction with them. So I just thought, why don't I just start posting and stop relying on other people to shout us out? That's how I kind of landed on that.

Having lived in New York City for so long and observing the way it's changed over the last ten years, I had a longer-term vision. If I can build my own platform to market our snacks and our business, why can't I use that to try to be like the Keith Lee of New York City? Not to the extent of what he's done, but just promoting places that typically don't get promoted. Places that have been around for 30 or 40 years, whose storefront isn't super aesthetic, with Gen Z fonts. I thought that would be really cool.

You have never reached out to or responded to influencers for collabs?

Correct. I have not reached out or responded. And honestly, it's been the other way—influencers have reached out to us for samples or collabs.

When did you post your first reel skewering influencers? Was there one particular video that really launched everything?

I want to say that was around springtime last March, if my memory serves me. Before that, sales were slow but steadily growing. We were doing pop-up events to get the word out. Then in June we had hundreds and hundreds of orders come in within like two days (I don't even know the exact number), which was just crazy.

I think the inflection point was when I made a video naming who it was that influenced me to start posting videos about not liking influencer culture. When I did that and people heard the story, that's when we went from around 70,000 to over 130,000 or 140,000 followers in a week or two.

Why do you think people are so engaged and responsive to what you're doing?

In New York City it just feels like there's this need for some degree of counterculture. It's been so overwhelming in terms of the growth of these NYC-based influencers with millions of followers, just drowning in brand deals. I think people have felt the need to push back on it for a while.

You nail that restaurant influencer voice so well. Why do you think these accounts are as successful as they are, even if you punch holes in what they're doing?

I think for a lot of the NYC influencers, their content doesn't connect super well with people who actually live here—but it can connect really well with people who aspire to live here. There was this article about how this has been a very mechanical way of repurposing the whole Carrie Bradshaw thing, selling people on a manicured, aspirational idea of being a West Village girl. New York doesn't need influencers to find great food.

You've accidentally become a content creator/influencer. Do you think there's a difference between the two, or are they one and the same?

To me, an influencer’s content basically just revolves around a perpetual cycle of brand deals, which they then market to their viewers, which then propels them to get more brand deals, and so on. Honestly, I feel like because we've been on this ridiculous post-COVID run. Beauty brands have so much money, and a lot of these CPG brands have scaled so fast—it's just been unchecked. People haven't had to put in the effort.

I make it a point to never go anywhere that DMs me and asks me to review their stuff. It's crazy some of the stuff you get offered once you build any kind of following. But I've never taken PR, never taken free stuff. I'm very clear about where I stand on all that.

When do you decide to make a response video? Is it just a gut thing, like something's annoyed you enough?

I'm very opinionated, and I legitimately feel like I'm right. I pick up my phone, stop everything I'm doing, and record my 30-second video in my office chair in the same crappy apartment lighting.

#97. The 38 Best Restaurants in Rome, According to a Best-Selling Local Cookbook Author

Where to eat in Rome, including the best pizza, pasta, wine bars, and more

Roman cuisine is a reflection of the city itself — layered, deeply rooted in tradition, and full of contrasts. After years of eating my way through Rome, I’ve found the best meals are shaped as much by history as the hands that prepare them. Family-run trattorias have served the city’s defining dishes for generations: cacio e pepe, carbonara, roasted lamb, and offal-based specialties, many of which trace their origins to Rome’s historic slaughterhouse economy. While these places remain essential, a wave of neo-trattorias constantly reinterprets the classics, and the broader dining scene continues to shift too. The influence of Rome’s immigrant communities and cuisines, from Ethiopian to Venezuelan, is stronger than ever.

Rome in February and March can feel like a damp intermission which pivots quickly toward spring. One day you’re ducking into bars to escape the downpour and the next you’re scanning patios for a table in the sun. If recent years are any indication, high season now revs up well before Holy Week, and by late March the city is already moving at full tilt. This is the narrow stretch to lean into artichokes simmered with the first peas, favas, and lettuce into vignarola, Rome’s definitive spring stew. Blink and you’ll miss it.

Eating and drinking well in Rome isn’t just about knowing where to go; it’s about knowing how to navigate the city’s idiosyncratic dining culture. Travelers often book tables months in advance, making last-minute reservations tough. While online booking is becoming more common, many places still rely on the phone, and it’s best to call at the very start or very end of service, when the staff actually has time to pick up. Plan ahead — but leave some room for spontaneity too.

We update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing dining scene in Rome. Our write-ups include insider tips from our experienced writers and editors, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in euros), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

New to the map in October 2026: In San Giovanni, Beppe e I Suoi Formaggi has moved beyond its former Ghetto shop, with a larger space where Beppe Giovale’s selection of Italian and French cheeses shares the table with dishes like tajarin with alpine butter. Near the Pyramid of Gaius Cestius, third-generation family-run Taverna Cestia serves Roman classics, seafood, and wood-fired pizza alongside a thoughtful wine list. In Prati-adjacent Della Vittoria, Vetro pairs natural wines with small plates that borrow freely from Roman and wider European traditions, making it as appealing for dinner as for a drink.

Katie Parla is a Rome-based food and beverage journalist, culinary guide, and New York Times best-selling cookbook author. Her latest cookbook, Rome, is available now.

We update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing dining scene in Rome. Our write-ups include insider tips from our experienced writers and editors, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in euros), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

New to the map in October 2026: In San Giovanni, Beppe e I Suoi Formaggi has moved beyond its former Ghetto shop, with a larger space where Beppe Giovale’s selection of Italian and French cheeses shares the table with dishes like tajarin with alpine butter. Near the Pyramid of Gaius Cestius, third-generation family-run Taverna Cestia serves Roman classics, seafood, and wood-fired pizza alongside a thoughtful wine list. In Prati-adjacent Della Vittoria, Vetro pairs natural wines with small plates that borrow freely from Roman and wider European traditions, making it as appealing for dinner as for a drink.

Katie Parla is a Rome-based food and beverage journalist, culinary guide, and New York Times best-selling cookbook author. Her latest cookbook, Rome, is available now.

Vetro’s sidewalk crowd can look like the cigarette-rolling Olympics, with drinkers claiming improvised seats and lingering over glasses of wine and beer. Inside, high-tops and tables offer a more settled way to explore a menu whose ingredients often speak Roman, while its sensibility ranges across Europe. Gildas and eggs with mayonnaise join tongue with sweet potatoes and piquillo peppers, while baccalà mantecato goes by brandade and comes with marinated zucchini and isot pepper. Order a few snacks and small plates, and suddenly staying for dinner becomes an appealing proposition. Set in a former alimentari on Viale Carso, the bar pairs its neighborhood hangout atmosphere with a thoughtful natural wine selection spanning Italy, Spain, and southern France, including wines served sfuso (on tap).

Vibe check: Stay outside for the people-watching; claim a table inside to work your way through the food menu.

Colombian chef Roy Caceres is a veteran of Roman fine dining. His landmark, Michelin-starred restaurant, Metamorfosi, didn’t survive the pandemic, but his signature dishes have found a place at Orma (an anagram of Roma) just a few blocks southeast of the Galleria Borghese. Orma is home to a number of distinct concepts: The bistrot is a power-lunch spot set on a shaded terrace, the cocktail bar specializes in tropical fruit- and herb-forward drinks, and the restaurant offers tasting menus and a la carte dishes that blend Caceres’s Colombian heritage with Italian flavors and ingredients. Fans of the chef’s Uovo 65° Carbonara (a soft-cooked egg floating in Parmigiano-Reggiano foam, served with a side of puffed pasta and tender strips of guanciale) will find it in the bistrot, while the restaurant serves his renowned lacquered eel with pickled onions.

Best for: The business lunch is a great deal for anyone into fine dining but not keen to linger.

A short walk from the Trevi Fountain, this friendly trattoria has been serving satisfying dishes from Emilia-Romagna, a region in northeastern Italy, since 1931; the current owners took the helm in 1967. The menu is rich in egg-based house-made pastas like tortelli di zucca (pumpkin pasta with butter and sage) and tagliatelle alla bolognese (long strands of fresh, egg-based pasta dressed with a rich meat sauce). Save room for meaty mains including bollito misto (assorted simmered meats) and fried liver.

Must-try dishes: Tortellini in brodo and the bollito misto.

Just 100 feet from Rome’s most intact ancient monument, Armando al Pantheon champions local food traditions. For more than five decades, the Gargioli family has been dutifully producing Roman classics like fettuccine con le rigaglie di pollo (fettuccine with chicken innards) and coda alla vaccinara (oxtail braised in tomato and celery). Among the seasonal side dishes, look for puntarelle (Catalonian chicory) with anchovy sauce and carciofi alla romana (simmered artichokes) in the cooler months. Save room for the torta antica Roma, a ricotta and strawberry jam pie. The lovingly curated wine list gets better every year.

Know before you go: Book online exactly one month ahead to secure a spot — it fills up fast.

Moriondo e Gariglio is a time capsule with a cocoa perfume. Founded in Turin by cousins Agostino Moriondo and Francesco Gariglio, former chocolatiers to the Savoy royal household, the chocolate shop followed the court to Rome in the late 19th century and eventually settled on Via del Piè di Marmo, a couple of minutes from the Pantheon. Glass counters hold more than 80 chocolates and bonbons, all made by hand. In autumn, locals stock up on the shop’s cult marrons glacés, sold whole or blended into a paste, while spring brings elaborately engineered Easter eggs with surprises hidden inside. A small box is an easy souvenir. A kilo feels like joining a noble Roman ritual.

Know before you go: Chocolate production winds down in the warm months, which see the arrival of pâte de fruits in their place.

After Settimio al Pellegrino, a cult favorite featured on Anthony Bourdain’s Parts Unknown, shuttered in 2022, Leonardo Vignoli and Maria Pia Cicconi (of Cesare al Casaletto fame) resurrected the restaurant. They’ve retained the institution’s signature tiled floors, midcentury furniture, and infamous doorbell required for customers to gain access. The trattoria near Campo dei Fiori serves a succinct menu, including minestra con broccoli e arzilla (romanesco and skate soup) and former chef-owner Teresa Zazza’s legendary pan-fried meatballs.

Best for: A dinner (or weekend lunch) when you’re ready to drink from the incredibly affordable wine list.

If Roman restaurants have become known for brusque, no-nonsense service, Hosteria Grappolo d’Oro did not get the message. Affable servers circulate through the dining rooms beneath exposed wooden beams, delivering pure versions of cucina romana classics like toothsome tonnarelli cacio e pepe and tender roasted suckling lamb.

Best for: The 36 euro, four-course Roman tasting menu is one of Rome’s best deals.

Open for: All dayPrice range: $In the southwest corner of one of Rome’s most touristy squares, Forno Campo de’ Fiori bakes sweet and savory Roman specialties like jam tarts and flatbreads. Look for pizza alla pala (long slabs baked directly in a deep electric deck oven), which is sold in slices by weight; the unctuous toppings and crispy bases make a surprisingly balanced pair. An annex across the alley on Vicolo del Gallo stays open during the main bakery’s afternoon break, from 2:30 to 4:45 p.m.

Must-try dish: The pizza con mortadella is one of the best bites in town.

Culinary power couple Francesca Barreca and Marco Baccannelli reopened their landmark restaurant Mazzo after a five year hiatus, and this time around, a relatively central location in San Lorenzo makes it considerably more accessible to many residents. The dining room has also grown from a single 12-seat communal table to full-fledged restaurant seating complete with a massive porthole peering into the brightly lit kitchen. Just like the original, the new Mazzo plays with nostalgic forms in dishes like wagon wheel pasta with braised beef and onions, which joins Barreca and Baccannelli’s classics like fried tripe with grated pecorino Romano in a pool of tomato sauce, a retooling of Rome’s signature offal dish, trippa alla romana.

Must-try dishes: The fried tripe, and the wagon wheels with an oniony braised beef sauce.

The Camerucci family’s well-loved trattoria is not actually in Monti, but rather the adjacent multicultural Esquilino district near Stazione Termini. The cuisine is heavily Marchigiano — from the Italian region of Le Marche — so expect lots of game like braised rabbit and roasted duck, meat-filled fried olives, and fresh pasta like the legendary raviolo filled with a runny egg yolk and dressed with butter and sage.

Must-try dish: The runny-yolk raviolo is not to be missed.

Founded in the Historic Center in 2004 by Rome’s premier baking family, Salumeria Roscioli does triple duty as a deli, wine bar, and restaurant. Though the menu is extensive, the real stars are the cheeses (burrata with semi-dried tomatoes is spectacular), cured meats (Culaccia and mortadella with Parmigiano-Reggiano are both stellar), and pasta classics (get the gricia, cacio e pepe, amatriciana, or carbonara). If you dine at lunch or on the early side at dinner, the bread basket will include warm bread from nearby Antico Forno Roscioli. The wine list is wide-ranging, and don’t miss the distilled spirits before closing out the meal.

Vibe check: Request a table upstairs or outside to avoid getting seated in the basement.

For two centuries, Rome’s Jewish community was confined to a walled ghetto along the Tiber River. The squalid buildings are long gone, but a historic ghetto-era bakery survives on what has become the transformed neighborhood’s main thoroughfare. The pizza ebraica — a sort of fruit cake studded with nuts, raisins, and candied fruits — is an easy specialty to eat on the go, but it’s worth seeking out a bench to get messy with a slice of ricotta and sour cherry tart. Also try the amaretti and biscotti made with heaps of cinnamon and a generous smattering of whole almonds.

Must-try dish: The ricotta and sour-cherry tart — grab it before it sells out.

Via Prenestina has been a hub for Ethiopian and Eritrean community and cuisine in Rome for decades, and Mrgda, situated on this wide avenue at the edge of Pigneto, is a standout example. Partake of the free-flowing tej, a heady, honey-fermented wine that pairs perfectly with dishes like richly spiced legumes, aromatic vegetables, tender braised chicken, and deeply seasoned raw beef. Each bite is scooped up with Mrgda’s ethereal, naturally leavened injera, which has a balanced tang.

Know before you go: There is a vegan restaurant from the same owners, Mrgda Vegano, just a few blocks away.

Routinely named among the best places to drink in Europe, this long-established craft beer pub in Trastevere pours around a dozen draft beers from Italy, the U.S., Belgium, Germany, and the U.K., in addition to a small but well-curated assortment of bottles. The staff is passionate and knowledgeable, and can guide you to the right choice for your palate. It’s worth waiting for the few tables on the street outside, set up during the pandemic, which offer a front row seat to Trastevere’s lively nightlife.

Best for: Drinking vintage sour beers from Italy and beyond, 365 days a year (it’s even open on holidays).

Open for: Dinner, with lunch Wednesday to Sunday

L’Elementare has multiple locations around Rome, but the Trastevere outpost is the one that stands out service-wise. The focus is Roman pizza tonda: thin, nearly rimless, crisp and chewy at the edges. It’s baked longer than a Neapolitan pie, lending structural integrity that prevents slices from collapsing under disappointing tip sag. Start with molten supplì ar telefono, fried bricks of lasagna, and fried parcels of tonnarelli cacio e pepe.

Know before you go: There are several locations, so double check you are booking the Trastevere address, and be warned that although they post all day hours Wednesday to Sunday, the kitchen actually does close from 3:30ish to around 6:45.

Trapizzino is a small street food chain with locations throughout Italy (and an outpost in New York). The concept is based on the trapizzino, a combination of the popular triangular tramezzino sandwich with long, slowly leavened pizza dough, invented by pizzaiolo Stefano Callegari in 2008. Callegari fills his tricornered creations with Roman classics like oxtail simmered with tomato and celery, chicken cacciatore, and tripe cooked with tomato, each going for just 5 euros.

Know before you go: Visit the Trastevere branch for table service and a full bar with Lazio wines.

The cool, windowless inner sanctum at number 10 on Via del Moro in Trastevere only has a handful of tables lining two walls, and they fill up quickly with 90-minute reservation slots beginning at 6 p.m. The interior design evokes the Orient Express with wooden accents and overhead racks above the seating, and the bartenders’ wardrobe and glassware are a throwback to the last century too. The menu of bottled classic cocktails, Champagne, and non-alcoholic drinks provides an oasis of refinement in the heart of Rome’s rowdy nightlife district.

Know before you go: Reservations are essential — book online for this hidden cocktail bar experience.

Latteria Trastevere is a wine bar and bistro in Rome’s nightlife epicenter focused on natural vino, cheeses, and cured meats culled from tiny, sought-after producers across Italy. There are some hot dishes too, and Sardinian owner Antonio Cossu brings in island specialties like sa fregola (pearl couscous) with crab and bottles from Barbagia, one of Sardinia’s most delicious wine regions. As a bonus, Latteria is open nearly every day of the year.

Must-try pairing: The Sardinian prosciutto and wines from small producers from the Barbagia.

Few restaurants in Rome are as deeply tied to the city’s culinary identity as Sora Lella. Founded in 1959 by Elena Fabrizi — actor, cook, and icon — this trattoria in a medieval tower on the Tiber Island has long been a standard bearer for the hearty cucina romana. While there was a period when the restaurant seemed to coast on its reputation, the third generation has brought it back to top form. Today, Sora Lella is once again a satisfying place to experience traditional Roman dishes executed with care. The wine list leans local, highlighting Lazio’s underappreciated labels. With its rustic wood-paneled dining rooms and medieval tower setting, Sora Lella is a nostalgic but enduring pillar of Roman dining.

Must-try dish: Go in spring for the coratella d’abbacchio (sauteed sucking lamb offal) with artichokes, or try the coda alla vaccinara (oxtail stewed in a rich tomato and celery sauce).

L’Antidoto sits on a cobbled Trastevere side street, far from the crowds queuing outside tourist-packed trattorie. What started as a simple natural wine bar in 2020 has evolved into one of the most compelling dining experiences in the city with the arrival of chef Mirko Pelosi in 2024. Pelosi’s training in France, Norway, and Scotland gives him a worldly sensibility, which he puts to work aging fish, fermenting vegetables, and sourcing spices from across continents. Each dish is rooted in ingredients, driven by technique, and free from ego. The menu changes constantly, but expect dishes like mahi mahi confit, chard, tendons, and grapes. In a Roman dining landscape crowded with derivative plates and copycat concepts, Pelosi’s food is a revelation.

Know before you go: Two hungry people definitely can — and should — order everything on the menu.

A short walk from the Colosseum, Tempio di Iside is an elegant fish restaurant known for its crudi (raw dishes) like fish carpaccio, sea urchin roe, langoustines, and oysters. The pasta with sweet red shrimp, cherry tomatoes, and fresh pecorino is excellent (and proof there are valid exceptions to the “no cheese with seafood” rule), as are the spaghetti with clams, whole roasted fish, and pasta with spiny lobster. Book ahead, especially to secure an outdoor table for dinner in the summer, and expect to pay a premium for access to some of the freshest fish around.

Know before you go: Book ahead for a coveted outdoor table in summer.

Located in the sprawling Centocelle district in eastern Rome, Menabò Vino e Cucina offers a veritable tour of Italian regional comfort food. Rigatoni is served with oniony braised beef in the style of Naples, while pasta with chickpeas and mussels evoke the coastal south. Meanwhile, unctuous local classics like pasta alla gricia get punched up with fresh, seasonal twists such as grapes or figs. As the name promises, wine shares the stage with the kitchen’s creations, and the list is populated primarily by naturally and traditionally made wines.

Know before you go: The menu is always changing and the wine list is consistently outstanding.

After a career working in Roman gourmet temples like Salumeria Roscioli, Pasquale Borriello struck out on his own in 2022. His small shop in Trastevere near the church of San Francesco a Ripa has a few high-top tables where you can sip natural wine or craft beer alongside Italy’s greatest cheeses. All the big names are on the menu — Parmigiano-Reggiano, gorgonzola, and mozzarella di bufala among them — but Borriello favors the smallest and most artisanal producers of these famous styles. In addition to formaggio, Forme sells cured meats, sandwiches, and pantry items like jars of obscure marinated vegetables.

Best for: Sit at a high-top table and try blue cheese from celebrated affineur Andrea Magi.

Marco Radicioni trained with Rome’s gelato maestro Claudio Torcè, embracing his sensibility of all-natural flavors, meticulous sourcing, and restrained sweetness. Since launching his own gelateria, Radicioni has grown into a maestro in his own right, churning some of the most exquisite gelato in Italy. His newest location in Monteverde Vecchio serves more than just Otaleg’s rich and creamy gelato made from the world’s best pistachios and chocolates. There are specialty coffee and artisanal pastries, too, which have transformed Otaleg into a point of reference for third-wave coffee drinkers.

Know before you go: Try the Monteverde location for gelato and coffee; Trastevere for pure gelato bliss.

A few minutes from the Circo Massimo, Pizzarium alum and Bonci protégé Alessandro Ruver runs a tiny laboratorio where pizza in teglia gets the kind of focus usually reserved for restaurant menus. The daily lineup of trays features long-fermented dough that bakes up light, crisp, and audibly crunchy. Pizzas get named with a sense of humor, and topped with ingredients from small farms in central Italy. The Ragùver is loaded with slow-cooked meat sauce and Parmigiano-Reggiano, reminiscent of Sunday sauce.

Know before you go: Like most Roman slice joints, you eat standing at a few outdoor high tops, so don’t wear yourself out too much wandering the nearby Colosseum and Forum before stopping by.

Santo Palato is chef Sarah Cicolini’s neotrattoria in Rome’s Appio Latino district, a residential area just beyond the city walls near San Giovanni in Laterano. When it first opened in 2017, the trattoria quickly became a pilgrimage spot for those craving a bold, updated take on Roman cooking. The new, larger location, which opened in the spring, stays true to that original spirit, serving deeply satisfying dishes like tender trippa, an ethereal chicken gizzard frittata, and the yolkiest carbonara around. With a bigger kitchen, Cicolini now has the space to turn out fresh pasta and a wider range of braised, grilled, and smoked meats. Diners can watch it all unfold through large windows that separate the kitchen from the dining room, bringing the action right into view.

Know before you go: The communal table near the entrance is available for walk-ins. Book well in advance if you’d rather sit anywhere else.

After nearly two decades in Rome’s historic Ghetto, cheesemaker Beppe Giovale closed his original shop at the end of 2025 and resurfaced in San Giovanni with a brighter, roomier version. The Via Gallia location still revolves around a refrigerated counter filled with more than 100 mostly raw-milk cheeses, including selections from Giovale’s family dairy in Piedmont and small producers throughout Italy and France. But there is now a real kitchen and around 20 seats, allowing the menu to venture beyond cheese and butter tastings into dishes like tajarin with alpine butter and tongue with bell peppers and salsa verde. For shopping only, Giovale maintains a small stall at boxes 227 and 228 in the Mercato Trionfale; the Ghetto location has closed.

Must-try dishes: A selection of cheeses made by Beppe and his family, accompanied by the smoked salted butter.

Located in Testaccio, Rome’s undisputed offal capital, Piatto Romano focuses on classics like rigatoni con la pajata (pasta with milk-fed veal intestines cooked in tomato sauce) and fettuccine con le rigaglie di pollo (fettuccine with chicken innards). There are plenty of pescatarian options as well, like the outstanding cod baked with onions, pine nuts, apricots, and prunes, and pan-fried anchovies spiked with vinegar and chile pepper, and the vegetable dishes are incredible.

Must-try dishes: Vegetable sides like the braised zucchini greens and foraged greens salad are showstoppers.

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and some Friday evenings

The Testaccio neighborhood market is the best place in central Rome to shop for seasonal produce, meat, fish, and baked goods all in one place. Get there in the morning to see it in full swing (it’s open Monday through Saturday until 2 p.m. and occasional evenings). Visit Da Artenio (Box 90) for takeaway pizza slices and pizzette, little pizzas topped with tomato sauce, potatoes, or onions. Don’t miss the essential Mordi e Vai (Box 15), where the Esposito family prepares sandwiches filled with offal and meat based on generations-old recipes, including disappearing historic dishes like alesso di scottona (simmered brisket). Nearby Da Corrado (Box 18) sells natural wines, artisan cheeses, and a handful of hot dishes — including incredible soups — while Casa Manco (Box 22) serves naturally leavened pizza by weight and Sicché (Box 37) specializes in Tuscany-inspired soups, sandwiches, and salads.

Must-try shops: Hit Mordi e Vai for offal sandwiches and Da Corrado for cheese, soup, and wine.

Founded in 1967 by Amatrice native Gioacchino Salvi, Taverna Cestia sits across from the ancient pyramidal tomb of Gaius Cestius that gives the restaurant its name. Now run by third-generation restaurateur and sommelier Valerio Salvi, the trattoria covers a lot of ground without losing focus. Roman staples like tonnarelli cacio e pepe and grilled abbacchio share the menu with locally caught seafood, seasonal vegetables, and thin, crisp Roman pizzas from the wood-fired oven. The sprawling dining room and outdoor tables attract families and large groups, while the unusually thoughtful wine list favors small producers and natural wines.

Must-try dishes: This very Roman trattoria serves a very Neapolitan dessert: babà. The rum-soaked pastry can be cloying and sodden elsewhere; here, it’s spectacular, with just the right balance of booze, sweetness, and airy crumb.

The sign teetering on the roof might read “Cafè Du Parc” in the most appealing mid-century font ever, but this kiosk at the nexus of the Aventino, Ostiense, and Testaccio districts now has new ownership and a new name, Mostro. It opens early for specialty coffee, cruises through the afternoon with restrained momentum, then pivots into low key drinking with draft cocktails and natural wines that attract locals who aren’t phased by the flurry of trams and buses that careen over the adjacent cobblestones. The vibe stays casual and the soundtrack vacillates between staff playlists and vinyl on the turntables by the bar.

Know before you go: This is largely an outdoor stop, so dress for the weather, and aim for earlier hours if you want a calmer moment with your drink before the aperitivo crowd clocks in.

Following careers in fine dining in Italy and abroad, Leonardo Vignoli and Maria Pia Cicconi went back to basics with Cesare al Casaletto, a straightforward trattoria the husband-and-wife duo took over in 2009. The menu features Roman classics with a few restrained twists, like fried gnocchi served on a pool of cacio e pepe sauce. The pasta alla gricia has achieved cult status, the suckling lamb mains are exceptional, and the beverage list spotlights stunningly affordable natural wines from Italy, France, and Slovenia.

If you take public transit: Take tram 8 for easy access, and stroll back to the center through Villa Pamphili park after lunch.

Pizzaiolo Sami El Sabawy first made a name in the Roman pizza world at the iconic slice joint Pizzarium (also on this list). But it’s the thin crust, wood-fired personal pizzas he makes today that attract diners to Torpignattara in eastern Rome. Named after the Roman phrase meaning “to do something continuously,” A Rota lives up to its name; once you try the impeccably crisp pizza and golden fritti, like supplì and battered squash blossoms, you’ll keep coming back for more. El Sabawy specializes in a hyper-thin, low-hydration dough that he rolls out with a pin before baking at a lower temperature for longer than its Neapolitan counterpart. The result is a shatteringly crisp base, sturdy enough to support both classic and creative toppings without losing its integrity. The traditional margherita is a lesson in balance, with bright tomato sauce, fior di latte, and fragrant basil, but don’t skip Sami’s specials, like April’s stuffed pizza filled with chard, potato, Parmigiano-Reggiano, and ham.

Must-try dish: Try the classic margherita to understand Sami’s style, then go for the seasonal special.

Located a short distance from Stazione Trastevere, C’è Pasta… e Pasta (translation: “There’s pasta… and pasta”) serves delicious kosher meals to eat in or take away. Order at the counter and don’t miss Roman Jewish classics like carciofi alla giudia (fried artichokes), filetti di baccala (battered fried cod), aliciotti con l’indivia (layered anchovy and frisee casserole), and concia (fried and marinated zucchini). As the name promises, they also serve pasta dishes and sell fresh pasta to cook at home.

Must-try dishes: The Roman Jewish concia and baccala are particularly special.

Bruno Persiani, an Umbrian transplant to the Italian capital, opened this homey trattoria in southern Trastevere in 1968 to serve a mix of dishes from Umbria and Rome. Tavernaccia is now run by Persiani’s daughters and Sardinian son-in-law, who throws in a few of his own regional specialties like suckling pig cooked in the wood-fired oven. The fresh pastas are excellent (especially Sunday’s lasagna, which sells out fast), and the wood oven-roasted brisket is otherworldly. Organic and natural wines from Italy and Slovenia round out the wine list. The service is patient and unbelievably kind — far from the norm in the Italian capital, so don’t get used to it.

Must-try dishes: Order whatever was made in the wood fired oven that day, whether it’s brisket, lasagna, or eggplant parm.

Nearly a decade in, Trattoria Pennestri is still one of Rome’s smartest answers to the question “where do I eat Roman food near the center but away from the tourists?” The room is relaxed and the cooking is grounded in the classics, but the kitchen knows exactly when a twist is worth making, like rigatoni con la pajata brightened with a measured hit of collatura (anchovy elixir) that elevates the sweetly lactic, milk-filled calf intestines with a savory note. The accessibly-priced wine list leans heavily toward small producers, with a strong showing from Lazio and central Italy.

Know before you go: Book ahead, especially on weekends, and ask the staff to steer you through the wine list.

Stecca is the Roman debut of Abruzzese chef Franco Franciosi of Mammaròssa in Avezzano, in partnership with Flavio De Maio of Rome’s Flavio al Velavevodetto. In a low-lit Garbatella space fitted with austere, Nordic-inspired design, the two turn the dining room into a kind of multisensory stage where Abruzzo’s mountain flavors meet Roman cooking. The menu shifts constantly and leans comforting: rigatoni with meat roll sauce; perfectly roasted lamb chops with puntarelle; a creamy soup of chickpeas, chestnuts, and dried figs. It’s all paired with excellent naturally leavened bread and a serious central Italy-leaning wine list

Know before you go: There are a handful of bar seats, ideal for solo diners.

After nearly 30 years at the helm of Rome’s first Thai restaurant, Beijing-born chef Ge Jing Hua opened Sinosteria in 2020 to serve a blend of Chinese regional cuisines featuring dishes like Beijing-style tripe with chile oil and cilantro, and Shandong-inspired squid with peppers, ginger, and bamboo. There are also signature creations like basmati rice with coconut milk, shrimp, capers, and oregano from Pantelleria. The front of house is expertly managed by Ge’s gregarious sommelier son Jun, whose natural wine list and coffee menu are outstanding.

Must-try pairing: Ask Jun to recommend a natural wine or tea.

Trecca is, for lack of a better term, a neo-trattoria. It delivers everything a Roman trattoria should: an informal setting, rigorously seasonal comfort food, and an offal-forward menu. But there’s also a natural wine list, an Instagram page, and two young brothers at the helm. Manuel and Nicolò Trecastelli lean into Rome’s powerful flavors and rich ingredients. Their carbonara and amatriciana are as loaded with pepper-spiked guanciale as any in the city, and tomato and vinegar are employed in the meaty mains to offset their unctuousness.

Must-try dish: Try the pajata in any and every way the restaurant serves it.

At Da Michele, two generations of the Pignotta family have perfected an incredibly high-level wine and seafood experience, presented without pretense. Since opening in the residential San Paolo district in 1991, this spot has become a neighborhood institution, drawing back regulars with its consistently fresh catch from local fish markets in Fiumicino and Anzio, and attracting wine connoisseurs from across the city eager to taste through the exceptional cellar. Pair mineral-driven white wines from across Europe — including older vintages — with al dente linguine with telline (wedge clams) and fried or roasted fish.

Must-try pairing: Pair linguine with telline or roasted fish with older vintage white Burgundy from the cellar.

Pizza Nader in the Roma 70 neighborhood — an area in the southern part of town once home to emperor Nerva’s grain reserves — is worth the detour. This unassuming shop might look like your standard Roman pizza al taglio joint, but step inside and you’ll find a level of care and precision that sets it apart. Sacks of stone milled flour from Le Marche, Campania, and Sicily crowd the entrance, where I ate a delightful supplì on a visit last month while waiting for a slice of pizza adorned with pecorino, black pepper, and guanciale. Owner Nader Abdelkader praises the dedication of the farmers and millers that make the flour for his deeply flavored pizzas and the dozen types of naturally leavened pane that he bakes.

Must-try dish: Don’t miss the legendary kebab, a favorite of regulars.

#98. 16 pumpkin recipes, from cakes and cookies to bars and bread: We've got a marbled pumpkin cake, chewy pumpkin cookies, and even pumpkin milk bread.

It’s that time of year when pumpkin spice everything starts appearing on store shelves — candles, lip balm, air fresheners, beer, and of course, the ubiquitous PSL (pumpkin spice latte). That means fall is here, and more importantly, that pumpkin should make a grand return to your kitchen! Pull out your canned pumpkin — or better yet, make your own pumpkin purée — and stock your pantry with pumpkin pie spice, because we have the best pumpkin recipes to bake this fall.

This Pumpkin Swirl Cake takes my breath away every time I unmold it from its intricate loaf pan. The anticipation keeps building until I slice into the pound cake-like loaf and reveal the swirled pattern inside, marbled with both vanilla and spiced pumpkin batter. (Don’t fret if you don’t have the specialty loaf pan — this can also be baked in a standard loaf pan and adorned with a simple confectioners’ sugar icing.)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Patch O Pumpkins Loaf Pan and Pure Vanilla Plus

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Sparkling Sugar

A cousin of Belgian-style Liège waffles, these Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles have caramelized edges and a pleasant chew that’s reminiscent of brioche. The yeasted batter has pumpkin in it for flavor and color, plus Swedish pearl sugar that melts into pockets of crispy sugar. The best part? The batter rests overnight, so if you prepare it the night ahead, all you have to do the next morning is scoop and cook the batter for hot, crispy waffles in just a few minutes.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles

To make this recipe, you'll need: Swedish Pearl Sugar

I used to make the same pumpkin pie recipe for years, and it always left me wanting a little more excitement. Then I found this Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie and never looked back! The generously spiced filling uses nutmeg, ginger, cloves, and Vietnamese cinnamon to create a more flavorful pie than traditional versions. The secret to its silky-smooth texture? Corn syrup, which is an invert sugar and keeps the custard from becoming grainy. Substitute another invert sugar like honey or maple syrup if you like; I use maple syrup.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon, Ginger, and Nutmeg

Whenever I have these tender, golden scones on hand, I look forward to getting out of bed the next morning because I know they’re waiting for me. They can be easily customized to use a range of mix-ins, depending on what you have in your pantry. My personal preference is a mix of crystallized ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits.

Get the recipe: Harvest Pumpkin Scones (or Gluten-Free Pumpkin Scones)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Mini Diced Ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits

If you’re looking for a way to make your whole kitchen smell like fall, these one-bowl, easy pumpkin muffins deliver — and fast. They’re ready in under an hour, so you can spend less time measuring, mixing, and cleaning and more time tackling your autumn bucket list.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Standard Muffin Pan

Making banana bread is an almost weekly activity in my house — except during fall, when we pivot to pumpkin bread instead. This is a quick, easy bake that satisfies my craving for something pumpkin-y, and it uses a simple trick to concentrate the pumpkin flavor and ensure the loaf is perfectly textured: The pumpkin purée is reduced on the stovetop to cook off excess moisture. (The process is similar to browning butter.) As a result, the final loaf is packed with pumpkin flavor.

Get the recipe: The Most Pumpkin Pumpkin Chocolate Chip Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: Ginger and Semisweet Chocolate Chips

These bars have all the cozy, spiced goodness of the classic dessert in a portable, crowd-friendly form. The buttery, brown sugar crust gets pressed into the pan (no rolling out pie dough!), and the silky pumpkin filling comes together with just a handful of ingredients. The (optional but highly recommended) sour cream whipped topping brings a slight tanginess and completes the traditional pumpkin pie experience.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Milk Bread is exceptionally soft, squishy, and feather-light, while also packing in a lot of pumpkin. Pumpkin can often weigh down baked goods, but here the combination of a tangzhong, bread flour, and a long mix makes this bread simultaneously moist and high-rising.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant Yeast

This tender pumpkin crumb cake is for people who double the chocolate chips in pumpkin bread and the streusel on coffee cake. Atop the thin layer of spiced pumpkin cake lays a heavy blanket of buttery crumbs with a bold chocolate flavor, thanks to Dutch-processed cocoa powder.

Get the recipe: Chocolate-Pumpkin Crumb Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Black Cocoa

These Pumpkin Cupcakes, with their piped swirl of cream cheese frosting, are the ideal way to celebrate fall birthdays. The cupcakes are super tender, thanks to the addition of cake flour and oil. Sour cream and brown sugar add tanginess and molasses-y sweetness while also preventing the cupcakes from being dry.

For more cupcake decorating ideas, see our YouTube video: Decorate Cupcakes Better Than Ever.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cake Flour (or Gluten-Free Measure for Measure Flour)

My husband’s favorite fall dessert is Pumpkin Whoopie Pies, hands down. He can’t resist these subtly sweet cakes sandwiching rich cream cheese filling. This recipe has a few extra bells and whistles to take it over the top: Bread and Cake Enhancer to keep the cakes extra soft and fresh, xanthan gum in the filling to give it a smooth mouthfeel, and diced crystallized ginger for a bit of extra zing in the filling.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Bread and Cake Enhancer, Xanthan Gum, and Mini Diced Ginger

The next time there’s a rainy weekend, I’m taking on a project bake: our Pumpkin Cream Cheese Danish. It’s a multiday process and laminating dough is a labor of love, but the final product is worth the effort: buttery, crisp pastries filled with pumpkin and sweet cream cheese.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cream Cheese Danish

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting is a show-stopping dessert featuring spiced layers of cake, not-too-sweet cream cheese frosting, and a blanket of melted caramel poured over the top. Will it be slightly messy to serve? Yes. Will anyone mind? Absolutely not.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Offset Spatula

The pumpkin spice recipe I’m most excited to bake this fall is a mash-up of greats: Part-coffee cake, part-Bundt cake, part-pumpkin bread, this Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake deserves a category all of its own. It has two layers of espresso swirl tucked within a moist, spiced cake. Make it in your favorite Bundt pan or serve it as a loaf if you’re more of simple-is-better person. Either way, it’s great for snacking all day long.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Espresso Powder and Bundt Pan

For more recipes that are ideal to bake as the seasons change, see our collection of Fall Favorites.

It is an error that needs correcting that in the near-20 years of plugging recipes into this url, only a few truly star cucumbers — and highly unrepresentative too, given that we are probably eating some format of cucumbers at half the nights of the week with dinner, and snacking on them throughout all of the other days. #100. Frico'ed Brussels Sprouts

A slick of oil and a sprinkling of salt are the only adornments brussels sprouts need to shine. But put a crispy Parmesan skirt on them and suddenly the humble veggie becomes the belle of the ball. This recipe does just that. By roasting the brussels sprouts snuggled into a blanket of grated Parmesan cheese, the cheese melts into a crispy, frico-like sheet that clings onto the sprouts, surrounding them in a lace-like halo. It’s a dramatic side dish, but one that makes a serious statement. If roasted correctly, and the stars align in your favor, you can peel off the entire sheet in one swift swoop, presenting it as the culinary masterpiece it is. Fans of fun, this is for you.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a baking sheet with a nonstick baking mat or a sheet of parchment paper generously coated with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a medium bowl to combine. Scatter 4 oz. store-bought grated Parmesan (pre-grated works better here than grating from a block) in an even layer over baking sheet, leaving a ½" border around edges. Arrange brussels sprouts, cut side down, in a single layer on top, spacing evenly to fill baking sheet. Bake until brussels sprouts are tender and browned and cheese is deep golden, 20–28 minutes. (If the cheese in the very center is browned, it’s done.) Let cool at least 5 minutes, then break into pieces to serve. (Or place another parchment-lined baking sheet upside down on top; holding together, swiftly turn over, peel away mat, and present cheese side up.)

#101. 12 Dishes and Drinks Everyone Should Try in Mexico City

Mexico City is a colossal, beautifully overwhelming metropolis and an absolute paradise for those who live to eat. Across thousands of restaurants, markets, street stalls, bakeries and fondas, food from every corner of the country converges. So deciding where (and what) to eat can feel daunting.

I’ve spent over a decade writing about Mexico’s food scene, along with popping up on TV shows to talk about it occasionally. My favorite way to navigate it all is still right here on the ground with my food tours. Sidestepping the obvious spots and encouraging travelers to go deeper into the food culture here constantly reminds me of the fascinating nature of how we chilangos eat.

To me, that means having the flexibility to move between completely different culinary worlds. We can spend lunchtime standing on a crowded sidewalk, leaning over a taco drenched in salsa and lime juice, then dress up that same evening for a multicourse dinner at a dimly lit restaurant. We’re fiercely loyal to the neighborhood places that have fed us for years and know our names, but we remain insatiably curious about the next opening or dish worth crossing town for.

That same flexibility shapes the city’s food. CDMX knows exactly how to pull tradition into modernity without losing its spirit. These 12 spots offer a taste of the city’s versatility: dishes and bites deeply rooted in history but shaped by the wonderfully chaotic, ever-evolving way we eat today.

Adolfo Prieto 1364 B, Tlacoquemecatl del Valle, Benito Juárez +52 55 5559 6358

I remember being dragged out of bed early on a weekend as a teenager to have breakfast here. Although I was still drowsy, the smell of the wood-fired stoves, the café de olla (traditional “pot coffee”) bubbling away, and sounds of the older musicians playing classic tunes on their guitars were enough to bring me around. I was fully awake by the time a plate of refried beans with scrambled eggs and a stack of warm tortillas made it to the table. It’s the kind of humble combination you’d find in almost any Mexican home. At Fonda Margarita, these eggs, which are cooked over a wood fire and enriched with lard, take on a different life. Getting here early is a requirement, as they open around 6:30 a.m. and by 10 a.m., all the food is gone.

C. Chilpancingo 35, Colonia Condesa, +52 55 5264 4976

Few breakfast menus are complete without chilaquiles. What started as a way to use up day-old tortillas is now one of the country’s quintessential breakfasts: triangles of tortillas, deep-fried until crisp, then bathed in salsa. At Chilpa in leafy Condesa, several salsas are available, from a red, tomato-based version to the bright, tangy tomatillo number, all with different spice levels. Pile on your choice of cecina, shredded chicken, or fried eggs. Crema, grated cheese, and chopped onion are standard, making it easy to order a different version every visit.

If you asked my Mexican grandma what breakfast looks like, she’d say coffee and a pan dulce—more often than not that would mean a concha. The quintessential Mexican pastry makes an appearance in virtually every bakery in town, from the most traditional versions made with a combination of lard and shortening to the tender butter-forward renditions found in most modern bakeries. At Panadería Gala, a speakeasy-style bakery, the extra-bouncy conchas get an extra layer of indulgence when topped with a white or dark chocolate ganache quenelle.

The Margarita may be known worldwide as the quintessential Mexican cocktail. Legend has it that the iconic drink was first conceived in Ensenada, Baja California, and its ties to coast and borderlands are still strong. But chilangos tend to save it for specific occasions and places such as a beach vacation, a favorite cantina, or a particular restaurant where we know they’ll make a killer one. At Despacho Margarita, the classic shaken version gets a new life, alongside spicy and frozen variations. In the slushy machine there are usually two flavors: a classic tequila and lime version and a seasonal mezcal-based one that changes monthly, with unique flavors such as nopal and shiso or raspberry and cayenne pepper.

Cantinas have long been places to gather over good food and several rounds of drinks. In these laid-back establishments, both are given equal importance. At Covadonga, a cantina without background music, generations mix at the tables, from the young and cool to sixty-somethings who come to play dominoes (available on request).

Banderas have been a popular order here from the beginning: three shot glasses lined up, one with tequila, another with lime juice, and a third with sangrita, a red-hued blend of tomato and fruit juices. Together they mimic the three colors of the Mexican flag (hence the name). They’re not meant to be knocked back but rather sipped slowly, alternating between glasses.

There’s a certain type of stand you’ll see repeatedly throughout the city centered around a large, round comal, usually fired with charcoal, with a bucket of corn masa and, more often than not, two women working side by side. Gorditas, quesadillas, and sopes are all on the menu, but the tlacoyo may be the most emblematic of central Mexico and Mexico City.

Football-shaped and stuffed with your choice of fava bean purée, requesón (a soft cheese similar to ricotta), or refried beans, tlacoyos are typically topped with cactus salad for a tangy contrast, grated queso fresco, and red or green salsa, depending on your preference. They're the kind of morning or afternoon snack you might grab during errands or before wandering into the adjacent market.

Petén 248 y, Avenida Universidad, Narvarte Poniente, Benito Juárez+52 55 5536 3060

The idea of stacking meat on a rotating spit was brought to Puebla by Lebanese immigrants. Once it reached Mexico City, it evolved into one of the city’s great late-night bites: the taco al pastor. At El Vilsito, a garage by day that moonlights as one of the city’s best taquerías, they take the pastor one step further, turning it into the most Chilango version possible by making it into a torta. A warm, lightly toasted telera gets a smear of refried beans, avocado, onion, tomato, and freshly shaved pastor, all finished with melted cheese.

Calle Versalles 113, Casa Versalles, Juárez+52 55 8568 7397

You can’t talk about Mexico City without talking about its obsession with seafood. It may seem strange for a city far from the coast, but seafood from both of Mexico’s coastlines makes its way here through the second-largest seafood market in the world (surpassed only by Tokyo’s Toyosu) before being distributed across the rest of the country.

At Taller de Ostiones, clams, barnacles, and tuna arrive three times a week by air from Baja California Sur, alongside sustainably farmed oysters. Those bivalves pair perfectly with a house-made sauce that’s rich, briny, deeply umami, and slightly spicy.

Mexico City runs on fondas and street food. These casual eateries serve homestyle food that’s quick, affordable, and feels like a warm hug. Stepping inside a fonda means being a part of a daily ritual known as comida corrida, where a meal typically unfolds in four acts: a steaming bowl of soup or broth to start, followed by your choice of rice or pasta. Next comes the main course, which at some places, like Nuevo Tehuacán, is what dictates the price of the meal; meatballs in chipotle, pork with tomatillo and purslane, and chicken in peanut sauce are classics. Everything is washed down with a pitcher of freshly made agua fresca and finished with a sweet treat like a cup of gelatin. Look around, and you’ll see schoolchildren sitting elbow to elbow with office workers all savoring the comfort of one of the city’s most democratic meals.

Mostly homemade, flan is a staple of casual Mexican cooking, but it’s one of those desserts that look deceptively simple. Getting the texture just right (silky, firm, not overly sweet) is way harder than it seems, which may be why the best versions are often found in homes. Siembra may be a temple dedicated to heirloom corn masa, tacos, and antojitos, but its flan has all the right qualifications to receive just as much attention.

Fernando Montes de Oca 89, Cuauhtémoc, Colonia Condesa+52 55 5286 1258

Ice cream parlors used to be an almost daily afternoon ritual for families and couples alike. Nevería Roxy was one of the early ones, and its 1950s-diner palate of teal and red has barely changed, even in the newer locations. Alongside the classic milk- and cream-based flavors, sundaes, floats, and banana splits, you’ll find nieves.

The word literally translates to “snow,” and the closest comparison might be a sorbet, though the texture tends to be a little coarser and the flavors typically center around seasonal fruits. Mamey, an endemic fruit, may have a short season, but Roxy keeps its nieve de mamey year-round. With a faintly nutty flavor reminiscent of baked sweet potato, it’s become a local favorite. And thanks to mamey’s lush, natural creaminess, it’s easy to forget there’s no dairy in the cup.

Avenida 5 de Mayo 39, Centro Histórico de la Ciudad+52 55 5521 1787

Stepping into Dulcería de Celaya feels more like entering a 19th-century jewelry store than a candy shop. Founded in 1874, this Centro Histórico institution still retains its original art nouveau interior, complete with French mirrors, tiled floors, and hand-carved oak cabinets, all filled with traditional sweets made in-house. Among the colorful sweet treats are candied lime skins stuffed with shredded sweetened coconut. The peel is candied and tender and, unlike fresh lime rind, is not bitter, so you can go ahead and bite into the whole thing at once.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

Seek out tlacoyos, chilaquiles, and nieves in this culinary capital.

Petén 248 y, Avenida Universidad, Narvarte Poniente, Benito Juárez+52 55 5536 3060

The idea of stacking meat on a rotating spit was brought to Puebla by Lebanese immigrants. Once it reached Mexico City, it evolved into one of the city’s great late-night bites: the taco al pastor. At El Vilsito, a garage by day that moonlights as one of the city’s best taquerías, they take the pastor one step further, turning it into the most Chilango version possible by making it into a torta. A warm, lightly toasted telera gets a smear of refried beans, avocado, onion, tomato, and freshly shaved pastor, all finished with melted cheese.

Calle Versalles 113, Casa Versalles, Juárez+52 55 8568 7397

You can’t talk about Mexico City without talking about its obsession with seafood. It may seem strange for a city far from the coast, but seafood from both of Mexico’s coastlines makes its way here through the second-largest seafood market in the world (surpassed only by Tokyo’s Toyosu) before being distributed across the rest of the country.

At Taller de Ostiones, clams, barnacles, and tuna arrive three times a week by air from Baja California Sur, alongside sustainably farmed oysters. Those bivalves pair perfectly with a house-made sauce that’s rich, briny, deeply umami, and slightly spicy.

Mexico City runs on fondas and street food. These casual eateries serve homestyle food that’s quick, affordable, and feels like a warm hug. Stepping inside a fonda means being a part of a daily ritual known as comida corrida, where a meal typically unfolds in four acts: a steaming bowl of soup or broth to start, followed by your choice of rice or pasta. Next comes the main course, which at some places, like Nuevo Tehuacán, is what dictates the price of the meal; meatballs in chipotle, pork with tomatillo and purslane, and chicken in peanut sauce are classics. Everything is washed down with a pitcher of freshly made agua fresca and finished with a sweet treat like a cup of gelatin. Look around, and you’ll see schoolchildren sitting elbow to elbow with office workers all savoring the comfort of one of the city’s most democratic meals.

Mostly homemade, flan is a staple of casual Mexican cooking, but it’s one of those desserts that look deceptively simple. Getting the texture just right (silky, firm, not overly sweet) is way harder than it seems, which may be why the best versions are often found in homes. Siembra may be a temple dedicated to heirloom corn masa, tacos, and antojitos, but its flan has all the right qualifications to receive just as much attention.

Fernando Montes de Oca 89, Cuauhtémoc, Colonia Condesa+52 55 5286 1258

Ice cream parlors used to be an almost daily afternoon ritual for families and couples alike. Nevería Roxy was one of the early ones, and its 1950s-diner palate of teal and red has barely changed, even in the newer locations. Alongside the classic milk- and cream-based flavors, sundaes, floats, and banana splits, you’ll find nieves.

The word literally translates to “snow,” and the closest comparison might be a sorbet, though the texture tends to be a little coarser and the flavors typically center around seasonal fruits. Mamey, an endemic fruit, may have a short season, but Roxy keeps its nieve de mamey year-round. With a faintly nutty flavor reminiscent of baked sweet potato, it’s become a local favorite. And thanks to mamey’s lush, natural creaminess, it’s easy to forget there’s no dairy in the cup.

Avenida 5 de Mayo 39, Centro Histórico de la Ciudad+52 55 5521 1787

Stepping into Dulcería de Celaya feels more like entering a 19th-century jewelry store than a candy shop. Founded in 1874, this Centro Histórico institution still retains its original art nouveau interior, complete with French mirrors, tiled floors, and hand-carved oak cabinets, all filled with traditional sweets made in-house. Among the colorful sweet treats are candied lime skins stuffed with shredded sweetened coconut. The peel is candied and tender and, unlike fresh lime rind, is not bitter, so you can go ahead and bite into the whole thing at once.

#102. The Creamy Jarred Sauce That Turns Pasta & Ground Beef Into A Classic Greek Comfort Food

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Every country has its signature comfort foods. In the U.S., we have our mac and cheese and crispy fried chicken, of course. Mexico has its birria and sopa, and Italy has ragù and a plethora of pasta dishes that will warm the soul. But there's one classic Greek dish that you may have never even heard of that is creamy, cheesy, and full of warmly spiced beefy flavor. It's called pastitsio, and at the risk of oversimplification, you can think of it as a sort of Greek lasagna or, maybe more correctly, a Greek mastaccioli of sorts because it features smaller pieces of pasta rather than layered sheets.

Pastitsio typically uses an ultra-smooth béchamel sauce as the final poured-over topping that will get nice and creamy and crispy with grated cheese and pasta. However, you can skip the hassle of making your own béchamel and use a jarred Alfredo or white sauce in its place — think Bertolli or Classico. Creating your homemade pastitsio is pretty simple. All you have to do is layer a casserole pan with cooked pasta, top it with cinnamon-spiced meat sauce, pour over your store-bought Alfredo, then a little Kefalotyri cheese (or Romano or parmesan if you really can't find any Greek cheese), and bake it until nice and golden brown. It's a wonderfully crispy, creamy, beefy bite with every forkful, and there are some special tips you can follow to get more spice and flavor.

Ideally, you'll be using authentic Greek pastitsio noodles for the recipe, but if you don't have a grocery store that carries a lot of Greek imports nearby, penne or ziti will work. You want something in a tubular shape that won't fall apart in the bake to give your pastitsio its signature layered look. As for your jarred white sauce, some store-bought Alfredos are better than others, but with all of the flavor you'll be adding, as long as it's creamy and relatively tasty, it should work just fine. For the sauce, you can use a jarred meat sauce as your base, but it needs to be thick enough to create a solid layer. To that end, you'll want to add more ground beef, some shredded carrots, diced onions, garlic, and maybe celery, but this is the point where you can spread your wings to personalize your pastitsio and pack it with herbs and spices. As long as cinnamon is the highlight, you can get creative.

If you want to really experiment with spices, you can think of the flavor of a good pastitsio as similar to a spiced British mince pie. Warming spices like ground cinnamon, nutmeg, and clove are common, and you can add them into the Alfredo sauce (just like a béchamel) to get a nice spread over the top, rather than sauteing them with the meat. A bit of oregano, thyme, and marjoram go great with the meat sauce, with maybe a splash or two of red or white wine. And if you want to up the salty, umami flavor, try a tablespoon or two of miso paste. Just like most casseroles, a pastitsio can start with the basics and build the flavor from there. It may contain quite a few ingredients, but it's no sweat if you already have everything in the pantry or fridge.
