#104. We Can't Stop Eating These Sour Candy-Coated Dates (And You'll Love Them Too)

Nature’s candy just got the Sour Patch treatment.

Delish editors love all things food, but we have a soft spot for sour candy. We’ve been known to sneak pieces from the decorative jars in our test kitchen. News and Features Editor Amanda Mactas has an overflowing communal candy bowl on her desk for afternoon treats. And we’re always on the lookout for the next great sour snack.

So when I discovered a new tangy treat from Joolies, I knew our office had to try it.

The California-based date brand recently unveiled its newest product line: Date Sours. Organic pitted dates get the sour-candy treatment with a tart coating. (If you’re already a fan of Fruit Riot from the freezer aisle, this combo will sound fairly familiar.) They’re currently available in four flavors: Watermelon, Blue Raspberry, Peachy, and Cherry Cola.

Our team of sour candy fanatics tasted all four. Here’s our verdict.

The ingredient list is brief. Beyond the dates themselves, Date Sours contain cornstarch, natural flavors, and a mix of citric and malic acids, which provide that signature pucker. There’s no added sugar, and each serving contains three grams of fiber.

The scent of each candy-inspired flavor hits as soon as you open the bag. Visually, though, they still look mostly like plain dates. The cornstarch helps the sour coating cling to the fruit, but because dates are naturally moist, we found that some of the crystals had fallen off and collected at the bottom of nearly every bag. An evenly coated date was more the exception than the rule, but it didn’t bother us much.

The flavors still came through. Each coating had a nostalgic familiarity that reminded us of classic sour candy, although the intensity varied. Watermelon was the overwhelming favorite, being bright, fruity, and probably the sourest of the bunch. Blue Raspberry and Peachy also went over well, reminding our editors of Jolly Ranchers and peach rings, respectively.

Cherry Cola proved more polarizing. In my opinion, the vanilla and warm spice notes of cola paired perfectly with the complex sweetness of the dates. Some editors, though, thought the sourness was too subtle. Still, no matter the flavor, people kept coming back for more. I even brought the leftovers home for friends to try, and the only word I could use to describe their reaction was “ravenous.”

Are Joolies Date Sours a 1:1 substitute for actual sour candy? No, and they’re not trying to be. But if you already enjoy dates and if you love sour candy as much as our editors, these are an absolute must-try.

#106. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#108. The History of This Must-Try Cheese Goes Back Nearly 1,000 Years

An authentic wheel of Grana Padano carries a signature brand burned into its rind—so you know that if you see a diamond pattern and the cheese’s name, it must have been produced in the Valle Padana (Po River Valley) of Northern Italy according to strict rules with roots in a 12th-century Cistercian monastery. At the time, the region surrounding the city of Milan was primarily soggy marshland. The monks who built the monastery—Chiaravalle Abbey—were followers of the Rule of Saint Benedict, which, along with devotion to prayer, mandated that they practice agriculture with a focus on responsible, sustainable use of land. They first figured out how to turn the marshy landscape into arable fields so they could grow high-quality feed for dairy cattle. Since milk (and fresh cheese) didn’t last long, the next challenge for the monks was how to preserve this nutritious, valuable food source to nourish themselves and their community.

The method they developed—heating the milk in copper cauldrons, adding rennet (a coagulating enzyme), cutting the curds into tiny pieces, and molding, salting, and aging the cheese—remains largely unchanged today. By producing the first iteration of what is now known around the world as Grana Padano, the monks of Chiaravalle Abbey earned the distinction of operating the world’s first cheese dairy.

Easy to like, portable, and a good source of protein, the cheese became an emblematic food, enjoyed by Italians at all levels of society through the Renaissance and into the modern era. Its iconic name, meanwhile, developed over time. The monks called it “caseus vetus”—Latin for “old cheese”—but since the peasants didn’t know Latin, they referred to it as “grana” for its distinctive grainy texture. As production spread well beyond the monastery, each province had its own grana: Cheese made in Milan was “grana Milanese,” and “grana Mantovano” was from Mantua.

It wasn’t until 1954 that the Italian government codified the name Grana Padano to unite the different varieties of grana cheese under a single wider geographical indication and that the Grana Padano Protection Consortium was established. In 1996, Grana Padano was awarded the European Union’s Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) designation. Today the consortium incorporates 134 member dairies, who together produced over 6 million wheels of cheese in 2025. In addition to safeguarding the name, the organization is also responsible for the global promotion of Grana Padano PDO and governs every detail of production to ensure that each wheel meets the strict standards established under the PDO.

The specifications start with the cows’ diet: All fresh forage and at least 75 percent of dry fodder (such as hay) must be grown within the cheese production area. Raw milk must be collected within 24 hours of milking and be partially skimmed, allowing for natural separation of the cream. After a natural whey starter is introduced to the copper (or copper-lined) milk vat, calves’ rennet is added for coagulation. The cheese is then broken into rice-size curds using a spino, which resembles a large whisk, and packed into round molds, where it sits for at least 36 hours. The wheels are immersed in brine for anywhere from 14 days to a month and aged for at least nine months and up to 24 months or longer. Wheels aged over 20 months can be labeled Riserva.

Bite into a chunk of Grana Padano PDO, and you taste the sweetness of fresh milk coupled with a savory hint of toasted nuts. Riservas may be flakier and more crystalline in texture than younger versions of the cheese but never dry or crumbly, and they must still have a delicate flavor. Grana Padano PDO is an exceptionally versatile cheese, equally delicious on a cheese board, wrapped with a slice of Prosciutto di Parma PDO and drizzled with aged balsamic for a sophisticated appetizer, as a filling for ravioli, or grated over soup or pasta.

It’s good for you, too. Lactose- and gluten-free, Grana Padano PDO is low in fat and an excellent source of protein, calcium, and vitamin B12. A 30-gram piece (just over one ounce) has as much nutrition as a pint of milk, making it a beneficial as well as tasty solution to the “afternoon slump” for both kids and adults. Whoever you share Grana Padano PDO with, be sure to tell them what they have in common with Italians from more than 1,000 years ago—that they’re savoring a taste of European culinary history.

Head to DistinctlyDeliciouslyEuropean.eu to learn more about Prosciutto di Parma PDO and Grana Padano PDO.

#109. London Broil Isn't A Cut Of Beef

With some beef dishes, it can be tricky to tell a cut apart from its application. Although you might see beef pot roast on a grocery label, the name refers to a simple slow cooker meal (one that only needs three ingredients). And despite the abundant prime rib recipes, the term is technically tied to a specific cut. Another frequent mismatch? London broil.

The name doesn't apply to specific beef cuts, but rather a preparation technique. While you might spot the term London Broil on raw beef labels, the phrase instead refers to transforming a lean cut of steak using a marinade. Spotted on menus as early as 1919, it's a long-running preparation method with storied American (not English) origins.

The essence of London Broil lies in elevating a cheap cut that's typically tough via a marinade to make it tasty when medium-rare. Most often, the cooking technique is employed with flank steak, although beef cuts like top round, sirloin, and chuck shoulder can also be London Broiled. The size of beef varies, ranging from a thin breakfast steak to a beefy 4-inch-thick slab of meat. Dependably, though, the cut spends time in a marinade and is then grilled or pan-seared into a delicious steak experience.

The concept of London Broil is simple: flavorful marinade meets a tough cut of beef. Subsequently, the interpretations of such a template are wide-ranging. The marinade alone can vary drastically, in turn creating many London Broil flavors. Dependably, though, this liquid must contain salt and acid, which function as the agents for tenderization. Many types of citrus and vinegar are poured onto the beef, but specifically lemon juice, balsamic vinegar, and apple cider vinegar show up frequently.

Complementary aromatics come in more varied choices, with options including fresh garlic and ginger, dried seasonings like paprika and oregano, as well as honey or sugar for sweetness. Worcestershire sauce — which happens to be lightly acidic –- is often included for both texture enhancement and flavor. Plus, a dash of soy sauce often lends a salty-umami component to a London Broil marinade. Oil (typically olive oil) rounds out the recipe, adding more moisture to the mix. Beef is stored in the resultant marinade for around three hours per inch of thickness; marination takes up the majority of a London Broil's assembly duration.

To cook, the meat is typically grilled, which is considered the best way to cook a London Broil, but can be pan-fried, too. Hit with high heat, the beef develops aesthetic sear marks, despite the marinade. And the meat is traditionally cooked to a still-pink medium-rare or medium. Following some resting time, London Broil is sliced thin and enjoyed, producing a beefy yet tender dining experience.

#110. Toasted Meringue Hazelnut Blondies

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Lightly coat a 9x9" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line pan with parchment paper, leaving overhang on two sides. Toast 2 cups blanched hazelnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown and fragrant, 15–18 minutes. Let sit until cool enough to handle, then coarsely chop; set aside.

Cook 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring often, until butter foams, then browns (do not burn), 7–9 minutes. Remove from heat.

Whisk 2 large eggs, room temperature, 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) light brown sugar, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¾ tsp. instant espresso powder (if using) in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium-high speed until mixture is pale and doubled in volume, 6–9 minutes (mixture will form an unbroken ribbon when whisk is lifted from bowl).

Reduce speed to low and with motor running, gradually pour in brown butter in a thin, continuous stream; beat until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Remove bowl from mixer and gently fold in 1½ cups (187 g) all-purpose flour with a rubber spatula, scraping down sides and bottom of bowl, until no large, dry streaks of flour remain. Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. Top with reserved hazelnuts and press in gently to adhere (surface will be smothered with nuts).

Bake blondie until edges are golden brown and center is just set, 35–45 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let blondie cool in pan. Using parchment paper to help, lift blondie out of pan and transfer to rack.

Meanwhile, combine 3 large egg whites and 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar in the clean bowl of stand mixer and set over a saucepan of just simmering water (make sure bottom of bowl does not touch water). Heat, whisking constantly, until sugar is dissolved and an instant-read thermometer registers 170°.

Fit bowl onto mixer fitted with clean whisk attachment. Beat egg white mixture until thick and glossy and mixture is barely lukewarm, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt; fold in with a rubber spatula just to combine. Taste meringue and season with more kosher salt if needed

Peel away parchment paper from blondie and transfer to a heatproof platter. Using an offset spatula, spread meringue evenly over blondie, covering from edge to edge. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue until deep golden brown. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Using a long knife and wiping off with a damp kitchen towel between cuts, slice blondie into 9 squares.

Do Ahead: Blondie can be baked 24 hours ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#111. Slow-Cooker Birria Tacos

Recipe by Ericka Sanchez, La Habra, California

Nothing tops slow-cooker birria tacos. This comfort food is cheesy, crispy, crunchy and dunked into a warm bowl of rich, umami-packed consommé.

If you’re new to the concept of birria, allow me to introduce you to the Mexican gift that is quesabirria, or cheesy birria tacos. Half taco, half quesadilla and 100% delicious, they’re the kind of midnight snack or after-work meal that will quickly earn repeat status in your recipe repertoire.

The only problem? Making traditional birria can be quite labor-intensive because the beef needs to simmer for hours on end. That’s where this slow-cooker version comes in. If you don’t have the time or patience for the traditional hours-long process, this recipe delivers all that comforting goodness in a fraction of the time.

With a few store-bought spices, a handful of fresh ingredients, and about 30 minutes of prep time, you’ll have the best-ever birria ready to dominate taco night. The only decision left is whether you’ll serve them with cervezas or margaritas.

In a large bowl, combine the chiles and hot water, and let them stand for 30 minutes.

Editor’s Tip: Rehydrating the peppers breathes new life into the dried chiles. You’ll know they’re ready when they’ve softened and plumped up.

Add the chiles and the soaking liquid to a blender, along with half an onion, the tomatoes, garlic, bouillon granules, peppercorns, thyme, oregano and cumin. Puree the mixture until smooth, then strain it through a fine-mesh sieve to eliminate any chunky pieces.

Editor’s Tip: You’re going for a silky consommé, not a chunky salsa, so the sieve is important. But if you don’t have one, a regular mesh strainer will also work. Just use the back of a spoon to press as much of the sauce through as possible. No sauce spared on our watch!

In a large skillet, heat the oil over medium-high heat, then add the chuck roast. Sear it until a nice golden brown crust has formed, about two to three minutes per side.

Editor’s Tip: Searing is the handy step that turns making birria beef from an all-day affair into a slow-cooker cinch—without sacrificing flavor.

Transfer the roast to the slow cooker. Add the bay leaves and remaining onion half. Add the strained sauce, and stir to combine. Cook the beef, covered, on low until it’s tender, five to six hours.

Editor’s Tip: You’ll know your beef is ready when your kitchen smells like a taqueria and the chuck pulls apart easily with a fork.

Remove and discard the onion pieces and bay leaves. Transfer the meat to a cutting board. Shred it with two forks before returning it to the slow cooker.

Working one at a time, dip a tortilla into the cooking liquid, coating it thoroughly. Place the tortilla onto a griddle, comal or cast-iron skillet over medium heat. Sprinkle it with cheese if desired, and cook it until the cheese melts. Top it with beef, and fold the tortilla over to form a taco. Serve tacos with your desired toppings and a side of the cooking liquid.

Editor’s Tip: For authentic texture, cook the folded tortilla until crisp and golden on both sides.

Store the birria beef filling in an airtight container in the fridge for up to four days. You can store the beef in the consommé cooking liquid, but keep it separate from the tortillas and toppings.

If you’re prepping birria tacos the day before a party or game, make the slow-cooked beef as directed and return the shredded beef to the cooking liquid. Keep it in the fridge until about an hour before you’re ready to fry up the tacos. Reheat the filling in the slow cooker until it reaches 165°F, or reheat it in the microwave or on the stovetop. Keep the tortillas in a sealed bag so they don’t go stale, and prep any toppings and herbs in individual containers so you can set up your taco bar at the very last minute.

You can freeze slow-cooked birria beef for up to three months. Transfer the beef and some of the consommé to a freezer-safe container and seal it tightly. Be sure to label it; a frozen pint of taco meat can look an awful lot like Bolognese or chili.

We wouldn’t recommend freezing fully assembled, cooked tacos, which can turn soggy and lose their signature crispness. Your best bet is to keep the beef and cooking liquid separate from the tortillas, cheese and toppings, then assemble and sear your tacos when you’re ready for round two.

We like to make slow-cooker birria with boneless chuck roast. It produces plenty of flavor-packed fat for the cooking liquid, and saves you the hassle of removing the meat from the bones. Plus, it becomes fork-tender after a few hours in the slow cooker.

That said, you can absolutely use a bone-in chuck roast or beef short ribs. The only cuts we wouldn’t suggest are especially lean ones like sirloin or tenderloin. They can dry out during the low-and-slow cooking process.

For 3 to 4 pounds of meat, plan on roughly six to eight hours on the low setting on your slow cooker. It may be ready closer to the six-hour mark since you’ll be quartering the chuck roast first. Either way, we highly recommend giving your meat the ol’ fork test toward the end to see how it’s doing. Once the beef pulls apart easily, you’re good to go. Slow-cooker birria tacos will save you a ton of time, but the last thing you want to do is overcook your meat and dry it out.

Most people are strictly divided when it comes to flour or corn tortillas for tacos, but in the case of birria tacos, you really want to lean into corn. They’re the traditional choice, and they crisp up beautifully once dipped in the rich, chile-stained fat from the m. Flour tortillas don’t have the same texture—and trust us, that crispy exterior is the whole point.

#113. Air Fryer Pumpkin Donut Holes

If you’re ready to jump into fall baking, but your kitchen is still running at 80°, these air fryer pumpkin donut holes are the perfect treat. Baked in tiny silicone liners and rolled in cinnamon sugar, these poppable, bite-sized donut holes promise to leave you with sticky fingertips and an extra dose of fall vibes. Baking in an air fryer is like baking in a tiny high-powered convection oven—so while it’s similar to regular baking, there are a few things to be aware of.

Every air fryer bakes differently:Every oven also bakes differently, but due to the smaller size and high convection power of an air fryer, the differences are often more pronounced. In testing these donut holes, I found that timings could vary a lot, depending on which brand and model of air fryer I was using. “Hot spots” can vary too. Because of this, I often test cooking a smaller batch or even just a single sample of something, just to see how the air fryer behaves before I try making a full-sized batch.

Drop the temperature by 25°:Because the extra air power creates additional heat and browning, a good rule of thumb is to set the air fryer 25° lower than you would a conventional oven. This ensures that the baked goods don’t brown too heavily on the outside before the inside is baked.

Decrease the time by 25%:Even with the decreased temperatures, air fryers tend to bake faster than a conventional oven. Specifics will vary by recipe, but in general, you can expect to decrease the time by about 25%.

Make ahead & storage:These donut holes are best on the day they’re made, but if you have leftovers, they can be stored in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. The cinnamon sugar mixture will dissolve and sort of melt into the donuts over time, but they’ll still taste great.

#114. Baltimore Yat Gaw Mein

Yat gaw mein, also known as Baltimore yak or dirty yak, is Baltimore carryout comfort food at its finest. A Chinese American remix of Beijing’s zha jiang mian, the dish dates back to the late 19th century, when Chinese immigrants started settling in the city. Setting up shop in traditionally Black and working-class neighborhoods, Chinese cooks adapted their recipes to locally available ingredients, swapping fermented pastes for a simpler, soy-based gravy. Over time, something new emerged: savory wheat noodles, stir-fried with shrimp, beef, and vegetables and punctuated with a hard-boiled egg. Today you can find the beloved dish at counter spots around town like Jimmy’s Carryout, Danny’s, and Pimlico Chinese Carry Out.

In this at-home version from Steve Chu, the chef behind Baltimore’s Ekiben, smoky wok-charred noodles are tossed with umami-packed soy sauce and oyster sauce, rich fat, and sweet caramelized onions. What makes the dish “dirty” is the flavor that develops when soy sauce, sugar, and aromatics scorch against the hot metal of the wok, creating deep savory notes balanced by subtle sweetness. Be sure to keep the wok on high heat and stir frequently, since this allows the wok hei—which translates to “the breath of a wok” and refers to that elusive smokiness—to work its magic. The finishing squeeze of ketchup might sound unusual, but it delivers the acidic punch that makes the dish complete.

#115. The Difference Between The McDonald's Quarter Pounder And Double Cheeseburger

With more than 44,000 locations worldwide, McDonald's has truly dominated the fast food game, largely thanks to its instantly recognizable, iconic menu. When the McDonald brothers first opened their restaurant in San Bernardino, California, in 1940, it was actually a barbecue drive-in with a sprawling 25-item menu. It wasn't until 1948 that they stripped things back to a handful of simple items, most of which weren't unique to the chain — think hamburgers, cheeseburgers, and, a year later, its world-famous fries. Today, thanks to its many franchisees and innovation within the company itself, the menu features a whole host of unique items, many of which you'll find on offer all over the world. Two of its most famous offerings are the Quarter Pounder and the Double Cheeseburger, both of which have been on the menu for decades, but what exactly sets these two heavy hitters apart?

At first glance, not much. A quick look at their respective ingredient lists reveals the two burgers share most of the same building blocks: beef patties, a bun, American cheese, pickles, onions, ketchup, and mustard. But dig a little deeper, and the differences start to show. Sure, the Double Cheeseburger packs two patties to the Quarter Pounder's one, but the Quarter Pounder makes up for it with the very patty it's named after. Beyond being heavier, however, it sets itself apart from the rest of McDonald's burger lineup in other ways, too — both nutritionally and in the quality and preparation of its ingredients.

While many of McDonald's most iconic menu items, including the Filet-O-Fish or the Quarter Pounder, were the brainchild of franchisees, the Double Cheeseburger was introduced by the company itself in the 1950s, becoming a permanent menu item in 1965. But the story really begins with the original Cheeseburger, which McDonald's founders Richard and Maurice McDonald added to the menu back in 1948.

The most obvious difference separating the Double Cheeseburger from the Quarter Pounder is its two patties. Interestingly, however, McDonald's nutritional figures list around 25 grams of protein for the Double Cheeseburger, compared with 30 grams for the Quarter Pounder. Despite having just one patty, the Quarter Pounder uses a famously heavier beef patty, which helps it creep ahead in the protein rankings.

A closer look at the ingredients also reveals a few more differences. The Double Cheeseburger comes on a regular bun, while the Quarter Pounder uses a slightly different sesame seed bun. Additionally, the Double Cheeseburger uses rehydrated diced onions, whereas the Quarter Pounder features fresh, slivered onions. That distinction became particularly significant in 2024, when fresh, slivered onions served on McDonald's Quarter Pounders were identified as the likely source of a widespread E. coli outbreak in the U.S. This led McDonald's to temporarily remove Quarter Pounders from restaurants in affected areas while the investigation was underway. The chain's diced onions — which are dried and then rehydrated — weren't implicated, so the Double Cheeseburger wasn't affected by the same recall.

The Quarter Pounder was invented in 1971 by Al Bernardin, a McDonald's franchisee in Fremont, California, who wanted a burger that would appeal to customers craving a higher meat-to-bun ratio than your standard cheeseburger. It rolled out nationally in 1973, but one thing that might surprise customers is that the fresh, never frozen beef the Quarter Pounder is now famous for didn't arrive until 2018. The move was likely nudged along by rivals like Wendy's, which had long built its brand on fresh beef and even took a Super Bowl swipe at McDonald's flash-frozen patties, and, of course, by customers looking for higher-quality fast food meals.

The patty is what puts this burger in a league of its own. It's a substantial 4.25 ounces before cooking, though the name comes from the original quarter-pound patty, which was bumped up in 2015. While most McDonald's burgers use frozen patties, the Quarter Pounder uses fresh beef, cooked to order. Every McDonald's patty is cooked on a clamshell grill that clamps shut to apply heat from the top and bottom plates at once, but the Quarter Pounder still stands out. A regular frozen patty takes around 42 seconds to cook, while a Quarter Pounder's cooking time nearly triples that at roughly 112 seconds (via McDonald's).

Unlike the Double Cheeseburger, whose only real variation is the regular old Cheeseburger, the Quarter Pounder comes in several styles. There's the Quarter Pounder with Cheese, the original, plus the Double Quarter Pounder with Cheese, the Bacon Quarter Pounder, and the Quarter Pounder Deluxe, an elevated version that adds beefy Roma tomatoes, crispy shredded lettuce, and creamy mayonnaise.

#116. 5 Quick Dishes Our Editors Make With Marinated Artichokes

Each month in Well Stocked, our staff shares unfussy recipe ideas that you can call upon any day of the week. Because yes, our editors love to cook, but sometimes we need to get dinner on the table 12 minutes ago. That’s when we look to pantry and fridge staples that can quickly morph into delicious meals. This month, it’s all about marinated artichokes.

Oh, the artichoke: an aloof green globe, made up of scale-like leaves and a fuzzy interior. But the flavor? So vegetal, so buttery. As a member of the thistle family, the raw vegetable takes a fair amount of trimming and coaxing (including removing the spiky part aptly known as the choke) before it’s good to go. And after you’ve wrestled it into submission, there’s not a ton to show for all that effort.

Which is part of the appeal of marinated artichokes—the kind you get in a jar. Tender, tangy, and genuinely ready to eat, they’re a shortcut worth taking, adding a bright hit of acidity and a satisfying meaty texture to all kinds of dishes. Toss them into a pantry-friendly pasta with speckles of salty pancetta. Mix them into a no-cook antipasto salad. Even nestle them into an unhinged sandwich. Read on for five smart ways our editors put them to work.

A last-minute galette happens to be my specialty, and marinated artichokes are the perfect addition. You could make this full recipe, which involves a simple cream cheese filling, those ’chokes, and asparagus, plus a vinaigrette-dressed arugula topping. But you could also just toss the artichokes with whatever other veg you have in the fridge and a couple spoonfuls of marinade, maybe some grated parm if you have it, into a rolled out puff pastry crust. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor

My team knows my love for a good potato salad, as I sing its virtues all the time. Marinated artichokes are a killer ingredient to add to a French- or German-style potato salad that’s heavy on the vinaigrette: Add chopped marinated artichokes and their brine to just-cooked potatoes, which will hungrily drink up the juice. Standard marinated artichokes are fine; grilled marinated artichokes (like the jarred ones at Trader Joe’s) are even better. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor

It’s saved my butt many times: antipasto pantry pasta. (Antipantry pasta? Hm. No.) I raid my cupboard for salty-savory-oily things like olives, capers, roasted peppers, sun-dried tomatoes, chickpeas, and, of course, marinated artichokes. Mix everything in a bowl while the pasta boils. Throw in some mozzarella if there’s any around. Takes 15 minutes tops and always hits the spot. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

My fanciest 20-minute dinner involves a couple of sheet-pan fish fillets surrounded by frilly burnished artichoke hearts. I’ll simply brush some of the marinating juices over salmon or whatever flaky white fish my seafood share provided that week, then save the rest for a finishing drizzle. The drained artichokes go right on the same pan. Then it goes into the oven for about 15 minutes and dinner’s ready. For what it’s worth, those crispy ’chokes are also great for a vegetarian Italian-style deli sandwich. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking

My bakery days taught me many things, chief among them that ricotta deserves a little fluffing. I loosely follow this recipe and whip it until smooth, then pile it onto pan-fried toast with sizzled artichokes and capers (two dependable ingredients always stationed in my pantry). I like to top the toasts with an herb salad: usually basil and dill dressed in the brine from the artichoke jar. Let no drop go to waste. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

#118. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

#119. Spiced Beef Baked Potatoes

Baked potatoes may not seem like a dish that requires much technique, but there’s a difference between a good baked potato and a great one. Wrapping them in foil can lead to a tender interior but render the skin too soft. For the most crisp skin, bake them right on the oven grate at quite a high temperature. (To make it taste almost like a potato chip, rub those scrubbed russets with vegetable oil and season with plenty of salt.) Shockingly, this doesn’t prevent a fluffy interior—that comes down to the internal temperature reaching at least 212°. Sure, it may seem strange to take your potato’s temperature, but it’s a fail-safe route to the most enjoyable potato.

Some, including the Idaho Potato Commission, swear that the way a baked potato is opened affects the texture, eschewing a knife for a fork to gently poke a plus sign into the surface. Others, like beloved food writer Nigel Slater, prefer to strike the potato as though it were part of a martial arts competition. “Bring your hand down fast and sharp as if you were doing a karate chop but only hard enough to crack open the potato skin,” he writes in a piece for The Guardian. (Whether or not to attempt this feat is literally in the hands of the potato-baker.) We found a single fork-pricked line down the length of the spud is the most effective.

Once opened, a baked potato can be filled with anything from tuna salad to cheesy baked beans. Here, it’s a picadillo-inspired mixture with ground beef (packed with protein, iron, and creatine—though ground turkey or chicken work nicely too) adorned with golden raisins and stuffed olives. A spicy tomato sauce will slowly soak into the potato, further seasoning it with every passing minute. Make sure to use a chili powder that’s a mix of spices like chiles, cumin, oregano, garlic (not just dried ground chiles).

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. Read more: White Potatoes Are Not Empty Calories. They’re Actually Great for You.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Prick 4 large russet potatoes (about 10 oz. each), scrubbed, patted dry, all over with a fork, then rub all over with 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil and sprinkle with 1¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Bake directly on oven rack until skins are crisp and flesh is very soft (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 212°–220°), 55–75 minutes. (If thermometer registers 210° before beef mixture is finished, turn off oven and leave potatoes inside until ready to use.)

Meanwhile, pick enough leaves from ½ bunch cilantro (about 2 oz.) to measure ½ cup; set aside for serving. Finely chop remaining leaves and all of stems (you should have about ¾ cup); set aside separately.

Heat remaining 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium. Add 1 medium red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is softened, 8–10 minutes. Add ¼ cup double-concentrated tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until deepened in color and slightly tacky, about 2 minutes.

Increase heat to medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground beef, 2 Tbsp. chili powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, stirring and smashing often with a heatproof rubber spatula to break up meat, until cooked through, about 4 minutes.

Reduce heat to low. Add ½ cup golden raisins, ¼ cup sliced pimiento-stuffed green olives, reserved chopped cilantro, and 1 cup water. Cook, stirring occasionally, until sauce thickens slightly and flavors come together, 8–12 minutes. Taste beef mixture and season with more salt if needed. Remove from heat and cover. Let sit until ready to use.

Transfer potatoes to a platter or plates and let cool 5 minutes. Using a fork, prick a 3"–4"-long line in the center down length of each potato, leaving 1" unpricked on each end. Using your hands, firmly press ends down toward platter to split potatoes open. Smash flesh as desired, then season inside of potatoes with salt. Divide beef mixture among potatoes and top with reserved cilantro leaves.

#120. Baked Potatoes on the Grill

Making baked potatoes on the grill means fluffy, tender spuds with buttery skins—all without turning on the oven.

When you already have your grill fired up for steaks or chicken, there’s no need to turn on the oven for a baked potato side. These grilled baked potatoes take just a few minutes to prep, and turn out fluffy and tender inside with buttery skins. Once they’re on the grill, you’re free to focus on the rest of the meal. Serve this grilled side dish with classic toppings like sour cream and chives, or set out a few options and let everyone build their perfect potato.

Making baked potatoes on the grill is just as easy as cooking them in the oven. Scrub and pierce the potatoes, then brush them with melted butter, season with salt and pepper (or any other seasoning you like), and wrap them in foil. Place the foil-wrapped potatoes over indirect medium heat, cover the grill and cook the potatoes until they’re tender.

Set up the grill for indirect cooking. For a gas grill, preheat the burners on one side to medium and leave the other side off. For a charcoal grill, arrange the coals on one side, leaving the other side empty. Close the lid and let the grill preheat to about 350°F.

Scrub the potatoes well and pierce each one several times with a fork or sharp paring knife. Place each potato on a 12-inch square of heavy-duty foil. Brush them with melted butter, then season them with salt and pepper. Fold the foil around the potatoes and seal the packets tightly.

Editor’s Tip: A pastry brush makes it easy to coat each potato evenly, but you can also use your fingers to rub the butter over the skin.

Place the foil-wrapped potatoes over indirect heat, away from the burners or coals. Cover the grill and cook the potatoes for 45 to 50 minutes, or until the potatoes are tender when pierced with a fork. Carefully open the foil packets to allow the steam to escape.

Let the potatoes cool, then remove them from the foil and transfer them to an airtight container. Refrigerate them for up to four days.

Reheat individual potatoes in the microwave or warm them in a 350° oven until they’re heated through. For crispier skin, reheat them in an air fryer or directly on the grill.

Yes! To freeze baked potatoes off the grill, unwrap the potatoes and let them cool completely, then rewrap them tightly in foil or storage wrap and place them in a freezer-safe bag or container. Freeze them for up to three months.

When you’re ready to enjoy the potatoes, thaw them overnight in the refrigerator, then reheat them in a 350° oven until they’re heated through. For crispier skin, finish them on the grill or in an air fryer for a few minutes.

Russet potatoes are your best bet for grilled baked potatoes. We like large Russets because they make a hearty side and hold up well on the grill. Their high starch content gives you that classic fluffy baked-potato center. Try to choose potatoes that are about the same size so they cook at roughly the same rate.

Baked potatoes take about 45 minutes on the grill. Larger potatoes may need a little extra time, while smaller ones can cook more quickly. Start checking at the 45-minute mark by piercing a potato with a fork; it should slide easily into the center when the potato is done.

Whether you choose the oven or grill, baked potatoes take about the same amount of time to cook. Potatoes on the grill take about 45 to 50 minutes, while oven-baked potatoes may take up to an hour. So there’s not much difference in cooking time. The grill does have one big advantage in warm weather, though: You can make baked potatoes outside without heating up the kitchen.

The topping possibilities for grilled baked potatoes are endless! Keep it classic with butter, sour cream, shredded cheddar, bacon and chives, or turn them into a substantial meal by topping them with chili, pulled pork, broccoli and cheese, or sauteed veggies. For a Tex-Mex twist, try your favorite salsa, sliced avocado or guacamole, and green onions. You can also set out a variety of toppings and let everyone build their own loaded baked potato.

#121. Lay’s Turned Thanksgiving Dinner Into Chips—And Somehow, They Actually Work

Turkey and scalloped potatoes just landed in the snack aisle.

Lay’s is betting big on America’s biggest food holiday this year. Just in time for Thanksgiving, the company is releasing new limited-edition flavors inspired by two of the dinner table’s biggest stars: turkey and potatoes.

Beginning in late October, fans can pick up Lay’s Cheddar Scalloped-Style Potatoes and Lay’s Roasted Holiday Turkey. And before you clutch your pearls over the more ambitious of those flavors, hear me out. They’re pretty damn good.

The Cheddar Scalloped-Style Potatoes chips aren’t a huge leap for Lay’s considering we’re starting with potatoes anyway. These go hard on the cheddar, while a sprinkling of parsley helps bring them surprisingly close to the dish they’re trying to emulate. They deliver that creamy, comforting flavor without being nearly as indulgent as actual scalloped potatoes. I’d call these a win.

The Roasted Holiday Turkey chips, however, had me a little uneasy. That disappeared after the first crunch. To me, they taste more like stuffing and gravy than an actual bite of turkey, but in this case, I’m not mad about it. Thyme, onion powder, and pepper come through strongest, reminding me of the sides that usually share the plate with the bird.

And Lay’s isn’t stopping there. On November 8, the brand is bringing Canadian favorite Maple Bacon to the U.S. for the first time. In fact, it’s shaping up to be a very Lay-tastic holiday season, as in late November, it’s embracing its sweeter side with Lay’s Wavy Milk Chocolate and Wavy Dubai-Style Dark Chocolate. As a sucker for chocolate and potato chips, I can’t wait to get my hands on these.

#122. Forget Regular Butter And Mayo: Spread This Rich Ingredient On Bread For Crispier Grilled Cheese

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Probably up there with boxed mac and cheese or an easy cold cut sandwich, grilled cheese is likely one of those first meals many American kids first learned to make by themselves. But, at least since I was a kid, the grilled cheese game has gotten a little more serious. You probably know you can go beyond butter and try some mayo on your grilled cheese (both inside and out), and there are certainly more cheese choices than just the plastic-wrapped American slices. But maybe it's time to step it up another level entirely and try spreading some ghee on your bread for a beautifully crispy toasted experience.

If you're unfamiliar, ghee is similar to clarified butter but is basically cooked longer with the milk solids as the butter breaks down. With clarified butter, on the other hand, the proteins are strained off just as they separate. Allowing them to cook longer in ghee imparts more flavor, a deep satisfying nuttiness. Plus, because the solids and water are removed, ghee ends up as pretty much pure fat, just like processed cooking oils. So, not only is it shelf stable, but it means you can use it at a much higher temperature than butter or mayo and add a whole lot more taste than your standard cooking oil. The stuff can be a little pricy, like Spring Sunrise's Grass Fed Organic, but you can even make ghee at home.

Regular butter is usually about 80% to 82% fat, around 16% water, 1.5% salt, and 1% milk solids. Because of the milk solids and high water content, butter has a lower smoke point and can burn your food easily, especially in a frying pan. With butter, you can get up to about 350 degrees Fahrenheit, but ghee can go all the way up to around 465 degrees Fahrenheit, so you can leave your grilled cheese in the pan longer to get the cheese sufficiently melted.

Ghee will help you get an ideally-browned and crunchy exterior because it melts more evenly under high heat, where butter or mayo could burn immediately in spots, if not evenly spread. While it's perfectly delicious with a couple classic slices of American cheese, its caramel-tinged flavor lends itself well to Comté and Gruyère that melt wonderfully and share some nutty undertones that ghee is loved for. From there, there are a number of tips for making a killer grilled cheese. Try some simple deli-sliced ham or go all the way with a classic Reuben.

And, while grilled cheese isn't typically the realm of the lactose-intolerant, because ghee has the milk solids removed, it's a lactose-free food. Maybe try it with a low-lactose aged cheddar or pecorino. And most cheeses made out of sheep or goat milk generally have much less lactose, so it might be worth giving them a shot. But, whatever goes inside, to get a perfectly-toasted grilled cheese on the outside, it's probably a good call to spread on the ghee.

#123. 5 Cookbooks That Go Deep on a Single Ingredient

If you’ve ever been starstruck by a perfect Cinderella pumpkin or a stately stalk of Brussels sprouts, you likely understand the appeal of a book focused on a single fruit or vegetable. While books like this aren’t always long, they typically go deep, with the fervor of an author who is fully obsessed.

One charming example, The Core of an Onion: Peeling the Rarest Common Food by Mark Kurlansky, melds authority with a dose of irreverence. First published in 2023, it’s a slim 200 pages, but the writer (who’s also written nonfiction books dedicated to oysters, salt, and cod) packs a lot in. “Onions have a way of taking on unexpected significance,” he posits. The first section covers the allium’s history and cultural impact. (Did you know that ancient Egyptians tied them to mummies’ feet as a preservative?) Kurlansky then offers loosely structured recipes for breads, sauces, and more, all centering the humble bulb.

Elevating a perhaps overlooked ingredient is a core tenet of single-­subject cookbookery. In The Compleat Squash: A Passionate Grower’s Guide to Pumpkins, Squash, and Gourds, a canonical 2004 ode to members of the Cucurbitaceae ­family, master ­gardener Amy Goldman Fowler’s passion is abundantly evident. “Sometimes I don’t know where pumpkins begin and I end,” she writes, before segueing into a series of squash and gourd portraits, each showing an individual specimen more striking than the last. Fowler shares recipes too, in addition to breed spotlights, resources for seed ­buying, and advice on growing your own.

Some such tomes aim to introduce the reader to the joys of less ubiquitous ingredients. Lane Selman and Margarett Waterbury’s Radicchio: A Celebration of the Beloved Italian Vegetable tells the “human and natural history” of the bitter chicory, along with instructions for how to grow it and cook with it. Selman is the founder of the Culinary Breeding Network, an initiative that rallies scientists, farmers, and chefs to geek out over new produce varieties. The book gets weird in the best way possible, with profiles of Italian growers and recipes including gnocchi with radicchio pesto, radicchio with prosciutto ­gratin, and chocolate–radicchio cake (why not?).

Radicchio reads almost like a community cookbook, and that’s intentional. Selman’s inspiration to pursue the topic was the sheer lack of writing on this oddball vegetable: “All of these people that we’ve met on our way down the rabbit hole needed to be included,” she says. “They’re the ones who have given us all this information. Sometimes it takes a village.”

Other single-subject cookbooks showcase pantry ­staples that are rarely in the spotlight. Anna Hezel’s Little Book of Olives: A Guide to Cooking, Eating, and Drinking for the Brine-Inclined presents recipes including cantaloupe and crushed-olive panzanella, Castelvetrano and pistachio pesto, and a whole chapter of olive desserts, plus shopping tips and a breakdown of varieties. The book’s retro aesthetic lends ­gravitas to an ingredient often relegated to garnish status.

Finally, some books exist more to dazzle than to inform, as is the case with pop artist Ed Ruscha and River Café chef Ruthie Rogers’s 2025 release Squeeze Me: Lemon Recipes & Art. In the pair’s high-gloss love letter to the lemon, pop art–coded photos with cheeky captions and a suite of minimalist recipes—such as lemon–­mascarpone tart and limoncello—make this ode to the simple citrus equally at home on a coffee table or the kitchen shelf.

While styles and forms vary, these books serve a ­common goal: to illuminate the sometimes surprising pleasures of a particular fruit or vegetable. That they manage to do so in such delightful fashion is proof that, once in a while, ­working with less really is more.

Hungry for even more stories to sink your teeth into?

#125. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

#126. These Are The 11 Best Italian Foods You Can Buy At Costco Right Now

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Oh Costco, the land of the plentiful. Aside from the sheer volume of affordable essentials available at Costco, one of the best things about the massive warehouse is that this land of the plentiful includes plenty from all lands! One of those lands is Italy... which, when it comes to food, is arguably the best land of all.

If you're looking for Italian goods and goodies, you've come to the right place. Costco warehouses across the U.S. offer a plethora of Italian foods to choose from, whether you're on the hunt for delicious cheeses, sweet treats, or go-to groceries for weeknight Italian dinners.

As always, though, some products are better than others — so we're rounding up the best of the best Italian foods that you should try at Costco. These particular products make the cut because they're either imported, authentic Italian goods, or they're Italian-style foods that have earned stellar reviews for great quality and taste. Just note that Costco usually has many different items in rotation, and inventory can vary from store to store, so be sure to check online to confirm what's currently available at your Costco location. Prices may vary based on your location.

Kirkland Signature Parmigiano-Reggiano is the perfect product to kick off this list, because this one of the most loved, and most authentic, Italian products on Costco's shelves. The Parmigiano-Reggiano at Costco is a must-buy for any cheese lover because it's a great price for a high quality Italian cheese that's actually the real deal.

The Americanized version of the cheese, called parmesan, is not the same thing as Parmigiano-Reggiano. Authentic Parmigiano-Reggiano comes from one of a handful of areas in Italy: either Parma, Reggio Emilia, Bologna, Mantua, or Modena. It's regulated by a consortium and must meet strict standards under DOC (Denominazione di Origine Controllata) law to be considered Parmigiano-Reggiano — aside from its origin, it must be made from cow's milk and aged at least two years. A good way to confirm authenticity is to look at the rind on the cheese; it should be stamped with a signature dotted "Parmigiano-Reggiano". You can also look for the Parmigiano-Reggiano Consortium logo on the packaging, which shows an image of a wheel of cheese next to a triangular wedge.

Costco's Parmigiano-Reggiano hits all the marks, and it tastes great, too. This cheese offers the rich, nutty, complex, and deeply savory notes you want from a Parmigiano-Reggiano. And once you taste the real thing, trust us — you'll never go back to "parmesan" again.

Speaking of delectable Italian cheeses, Kirkland Signature Pecorino Romano is another stellar find at Costco, because again it's both delicious and authentic. Similar to Costco's Parmigiano-Reggiano, you can tell the cheese is real thanks to the words "Pecorino Romano" you'll find stamped on the rind, as well as a PDO (Protected Designation of Origin) seal on the packaging. Kirkland sources this cheese from Sardinia, Italy.

While Parmigiano-Reggiano is made from cow's milk, Pecorino Romano is made from sheep pasture-raised sheep's milk. During the cheese-making process, Pecorino Romano is salted, which gives it a beautiful sharpness. It's typically aged for at least five months; Kirkland brand Pecorino Romano is aged for nine. The result is a very sharp, salty, earthy, and slightly tangy hard cheese that tastes amazing mixed into any risotto or pasta dish (especially cacio e pepe), shaved onto soups and salads, or just bitten into by itself in all of its sharp and salty glory. Pecorino Romano is a special cheese, and Costco is the go-to place to find the good stuff at a great price.

Costco offers no shortage when it comes to olive oil selection, so there is always some debate over which product is the best. With various olive oils in and out of rotation, the answer tends to change a lot, but there's no question that Kirkland Signature Toscano Extra Virgin Olive Oil is one of the higher-quality Italian olive oils to grace Costco's aisles.

This is a great choice for several reasons. First, it's a cold-pressed extra virgin olive oil, which means it's the freshest, highest quality grade available (as opposed to a "virgin olive oil", or an unspecified "olive oil" which tend to be blends with various extraction methods). It's also produced in a dark, glass bottle (rather than a transparent or plastic one), which is the best way to preserve the oil's quality and freshness. This extra virgin olive oil in particular is not only certified Organic, but it's also a single-origin oil — the olives used to make it are all traceable to a single region in Tuscany (versus bottles made from vague blends that don't disclose sourcing).

This PGI (Protected Geographical Indication) extra virgin olive oil has a slightly bitter finish which is characteristic of most good olive oil, but it's also got some pleasant peppery notes and a bit of fruitiness and brightness. It's great for dipping, finishing off dishes, and creating dressings, so use it anywhere that you want that beloved olive oil flavor to shine through.

If you're a prosciutto person, look no further than Costco to stock up on your favorite cured meat. The Citterio 18 Month Prosciutto Di Parma that you'll find at the warehouse is another authentic Italian product that won't disappoint. Sliced paper-thin, this prosciutto is a little salty and a little sweet, with a delicate texture and that signature cured, clean finish.

This product also contains the DOP (Denominazione di Origine Protetta) label, which means it's produced and packaged in Italy, and because this is Prosciutto "Di Parma", it's made specifically from the hind legs of pigs that come from one of 11 regions in Italy (similar to how Parmigiano-Reggiano and Pecorino Romano are regulated). Citterio's Prosciutto Di Parma comes from Felino, Parma, and the pork is dry-air cured using only sea salt (with no other additives) for a minimum of 140 days.

This Italian staple is the perfect addition to any charcuterie board and great eaten on its own, but it also pairs wonderfully with something sweet or salty like ripe melon or creamy burrata. Throw it on sandwiches, or crisp it up and add it to a veggie dish to level things up. You can't really go wrong.

Pesto is one of those staples that's great to have handy in the fridge because it's good on just about anything, and Costco does a great pesto. The Kirkland Signature Basil Pesto gets rave reviews from customers for being one of the best jarred pesto products out there and a fan favorite at Costco. And, it's only $10 for a large 22-ounce jar. If that seems like a lot of pesto to eat, don't worry, this stuff freezes excellently.

Why is this pesto such a winner? First off, it's another product that uses authentic Italian ingredients: This time, imported Genovese Italian basil (DOP). Aside from the fresh, vibrant basil, Kirkland's pesto is made with both Parmesan cheese and Pecorino Romano cheese (also DOP), pine nuts, garlic, and a blend of extra virgin olive oil and sunflower oil. The herbaceous flavor shines through without being overly garlicky, and it's a bright pesto with a delicious, subtly chunky texture to it that allows you to really taste each ingredient.

It's obviously amazing on pasta, but there are plenty of other deliciously creative ways to use this pesto, from eggs, toast, and soups to chicken and salmon. It's a great addition to just about any meal, so it's definitely worth keeping in your fridge or freezer for that easy extra zing.

There obviously had to be a pasta included on this list, because what's more Italian than pasta? Garofalo Organic Pasta is one of the best Italian options you'll find on Costco's shelves. Dried pasta is a great kitchen staple to buy in bulk because it doesn't go bad, and it's one of the most versatile ingredients out there.

While dried pasta is generally very low-cost and easy to come by, not all pastas are created equal; once you use a higher quality brand, you'll taste the difference. Garofalo Organic Pasta is obviously organic which is great, but it's also made in Italy with 100% durum wheat semolina. That matters because this coarse, ancient grain is high in protein density, which is what allows pasta to hold up well while it cooks, resulting in a perfect al dente with that chew that you're looking for. The nutty, earthy flavor of the wheat can also come through without being muddled by other cheaper flour blends.

The package of Garofalo Organic Pasta at Costco comes with six bags that over a pound each, which makes it a great deal. And the best part is that the six-pack includes three different pasta shapes — penne ziti regate, casarecce, and gemelli — so you can whip up a whole array of different pasta dishes at home that don't feel repetitive.

If you're looking for a ready-made pasta option that makes for a quick, easy, delicious meal during the week, the Kirkland Signature Five-Cheese Tortelloni available at Costco is a great go-to that customers love. This tortellini is a fan favorite because it freezes well, cooks in just two minutes, and tastes delicious with all kinds of different sauces and preparations, whether you're tossing them in a pesto or marinara sauce or even adding them to a homemade soup.

This product isn't imported from Italy like some of the others, but it does use a few authentic Italian ingredients. The five cheeses that make up the filling in this five-cheese tortelloni: Parmigiano-Reggiano (yes, the real deal), ricotta, mascarpone, Pecorino Romano, and mozzarella. It's hard not to like that medley of creamy, salty, and sharp cheeses. The tortelloni includes a few other ingredients like breadcrumbs, various types of vegetable fibers, and potatoes, and the pasta itself is made with semolina, eggs, and water.

Costco's tortelloni comes in a 3-pound package, so it'll last for several meals. It's the perfect thing to have on hand when you want a no-fuss, comforting Italian meal that you can make in a matter of minutes.

Similar to its extra virgin olive oil products, Costco offers a great option for an authentic balsamic vinegar as well. Kirkland Signature Organic Modena Balsamic Vinegar is a high-quality vinegar at a solid price that delivers on the sweet, syrupy, velvety goodness you want from a good balsamic.

To clarify, this product isn't DOP Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale, which is the highest designation with the strictest standards; that would mean its made only of grape must from grapes grown in Modena or Reggio Emilia and aged for a minimum of 12 years (and it would be way more expensive). However, Kirkland Signature Organic Modena Balsamic Vinegar is labeled PGI — Protected Geographical Indication which means it's still made in Modena. Within PGI, there is a tiered leaf system that indicates quality with one to five leaves; this particular balsamic has earned five leaves, which means it's pretty much as good as it gets without being DOP. Costco's balsamic vinegar is thick and syrupy with notes of plum and sweet spices, making it delicious for drizzling on anything from cheese to salads to ice cream.

Nothing beats a homemade marinara sauce with simple, fresh ingredients... but sometimes you just don't have time to make everything from scratch. When it comes to jarred pasta sauces, Rao's Homemade Marinara Sauce is surprisingly tasty and gets a lot of love from consumers. And it probably has something to do with the fact that it's made in Italy.

This pre-made marinara sauce is so easy to add to pastas, meatballs, and other dishes you can make at home, but the great thing about Rao's is that this brand is intentional with its ingredients and doesn't sacrifice quality. The marinara sauce is made with whole peeled Italian tomatoes, olive oil, onions, garlic, basil, salt, pepper, and oregano. That's it. No other additives, preservatives, or other ingredients that have no business being in a marinara sauce. The sauce is slow-simmered in small batches before its jarred, and because the ingredients are so pure and simple, its homemade taste really holds up.

Can't make a Costco trip without getting a little something sweet, so why not try some delicious Italian desserts? First up are these La Dolce Vita Classic Almond Biscotti, which get high praise from customers for their quality, authenticity, and delicious, just-right almond flavor.

Biscotti, which actually means "twice-baked" in Italian, are made by baking the dough and then cutting it into the signature slices and baking it again to get it extra toasty and crispy. These classic almond biscotti don't disappoint with their delightful crunchy texture and whole toasted almonds, and they make the perfect companion to dunk in your coffee.

And if you need some great coffee to dunk that biscotti into, Lavazza Whole Bean Espresso is definitely up for the task. This whole bean coffee is an Italian-style light roast that's made with 100% Arabica beans from Central and South America. The coffee is richly bodied with a fruity and floral aroma, and it's a great option at Costco for the price.

Lavazza is a company with deep Italian roots that started as a coffee shop in Turin, Italy all the way back in 1895. The once small coffee business eventually became the largest company in Italy, and today it's a global brand with products across the globe. Lavazza a very trusted and respected brand when it comes to good quality coffee, and its Italian heritage has a lot to do with that.

With an intensity level of 5 out of 10, this coffee is super versatile, and customers love using it for variety of preparations, from pour over and cold brew coffee to classic espresso and drip coffee. It's a little sweet and a little nutty, mellow enough to work across several applications, and balanced enough to make a delicious espresso.

#127. I Tried the Most Popular Ranch Dressings, and This One Is By Far the Best

It's tailgate season, and that means you'll be going through ranch faster than halftime rolls around. Here are the best store-bought ranch dressings to keep in your fridge.

It’s easy to take ranch dressing for granted. Whipping up homemade ranch is easy, store-bought versions are available in just about any supermarket, and most restaurants have it on the menu. We reach for a bottle to drizzle on salads, veggie platters and sometimes even pizza. I remember watching tourists come to the U.S. for the World Cup and raving about the condiment. Visitors from all over the globe packed bottles in their bags before departing. And for us, it’s just another condiment in the fridge.

That got me thinking—which brand makes the best ranch on the market? I tasted the following eight ranch dressing brands to find the most tangy, dill-forward version you can buy in a store:

To keep things accurate, I grabbed a bag of baby carrots and got dipping! My ranking parameters were taste, texture and value.

Honestly, I was quite shocked that the bottle of organic ranch dressing from Trader Joe’s came in at the bottom of my ranked list. I’m a huge fan of TJ’s and am usually very pleased with its products. Unfortunately, this ranch dressing wasn’t up to the brand’s usual standards.

It came out of the bottle with a thin and watery texture. That’s why it wasn’t a big surprise when I turned the bottle around to read the ingredient list and saw that the first one listed was, in fact, water. For comparison, every other ranch dressing on this list uses some sort of oil as the first ingredient. Taking a bite didn’t change my mind. The flavors were muted and uninspired.

Bottom Line: Though the $2.99 price point is nice, the Trader Joe’s ranch is too watered down for me to purchase again.

I was also surprised to rank Litehouse Ranch lower on this list. I tend to prefer refrigerated salad dressings sold in the produce section rather than shelf-stable options in the grocery store aisles. I have purchased other varieties of Litehouse products in the past and liked the taste, but this ranch dressing didn’t have the flavor punch I was hoping for.

Selling for $3.99 per 13-ounce jar, this ranch comes out to about 30 cents per ounce, which is on the higher end compared to other options on the market. I did like that this was the only product sold in a glass jar with a screw top, rather than in a plastic container or a squeeze bottle.

Bottom Line: Litehouse Ranch needs more herbs and seasonings to really be considered a contender in the jam-packed ranch dressing space.

I’ve always had good luck with Ken’s products. The dressings are typically sold in large, 16-ounce bottles with a respectable price point. This ranch retails at my local store for $3.29, which comes out to about 21 cents an ounce. Ultimately, both the price and flavor of this dressing were middle-of-the-road. I did like the velvety texture of the dressing, so I might keep it on hand when making recipes that call for ranch, rather than just using it on a basic salad or as a dip.

Bottom Line: Ken’s Steak House offers a diverse line of salad dressings, but its ranch wasn’t a standout in this ranking.

Tuscan Garden is a product line from Aldi, and a 16-ounce bottle of its ranch dressing sells for a bargain at $1.99. That comes out to about 12 cents an ounce and is one of the most budget-friendly options in this ranked list. This ranch skews a little sweeter than others I tasted and has a muted vinegar tang. Depending on your palate, this could be right up your alley or not your thing.

Bottom Line: While this might not become my go-to ranch dressing, it will certainly be on my radar whenever I’m entertaining a crowd and need to save on groceries.

Marie’s is another refrigerated ranch dressing option. The Creamy Ranch comes in a 12-ounce screw-top plastic jar for $3.99, or about 33 cents per ounce. Refrigerated dressings tend to cost more than shelf-stable dressings.

Sour cream is listed in the ingredients, which sets this ranch apart from others I tested. It resulted in more of a dip consistency rather than an easy-to-drizzle dressing for a salad. I did enjoy the rich, thick texture of this dressing, but I also felt the sour cream slightly muted the vinegar’s tang.

Bottom Line: This would be my choice for a ranch to serve as a dip or a spread rather than drizzled on a salad.

The tiny but mighty bottle of Classic Ranch Dressing from Kraft was the biggest surprise of this taste test. At only $1.00 for an 8-ounce container, this ranch was the least expensive of the bunch. I presumed that the big brand name and the low price point might mean a lower-quality product, and I was proven wrong. Just looking at this dressing, you can see more specks of herbs and spices than in other brands. It also has a delightful tang that I have mentioned missing in other products. Given the fact that it is also such a deal, I was blown away.

Bottom Line: If you want the best-tasting ranch dressing on a budget, look no further than Kraft.

I wasn’t surprised when the Marzetti Classic Ranch ranked quite high on this list. The Marzetti brand is one I reach for over and over again with consistently delicious results. This 13-ounce refrigerated jar retails for $3.99.

The flavor profile was the perfect balance of herbaceous and zesty, all while having the ideal texture and thickness for a dressing. It perfectly hovers that line between feeling substantial enough for a veggie tray and still having the ability to drizzle over a salad. This brand uses real buttermilk in its recipe, and it is the second ingredient after oil. I think that leads to the tartness and richness I have come to love in a great ranch dressing.

Bottom Line: Marzetti makes the best of the refrigerated ranch dressing options.

It’s no surprise that the best ranch on this list was awarded to the brand that started it all, Hidden Valley Ranch. What began as one cowboy’s signature recipe in the 1950’s has transformed into an iconic American staple. I purchased an 8-ounce bottle for $2.49, or about 31 cents an ounce, which is an average price for a bottle of ranch.

The classic flavor settled right into the perfect ranch balance of creamy, tangy and savory, with an ideal drizzling consistency. I also like how Hidden Valley Ranch offers a variety of products so you can make ranch for different needs. If you want to make a more homemade version of this legendary dressing, you can purchase a spice blend packet and mix it with mayonnaise and buttermilk or grab some sour cream and cream cheese and whip up a Loaded Hidden Valley Ranch Dip.

Bottom Line: I’d say go straight to the source! Hidden Valley Ranch created the legendary ranch flavor, and it continues to be the best today.

Which is your favorite brand? Let us know in the comments below!
