#129. A Chef’s Guide to the Best Restaurants in Asheville, North Carolina

By Meherwan Irani as told to Jamie Feldmar

Part of what gives me so much joy about eating in Asheville is recognizing that we’re all part of a very integrated ecosystem. It feels like every restaurant I love is either run by an alum of one of the places I’ve been involved in, or by people that I’ve worked side by side with at hurricane-relief events, or by someone I know I’m going to see at the farmers market.

That’s what makes Asheville special. The folks that come in from out of town are lucky that there’s a virtuous cycle of talent here to keep the pipeline full. It’s so cool to see the evolution of this place, even if we locals don’t always realize how good we have it.It’s almost funny how not a big deal eating out here is. It’s so laid-back. We take it for granted that it’s going to be a great restaurant—of course it is! Having said that, the sheer range of restaurants is incredible. Given how small our town actually is, I sometimes find myself thinking, How lucky are we?

A hallmark of most of the restaurants I love is their connection to nearby farms. At my last count, there were more than a dozen farmers markets happening in Asheville, and there are probably more than twice as many local farms within an hour of here. Most people know the farmers by name, and nobody is precious about it. So when you go to a restaurant, they’ll just say, “It’s Evan’s greens tonight,” and everybody knows who Evan is.

The last thing is that whether it’s an Indian restaurant or a Filipino restaurant or Italian or Spanish, I love the Southern throughline in all of the dishes and hospitality here. That doesn’t mean there’s cornbread or okra in every dish; it’s honoring the fact that we all chose to open Indian or Italian restaurants here in Appalachia, so let’s not divorce the two from each other.

Let’s find a way to make it feel holistic. We do that really well. I was worried after the pandemic and Hurricane Helene that Asheville might not bounce back, but we have. I know that this place is going to continue to trailblaze for years to come.

20 Battery Park Avenue, Floor 1(828) 271-9808

Luminosa is hands down my wife, Molly, and my favorite date- night restaurant. It checks every box so beautifully. It’s intimate, but also a showstopper. It’s visually exciting to be in there, and yet [the design] doesn’t detract from the food, which they describe as “hyper-local Italian.” In the two years that they’ve been open, they’ve picked up a Michelin Green Star and a Michelin Bib Gourmand, and they deserve it. Everything about it just feels very intentional. The food is brilliantly delicious and the menu changes a lot—which sometimes drives me crazy, but it works here, because I know there’s going to be something fun and new every time I go. Their style of service and hospitality is so old-fashioned it almost borders on being antiquated, but I love it. It’s a small town at the end of the day, and everybody touches your table.

One word: respect. Katie Button and her crew have been at the top of their game for so long, you almost forget that continuing to win the championship is really hard to do. But they execute at the exact same incredibly high level as they did the first time I walked in years ago. I go there because what they do is incredible, and it’s always good to be reminded of how well they represent the tapas side of Spanish cuisine. It’s also a really exciting restaurant to be in—there’s an energy and a vibe because of the open kitchen, and it feels so intimate and fun. It’s always packed—they’re a victim of their own success—but even if I’m just going in for a glass of sherry and a plate of jamón ibérico, it’s worth pulling whatever favors I must to get in.

701 Haywood Road, Suite 102(828) 552-3880

This is a true only-in-Asheville pick, a chest-swelling-with-pride kind of choice. The chef, Silver Iocovozzi, worked with me at [two of Irani’s erstwhile restaurants] MG Road and Buxton Hall, and now they get to showcase their own cuisine, Filipino. Neng Jr.’s feels like the kind of restaurant that this city is built for. It’s so tiny and so intimate, with maybe 12 seats, so you’re packed in and you really feel like you’re eating dinner at Silver’s house. The food feels so personal—it’s brilliant and fun and totally them, with flavor profiles that remind me of Indian street food in some ways, full of fermentation and funk.

First of all, this space was converted into a restaurant without doing much to disguise the fact that it used to be a house. You’re dining on the front porch or in the side yard or in the living room, but somehow it manages to make you feel like you’re in a small village in Provence. The food has a French focus, as well as an Americana element. They win all kinds of awards for their wine program, deservedly so. Leo’s is hard to describe. It feels like this rustic little bistro where you might order something as simple as a grilled cheese sandwich and tomato soup, but when it shows up, you realize this could actually be the best grilled cheese and tomato soup you’ve ever had in your life. It’s totally unique and transportive, and it’s become my go-to spontaneous dinner recommendation for friends visiting from out of town.

I’m going to throw it back a little to one of the first places that really popped in West Asheville. Ten or 15 years ago, The Admiral was essentially a dive bar in a cinder-block building next to a gas station where probably 80 percent of Asheville’s pot deals went down. There, a young chef named Elliot Moss [ed note: later Irani’s partner at Buxton Hall] was putting out gastropub food that was blowing people’s minds. After service, they’d push all the tables to the side to clear room for these legendary dance parties. Now the neighborhood isn’t as sketchy, Elliot is long gone, and they no longer push the tables aside, but the food has not lost an inch. When you’re eating, you can just feel that it’s world-class cuisine, and reservations are hard to get, so it still feels special to get to go to The Admiral.

The best way I can describe chef Matt Dawes’s food, or at least my experience of it, is that it’s elevated British pub cuisine with a French influence and a Southern twist. The menu swings from steak frites au poivre to the best shepherd’s pie you’ve ever had to a pitch-perfect Welsh rarebit (it’s also the first place I had Welsh rabbit). The restaurant is located maybe 30 feet from the railroad tracks, next to a dirt field and one of the noisiest outdoor breweries in Asheville, but don’t let that deter you. It’s one of the most reliable and satisfying restaurants in the city.

This is a newcomer to the scene. Chef Ashleigh Shanti Santi, a James Beard Award–winner and prominent Top Chef contestant, has been a passionate advocate for Black Southern foodways. Good Hot Fish is exactly what it sounds like: a fish counter with amazing hot fish sandwiches and seafood, plus the perfect sides. All of the fish she serves comes from local waterways. There’s fried catfish and Gulf shrimp burgers and fish dip with fried saltines. It’s literally just a counter with a few stools against the wall, but the technique is immaculate. The sandwiches are served on squishy white bread with buttermilk tartare sauce, and it delivers on its promise of being the best damn hot fish sandwich you’ve ever had.

I have to give a shout-out here to one of the OGs. To call All Souls just great pizza does it a disservice; you need to understand the backstory. David Bauer, was one of the first bread gurus/savants of Asheville. Farm and Sparrow, his bakery, helped usher in the modern renaissance of heirloom grains and bread that you now see everywhere. He grew his own grain, milled his own flour, and made these amazing breads. Then he helped open All Souls, which makes pizza using stone-ground heirloom grains, in a style I can only describe as Carolina pizza. It’s our own thing, with our own grains, cooked in a wood-fired oven with toppings that come from within 50 miles or so. It’s in a building that was a diner for decades in West Asheville, next to a big old field where you can spread out a picnic blanket if the restaurant is full. All Souls is a classic example of doing one thing, doing it well, and not being too uptight about it, which is everything I love about Asheville.

244 Short Coxe Avenue, #110(828) 505-1003

I have to include two bakeries here. Mother serves a full lunch and dinner menu, so it’s a little more on the restaurant side of things. It’s again in a weird part of Asheville, sandwiched between a sauna and a tire shop, with garage doors that open to a front patio that looks like a loading ramp for trucks. And yet, like so many places here, it’s totally transportive. You feel like you’re eating in Europe somehow. Their jambon-beurre sandwich is the closest I’ve had to Fauchon’s in Paris, and their pumpernickel bread is divine. It feels like a restaurant run by a group of passionate friends that care deeply about food and hospitality, who all got together to open a little place as a gift to the community, because that’s exactly what it is.

I would describe Owl as a bakery with Southern sensibilities and French technique. I’d put the lamination on their croissants up against anything in Stockholm. They’re known for their almond rose croissants, cardamom buns, and squirrel bread [a seed-and-nut loaf], and if you don’t get there right at 8 a.m. they’re going to be sold out. Sometimes I look at the people lining up, and I want to shake each and every one of them and yell, “Do you have any idea how good you have it right now?!” I actually have to resist doing that as I see them gabbing away over their morning pastries and lattes without a care in the world, not recognizing that the rest of us have to schlep around the world God knows how many times to find anything even close to this good in terms of quality and execution. And that’s just life in Asheville.

It’s an honorable mention, because I haven’t stepped foot in the restaurant for 17 years, but I get takeout from Rocky’s almost every Sunday, when I host a men’s group at my house where we discuss things like “How do you actually define electro music?” and play Crocodile, a weird Canadian board game. In the very crowded field of hot fried chicken, Rocky’s stands at the top, because their chicken is actually melt-your-face hot, not “oh-look-how-cute” Nashville hot. Beginners should get the medium. The hot is for veterans, and the extra hot is something the CIA should use to extract information. The crust is thin and it has the perfect amount of crunch, and the seasoning goes all the way through. But most importantly, every week we get the same order, and never once in 17 years have they messed up that order. I feel like a highly underrated aspect of a great restaurant is doing exactly the same thing 52 weeks out of the year, and I have mad respect for Rocky’s.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

It’s an honorable mention, because I haven’t stepped foot in the restaurant for 17 years, but I get takeout from Rocky’s almost every Sunday, when I host a men’s group at my house where we discuss things like “How do you actually define electro music?” and play Crocodile, a weird Canadian board game. In the very crowded field of hot fried chicken, Rocky’s stands at the top, because their chicken is actually melt-your-face hot, not “oh-look-how-cute” Nashville hot. Beginners should get the medium. The hot is for veterans, and the extra hot is something the CIA should use to extract information. The crust is thin and it has the perfect amount of crunch, and the seasoning goes all the way through. But most importantly, every week we get the same order, and never once in 17 years have they messed up that order. I feel like a highly underrated aspect of a great restaurant is doing exactly the same thing 52 weeks out of the year, and I have mad respect for Rocky’s.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

#131. Farmers Market Salad With Miso Maple Dressing

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

The farmers market is my biggest hack for solo cooking. Instead of committing to a three-pound bag of carrots, you can buy just one, and choose your produce based on beauty or mere curiosity. That’s how I came up with this fall salad, comprising a single head of Little Gem lettuce and some crunchy produce, including that carrot we mentioned, cucumber, watermelon radish, and an Asian pear. Slicing those elements thinly with a mandoline and throwing them in an ice bath for a brief soak helps keep everything cold and crisp.

The dressing is equally important. I start with Kewpie mayo for its richness and savory depth—it’s made with only egg yolks and contains MSG, giving it a fuller flavor than standard mayonnaise. White miso brings even more umami, while rice vinegar keeps things bright. The result is a creamy finger-licking dressing that clings to every bite. Serve with a fried egg (or your protein of choice) and a piece of fresh bread to scoop up the leftovers. Make a double batch of dressing for dipping crudités or marinating salmon, chicken, or roasted vegetables.

Read More: The Farmers Market Is Built for Solo Cooking

Combine 1 small head of Little Gem or other crunchy lettuce, leaves separated, cut into 2"–3" pieces, 1 rainbow carrot, peeled, very thinly sliced lengthwise into ribbons with a mandoline or vegetable peeler, 1 Persian cucumber, thinly sliced, preferably with a mandoline, ½ small watermelon radish, peeled, halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, and ¼ medium Asian pear, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, in a large bowl of ice water. Let soak 10–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 Tbsp. seasoned rice vinegar, 2 Tbsp. white miso, 2 tsp. Kewpie mayonnaise, 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, and 1 tsp. toasted sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth and emulsified (or combine in a small glass jar, cover, and shake). Taste dressing and season with kosher salt.

Drain vegetables and run through a salad spinner or pat dry with a kitchen towel to remove excess water. Wipe out large bowl, return vegetables to bowl, and drizzle 2 Tbsp. dressing over. Toss, adding more dressing as needed, until evenly coated (reserve any remaining dressing for another use).

Transfer salad to a shallow bowl or rimmed plate. Top with a fried egg and serve with country-style bread if desired.

Do Ahead: Dressing can be made up to 3 days ahead. Cover and chill.

#132. Is An Apple A Day Actually Good For You? A Dietitian Weighs In

The classic snack supports your health—but with a few caveats.

An old proverb says one apple a day keeps the doctor away, but does nutrition science back that up? For most people, yes: An apple is a healthy way to add fruit to your diet and help you meet the recommended daily amount. But a few caveats—like apple variety, washing, and digestive sensitivity—are worth keeping in mind.

Current dietary guidelines recommend two servings of fruit per day, and since an apple is about one serving, it can help you meet those needs. But most types of apples are high in fiber and natural sugar, so eating too many could mean problems for your gut health, according to Lauren Manaker, M.S., R.D.N.

Let’s dig into the science to learn how to safely add apples to our diets.

“Apples offer a range of health benefits, including supporting heart health, supporting immune function, and reducing inflammation,” Manaker says. She credits vitamin C with supporting the immune system and flavonoids, a type of antioxidant, with helping lower the risk of heart disease.

While nutrient content varies by apple type, a medium Golden Delicious is mostly water. A single apple contains roughly 96 calories, 23 grams of carbs (17 of which come from sugar), and about four grams of fiber. That fiber, especially soluble fiber like pectin, can help regulate blood sugar and support gut health.

“Eating an apple every day can be incredibly healthy, as apples are a nutrient-dense fruit full of fiber, vitamins, and antioxidants,” Manaker says. “Since most people don't eat the recommended servings of fruits and veggies daily, making a habit of having an apple a day can be a good thing.”

Just don't forget to wash them. “Eating unwashed apples may pose a risk of pesticide exposure, so washing them thoroughly is recommended,” she notes. Apples often appear on lists of produce with higher pesticide residues, such as the Environmental Working Group's Dirty Dozen. Of course, washing is recommended for all produce, and conventional (versus organic) apples still provide nutritional benefits.

“While apples are healthy, over-consuming them in excessive amounts could lead to excess calorie intake or digestive issues due to their high fiber and natural sugar content,” Manaker says.

For most people, it's hard to overdo it enough to cause harm. However, she cautions that too much fiber and natural sugars could cause mild discomfort for those with IBS or more sensitive stomachs, and people managing blood sugar may want to pair apples with protein or fat.

One apple per day is a healthy choice for most people, but rotate fruits, wash produce, and adjust portions if apples trigger digestive symptoms. Your doctor—and your gut—will thank you.

Lauren Manaker M.S., R.D.N., L.D., C.L.E.C. is a registered dietitian based in South Carolina. She earned a bachelor's degree in Food Science and Human Nutrition at the University of Florida before going on to complete her master's and dietetic internship at Rush University Medical Center. Manaker received the Emerging Professional in Women’s Health Award from the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics in 2018 and provides her expert advice at CNN, Women’s Health Magazine, SHAPE, The Oprah Magazine, and Cooking Light.

#133. Skip The Sponge: There's A Better Way To Clean Cast Iron Without Dish Soap

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

There are plenty of reasons to invest in a high-quality cast iron pan. Beyond its excellent heat retention and naturally non-stick surface, cast iron is an incredibly durable material. Look after it, and a single pan can last for decades, even generations. That said, cast iron does come with a few basic ground rules. Follow them, and it'll reward you with years upon years of reliable cooking. Ignore them, and you could find yourself dealing with rust or a damaged seasoning layer. That's where a cast iron ringer comes in handy, like the Amagabeli cast iron ringer on Amazon.

Cleaning is one area where cast iron has earned an unnecessarily intimidating reputation. Its nonstick qualities come from a baked-on layer of polymerized oil, commonly known as seasoning. This protective layer helps prevent food from sticking and shields the iron beneath it from moisture. Leave your pan wet for too long, and rust can develop. Scrub too aggressively, and you risk damaging the seasoning; the same goes for the old advice about avoiding dish soap. Traditional soaps sometimes contained lye, which could strip away seasoning, but modern dish soaps are almost always mild enough to use on a properly seasoned pan. Even so, the aversion to dish soap has stuck around — even Bobby Flay chooses to avoid it.

If you'd rather keep things traditional or avoid dish soap altogether, a cast iron ringer is a useful alternative. Made from interlocking rings of rust-resistant stainless steel, this chainmail scrubber works much like a metal scourer, using friction to lift stubborn grease and baked-on residue. The difference is that, when used correctly, it can remove stuck-on food without wearing away a well-established seasoning layer.

Using a ringer to clean your cast iron is incredibly simple. Just run warm water over your pan and gently scrub away the residue with the ringer, working in circular motions where needed. To make lifting stains even easier, you can also pair it with dish soap — just don't let the traditionalists know! The cleaning is the easy bit; what really matters is how you treat the pan after.

Everybody knows that cast iron and water don't mix. Why? Science, of course. Iron is highly reactive to oxygen and water, and when the two meet, the iron oxidizes and forms iron oxide — better known as rust — surprisingly fast. Cast iron can usually tolerate a quick wash, but it despises sitting in water for long stretches. To keep it in top shape after cleaning, dry it vigorously with a kitchen towel, or set it on a warm stovetop to evaporate any trace of leftover moisture. If you do end up with rust, you can easily scrub it off with a simple mixture of lemon and kosher salt.

One of your greatest protections against rust is the seasoning. Unlike an enamel coating, however, this layer of polymerized oil isn't as hardy. It can be stripped away, worn down, or built back up over time. To keep it in good condition, avoid cooking large amounts of acidic ingredients, never soak the pan, and keep long, roiling boils to a minimum. That's not to say you should baby your cast iron. In fact, cooking is one of the best ways to maintain seasoning, as cooking with oil naturally builds it up. After cleaning, you can also rub a small amount of neutral oil onto the surface to keep it protected.

#136. What Goes Into Making Real-Deal Prosciutto di Parma PDO

There are precious few food products that have been enjoyed for as much of human history as Prosciutto di Parma. The signature silky texture and buttery, sweet-savory flavor of the “King of Hams” is recognized around the world as the result of carefully controlled production methods, dedication to quality, and traditions continued for centuries.

The history of Prosciutto di Parma reaches back more than 2,000 years, to Roman times, when the art of preserving pork through salting and natural drying was already well established in the Po Valley. As early as the 3rd century BC, Cato the Elder described methods for curing pork legs with salt and allowing them to dry and mature. Today, Prosciutto di Parma is produced exclusively in a strictly defined area of northern Italy, in the province of Parma in the Emilia-Romagna region, where local know-how combines with distinctive climatic conditions. Humid breezes from the Tyrrhenian Sea become drier as they flow over the Apennines and down onto the hills. Prosciutto producers discovered that this created an ideal environment for dry aging, and they built storerooms with tall windows that could be opened and closed as necessary, allowing the air to circulate through the racks of hams for gradual drying.

The specifics of aging, like every step in the process, are governed by a consortium—the Consorzio del Prosciutto di Parma—that was founded in 1963 to protect the authenticity of the product. In 1996, Prosciutto di Parma obtained the European Union’s Protected Designation of Origin (PDO). These have a red and yellow seal to show that a product is made in a certain geographical area using time-honored, traditional methods. Grana Padano, a nutty, aged hard cheese also from Northern Italy that’s often paired with Prosciutto di Parma on a charcuterie plate, was awarded a PDO the same year.

Grana Padano PDO and Prosciutto di Parma PDO also share the distinction of being fire-branded—a sign for consumers that you are buying the real thing. Only Parma hams that meet the PDO’s specifications can receive the five-pronged Ducal Crown that signifies a true Prosciutto di Parma.

Well before that brand is applied, production starts with the pigs. Which breeds, where they can be bred and raised (in 11 Italian regions), and what they are fed (a list that also includes whey from local cheesemakers) are all precisely detailed. Within the 28th day from birth, the piglets receive a breeder tattoo that will also appear on the final product along with the crown brand. The fresh pork (hind legs only) sent to prosciutto producers must weigh between 26 pounds and 40 pounds, with a set amount of fat coverage. After they arrive at the production facility, the legs are trimmed to form the characteristic rounded shape, chilled to a precise temperature, and salted by hand with sea salt, which joins the pork as the only two ingredients that go into the making of Prosciutto di Parma PDO.

Following a resting period of at least 90 days, the hams are washed then hung in windowed storerooms to dry slowly. The next step is called sugnatura: The parts of the ham not covered by rind are rubbed with sugna—a mixture of pork fat, salt, and pepper—to keep the meat from drying too quickly. For final aging, the hams hang in cool, dimly lit cellars. From start to finish, the process cannot last less than 14 months (many producers continue aging for 24, 30, or even 36 months and beyond). The last step before inspection may be the most fascinating: The hams are tested using a needle made from horse bone, selected because the bone is able to absorb the aroma and quickly shed it. By inserting the needle into different parts of the cured meat and smelling it, experts can determine if a whole ham leg has the qualifications to be named Prosciutto di Parma PDO.

The Consorzio, which started with 23 producers, now numbers 125, and in 2025 they turned out 6.75 million Prosciutto di Parma PDO hams. Beyond its economic significance to the region, the “King of Hams” is a cultural icon and a tourism magnet. The annual Parma Ham Festival is held in September, and there’s even an entire museum dedicated to the region’s signature product—with a tasting room, of course.

However you experience the exceptional flavor and texture of Prosciutto di Parma—on a visit to the museum or from your local specialty store—look for the crown and PDO seal, and take a moment to remember that you are tasting a distinctly delicious slice of history.

Head to DistinctlyDeliciouslyEuropean.eu to learn more about Prosciutto di Parma PDO and Grana Padano PDO.

Within the 28th day from birth, the piglets receive a breeder tattoo that will also appear on the final product along with the crown brand. The fresh pork (hind legs only) sent to prosciutto producers must weigh between 26 pounds and 40 pounds, with a set amount of fat coverage. After they arrive at the production facility, the legs are trimmed to form the characteristic rounded shape, chilled to a precise temperature, and salted by hand with sea salt, which joins the pork as the only two ingredients that go into the making of Prosciutto di Parma PDO.

Following a resting period of at least 90 days, the hams are washed then hung in windowed storerooms to dry slowly. The next step is called sugnatura: The parts of the ham not covered by rind are rubbed with sugna—a mixture of pork fat, salt, and pepper—to keep the meat from drying too quickly. For final aging, the hams hang in cool, dimly lit cellars. From start to finish, the process cannot last less than 14 months (many producers continue aging for 24, 30, or even 36 months and beyond). The last step before inspection may be the most fascinating: The hams are tested using a needle made from horse bone, selected because the bone is able to absorb the aroma and quickly shed it. By inserting the needle into different parts of the cured meat and smelling it, experts can determine if a whole ham leg has the qualifications to be named Prosciutto di Parma PDO.

The Consorzio, which started with 23 producers, now numbers 125, and in 2025 they turned out 6.75 million Prosciutto di Parma PDO hams. Beyond its economic significance to the region, the “King of Hams” is a cultural icon and a tourism magnet. The annual Parma Ham Festival is held in September, and there’s even an entire museum dedicated to the region’s signature product—with a tasting room, of course.

However you experience the exceptional flavor and texture of Prosciutto di Parma—on a visit to the museum or from your local specialty store—look for the crown and PDO seal, and take a moment to remember that you are tasting a distinctly delicious slice of history.

Head to DistinctlyDeliciouslyEuropean.eu to learn more about Prosciutto di Parma PDO and Grana Padano PDO.

#137. Sweater Weather Spritz

Recipe by Christine Rukavena, Milwaukee, Wisconsin

The Sweater Weather spritz is what happens when your Aperol spritz goes apple-picking and turns into a bubbly drink built for flannel season.

I’m a die-hard Aperol spritz enthusiast. But the minute Chicagoans put away the patio umbrellas and pull out the parkas, I feel like folks start giving me the side-eye when I reach for the Prosecco and bright orange Aperol bottle. Like white pants, are spritzes supposed to be retired after Labor Day? Not on my watch. I say it’s time for swimsuits to meet snowsuits with this apple cider Aperol spritz, which we affectionately named Sweater Weather spritz.

This fall-themed spritz keeps the bittersweet orange sparkle I can’t quit and includes a pour of crisp, chilled apple cider, so it tastes less like a beach vacation and more like an afternoon of corn mazes. Apple cider softens Aperol’s bitter edge, and a splash of soda keeps things bright and bubbly. It’s made for Friendsgiving, bonfire nights, football Sundays or any evening that calls for a cozy blanket and bubbly sip.

Best of all, it’s just as simple to make as its summery sister cocktail. No shaker, no muddler, no simmering syrup on the stove while your guests hover in the kitchen. Just pour four ingredients into a wine glass and give it a gentle stir.

Fill a wine glass with ice and add the chilled Prosecco, apple cider, Aperol and soda. Give it a gentle stir to combine, just enough to swirl the cider and Aperol through the bubbles.

Editor’s Tip: You can always skip the ice if you pre-chilled your ingredients ahead of time.

If you like, tuck a sprig of fresh rosemary and a few apple slices into the glass. Serve your spritz right away while it’s cold and fizzy.

Editor’s Tip: If rosemary feels too woodsy and wintry for you, swap in mint to add a fresh, cooling finish.

Like bubbly Champagne cocktails, this spritz is best enjoyed the minute you mix it because those bubbles wait for no one. If you have leftover Prosecco, seal the bottle with a sparkling wine stopper and refrigerate it for a day or two. Keep opened apple cider in the fridge for about a week.

You can stir together the apple cider and Aperol up to a day ahead and stash it, covered, in the fridge. When guests arrive, pour the cider mixture into glasses and top each one with chilled Prosecco and soda so every spritz stays perky and fizzy.

You can make an apple cider spritz with or without soda. We like it because it adds a little extra sparkle and sweetness, but the drink holds up just fine without it. Skip it for a more cider-forward, slightly less sweet spritz, which is my move when my cider is already on the sugary side.

You can make an apple cider spritz with any type of spirit. Try Campari for a bolder, more bitter version that’ll speak to the Negroni lovers in the crowd, or go with an orange liqueur like Cointreau to lean into citrus and omit any bitterness at all. For a zero-proof option, a nonalcoholic bitter aperitivo will add the same gorgeous color and bittersweet bite without any alcohol. If you’re feeling experimental, steer away from the classic orange flavor profile found in many spritz recipes and try bourbon or brandy.

If you want to experiment and create your own spritz recipe, look for cozy fall flavors from orchard fruits and warm baking-type spices. Apple, pear and cranberry all shine next to sparkling wine, and a touch of ginger, cinnamon or maple adds instant sweater-weather warmth. For garnishes, woodsy herbs like rosemary and thyme are your best friends.

#138. The Boxed Side Dish That Turns Leftover Ground Beef Into A Hearty Meal

These days, a cheap meal that can be cooked up in one pot or pan is akin to a unicorn: A rare find that you'll want to tell everyone about, to share your good fortune. And if you don't have to spend an eternity slaving over a hot stove? Even better. That's why boxed side dishes, which you can find for a great price at Aldi, are so clutch — they're inexpensive, cook quickly, and with the addition of a protein, you have a complete meal. Boxed scalloped potatoes have been saving people the hassle of scrubbing, peeling, and thin-slicing potatoes since at least the 1960s, and with the addition of some leftover ground beef, you have a dish that is both quick and hearty — and doesn't leave you with a pile of dishes to do after.

You can reheat the ground beef in a pot or a pan with taller sides, and then use that same pot or pan to make the boxed scalloped potatoes. Just follow the stove-top directions on the package, add in any additional seasonings you want, and stir in the cooked beef. You can mix in cheese to add further creaminess and richness to the meal (or to help thicken the sauce if it's a bit too thin), or use it as a garnish on individual plates. Ground beef scalloped potatoes are warm and comforting, and you can round out the meal with a side salad or perfectly roasted veggies and breadsticks.

If you love this idea of combining boxed scalloped potatoes and ground beef, but you want all the ingredients to get nice and bubbly, and for the cheese to turn golden on top, this dish is versatile enough that you can actually dump the ingredients in a baking dish and make it casserole-style. While it bakes, you're free to do whatever else it is you need to do, so this is a good option if you prefer being able to multitask and prep whatever side dishes you want to accompany the meal. You will need to cook up the beef and prepare the scalloped potatoes' sauce separately, but you can actually do both at the same time, on separate stove burners.

Making this dish casserole-style is also a good opportunity to add some flavorful ingredients, such as aromatics like freshly sliced and minced onion and garlic, which you can cook with the beef, crumbled bacon, or even a vegetable element, like bell pepper or canned peas and carrots (there's a reason they make the list of inexpensive canned foods you'll use all the time). Add a fajita or taco seasoning packet, and serve it with a side of salsa and tortilla chips. This low-fuss meal is perfect for busy weekdays, but rich and creamy enough that it feels like a treat for the weekend. And there is just something so cozy and warm about taking a casserole dish out of the oven at dinnertime.

#139. The Best Apples for Baking

Not every apple is cut out for the oven. The best apples for baking—whether you’re making BA’s Best Apple Pie, a Buttery German Apple Cake, or Suspiciously Cheesy Apple Crumb Bars—have firm flesh that softens when cooked without turning to mush. A good balance of sweetness and acidity helps too. Granny Smith, Pink Lady, Braeburn, Honeycrisp, Golden Delicious, Jonagold, Mutsu, and Winesap are among our favorites.

But say you’re at the farmers market and none of those varieties is in sight. Don’t panic. Cookbook author and former BA food editor Claire Saffitz has a simple trick for finding a worthy substitute: Press your thumb against the apple. If it’s firm enough that you don’t leave an indent, you’re probably in good shape.

Softer apples—those that yield to the pressure of your thumb—are higher in water content and more likely to lose their shape or get soft and mushy when cooked. Save them for applesauce or apple butter, where a little breakdown is exactly the point. For more on why those apples listed above top our list of apple picks, read on.

Whether you’re making a classic apple pie or one with a cheddar-laced crust, the fruit you pick matters.

Granny Smith apples have long been a go-to for baking thanks to their pronounced tartness, firm texture, and year-round availability. Their bright, citrus-like acidity balances the sugar in pies and other desserts, like Gourmet’s classic Apple Strudel, and has made them a favorite among professional bakers for decades.

But they’re not everyone’s first choice anymore. During recipe development for BA Bake Club, senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic found that Granny Smiths repeatedly turned mushy in baked desserts, including their Apple-Cranberry Tarte Tatin and Caramel Apple Monkey Bread. Switching to Honeycrisp produced desserts in which the fruit held its shape—and offered more complex flavor. Granny Smith remains a classic, but if you want distinct pieces of tender fruit, another apple may be a better bet.

Pink Lady apples strike an ideal balance of sweet, tart, and tannic notes. They hold their shape in the oven and are relatively slow to oxidize, so the slices won’t brown as quickly while you’re assembling your dessert. Their bright flavor and relatively wide availability make them our first choice for BA’s Best Apple Pie.

Pink Lady is also a favorite of Christa Campbell of Rainbow Orchards in Camino, California, where they bake plenty of pies. “They keep that divine sweet-tart flavor,” she says, “and have the perfect oh-so-soft crunch and juiciness when baked.”

This superbly crisp apple has a concentrated taste and bakes up juicy but not mushy. Braeburns have pronounced sweetness balanced by tartness, and their flavor becomes richer, almost spicy, in the oven.

They release relatively little liquid during baking, which makes them particularly good for a crumb-topped apple pie: Less excess moisture means less risk of a runny filling or soggy crust. They’re equally at home beneath the streusel topping of Saffitz’s Yeasted Apple Coffee Cake, where their concentrated flavor can stand up to plenty of cinnamon.

Use a mix of apples with the skins on for this colorful Fall Fruit Galette.

Honeycrisps are the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen’s desert island apple. With their shatteringly crisp texture, juicy sweetness, and ability to hold their shape, they are as appealing baked as they are eaten out of hand.

The catch? Honeycrisps can be expensive. Shilpa suggests saving them for recipes that showcase the fruit, like Apple Dumplings, an Apple-Walnut Upside-Down Cake, or old-fashioned baked apples. For recipes where the apples are sliced or chopped and cooked down with sugar and spices, she recommends sticking to “something cheaper and just as effective.”

Golden Delicious apples might not be the most exciting choice for snacking, but their mild flavor becomes sweet, tart, and honeyed in the oven. They soften more than some of the other varieties on this list, making them a good option when you want a tender filling rather than distinct, firm slices.

Freshness is key: Older Golden Delicious apples can become mealy. They’re also less acidic than other varieties on this list, so pair them with a tarter variety or add an extra tablespoon of lemon juice to your pie filling. Their relatively thin skins make them a good candidate for leaving unpeeled in a rustic apple galette.

Tart with a honeyed sweetness, Jonagolds hold up exceptionally well in the oven. Related to Golden Delicious, they have a similarly mellow flavor but a firmer texture, making them excellent for pies and other baked desserts where you want recognizable pieces of apple.

The downside is their short window of peak quality. Jonagolds don’t store particularly well, so look for them early in the fall, especially at farmers markets and orchards. If you find good ones, put them to work in a Naked Apple Tart when they’re at their best.

Firm apples stay suspended in batter better than softer, wetter apples. Try your favorites in this Dutch Apple Snacking Cake.

Also known as Crispin, Mutsu apples are juicy, crunchy, and on the sweeter side. A cross between Golden Delicious and Indo apples, they have a similar flavor to Golden Delicious but a firmer texture that holds up particularly well during cooking.

They’re a great choice for pies, tarts, and other desserts, like Shilpa’s Glazed Apple Pie Fritters, where you want tender apple pieces that don’t disappear.

Winesap apples bring intense, full-bodied flavor with deep cider-like notes, and are equally suited to cooking, eating fresh, and making cider. They resist breaking down during cooking, adding complexity to baked desserts while keeping their shape.

Their assertive flavor makes them especially good in recipes with other fruits like an Apple-Rhubarb Crumble, or strongly flavored ingredients like a puff-pastry apple tart with almonds, maple syrup, and brandy.

Can you use the same apples for pie, cake, and crisp?

Generally, yes. Firm, flavorful apples work well in a range of baked desserts, but the ideal variety depends on the texture you want. For pies and tarts with distinct slices, prioritize apples that hold their shape. In cakes, crisps, and cobblers, a slightly softer apple can work well too.

Which apples should you avoid for baking?

Soft or mealy apples are less suited to desserts where you want the fruit to retain its shape. McIntosh, for example, tends to break down readily when cooked, making it better suited to applesauce or apple butter. But if you’re making a dessert where a softer filling is welcome, that tendency isn’t necessarily a drawback.

Do you need to peel apples before baking?

Not always. Leaving the skins on can add color and texture, especially in rustic desserts. For a more uniform filling, peeling is usually preferable. It ultimately depends on the recipe and whether you enjoy the texture of cooked apple skins.

#140. Pumpkin Cheesecake Muffins

Loaded with pumpkin seeds, canned pumpkin purée, and pumpkin pie spice, these big streusel-topped muffins are every fall lover’s dream come true. And to make things even better, the inside of each muffin is stuffed with a soft, lightly sweetened cream cheese mixture. Make the cheesecake filling and the streusel ahead of time to pace things out if it’s helpful. Don’t, even for a minute, consider using anything other than Libby’s 100% pure pumpkin purée (not pie mix). Nothing is better. We promise.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Whisk ⅓ cup coarsely chopped raw pumpkin seeds, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. light brown sugar, ½ tsp. pumpkin pie spice, and a pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl to combine. Using your fingers, rub in 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, until moist pea-size lumps form. Chill until ready to use.

Do Ahead: Streusel can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and keep chilled.

Vigorously whisk 6 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar, 2 tsp. all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. vanilla extract, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl until combined and smooth.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and chill.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Line cups of a standard 12-cup muffin pan with paper liners. Whisk 2 large eggs, 1½ cups (packed; 300 g) light brown sugar, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, ¼ cup whole milk, 1 Tbsp. pumpkin pie spice, 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth, about 1 minute. Whisk 1¾ cups (219 g) all-purpose flour and 1½ tsp. baking powder in a small bowl to combine. Add to pumpkin mixture and fold in with a rubber spatula until just incorporated and no large dry streaks of flour remain (don’t overmix; batter will be lumpy).

Bake muffins until streusel is crisp and muffins spring back when gently pressed, 24–27 minutes. Let muffins cool in pan 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and let cool until just warm or completely.

Do Ahead: Muffins can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

#141. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#142. Pecan Pie Cheesecake

Ditch the same old Thanksgiving desserts and try this fun twist on classic pecan pie this year. Cheesecake makes basically everything better, and that’s especially true for this dish. This recipe takes the classic pie to new heights by introducing an extra creamy base and a sweet, sticky pecan topping that we’d add to practically anything. Whether you’re a classic cheesecake lover at heart or are simply looking to go beyond pies this season, this pecan pie cheesecake will be the star at any holiday spread.

Once your cheesecake is done, turn off the heat, prop open the oven door, and let the cheesecake cool in the oven for around 1 hour. Then, remove the aluminum foil and refrigerate the cheesecake in the pan until firm, at least 5 hours and up to overnight. Serve it right away, or wrap it in plastic wrap and keep it refrigerated for up to 5 days. We recommend not topping the cheesecake until you’re ready to serve, but if you’re storing prepared cheesecake, be prepared that the topping will change texture.

#143. These Immersive Coffee Tours Follow the Beans From Tree to Cup

Travelers who can’t go a day without press-and-go espresso pods or a ­meditative pour-over ritual, rejoice! Coffee tourism is on the rise, and, thanks to expert tour operators with access to the best farms and baristas, your next visit to Latin America, East Africa, or Southeast Asia can be as caffeinated as you want. That could entail lingering with like-minded locals in cafés or stomping on the very soil in which these prized beans grow. If you’re eager to geek out on the whats and hows of it all, immersive education is always on the table—and in the cup.

In the Antioquia region, a custom itinerary with True Colombia Travel balances exclusive access to three of the country’s best producers with myriad adventures (like coffee in a village where locals still get around on horseback). Enthusiasts will marvel at coffee trees on volcanic slopes and learn about fermentation techniques. A visit to Café Cocondo Orgánico, where coffee is cross-­pollinated with mango, avocado, orange, and soursop trees, is especially thrilling.

Known for high-quality ­arabica and robusta beans, this East African nation is paradise for those who crave a brightly flavored brew. Arusha Coffee Lodge by Elewana is conveniently located between Mount Kilimanjaro and the Ngorongoro Conservation Area. It’s also surrounded by 100 acres of coffee trees. Hotel guests can tour the roasting facilities and sample as much of the final product as they’d like. Don’t miss the day’s rotating selection of java-flavored treats, which might include nutty cakes, tiramisu, or scones.

Every year, Augusto Carneiro—founder of Nossa Familia Coffee in Portland, Oregon—leads tours of Guatemala City’s third-wave scene. Travelers start by sharing breakfast with the owners of the trendy café Coffee District, then help with the harvest at a farm partway up Volcán de Agua. Later, they head to Finca San Jerónimo Miramar in the Atitlán region to learn about grafting arabica plants onto robusta roots. There are also many sorts of excursions, from a hike on Acatenango mountain to swimming in Lake Atitlán.

Guided experiences around the globe offer a chance to meet the makers behind your single-origin roast.

#144. Give Greek-Style Burgers 10x The Flavor (Grab One Creamy Ingredient)

Despite the dish's all-American reputation, a burger welcomes global influences. From Denmark's classic gravy-topped Bøfsandwich to the omelette-wrapped Malaysian Ramly burger, worldly reinterpretations are plentiful. And for a spin with a distinctly Mediterranean touch, look towards the Greek biftekia. A comforting home staple, this beef dish is akin to a meatball meets burger, full of bold flavor.

Biftekia consists of flavorful patties made with a heavily seasoned lean beef mix, held together with breadcrumbs and eggs. As it comes, it's already quite a flavorful construction. Yet the dish's texture and flavor can be enhanced even further by stuffing the patties with feta, making a riff called biftekia gemista. Reminiscent of a Juicy Lucy cheeseburger, the salty dairy melts right into the meat, enhancing the beef patties with a unique creamy touch.

The construction looks elaborate, but actual assembly is a breeze. While forming the beef patties, it's simply necessary to make a space big enough for a slice of feta, then enclose the cheese with meat on all sides, thereby preventing run-off. The patties are then traditionally charcoal grilled or pan fried, producing a burger rendition full of Greek character.

Unlike a traditional American burger, biftekia are not always served on bread, but instead often consumed standalone. To cut through the meaty richness, it's common to garnish the patties with fresh vegetables like tomatoes and onions. Rather than ketchup, mustard, or relish, a bowl of tzatziki sauce is a classic accompaniment. And like its American counterpart, a serving of fries or roasted potatoes rounds out the experience.

Enjoyed with a fork and knife, feta-stuffed biftekia makes for a distinct burger-eating experience. The patties are often richly seasoned, featuring additions like hot smoked paprika and oregano, as well as fresh herbs like parsley, mint, and thyme. Once sliced in, the melted cheese pours out of the burger core, moistening the lean beef, and adding a salty flavor. Especially when chargrilled, the meal can feel more like a kebab rather than a burger.

It's a delicious experience — but don't rule out stuffing feta into a classically American burger build, too. Worked into a thin patty, the cheese can delectably flavor a less intricate beef burger composition, no egg and breadcrumbs necessary. And feel free to try a ground turkey version or even Impossible burgers with feta, too. A serving of traditional biftekia is delicious, but the feta cheese shines in a wide array of burger recipes.

#145. What’s the Difference Between Apple Juice and Apple Cider?

Apple cider gets all the attention in fall, but what sets it apart from ordinary apple juice?

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Apple season is a big deal in Oregon, and cider is one of my favorite things about it. Of course apple pies and crisps and tarts are wonderful, but there’s something especially cozy about freshly pressed cider with its cloudy appearance and robust apple flavor. We have a few apple trees on our property—although calling them our trees might be a little generous. The deer seem to have a stronger claim to the fruit, and have been remarkably unwilling to share. Fortunately, our neighbors have a more productive relationship with apples (and fences). Every fall, they turn their harvest into fresh apple cider, which they generously share with us. It’s a pretty nice arrangement.

We were enjoying some of our neighbors’ delicious hot cider recently when my son asked me what makes apple cider different from apple juice. It’s a good question, considering both are made by pressing apples, and the answer isn’t quite as straightforward as the labels might suggest.

If you’ve ever had cider fresh from the orchard, you’ve probably noticed that it looks and tastes different from the apple juice you buy at the grocery store. Apple cider is usually cloudy, with a fuller apple flavor and sometimes a little tartness. Depending on the types of apples used, one batch can taste quite different from the next, with some leaning sweeter and others having a sharper, more tart flavor.

The difference generally comes down to processing. Both drinks begin with apples that are crushed and pressed for their juice, but apple cider is typically left unfiltered or only lightly filtered. Apple juice usually goes through additional filtering, which removes the fine apple particles responsible for cider’s cloudy appearance. That’s why most commercial apple juice is clear and golden, while fresh cider tends to look as though it came straight from the press. The additional processing gives commercial apple juice its familiar clear appearance and helps manufacturers produce a consistent product year-round.

The distinction isn’t quite as clear-cut as it might seem, though. While apple cider is commonly less filtered than apple juice, there’s no legal requirement that one must be cloudy and the other clear. That’s why you’ll occasionally come across unfiltered apple juice—or cider that’s been processed much like ordinary juice. And outside the United States, the terminology changes again. Order cider in England, for instance, and you’ll be served the alcoholic version that Americans call hard cider.

There’s one other difference worth checking before you buy fresh apple cider: whether it’s been pasteurized. Some orchard-pressed ciders are sold unpasteurized, which means they haven’t been heat-treated to kill potentially harmful bacteria. The FDA advises that children, pregnant people, older adults and people with weakened immune systems avoid unpasteurized juice and cider. If you’re buying directly from a farm or orchard, it’s worth asking how the cider was pasteurized.

Generally speaking, yes. In most recipes, you can substitute apple juice for apple cider, or vice versa, without making any other adjustments. Both bring apple flavor, sweetness and a little acidity, though the proportions can vary depending on the apples and how the drink was made.

I’d pay closer attention to recipes that depend on a pronounced apple flavor. Apple cider doughnuts are a good example. Many recipes call for simmering apple cider until it’s reduced, which concentrates the flavor before it goes into the batter. You can do the same thing with apple juice, although the flavor of the finished doughnuts will depend on what you started with. The same applies to apple cakes, muffins and other baked goods that call for apple cider. In most cases, either will work, but when apple flavor is the point, I’d reach for cider.

I also love cooking with apple cider, especially when pork is involved. A splash in a roasting pan or a slow braise adds sweetness and acidity, both of which work beautifully with richer cuts of pork. Apple juice can do the same job, though I’d be sure to taste the sauce before serving. If it’s sweeter than you’d like, a little lemon juice or apple cider vinegar can bring it back into balance.

If you’re making a drink like mulled cider, the difference isn’t quite as important. Apple juice takes perfectly well to cinnamon, cloves, orange peel and a gentle simmer on the stove. Fresh cider will generally give you a fuller apple flavor, but either makes a perfectly cozy fall drink.

Ultimately, you should choose based on what you’re making and what’s available. For everyday cooking and baking, there’s rarely a compelling reason to make a special trip for one if you already have the other. But when fresh cider is in season, it’s definitely worth enjoying. Especially when someone has been generous enough to do all the pressing for you.

#146. 39 Food Gifts We’re Giving (and Secretly Hoping to Get) in 2026

It’s never too early to get a head start on holiday gifting. After all, getting your shopping done now means you can focus on the important things once the holidays actually roll around—you know, like spending time with family, cooking a festive feast, and enjoying plenty of mulled cider and wine. If you’re in need of gifts for the food people in your life, look no further. These are the 27 gifts we’re planning to give (or hoping to receive) this year.

A handmade mug is a little luxury they’ll use every day (and think of you when they do!). Tailor your pick to your giftee’s caffeine preferences to make it feel more personal: opt for an oversized mug for the friend who needs drip coffee on an IV, or a more petite cup for the cappuccino drinker.

Cookbooks make for great gifts, and lucky for you, we’ve spent all year cooking through dozens of them to find the best ones. These are a few favorites from our quarterly best new releases roundups, like Yotam Ottolenghi’s latest collection of weeknight-friendly recipes and Roxana Jullapat’s ode to morning baking.

Get the friend who nerds out on coffee roasting and fermentation processes a subscription to Podium Coffee Club’s Platinum tier, which sources its monthly beans from award-winning roasters across the country. The Platinum tier is focused on rare coffee varietals made using experimental techniques, so it’s perfect for someone who likes an expressive, unique roast.

If you’re the kind of person who’s always ordering the fun new seasonal pour-over option at your local craft coffee shop, or who hunts down rare bean varietals like it’s your job, Podium Coffee Club’s Podium Platinum is the coffee subscription for you. Founded in 2023, Podium is a relatively new kid on the block in the world of coffee subs. The concept? A subscription service that solely sends out coffees that have stood on the podium (hence the name) at a major US coffee competition. The brand’s Podium Platinum subscription focuses on coffees that are unique and experimental in some way, be it flavor-wise, varietal-wise, or through the processing technique used.

Testers: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor, and Alaina Chou, commerce writer In the two months we’ve tested this service, we’ve received two bags of coffee that have lived up to that claim. The first bag was a light roast from Royal Flamingo Coffee, a micro-roaster based in Columbus, Ohio. The notes of blueberries, white chocolate, and florals definitely came through in the brewed coffee in both smell and taste, though not too aggressively. We quite enjoyed this one.

The next coffee hailed from Wonderstate Coffee in Wisconsin and claimed notes of gummy bear, melon, and cooked berries. That might seem like a crazy flavor profile for a bag of coffee, but the brewed stuff was subtle and highly drinkable.

The bottom line: This is a great coffee subscription to get if you’re looking to explore, nerd out on coffee-making processes, or discover award-winning roasters from across the country. Note that Podium also offers a less expensive Podium Gold subscription option, which does not get you the same unique selection that the Platinum offers.

We all know someone who finishes every dish with flaky salt. Get them this pack of tins from Jacobsen Salt Co., each of which is filled with a different kind of infused salt. These all-natural firestarters are a chic alternative to the typical firestarter logs, and would make an excellent host gift for the friend who’s lucky enough to have a fireplace or outdoor fire pit.

An olive oil can is the kind of thing that’s meant to live on your counter, so why not upgrade to a beautiful one? It goes with multiple different home aesthetics and looks equally at home by the stove as it does on a dinner party table.

Your shoppy shop-obsessed friend will jump at the chance to rep their favorite pantry brand, whether that means donning a “Fish Dad” hat from beloved conservas company Fishwife or throwing on a bright blue Fly By Jing sweatshirt to keep them toasty this winter. Any friend who cooks will appreciate receiving this set of ramekins from cult-favorite pottery brand East Fork. At four ounces, they’re a versatile size that works for equally as well for portioning mise en place as it does for serving condiments or sauces.

This stylish pepper grinder looks incredibly cool, but it’s also made with function in mind. That swanky-looking handle? This gift set brings a taste of Richard Christiansen’s Flamingo Estate to your pantry. It’s full of high-quality products you’ll actually use—no weird spice blends or waxy chocolates here.

These stunning wood cutting boards are truly heirloom-worthy, handcrafted by expert woodworkers from sturdy hardwood. They're versatile pieces that are durable enough to be your everyday chopping boards and beautiful enough to serve as serving vessels for cheese and charcuterie.

For the friend who would gladly eat tinned fish for dinner every night, I suggest this 10-pack of greatest hits from Fishwife. It’s got a little bit of everything, from the brand’s smoked salmon collab with Fly By Jing to the fan-favorite Smoked Rainbow Trout with Chimichurri, plus their limited-edition Little Sardines, which are only available as a part of the brand’s holiday sets.

The iced beverage fiend in your life will go gaga for this mini version of our longtime favorite ice maker, the GE Opal. Despite its more compact footprint and lower price tag, it produces the same crunchy nugget ice we know and love—and it’s available in some cute colorways.

You can’t go wrong with a beautiful vase, especially if you fill that vase with a bouquet of fresh flowers. This colorful glass number is sure to earn your giftee compliments, and I love that it’s hand-blown, which means every piece is one-of-a-kind.

Give the latte lover who also values convenience this do-it-all machine from Nespresso, which combines the brand's signature pod technology with an automatic milk frother that'll have them pouring latte art like a pro.

When in doubt, opt for wine. But instead of picking up a random bottle, treat your giftee to a month (or three, or six!) of deliveries from New York City wine bar and shop Parcelle, whose Wine Drop subscription service has been a longtime BA fave. Choose between red, white, rare, or a curated monthly mix, and Parcelle will take care of the rest.

#147. Pumpkin Enchiladas With Black Beans

Homemade enchiladas might sound like a laborious weekend project, but with a few clever tricks, this version made with black beans and pumpkin can be whipped up on even the most hurried of work nights. For starters, canned pumpkin creates the base of a quick sauce that requires no precooking. And because they are vegetarian, the filling—a combination of canned black beans, onion, and bell pepper flecked with cilantro—comes together in a flash. In lieu of baking the enchiladas, this version opts for broiling in order to brown the tops while also heating the enchiladas through in the same skillet you cook the beans in. A flourish of pumpkin seeds, sliced onion, cilantro, and fresh lime brightens up everything, although serving them straight from the oven would be just as delicious.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large broilerproof skillet over medium-high. Add 1 large white onion, finely chopped, and 1 medium green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, and cook, stirring often, until browned in spots and fragrant, 7–9 minutes. Add 4 garlic cloves, finely grated, two 15-oz. cans black beans, rinsed, and 2 Tbsp. chili powder and cook, stirring occasionally, just until combined and beans are warmed through, about 3 minutes. Transfer bean mixture to a large bowl; reserve pan.

Smash bean mixture with a spoon or potato masher until about half of the beans are mashed. Mix in juice of 1 lime and ¼ cup coarsely chopped cilantro; season with kosher salt. Set bean mixture aside.

Whisk together one 15-oz. can pumpkin purée, 1 tsp. Tabasco, and 1¼ cups water in a large bowl; season pumpkin sauce with salt.

Place 1 of twelve 6" flour tortillas on a surface. Scoop out ¼ cup (heaping) reserved bean mixture and arrange in center down length of tortilla. Scatter some of 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup), over, then roll up tortilla into a cylinder. Place, seam side down, in reserved skillet. Repeat process with remaining tortillas. Brush tops with oil.

Place a rack in upper third of oven; heat broiler. Broil enchiladas until tops are deeply toasted and charred in spots, 4–7 minutes (depending on your broiler; watch carefully as they can go from browned to burnt very quickly). Pour pumpkin sauce over enchiladas and spread into an even layer. Top with remaining 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup) and raw pumpkin seeds (pepitas; if using). Broil until cheese is melted and deeply browned in spots, 4–7 minutes (watch carefully). Remove enchiladas from broiler and top with thinly sliced white onion and cilantro leaves with tender stems. Serve with lime wedges for squeezing over.

#148. 17 apple dessert recipes for fall baking: Embrace the season with apple tarts, cookies, cakes, and more.

There’s an apple dessert for everyone. For the purists, there are lattice-topped pies and shingled galettes. For the non-traditionalists, there are caramel-frosted cakes and fritter-inspired loaves. And for apple lovers that hate cinnamon? Well, there are custardy cakes and classic French tarts. Ready to start baking with fall’s best fruit? Read on for our best apple dessert recipes.

There’s no shortage of apple in this cake — applesauce keeps things moist while boiled cider adds sharp, tangy fruit flavor. The cake is great on its own, but pair it with light, creamy Whipped Caramel Frosting, and you’ve got an irresistible baked version of a caramel apple (with none of the fears about your teeth).

You only need one apple (and two people eager for an apple dessert) to make a pair of these adorable galettes. Half the apple is sliced, while the other half is grated, which creates a hidden layer of jam beneath the shingled slices. Flaky fruit tarts don’t get easier (or cuter!) than this.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

Get the recipe: Apple Cider Snickerdoodles

This super-easy one-bowl cake is loaded with chopped apples and walnuts, which give this moist, spiced cake heft and texture. The frosting, akin to a velvety brown sugar fudge, adds a textural counterpoint and an extra dimension of richness.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" x 13" pan

Cinnamon and apple go together like a flannel and a beanie, but this recipe one-ups that perfect pairing with the addition of cinnamon chips. Diced apple and melty pockets of cinnamon-sugar are also studded throughout these autumnal scones, which are then finished off with an extra-crunchy sugar coating.

Get the recipe: Fresh Apple Cinnamon Scones

Ribbons of gooey, cinnamon-scented apples are twisted throughout this striking enriched loaf. Beautiful to behold (and easier to make than you’d think), this braided babka would be a welcome addition to any Rosh Hashanah table or fall celebration.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

Spoiler alert: The eponymous secret ingredient in this special pie is boiled cider! Made by cooking down apple cider into a concentrate, a few drops deliver big apple flavor. When used in apple pies, it super-charges the fruit’s tart, tangy flavor, delivering a pie with over-the-top apple goodness.

Get the recipe: Secret Ingredient Apple Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider

If your go-to doughnut order is an apple fritter, this mash-up cake was made for you. The batter is made using the reverse creaming technique, which ensures a velvety crumb and tender texture. In each slice, there’s a filling and topping of cinnamon-dusted apples and a final drizzle of icy-white vanilla glaze. A slice rivals anything you can get at your local doughnut shop.

This time of year, apples don't need much to make them shine. The paper-thin, crackly top layer of this cobbler highlights the juicy fruit beneath. It doesn’t need a lot of adornment, but a scoop of vanilla ice cream never hurt anything.

Is it a bar? A slab pie? Both! This breezy recipe swaps the flaky pastry for a buttery shortbread crust but keeps the warm, gooey apples and classic spices for a sliceable, portable dessert. To finish, there's a crumbly streusel topping inspired by Dutch apple pie.

When you want a fruit dessert fast, you can always count on crisps — no rolling, no resting, and most importantly, no special equipment required! This crisp is made with a handful of baking basics, so when you find yourself with a surplus of apples, dessert is barely an hour away.
