#149. The 15 Cookbooks We’re Most Looking Forward to This Fall

Fall cookbook season is upon us, and in advance of the holidays and cooler nights, that means big-name releases from restaurant-world heavyweights (ahem, Eric Ripert and Kwame Onwuachi) along with topic-based books delving into underrepresented cuisines (Basque, Taiwanese, and plant-based Ghanaian, to name a few) and even specific courses. There’s plenty to choose from this year, which is why we’re presenting a special supersize fall cookbook preview, with 15 of the titles we’re most looking forward to.

Ghanaian author Afia Amoako has amassed hundreds of thousands of followers on social media, where her account @eatwithafia highlights Ghanaian and West African cultural traditions and recipes through a plant-based lens. In her lush, colorful debut cookbook, Amoako builds a deeply researched archive of a cuisine that’s often passed down only orally, and we all benefit from her efforts: More than half of the recipes are traditional and unmodified, not modern interpretations, creating an essential record of Ghanaian foodways. Recipes include classics such as jollof rice and okra stew, plus “roadside snacks” like ofam (a sweet plantain-based snacking cake) and drinks including iced Moringa milk tea. (Avery, Aug. 18)

Pim Techamuanvivit is a legend. A former food blogger turned chef of several Michelin-starred Thai restaurants in San Francisco and Bangkok, she is uniquely poised to help guide home cooks interested in understanding the nuances of Thai cuisine. Teaming up with fellow food writing superstar Andrea Nguyen, Techamuanvivit created more than 100 new recipes covering an expansive range of Thai flavors and techniques, including chapters dedicated to “Grilled, Roasted, Simmered, and Steamed” dishes, along with “Stir-Fried and Deep Fried” delights, plus soups, curries, noodles, and more. (Ten Speed Press, Aug. 25)

Ali Stoner, aka the delightfully named @rovinghaggis on social media, is a Glasgow-born, Melbourne-based home cook and former Masterchef Australia contestant who tackles the flavors of her heritage in her debut cookbook (the title is Scottish slang for a simple, comforting meal). There are plenty of hearty breakfasts and handheld “savouries” (tattie scones and bacon pieces, “wee tongue sandwiches,” and chicken Balmoral sausage rolls), plus sweet puddings (try the Tipsy Laird trifle), soups, and breads. It’s refreshing to see modern Scottish cuisine given the spotlight, especially in such an approachable, home-cook-friendly fashion—with moody, evocative photos, to boot. (Mitchell Beazley, Sept. 10)

PBS host and Mexico City native Pati Jinich is back with a new cookbook (following 2021’s Treasures of the Mexican Table). This time she focuses on the cuisines of the borderlands between Mexico and the U.S. (or, as she prefers to call it, “la frontera”). What that translates to is thoughtfully researched dishes that go far beyond Tex-Mex, including skirt steak and shrimp hot pot, seafood fried rice with asparagus and mushrooms, and smashburger tacos with poblano peppers. Throughout, she intersperses personal stories of growing up between two cultures and challenges readers to think beyond the confines of a single place. (Harvest, Sept. 15)

Enrique Salmón is a Rarámuri (Tarahumara) scholar at Cal State University, East Bay, and an expert in the connection between Indigenous foodways and land-management practices and climate change. In his second cookbook, he explores the concept of “kincentricity,” an Indigenous worldview emphasizing the interconnectedness of all living beings and our responsibility to be good stewards of the planet we share. After a comprehensive introduction, Salmón dives into the history, harvesting, and cooking methods of more than 50 Indigenous ingredients, ranging from huckleberries to black walnuts to wild onions. The result is as much an ethnography as it is a cookbook, from an author with the lived experience to guide the newly kincentric-curious. (Rizzoli, Sept. 15)

In his second cookbook, Kwame Onwuachi, the Bronx-raised chef behind Tatiana in New York and Dōgon in Washington, D.C., promises personal recipes “about how I really eat” at any and all hours of the day. What that translates to is big, bold dishes that aren’t afraid to mash up cultures and cuisines, like Red Stew Chicken Parm and Drunken Noodles Alla Vodka. (“That’s not a thing! Well, it wasn’t a thing, but now it is,” he explains.) There are chapters dedicated to sandwiches, the “Holy Grail of the Bronx” (aka New York Chinese food), and “Goddamn Veggie Sides,” which should give you some indication of the verve and voice behind this raucous collection. (Knopf, Sept. 22)

Dona Murad is the Bahrain-born owner of New York’s beloved Librae, a self-described “third culture bakery” that draws equally from SWANA flavors and Danish technique. With recipes for pastries like rose and pistachio croissants, za’atar and labneh morning buns, and loomi and lemon curd babka, her debut book is aimed at home bakers who revel in a project, but Murad walks readers of all levels through techniques like lamination with a steady, gentle hand. And with step-by-step photos throughout (plus plenty of beginner-friendly bakes), you’ll be turning out pastries that inspire lines down the block, just like Librae, in no time. (Quadrille, Sept. 22)

In his ninth book, Eric Ripert, the celebrity chef and owner of New York’s fine-dining temple Le Bernadin, draws on his travels to Buddhist monasteries across Korea and Japan to put together 75-plus recipes designed to emphasize the joy and mindfulness that cooking with plants can bring. The recipes here hopscotch across Asian, European, and Latin cultures, in chapters introduced by “guiding principles” like gratitude, intention, and joy. That translates to recipes like Radish & Turnip Carpaccio With Yuzu Kosho Vinaigrette, Tamales Rojos, and Seared Tofu With Chili Crisp, among others. Through it all, the boundlessly enthusiastic Ripert encourages home cooks to consider cooking itself as a meditative act and to enjoy the process of nourishing ourselves in both body and spirit. (Random House, Oct. 6)

The crew behind the acclaimed Montreal wine bar Mon Lapin—namely co-chefs Marc-Olivier Frappier and Jessica Noël, along with sommelier Vanya Filipovic and coauthor Mireille Silcoff—team up for a cookbook that’s every bit as chic and vibey as the restaurant that inspired it. With chapters like “What Is a Wine Bar Anyway?” and “Every Vegetable Is a Summer Vegetable in Quebec,” their collective voice shines through, and recipes like White Asparagus Soldiers with Good Anchovies and Eggplant-and-Cantaloupe Ceviche belie a deep understanding of quality ingredients and elegant presentation. As to be expected, there’s plenty of wine writing throughout, making this a must for future dinner parties. (Phaidon, Oct. 7)

Award-winning New York-based pastry chef Caroline Schiff (formerly of Gage & Tollner) makes her cookbook debut with this bright, cheerful baking book, which encourages readers to consider making and eating some form of sweet treat as a daily ritual. Yes, there are a few advanced-level pastries (such as Hazelnut Roche Profiteroles with Glossy Chocolate Sauce), but most of the recipes are approachable and friendly, as outlined in chapters like “Bake Once, Snack All Week” (snacking cakes) and “Little Bakes Just for You (and Maybe a Friend)”. With a section dedicated entirely to doughs, toppings, and crumbs, Schiff equips bakers of all levels with the confidence they need to make dessert a regular part of their day. (Abrams, Oct. 13)

Ernesto’s chef Ryan Bartlow is American, but he spent years living and cooking at the three Michelin-starred Akelarre in San Sebastián, Spain. Despite his fine-dining bona fides, though, what Bartlow really fell for during his time abroad was the rustic, humble side of Basque cooking, codified, as he writes, “on farms, in fishing ports and cider houses.” In his handsome debut with coauthor Laurie Woolever, Bartlow champions recipes with simple ingredients, like a classic tortilla de patatas, callos de Madrileña (a smoky, spicy tripe stew), and a lush crème caramel, along with pintxos and cocktails. This is a book fully steeped in a sense of place, including helpful guides to the Basque language and Basque-Spanish drinking culture, and a travel guide to the region itself, with gorgeous photographs. (Abrams, Oct. 13)

Eric Sze, the chef behind 886 and Wenwen in New York, teams up with veteran food writer Elyse Inamine for a voicey, intimate, and delightfully neon-soaked exploration of the foods of Taiwan, where he was born and raised. The first half of the book focuses on Taiwanese dishes as they’re presented in Taiwan itself, while the second half is more experimental, covering the fusion-y (a term the chef embraces) recipes Sze has perfected cooking at his New York pop-ups and restaurants, such as Mochi Gnocchi with Chili Oil Pumpkin purée and Beef Noodle Soup Ragu). Shot colorfully on location, this is a book brimming with personality—and a sneakily impressive amount of research—on every page. (Hardie Grant, Oct. 20)

Siberia-born, London-based academic and food writer Alissa Timoshkina is the author of two previous cookbooks on Eastern European foodways, though she’s perhaps best known as the founder of #CookForUkraine, a global fundraising campaign supporting humanitarian relief. It’s fitting, then, that her latest title is focused on humble-yet-mighty soups and stews from across a borderless collection of Ukrainian, Jewish, Tatar, Hungarian, Polish, Slovak, and Roma traditions. Organized into “Soups & Broths,” “Stews & Grains,” “Dumplings & Pasta,” and “Sweet Comfort,” the chapters highlight the myriad ways in which foods eaten with a spoon have the power to soothe, surprise, and connect people across cultures and conflicts. (Quadrille, Oct. 20)

Fuchsia Dunlop, who graduated from culinary school in Sichuan Province, is one of the West’s foremost experts in Chinese cuisine, guiding home cooks with a knowledgeable and compassionate hand. The author of several renowned cookbooks on the topic, she’s back with a strikingly illustrated new volume, focused on the five taste sensations (sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and pungent) that a Chinese cook strives to balance harmoniously within a dish. Instead of a dogmatic approach to traditional dishes, she encourages cooks to apply Chinese seasonings and flavoring techniques to “whatever ingredients you have on hand,” assuring readers that “the ways of the Chinese kitchen travel well.” (W.W. Norton, Oct. 20)

Hungry for even more stories to sink your teeth into?

From underrepresented cuisines to restaurant-world heavyweights, this season’s crop of new releases has something for everyone.

Fall cookbook season is upon us, and in advance of the holidays and cooler nights, that means big-name releases from restaurant-world heavyweights (ahem, Eric Ripert and Kwame Onwuachi) along with topic-based books delving into underrepresented cuisines (Basque, Taiwanese, and plant-based Ghanaian, to name a few) and even specific courses. There’s plenty to choose from this year, which is why we’re presenting a special supersize fall cookbook preview, with 15 of the titles we’re most looking forward to.

Ghanaian author Afia Amoako has amassed hundreds of thousands of followers on social media, where her account @eatwithafia highlights Ghanaian and West African cultural traditions and recipes through a plant-based lens. In her lush, colorful debut cookbook, Amoako builds a deeply researched archive of a cuisine that’s often passed down only orally, and we all benefit from her efforts: More than half of the recipes are traditional and unmodified, not modern interpretations, creating an essential record of Ghanaian foodways. Recipes include classics such as jollof rice and okra stew, plus “roadside snacks” like ofam (a sweet plantain-based snacking cake) and drinks including iced Moringa milk tea. (Avery, Aug. 18)

Pim Techamuanvivit is a legend. A former food blogger turned chef of several Michelin-starred Thai restaurants in San Francisco and Bangkok, she is uniquely poised to help guide home cooks interested in understanding the nuances of Thai cuisine. Teaming up with fellow food writing superstar Andrea Nguyen, Techamuanvivit created more than 100 new recipes covering an expansive range of Thai flavors and techniques, including chapters dedicated to “Grilled, Roasted, Simmered, and Steamed” dishes, along with “Stir-Fried and Deep Fried” delights, plus soups, curries, noodles, and more. (Ten Speed Press, Aug. 25)

Ali Stoner, aka the delightfully named @rovinghaggis on social media, is a Glasgow-born, Melbourne-based home cook and former Masterchef Australia contestant who tackles the flavors of her heritage in her debut cookbook (the title is Scottish slang for a simple, comforting meal). There are plenty of hearty breakfasts and handheld “savouries” (tattie scones and bacon pieces, “wee tongue sandwiches,” and chicken Balmoral sausage rolls), plus sweet puddings (try the Tipsy Laird trifle), soups, and breads. It’s refreshing to see modern Scottish cuisine given the spotlight, especially in such an approachable, home-cook-friendly fashion—with moody, evocative photos, to boot. (Mitchell Beazley, Sept. 10)

PBS host and Mexico City native Pati Jinich is back with a new cookbook (following 2021’s Treasures of the Mexican Table). This time she focuses on the cuisines of the borderlands between Mexico and the U.S. (or, as she prefers to call it, “la frontera”). What that translates to is thoughtfully researched dishes that go far beyond Tex-Mex, including skirt steak and shrimp hot pot, seafood fried rice with asparagus and mushrooms, and smashburger tacos with poblano peppers. Throughout, she intersperses personal stories of growing up between two cultures and challenges readers to think beyond the confines of a single place. (Harvest, Sept. 15)

Enrique Salmón is a Rarámuri (Tarahumara) scholar at Cal State University, East Bay, and an expert in the connection between Indigenous foodways and land-management practices and climate change. In his second cookbook, he explores the concept of “kincentricity,” an Indigenous worldview emphasizing the interconnectedness of all living beings and our responsibility to be good stewards of the planet we share. After a comprehensive introduction, Salmón dives into the history, harvesting, and cooking methods of more than 50 Indigenous ingredients, ranging from huckleberries to black walnuts to wild onions. The result is as much an ethnography as it is a cookbook, from an author with the lived experience to guide the newly kincentric-curious. (Rizzoli, Sept. 15)

In his second cookbook, Kwame Onwuachi, the Bronx-raised chef behind Tatiana in New York and Dōgon in Washington, D.C., promises personal recipes “about how I really eat” at any and all hours of the day. What that translates to is big, bold dishes that aren’t afraid to mash up cultures and cuisines, like Red Stew Chicken Parm and Drunken Noodles Alla Vodka. (“That’s not a thing! Well, it wasn’t a thing, but now it is,” he explains.) There are chapters dedicated to sandwiches, the “Holy Grail of the Bronx” (aka New York Chinese food), and “Goddamn Veggie Sides,” which should give you some indication of the verve and voice behind this raucous collection. (Knopf, Sept. 22)

Dona Murad is the Bahrain-born owner of New York’s beloved Librae, a self-described “third culture bakery” that draws equally from SWANA flavors and Danish technique. With recipes for pastries like rose and pistachio croissants, za’atar and labneh morning buns, and loomi and lemon curd babka, her debut book is aimed at home bakers who revel in a project, but Murad walks readers of all levels through techniques like lamination with a steady, gentle hand. And with step-by-step photos throughout (plus plenty of beginner-friendly bakes), you’ll be turning out pastries that inspire lines down the block, just like Librae, in no time. (Quadrille, Sept. 22)

In his ninth book, Eric Ripert, the celebrity chef and owner of New York’s fine-dining temple Le Bernadin, draws on his travels to Buddhist monasteries across Korea and Japan to put together 75-plus recipes designed to emphasize the joy and mindfulness that cooking with plants can bring. The recipes here hopscotch across Asian, European, and Latin cultures, in chapters introduced by “guiding principles” like gratitude, intention, and joy. That translates to recipes like Radish & Turnip Carpaccio With Yuzu Kosho Vinaigrette, Tamales Rojos, and Seared Tofu With Chili Crisp, among others. Through it all, the boundlessly enthusiastic Ripert encourages home cooks to consider cooking itself as a meditative act and to enjoy the process of nourishing ourselves in both body and spirit. (Random House, Oct. 6)

The crew behind the acclaimed Montreal wine bar Mon Lapin—namely co-chefs Marc-Olivier Frappier and Jessica Noël, along with sommelier Vanya Filipovic and coauthor Mireille Silcoff—team up for a cookbook that’s every bit as chic and vibey as the restaurant that inspired it. With chapters like “What Is a Wine Bar Anyway?” and “Every Vegetable Is a Summer Vegetable in Quebec,” their collective voice shines through, and recipes like White Asparagus Soldiers with Good Anchovies and Eggplant-and-Cantaloupe Ceviche belie a deep understanding of quality ingredients and elegant presentation. As to be expected, there’s plenty of wine writing throughout, making this a must for future dinner parties. (Phaidon, Oct. 7)

Award-winning New York-based pastry chef Caroline Schiff (formerly of Gage & Tollner) makes her cookbook debut with this bright, cheerful baking book, which encourages readers to consider making and eating some form of sweet treat as a daily ritual. Yes, there are a few advanced-level pastries (such as Hazelnut Roche Profiteroles with Glossy Chocolate Sauce), but most of the recipes are approachable and friendly, as outlined in chapters like “Bake Once, Snack All Week” (snacking cakes) and “Little Bakes Just for You (and Maybe a Friend)”. With a section dedicated entirely to doughs, toppings, and crumbs, Schiff equips bakers of all levels with the confidence they need to make dessert a regular part of their day. (Abrams, Oct. 13)

Ernesto’s chef Ryan Bartlow is American, but he spent years living and cooking at the three Michelin-starred Akelarre in San Sebastián, Spain. Despite his fine-dining bona fides, though, what Bartlow really fell for during his time abroad was the rustic, humble side of Basque cooking, codified, as he writes, “on farms, in fishing ports and cider houses.” In his handsome debut with coauthor Laurie Woolever, Bartlow champions recipes with simple ingredients, like a classic tortilla de patatas, callos de Madrileña (a smoky, spicy tripe stew), and a lush crème caramel, along with pintxos and cocktails. This is a book fully steeped in a sense of place, including helpful guides to the Basque language and Basque-Spanish drinking culture, and a travel guide to the region itself, with gorgeous photographs. (Abrams, Oct. 13)

Eric Sze, the chef behind 886 and Wenwen in New York, teams up with veteran food writer Elyse Inamine for a voicey, intimate, and delightfully neon-soaked exploration of the foods of Taiwan, where he was born and raised. The first half of the book focuses on Taiwanese dishes as they’re presented in Taiwan itself, while the second half is more experimental, covering the fusion-y (a term the chef embraces) recipes Sze has perfected cooking at his New York pop-ups and restaurants, such as Mochi Gnocchi with Chili Oil Pumpkin purée and Beef Noodle Soup Ragu). Shot colorfully on location, this is a book brimming with personality—and a sneakily impressive amount of research—on every page. (Hardie Grant, Oct. 20)

Siberia-born, London-based academic and food writer Alissa Timoshkina is the author of two previous cookbooks on Eastern European foodways, though she’s perhaps best known as the founder of #CookForUkraine, a global fundraising campaign supporting humanitarian relief. It’s fitting, then, that her latest title is focused on humble-yet-mighty soups and stews from across a borderless collection of Ukrainian, Jewish, Tatar, Hungarian, Polish, Slovak, and Roma traditions. Organized into “Soups & Broths,” “Stews & Grains,” “Dumplings & Pasta,” and “Sweet Comfort,” the chapters highlight the myriad ways in which foods eaten with a spoon have the power to soothe, surprise, and connect people across cultures and conflicts. (Quadrille, Oct. 20)

Fuchsia Dunlop, who graduated from culinary school in Sichuan Province, is one of the West’s foremost experts in Chinese cuisine, guiding home cooks with a knowledgeable and compassionate hand. The author of several renowned cookbooks on the topic, she’s back with a strikingly illustrated new volume, focused on the five taste sensations (sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and pungent) that a Chinese cook strives to balance harmoniously within a dish. Instead of a dogmatic approach to traditional dishes, she encourages cooks to apply Chinese seasonings and flavoring techniques to “whatever ingredients you have on hand,” assuring readers that “the ways of the Chinese kitchen travel well.” (W.W. Norton, Oct. 20)

#150. Chicken Pot Pie Casserole

Chicken pot pie is a warm, hearty crowd-pleaser. But for all the comfort it delivers, it can be a difficult dinner dish, with hours of work required to make the perfect pie crust. So, we came up with the perfect solution: chicken pot pie casserole. Classic chicken pot pie filling is baked into a stress-free casserole, topped with buttery biscuits (my favorite store-bought hack) for that tantalizing golden-brown finish. In a little more than an hour, you’ll have a crowd-pleasing weeknight dinner on your hands—no pie crust required.

This casserole is all about ease. After preheating the oven to 375º, melt butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add your diced carrots, celery, onion, thyme, and salt to the skillet, and cook until softened. This should take around 5 to 7 minutes—make sure you are stirring often! Once softened, add the flour and stir to fully coat the vegetables.

After cooking for a couple of minutes more, add the milk, broth, mustard, garlic powder, and even more salt. Whisk to combine, then increase the heat to bring the mixture to a boil. Once boiling, immediately reduce the heat to medium so the mixture can simmer. Let simmer, stirring often, until it has visibly thickened. This should take around 3 to 5 minutes. Once thickened, fold in the chicken and peas. Give it a taste, and add more salt as needed.

Once your mixture is to your liking, transfer it to a baking dish. Grab your biscuits, separate them, then arrange them on top of the filling. Give the entire dish a good sprinkle of salt and pepper, then bake.

Bake until the filling is bubbling, and the biscuits are golden and risen. This should take around 22 to 25 minutes, but depending on the size of your biscuits, they may need longer in the oven. Once done, let the casserole cool for around 5 minutes before serving.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

If you have any leftovers, store them in the fridge in an airtight container for around 3 days. Keep in mind that as time goes on, the biscuits will start to lean more on the soggy side. For the crispiest biscuit topping possible, enjoy this casserole the day of, or separate the biscuits after cooking.

#151. 12 Smart Ways To Use Store-Bought Italian Dressing (That's Not Salad)

You probably won't find a bottle of Italian dressing in a Roman kitchen or Sicilian cupboards. Like many of today's most popular pantry staples, Italian dressing has its roots in American soil. But that's not to say it was invented without Italian influence. One origin story pegs its creation to a Kansas City steakhouse — the Wishbone Restaurant — where the owner's Italian-immigrant mother had brought with her a recipe for a zippy vinaigrette.

Italian dressing as we know it today has adorned salad greens for decades. At its core is an electrifying combination of ingredients that immediately wake up the taste buds, then quickly soothe them with a gentle finish. For this article, we focused on the most traditional store-bought varieties — no eggs or extra cheese: just water, oil, vinegar, salt, sugar, spices, and the additives necessary to preserve the emulsion and deliver that slick, satisfying texture. This unique mix of characteristics makes Italian dressing a great addition to everything from antipasto salads to baked fish to garlic bread. Here are smart ways to use store-bought Italian dressing that aren't salad.

Marinating is a simple and effective way to infuse your food with flavor. The best part is, there aren't too many rules you need to follow. For a basic marination, simply combine a mixture of oil, acid, herbs, and spices. Submerge your vegetables and proteins, and then wait for the chemistry to occur. But while the idea of no guardrails may appeal to your inner culinary daredevil, this fly-by-the-seat approach can lead to a few missteps, especially if you're relatively new to marinating. That's why a store-bought Italian dressing is such a useful shortcut. In one inexpensive bottle, you get all the elements of a good marinade neatly packaged in the right ratios.

So which foods benefit from a marinade of Italian dressing? It's hard to find many that don't. For grilled vegetables, anything you can slice into rounds is fair game: eggplant, zucchini, butternut squash, red or white onions, etc. Strips of bell pepper work, too. With beef, chicken, or pork, a marinade can help flavor and tenderize the meat before it hits the grill, skillet, or flat-top. Just be conscious of marination time. The acid in Italian dressing is so high that it can actually break down or denature the proteins, resulting in meat that's soft or mushy. It also draws out water, making the interior tougher and less juicy, which is why you want to only marinate most meats for two to four hours.

All you need for a good antipasto salad is a simple combination of cured meats, sharp and creamy cheeses, olives, diced vegetables, and a few marinated goodies. Now, it might seem cliché to make an antipasto salad with bottled Italian dressing, but the combination works beautifully — which probably shouldn't come as a major surprise. Italian dressing is both bright and herbaceous, two tasting notes that are necessary to cut the richness of the meat and cheeses while livening up anything that suffers from under seasoning.

Not only does Italian dressing bring harmony and balance, but it makes almost any ingredient a potential addition. You can add meats, cheeses, and marinated vegetables to a bowl of chilled noodles for a charcuterie-loaded pasta salad, or opt for a sweet-and-savory mix with cantaloupe, prosciutto, and butter lettuce. Another variation that can be prepared ahead of time centers on bocconcini (mini mozzarella balls), chunks of bell peppers, and cubed roasted eggplant. As long as you use Italian dressing, all food options are in play.

Fish cookery is at once simple to execute and very easy to screw up. While fattier fish, like salmon or halibut, are more forgiving, your typical white fish — tilapia, flounder, perch — are easy to overcook and can come with a surprisingly assertive fishy flavor. Simply ½ cup of Italian dressing can address both of those culinary conundrums at once. But how?

In this case, the Italian dressing serves as a flavoring, cooking liquid, and sauce for an elegant baked fish. The process is so simple it hardly requires a recipe. Just place the fish in a baking dish, cover it with Italian dressing, and roast until firm and opaque — about 12 to 15 minutes, depending on the thickness of the fish. Once the fish is done cooking, you can remove it from the pan and use the drippings as a sauce to pour over rice or any other supporting side dish. If you don't have any fish on hand, you can use a similar method to cook frozen shrimp.

If you want to create an effortless weeknight dinner without tons of prep or dirty dishes, go with roasted meat. A hot oven and a quality protein will get you most of the way there, but it's the Italian dressing that will help you cross the finish line. Like the baked fish above, Italian dressing can instantly transform an ordinary piece of chicken or pork into a dynamically flavored dish. In this scenario, you can use Italian dressing as a marinade, as well as a sweet and tangy sauce to glaze your meat.

The secret is using equal parts brown sugar to Italian dressing. Combine the dressing, sugar, and a few dashes of soy sauce, add the meat for a few hours, then pour the whole mixture into a baking dish and cook until the meat reaches the proper temperature (145 F for pork chops, 165 F for chicken). After it's done cooking, you can pour the remaining sauce/marinade into a pot and simmer away on the stovetop until it's thick and syrupy. Another option is to grill the pork chops (or chicken thighs or breasts) and make the sweet-and-sticky glaze separately, then pour it over after the meat is finished cooking.

Cabbage — a whole head or pre-shredded — is one of the best values in a grocery store. This hearty vegetable is as versatile as it is affordable, adding crunch to stir-fries and a soft, velvety chew when braised alongside a hunk of meat. But cabbage is most often used for coleslaw. You can make it sweet and creamy with some Kewpie mayonnaise and celery salt, or nutty and tangy with a few shakes of sesame oil and rice wine vinegar.

Or, you can give it the best of both worlds with a few tablespoons of Italian dressing. Cabbage is an inherently tough veggie, but the acid and fat help pacify its fibrous nature and cruciferous bite. Another benefit is that the emulsifiers and stabilizers so common in most commercial Italian dressings help coat the individual shreds, giving the whole coleslaw an even, glossy sheen that makes each bite more pleasant. You can pair the shredded cabbage with other ingredients, like cherry tomatoes, cashew pieces, scallions, sesame seeds, dried fruit, corn, or crispy tortilla strips, depending on the theme or direction of your meal. Try to prepare your slaw the night before serving to develop the flavor and tenderize the cabbage.

Garlic bread is one of those foods that you can't really screw up. Although not rooted in traditional Italian culture, it's a staple food in Italian-American kitchens across the United States, beloved for its crusty crunch and warm, buttery middle. There are a lot of ways to make garlic bread, and the path you ultimately follow depends entirely on your level of commitment: You can shuck, dice, and sprinkle the bread with fresh garlic and butter, use pre-chopped garlic, or take the ultimate shortcut and simply add a drizzle of olive oil followed by a heavy dusting of garlic powder.

It turns out there's another terrific garlic bread hack — you guessed it, Italian dressing. The magic elixir turns out to be the perfect addition to your garlic bread. And, no, you don't just squeeze it on a butterflied loaf of semolina and pop the whole thing in the oven. But the prep is far from difficult. To upgrade your garlic bread with Italian dressing, whisk it into your butter and garlic before brushing the mixture on the cut side of the bread. Remember to keep the butter warm and spreadable — not totally melted. Otherwise, this can lead to excess moisture and a somewhat soggy crumb. You can then dip the bread in balsamic vinegar or use it as a decadent carbohydrate cradle for a chicken parm hero or Italian sub.

On their own, potatoes don't taste like much. The starchy tuber has a mellow and earthy flavor, kind of like sun-kissed soil. But add butter, cheese, cream, or sour cream, and you've transformed the spud into a gourmet side dish worthy of both fine-dining menus and fast food combo meals. While it's popular to mash, fry, and bake them, one could argue that potatoes are at their best when cut into wedges, boiled, and served as a cold or room-temperature salad.

And once again, the ultimate shortcut is a few glugs of Italian dressing. The acid tang, garlicky seasoning blend, and coating of fat help impart the moisture necessary to combat their inherent chalkiness. Equally important is your potato selection. Fingerlings are creamier and absorb more dressing, while Yukon Gold or Red Bliss will hold their texture after you sprinkle them with oil. Now, the dressing alone won't lead directly to potato salad nirvana, but it'll get you a good part of the way there. Consider reinforcing the flavors with sliced cornichon pickles, sliced olives, capers, scallions, or a spoonful of grainy mustard.

The grill is typically reserved for burgers, steaks, and sausages, but there are a few vegetables that make it to the grates, and corn is one of them. There are plenty of ways to grill corn, from soaking to shucking to brining to parboiling. Ultimately, the goal is to highlight the corn's natural sweetness or infuse as much additional flavor as possible. You can oil and season the corn before it goes on the grill, or you can slather it with mayonnaise or butter after it comes off, but a little rub of Italian dressing might be the most effective method of all.

In this scenario, the dressing serves as both oil and seasoning, helping to kickstart caramelization, prevent the corn from sticking, and keep the kernels succulent and juicy. After the corn comes off the grill, brush on more dressing and sprinkle with Parmesan or cotija cheese, chile powder, smoked paprika, or any other seasoning that fits the rest of the meal. Another option is to cut the freshly-grilled kernels off the cob and use as the base of a corn, black bean, red onion, and avocado salad — or some other variation, depending on what sort of ingredients you have on-hand.

Grains don't get the respect they deserve. Brown rice, farro, buckwheat, millet, amaranth — these hearty little kernels can be so much more than just a landing place for beans, chili, or stew. Yes, they're a nutritious side dish, but if you rebrand them as a salad, grains can suddenly be considered suitable for a main course. To make your salad, cook the grains, let them cool to room temperature, mix in shelled edamame, chopped bell pepper, marinated artichoke hearts, and some cubes of feta cheese, then toss everything with a few tablespoons of Italian dressing.

Whole grains, like potatoes, are inherently starchy and full of fiber, which is why you need something sweet, tangy, and oily to break up the monotony of each mouthful. Note that grains are notorious for soaking up moisture like a sponge, so you may need to add a bit more dressing as the salad sits in the fridge. And while Italian dressing is potent, you may still want to add additional seasonings, like fresh mint, cilantro, or basil, lemon zest, Dijon mustard, or diced shallots.

Cured meats have existed for millennia as a way to preserve meat from spoilage. Today, they are a staple of American lunch culture, delivering a holy trinity of cost, taste, and convenience. You can find cold cuts at any supermarket across the country, in dozens of varieties, from classic salami and bologna to smoked ham and honey-roasted turkey. Any way you slice it, a hoagie layered with meat, cheese, tomato, and shredded lettuce is as comforting as it is satisfying.

These sandwiches, which you can customize with any number of ingredients, do need a little help in the flavor department. Although salty, crisp, and creamy, they lack a lubricating oil and burst of acid. An Italian cold cut sandwich is typically served with olive oil and either balsamic or red wine vinegar, but you can save yourself a step or two with a squirt of Italian dressing. What's good about a bottled dressing is that it contains certain emulsifiers that help it cling to the slippery surface of the lettuce and meat. This means your taste buds get an even balance of fattiness and tang with each bite.

A quick dip is invaluable, serving as a sauce, spread, or destination for dunking. The supermarket has plenty of options, but a premade dip doesn't quite hit the same way as one you make from scratch. And we use the phrase "from scratch" loosely. You can combine a few common condiments and get something truly mouthwatering: yogurt and wasabi, mustard and honey, ketchup and horseradish.

Italian dressing doesn't really work as a standalone dip: The acid, salt, and seasonings are too bold and astringent, even in small amounts. But these characteristics make Italian dressing the ideal addition to another classic refrigerator staple — mayonnaise. The mayo's richness is a natural foil to the potent nature of Italian dressing. You can add the supercharged dip to sandwiches, grilled cheese, garlic bread, or serve it alongside a plate of chips, celery, carrots, and radicchio. If you want to take it a step further, add a sprinkle of red pepper flake, lemon zest, or fresh herbs to brighten up the flavor.

When it comes to your appetizers, it never hurts to err on the side of simplicity. Sure, you can prepare platters of Oysters Rockefeller, hand-fried croquettes, or cheesy gougères, but you can make your life that much easier by supplementing your menu with a few dishes that require minimal preparation. Bruschetta is a popular pass around for this very reason. It doesn't take much to put together — just roughly chop some plum tomatoes (or roast them for a flavorful upgrade), add garlic, basil, and salt, and spoon over a toasted crostini.

In this scenario, think of your Italian dressing as a finishing oil. It's not an 18-year-aged balsamic or cold-pressed extra virgin olive oil, but it adds a balanced finish of tart sweetness to your otherwise naked tomatoes. This same process can be applied to other appetizers, like roasted vegetables, canned artichoke hearts, or hearts of palm. If you're worried about the flavor being too concentrated, gently toss your ingredients with the dressing ahead of time — whether chopped tomatoes, sliced zucchini, or roasted asparagus — so the flavor is evenly distributed.

How adorable is this gingerbread man pillow? This cutie is made from textured brown fabric with white, icing-inspired designs and finished with a red velvet bow tie. We’re absolutely in love with the shaped design and thoughtful details that make this gingerbread man as sweet as he is comfy.

Have friends and family heading home for the holidays? Welcome them with this 30-by-48-inch Merry Christmas doormat before they even step inside. Featuring a rough coir surface that scrapes the dirt off shoes, it’s the perfect outdoor doormat for holiday hosts.

Spruce up your bed or sofa with this vintage-inspired Christmas tree pillow. It measures 20-by-20 inches and pairs perfectly with this green velvet bow decorative pillow.

#153. I Tried GLP-1 Supplements for a Week. I'm Still Hungry.

A couple colleagues returned from a trip to Italy this week. Were they raving about the world-class food? The beautiful views? Their truffle hunting expedition? No, they came into the office chatting about the big wine heist that, according to them, everyone in Italy was talking about.

Basically, a group of men stole 30,000 bottles of wine from a warehouse in Tuscany, estimated to be worth $5.5 million. “Could they simply be passionate oenophiles who plan to drink the 30,000 bottles of Tuscan red themselves?” asks The New York Times. Ever the optimists over there.

Is there a single recipe that you love enough to make your legacy forevermore? That’s presumably the idea behind the recipes people have carved into their tombstones, which, yes, is a real thing that happens quite often. Archivist Rosie Grant has chronicled these recipes online and in her aptly named cookbook To Die For, but in putting the book together she discovered something much more profound about them.

Also in today’s Open Tab: Are GLP-1 supplements just another kind of snake oil? The Michelin scandal unfolding in Texas, new tech from Square that could change restaurants forever, and an essay from Daniel Humm on the frenzy of opening his latest restaurant.

My colleague Nina Moskowitz flagged something to me that caught her eye: A smoothie shop with locations around the country was offering what she called “GLP-1 powder.” Odd, I thought to myself. I investigated and found that it was listed as “GLP-1 Fiber Booster” on the shop’s menu. Naturally, I ordered a scoop in my smoothie; it was $30 with tip.

The powder is made by a company called Supergut, which named it GLP-1 Daily Support. It’s one of many such GLP-1-adjacent powders on the market. On its website, Supergut claims the powder “supports GLP-1 levels”—with an asterisk that notes that the claim hasn’t been evaluated by the FDA.

Babak Orandi, MD, PhD, an obesity specialist at NYU Langone, told me that there’s no evidence these powders can boost the effects or the levels of GLP-1s. “And even if it were to, it is unlikely to have a meaningful effect,” he wrote in an email. “The medications act at concentrations hundreds to thousands of times higher than the body’s own GLP-1 and are designed to last for days, while the body’s own GLP-1 is broken down within minutes.”

In fact, these supplements are something much simpler: fiber.

In an email statement, a spokesperson from Supergut said, in part, that the powder is “not a GLP-1 medication,” but is “designed as companion nutrition for people on GLP-1 medications and anyone supporting their gut health.” The supplement, they said, “may support feelings of fullness and beneficial gut bacteria associated with natural GLP-1 production.”

The $79 billion industry of GLP-1s has changed the way we eat. GLP-1s may even be supercharging nutritional therapy, and along the way they’ve become buzzwords in the weight-loss and wellness space. Slapping the phrase GLP-1 on the label is an easy way to sell more fiber powders (and smoothie supplements), even if it’s misleading consumers. “I think the name oversells it,” Dr. Orandi told me.

It’s telling, too, that the Supergut’s CEO herself has noted that it’s risky to use the term GLP-1 booster. When I first visited the smoothie shop and asked the guy working the counter about the term, he told me, “It’s the same stuff that goes into Ozempic.”

When I returned the next day for another GLP-1 supplement-laden smoothie (might as well see what drinking this supplement for a week does, I’d decided), a different cashier told me the GLP-1 supplement was actually more of an appetite suppressant, but that it wasn’t the same thing as an actual GLP-1.

For what it’s worth, after a week of consuming GLP-1 boosters I feel exactly no difference. Didn’t even keep me full, really.

Dallas landed five new spots on Michelin’s Texas guide this year, part of the guide’s ever expanding remit. But D Magazine’s dining critic Brian Reinhart noticed something strange in the guide’s write-ups. They didn’t read quite right. After putting the text through an AI detector, it looks like the majority of the reviews of the new restaurants were created by AI.

Reinhardt’s reporting points to the overuse of grammatical structures and specific words, such as serene or careful, which LLM’s tend to use more frequently than humans. Michelin denied that AI was used to write the restaurant reviews, and also refused an interview or to review Reinhardt’s findings.

The Michelin guide is known and lauded for its rigor. In a sea of influencers, Michelin’s century of dining expertise and its strict code of secrecy stand out. It is widely considered one of the last international authorities on food and restaurants. But critics have noted that trust has begun to erode as Michelin accepts cash in exchange for coverage, and accusations of AI use would further undermine the rigor and thoroughness on which Michelin has built its reputation.

Do you remember when, seemingly overnight, every coffee place and bakery suddenly had those tablets that would work as cash registers. Point-of-sale (POS) systems, they’re called—the kind that swivel around and ask you if you’d like to add a tip. Those systems are basically made by two companies at this point: Toast and Square.

This week, the latter released the next product in the POS line, simply dubbed Kiosk. It’s an AI-enabled tablet on a stand with microphones and speakers, and it does everything a human working a register would do: take orders, recommend dishes, explain menu items, and upsell, among other things. In short, it seems primed to take a lot of jobs.

Tech optimists would say that Kiosk will help independent restaurants cut costs and stay open, but I’m no tech optimist. I wonder if the idea of Kiosk is built on a fundamental misunderstanding of restaurants. We don’t go out to eat just to satisfy our hunger. We go out to feel like we’re a part of the world, to interact with people, to feel wrapped in and a part of the hum of servers and conversations and disagreements and sly jokes happening all around us. Optimizing that friction out of the restaurant experience with AI isn’t solving for a problem most customers experience. Just as self-checkout machines have made the grocery store experience more lonely, so too might Square’s new devices.

“Opening a restaurant is an insane thing to do,” chef Daniel Humm writes in an essay for Bon Appétit. He’s spent months obsessing over the details—the light fixtures, the perfect shade of red paint—all in service of getting his latest restaurant just right. Read on to see how Humm made it through the madness to open Humm, the first restaurant to bear his name.

#154. Pumpkin Bolognese

Classic Bolognese, with its multi-hour cook time, can be truly remarkable, if you ever have a stretch to make it. In this version, a scoop of canned pumpkin purée is the head-turning ingredient that gives it full-blown flavor and body, without the wait typical of a nonna-style sauce. Lightly caramelizing the pumpkin in the pot along with tomato paste gives it a nutty, savory edge. Milk is the other surprise ingredient here, especially in the quantity of a full cup. Think of it as a tenderizer, making the final sauce soft and delicate. Pay attention to the order in which the ingredients appear—the milk goes in first with the wine to follow. If you switch the order, the acidic wine will curdle the milk.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 1 large white or yellow onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. freshly grated nutmeg and stir to combine. Cover pot and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are very soft, 8–10 minutes. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are golden around the edges, about 5 minutes.

Uncover pot and add 1 lb. ground beef, preferably 20% fat; season lightly with salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until beef is very lightly browned but not crisp (it will still be pink in spots), 6–8 minutes. Pour in 1 cup whole milk and cook, stirring occasionally, until milk has evaporated and fat is pooling on surface of meat, 7–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until wine has evaporated, 6–8 minutes. Add 1 cup canned pumpkin purée and 2 Tbsp. double-concentrated tomato paste; season generously with freshly ground pepper. Cook, stirring often and scraping bottom of pot, until combined and pumpkin darkens slightly, 8–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup water, reduce heat to low, and cook, stirring occasionally, until mixture is saucy, 12–15 minutes. If meat seems dry, add an extra ½ cup water and continue cooking another 3–4 minutes. Taste sauce and season with salt if needed. Keep warm.

Meanwhile, cook 12 oz. fresh tagliatelle or pappardelle or dry rigatoni, in a large pot of boiling salted water. If using fresh pasta, cook about 3 minutes. If using dry, cook until very al dente, about 2 minutes less than package directions.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to pot with sauce. Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid and 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup). Increase heat to medium, bring to a simmer, and cook, tossing constantly, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Transfer pasta to shallow bowls and sprinkle with more Parmesan.

#155. 14 Thanksgiving desserts that aren't pie : Do something a little different with your holiday dessert table.

Yes, Thanksgiving is a pie-centric holiday. But what if you don’t like pie? Or maybe you just don’t want it. Either way, we’ve got lots of non-pie Thanksgiving desserts, from spiced pumpkin cupcakes to sugary apple cobblers, plus plenty of autumnal cakes.

This adorable cake pulls double duty, serving as both a scene-stealing centerpiece and a feast-ending dessert. To make, stack two mini Bundt cakes together and frost with orange buttercream. Carving this frosted pumpkin at the end of the meal may just upstage the turkey!

Get the recipe: The Great Pumpkin Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Mini Bundt Pan Set

Cranberry sauce can be a polarizing side dish, but everyone will love this New England-inspired cake, which pairs tart cranberries with walnuts and vanilla for a simple, satisfying dessert. (Because it’s so quick to make, this is a particularly good recipe for any last-minute holiday baking.)

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Sparkling Sugar

Sweet potatoes belong on the dessert table, and this recipe proves it. This ultra-soft cake is gently spiced and glows orange from the sweet potato purée, and it’s finished with a fluffy meringue that mimics marshmallow-topped sweet potato casseroles.

Get the recipe: Sweet Potato Sheet Cake with Marshmallow Frosting (make it gluten-free with Measure for Measure Flour)

To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9” x 13” pan

For a dessert that’s rich but not too sweet, turn to this recipe, which pairs pumpkin and pumpkin spice with chocolate chips. Baked in a decorative Bundt pan, it can be served unfrosted for an easy-yet-elegant dessert.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin-Chocolate Chip Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Soft Swirl Bundt Pan

Instead of apple pie, try an apple pan dowdy on your Thanksgiving dessert table. The pan dowdy is a traditional American dish from the 1800s and early 1900s. A combination of pie and pudding, the name comes from the method in which the recipe is completed: After an apple-based filling is baked in a crust-lined casserole, the baker takes a fork and "dowdies" the crust, breaking it into pieces that remain crisp despite being partially immersed in the juicy filling.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9" square pan

“Thanksgiving cheesecake” may not have quite the same ring as “Thanksgiving pie,” but when your guests are eating this ultra-creamy dessert, they won’t care. With its burnished top and custardy interior, this Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake reimagines the classic with bold autumnal flair, thanks to golden pumpkin purée and warm spices.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

Don’t be fooled by its stodgy name or humble appearance: This cake is so good, we named it our #1 best fall recipe! In fact, my colleague Jessica Battilana made it for Thanksgiving last year and declared it the biggest hit of the day; her guests fell in love with the moist, apple-loaded cake and fudgy brown sugar frosting.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Vermont Boiled Cider

If you don’t want to fuss with pie, we suggest making a cobbler instead. This fruit-filled version pairs juicy spiced apples with a crackly brown sugar crust — both prep and serving are easy, and the resulting cobbler will absolutely steal the show.

Get the recipe: Sugar-Crusted Apple Cobbler

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon

Apples are great, but seasonal pears deserve some love too. This simple cake, made with a combination of almond and all-purpose flours, has a rich, buttery texture and an almost marzipan-like chew. Studded with fragrant cubes of ripe pear, it's an elegant after-dinner dessert.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Almond Flour

The boozy Bundt cake features potent maple flavor thanks to the 1/2 cup (!) of maple syrup in the batter, plus the sticky maple-and-rum glaze to finish. Made with cake flour and sour cream, the cake itself is dense and velvety, like all great pound cakes should be.

Get the recipe: Maple Pound Cake with Maple-Rum Glaze

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Vermont Maple Syrup and Natural Maple Flavor

Instead of slicing and serving dessert, bake every guest their own individual mini cake. Start with a moist, spicy sheet cake, then use a biscuit cutter or overturned glass to cut rounds for individual layer cakes sandwiched with cream cheese frosting.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Apple Pie Spice

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

For a little French flair at your Thanksgiving table, make this classic tarte tatin. This dessert can be a little fussy, but we’ve endlessly tested our version to make sure it goes off without a hitch in your kitchen. And it’s worth it for the deeply caramelized apples layered over shattering pastry.

Get the recipe: Classic Apple Tarte Tatin

To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9” round cake pan

Make serving Thanksgiving dessert a breeze by baking up a big batch of cupcakes. These are packed with pumpkin flavor and spice, then finished with an easy swoop of cream cheese frosting. If you really want to level up your presentation, check out these cupcake decorating techniques for a pro-level finish.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cupcakes (make them gluten-free with Measure for Measure Flour)

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Unbleached Cake Flour

#156. Skip Pie Crust: Make Chicken Pot Pie 10x Easier With This Frozen Side

Chicken pot pie is one of those comfort foods that aren't just full of flavor but nostalgia, too. When you're a fan of the creamy pastry-coated pie, just the thought of it may warm your soul. If you're buying a pie from the freezer aisle to heat up at home, there are some hacks to make frozen pot pies even better. If you're planning to make one from scratch, it can be a little intimidating, but with a simple hack, you can tweak your dish to maximize flavor and get a beautifully chewy crunch on top. Try using a bag of frozen tater tots  in place of the pastry crust to make a chicken "tot" pie that requires much less work.

A classic chicken pot pie is certainly delicious, and it can be relatively easy to make using frozen puff pastry — but you still have to form the filling into the pastry and get the top just right. And, even then, the crust can burn easily, especially if you're an inexperienced baker. When you use tater tots as your crust (as it were), they're much more forgiving. The end result is more of a casserole than a pie, but the flavor and texture perks are undeniable. You can make your chicken pot pie filling with just a few ingredients you probably already have in the fridge, freezer, or pantry: a little canned soup, chicken, and frozen veggies. Then, add the tater tots to the top, and your pie will come out of the oven hot and sizzling, with the chicken and veggies blending beautifully with the crispy, crunchy topping that only taters can provide.

The most essential parts of your base are going to be the chicken and a creamy condensed soup. Rotisserie chicken is a great choice because it's ready to go and just needs to be shredded before mixing in, but cubed, cooked chicken breast will also work just fine. For the soup, cream of mushroom will give a bit more umami, while cream of celery is great for some peppery, herbaceous flavor. That said, there are plenty of other options, including cream of chicken, that you can use to get the exact taste profile you're going for. From there, almost any bag of frozen veggies will work, but for the classic chicken pot pie filling experience, you'll want something with peas and carrots.

For more aromatic flavor, you can sauté some diced onions and garlic. Adding shredded cheddar and using milk to reconstitute the condensed soup will give you a creamier, thicker casserole and more salty notes. Plus, a little sour cream doesn't hurt for a hit of tang. Once everything is mixed, you just need to pour it into a casserole dish, spread frozen tater tots across the top, and toss it in the oven. Depending on how quickly the tots brown, you're best leaving the dish uncovered in the oven for prime crunch, and it's easier to watch over than that finicky pastry crust. And, sure, if you're from the Upper Midwest, this may simply sound like a classic "hot dish" to you, and there are dozens of ways to tweak the recipe. But if you go with the classic chicken and veggie-based flavors, you're going to be right on target.

#157. 1.5 Million Pounds Of Hot Dogs, Sausage & Meat Products Recalled Due To Temperature Abuse

Check your fridge and freezer before your next cookout.

Over 1.5 million pounds of meat and poultry products are being recalled because they were stored at improper temperatures.

Kayem Foods Inc. is recalling approximately 1,584,361 pounds of ready-to-eat products sold under various brand names. The affected products were produced between March 31, 2026, and October 7, 2026, and bear the establishment numbers EST. M/P 7839, EST. P 20935A, or EST. M 9520.

Recognizable products include Kayem Old Tyme Beef & Pork Franks, Kayem Fenway Franks, Genoa Hot Ham, Al Fresco Chicken Breakfast Sausage, McKenzie Cob Smoked Bacon, and many more meat and poultry products. A full list of product labels and UPC codes can be found here.

The firm shipped the affected products to retail and foodservice locations nationwide.

The recall began after a retail customer reported receiving products at warm temperatures on October 1. An investigation found that meat and poultry products had been stored in a warehouse cooler that experienced temperature deviations. Kayem says the problem was caused by a malfunction in the warehouse cooling system.

Temperature matters when storing perishable food. According to FoodSafety.gov, refrigerators should remain at 40°F or below and freezers at 0°F or below. Bacteria can grow rapidly in the “Danger Zone” between 40°F and 140°F, which is why perishable foods generally shouldn’t remain in that temperature range for more than two hours.

No illnesses have been reported in connection with the recall. Consumers should not eat the affected products and should instead throw them away or return them to the place of purchase. Anyone concerned about a possible illness should contact a healthcare provider.

#158. Our 20 Favorite Rosh Hashana Recipes

Rosh Hashana marks the beginning of the Jewish New Year and the first of the High Holy Days that take place each autumn. For many, it’s a time of year to pause, reflect, and take stock of life’s simple pleasures. Family and friends gather to celebrate over generous shared meals made up of dishes that reflect the season and traditions passed down through generations. From slow braises and hearty sides to crisp fall desserts and plenty of challah, the food served during Rosh Hashana is an important part of the celebration. Here are some of our favorite recipes.

“On the red carpet of Rosh Hashana desserts, honey cake has a far smaller fan base than some of its glittering apple counterparts,” writes baker Ellen Gray. “Yet honey cakes are iconic, tethered to the High Holidays as a symbol of hope for a sweet New Year.” Here, Gray upgrades her grandma Minnie’s Rosh Hashana cake with a splash of cream soda and a slick of dark chocolate icing. Get the recipe >

Rings of fresh apple are dipped into a lightly sweet batter, fried until crisp and golden, and tossed in vanilla sugar while still warm. The result is a simple fall treat with a tender center and a fragrant, crackly coating. Get the recipe >

Beef and an assortment of root vegetables slowly braise together in this hearty, gently sweet stew. The long cooking time allows the meat and vegetables to soak up the flavors of the rich braising liquid. Get the recipe >

Instead of one large loaf, braided challah dough is shaped into individual knots before baking, giving each piece a soft, fluffy center and beautifully golden crust. Serve them alongside a holiday meal, or pull them apart and eat them warm with morning coffee or afternoon tea. Get the recipe >

This savory take on classic noodle kugel combines egg noodles with caramelized onions, eggs, and plenty of black pepper. Baked until set and lightly browned on top, it makes a comforting addition to any table. Get the recipe >

New York City chef Elyssa Heller shares her mom’s secrets to a richly flavored matzo ball soup, including roasting the chicken bones separately and adding lots of parsnip to the stock. Get the recipe >

Lightly sweetened dough is filled with a fragrant mixture of date syrup and pistachios before being rolled and baked until golden and crisp around the edges. A drizzle of rosewater-infused honey adds a floral finish to these bite-size pastries. Get the recipe >

Chicken roasts alongside sweet apricots and tart currants, which soften and mingle with the savory pan juices as they cook. The combination of tender meat and jewel-like dried fruit makes for a festive main course with a pleasing balance of sweet and savory flavors. Get the recipe >

Apples are roasted with honey and butter until tender and lightly caramelized, then tossed with their cooking juices, French apple brandy, and toasted sesame seeds and served warm with crème fraîche for a simple but memorable dessert. Get the recipe >

Whole smaller fish like branzino or porgy are coated in a mixture of herbs and spices and fried until deeply golden and crisp, letting the aromatic crust lock in the tender, flaky flesh. A garlicky parsley-and-chile rub adds brightness and heat, while lemon brings a fresh, citrusy finish to balance out this impressive centerpiece. Get the recipe >

Sweet, crisp carrots, bitter radicchio, and crunchy pistachios come together in this colorful salad that’s sweetened with dates and brightened with citrus and punchy balsamic vinegar. Get the recipe >

This dessert splits the difference between cake and pie, with a buttery, pie crust surrounding Granny Smith apples, raisins, and walnuts. Honey and warm spices flavor the filling, while pieces of dough scattered over the top bake into a rustic streusel-like finish. Get the recipe >

Raspberries do double duty here: a few spoonfuls of raspberry jam are added to the chocolate filling, and a raspberry syrup is used to lacquer the final loaf. Get the recipe >

Beans, barley, potatoes, and beef simmer slowly together overnight, allowing their flavors to deepen and mingle. The result is a hearty, deeply savory stew with tender meat, creamy beans, and a rich broth. For a faster version, the dish can be braised on the stovetop in just a few hours. Get the recipe >

Made with French miel de lavande from Provence, this simple custard combines milk, egg yolks, sugar, and honey, then is churned until firm. The honey gives the ice cream its distinctive floral aroma and flavor. If you’re unable to find miel de lavande, regular honey and dried lavender make a suitable substitute. Get the recipe >

Cooked carrots are blended until silky smooth and brightened with orange juice and a gentle hit of fresh ginger. The resulting purée is sweet, citrusy, and warmly spiced, making it an elegant accompaniment to a holiday spread or autumn table. Get the recipe >

Perfumed with warm spices including cinnamon, allspice, and ginger, then finished with a brighly flavored orange glaze, this dessert is a classic at Jewish holiday tables. Get the recipe >

Tender cabbage leaves are wrapped around a savory filling of beef and rice, then nestled into a rich tomato sauce to braise. As the rolls cook, the cabbage softens and the filling takes on the sweet, savory flavors of the sauce seasoned with cayenne, paprika, raisins, and honey. Get the recipe >

After a quick blanch, the sprouts are halved and broiled with olive oil and smoked paprika until caramelized. Lemon juice and zest plus white wine vinegar add acidity, while grated horseradish and pomegranate seeds bring heat and bursts of tartness. Get the recipe >

#159. This Trick Makes Cutting Winter Squash So Much Easier

A little heat makes a big difference when it comes to cutting a stubborn squash.

I love winter squash, but I’ve never been fond of the effort required to get some varieties onto the dinner table. Butternut squash is manageable enough, but a stubborn acorn or Hubbard squash can make even the sharpest chef’s knife feel inadequate. And while I have no objection to a little prep work, I’d rather spend my time cooking dinner than trying to negotiate with a vegetable.

Of course, the reward is usually worth it. Roasted squash is one of fall’s greatest gifts, and there’s no shortage of ways to put it to work in soups, sides and even desserts. But the effort (and fear of accidental finger amputation) is off-putting. Then I came across a video demonstrating a simple way to make cutting winter squash easier, and I put it to the test.

The technique itself isn’t new or complicated. What caught my attention was how little effort it took to dramatically simplify the process of preparing an otherwise stubborn squash.

In the video, the creator places a whole squash in a 400ºF oven for 20 minutes before cutting it.

Afterward, her knife passes through the squash with remarkably little resistance, and she removes the seeds in a single scoop. It’s an impressive demonstration, even though the principle behind it is familiar enough: Heat softens vegetables, and winter squash is no exception.

The question is whether 20 minutes is enough to make a meaningful difference without cooking the squash all the way through.

To find out, I picked up two similarly sized Danish squash—a classic type of acorn squash, recognizable by its dark green, deeply ridged exterior and sweet, golden flesh. Like other types of winter squash, it has a tough rind that can make cutting it in half more challenging than its relatively modest size might suggest.

I left one squash raw and baked the other for 20 minutes in a 400º oven, piercing the skin first to let steam escape. After letting the roasted squash cool long enough for me to handle it, I cut both in half using the same knife.

The difference was immediately obvious. Cutting through the raw squash required much more pressure, while the partially roasted one offered much less resistance. Removing the seeds was easier, too, and the softened flesh was still firm enough to be cut into wedges without falling apart.

Admittedly, putting a squash in the oven before cutting it raises a reasonable question: Why not just roast it all the way through? The answer depends on what you’re making. If you’re planning to scoop out the flesh for soup or puree, you might as well go all the way. But if your recipe calls for wedges, cubes or slices that need to hold their shape and brown in the oven, you need to cut the squash before it’s fully cooked.

Those exposed surfaces are what allow roasted squash to develop its beautifully browned, caramelized edges. And if you’re making a squash gratin, a roasted squash salad or a soup that begins by sauteing cubes of squash with onions and aromatics, the shape and texture of those pieces matter.

This technique doesn’t save time from start to finish. You still have to preheat the oven, roast the squash and allow it to cook before cutting into it. What it does save is the physical effort of cutting through a dense, raw winter squash, which can be complicated if you struggle with hand strength or find vegetables tough to manage. You’ll still want a sharp knife and a stable cutting board, but there’s something to be said about a little less resistance.

Danish squash worked beautifully for me, but the technique certainly isn’t limited to acorn varieties. Other hard-skinned winter squash like kabocha, Hubbard and buttercup can benefit from a brief period in the oven before cutting. Butternut squash is another good option, especially if you’re working with a large one that needs to be halved and cubed.

The size of the squash matters, too. Twenty minutes at 400º may be enough to make a noticeable difference in a smaller squash, but a large variety may need more time. The goal isn’t to cook it until it’s tender; it’s to soften it just enough that your knife can pass through more easily. If I don’t have to test the limits of my chef’s knife, I’ll happily take it.

Have you tried this hack before? Let us know in the comments below!

#161. 8 Foods That Taste Better With A Pat Of Butter

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

"Everything's better with butter" is a common phrase, and for good reason. Granted, part of that reason is decades-old ad campaigns waged by the American Dairy Association, which drove the notion into consumers' minds. Celeb chefs like Paula Deen and Julia Child have also eloquently pounded the idea home (Child is famously quoted as saying, "With enough butter, anything is good"). But the other part of the delicious equation is ... it's true. It's simply a fact that adding butter makes so many foods richer, tastier, and just overall enhanced in almost magical ways.

Narrowing things down a bit ("everything" would make for a ridiculously long list, after all), we've pinpointed some specific foods that absolutely, unequivocally need a pat of butter if you want them to reach their flavor potential. We could also get into the various types of butter and specific best practices for using them. At the end of the day, any variety has the potential to work its wizardry on food. So, for our intents and purposes here, we'll leave it to your culinary creativity to decide which brand of butter you want to slather on when duplicating these dairy-enriched creations. If you still feel like you need some recommendations, though, pretty much every revered chef has their go-to. Ina Garten's favorite butter, for instance, is Beurre de Baratte, a pricey French variety with flaked sea salt. But you don't need to break the bank to execute a scrumptious butter hack — an ordinary supermarket product will do just fine, too. (If you want a rec that's easy to locate, Kerrygold has been found to be the best store-bought butter brand.) Now, onward to buttery bliss!

In the U.S., we're all about spreading mayonnaise on savory sandwiches, so it may come as a surprise that the British often put butter on theirs — but when you understand the reasons behind the practice, it starts to sound like a trend that should cross the pond.

We've already established that butter adds yummy flavor to virtually everything, and sandwiches are no exception — the subtle sweetness of the dairy product balances and accentuates salty cold cuts and also helps them adhere to the bread better. In addition to the meat-and-cheese variety, the Brits also put butter on jam sandwiches, because it adds a lubricating element to help keep the bread from tearing when you're spreading the fruit. Buttering one's bread before applying other sandwich condiments additionally adds a barrier that keeps one's bread from getting soggy. On the flip side, it simultaneously adds its own brand of moisture to prevent dryness. In other words, don't knock it until you try it.

You may already be adding milk to your oatmeal and other hot cereals, but butter is another dairy add-in that similarly brings creaminess and so much more to the breakfast staple. Dropping a pat into your finished cooked cereal lends a silky texture, and the fat in the butter acts as a flavor carrier to help more evenly distribute and more fully develop your cereal's spices or sweeteners, making that hot sauce, garlic, cinnamon, brown sugar, or whatever flavor jam shine much more fully.

In addition to finishing your cereal with a dollop, you can also toast your oats in butter at the start of the cooking process for another big flavor boost. Toasting them not only adds notes of nuttiness and caramelization, but when the oats absorb the butter, it results in a softer final texture. Pro tip: Toasting your oats in brown butter — or stirring in brown butter at the end — takes the dish even further into the flavor stratosphere, making it almost dessert-like in its deliciousness. You're welcome!

Frying and scrambling eggs in butter is a given, but I must confess that the notion of putting butter on a boiled egg has never once occurred to me in my multiple decades of life. But apparently, it's a thing, lending an Eggs Benedict-esque lusciousness to the somewhat banal breakfast staple. It could be easily argued that the boiled version of an egg is its most simplistic form, but adding a pat of butter on top of that solid, little white orb is evidently quite transformative. When the rich dairy staple combines with the (also rich) boiled yolk, it's a creamy, velvety match made in heaven. Using a salted or compound butter takes the boost even further, with flavor profiles like garlic and herb making particularly scrumptious toppers to heap over (and melt into) your eggs.

When I was in first grade, a lady came to my school classroom and taught us how to make butter by putting cream inside a mason jar and then shaking it — until your arm fell off or butter formed, whichever came first. She then produced saltine crackers for us to spread the pale, newly churned substance onto, so we could sample the fruits of our labor. That mystified me, as it seemed honestly unusual, even to a 6-year-old with limited culinary sophistication, to put butter on a saltine. However, then I tried it, and I was a believer.

Something about the cool creaminess of the butter and the savory, salty crispness of the cracker forms a perfectly satisfying snack when paired together. The spread simultaneously amplifies and mellows the saltiness, too — don't ask me how; it's food voodoo. Whatever the culinary witchery that makes this combo great, it's one I highly recommend trying — please try toasting your crackers in a compound butter of your choice, if you feel fancy. As an added note, while my butter and cracker expertise begins and ends with the saltine hack (it's the only pairing I've personally tried), others heartily recommend spreading the rich dairy good on additional types of crackers, including grahams.

Most have at least heard of the concept of a butter burger. Fast-food chain Culver's is famous for its version (though, despite the name, Culver's sandwiches only include butter on the buns, not the meat patties themselves). Adding butter to the meat is where it's at, though. You can fry the patties in it, dollop it on top, or mix it right into your ground beef blend. (Technically, you could do all three, but your cardiologist might not approve.) Whichever approach you take, the result is added richness, flavor depth, juiciness, and a beautiful, caramelized crust on the meat. In a word, yum.

It started as a very Simon and Garfunkel-esque duet on the animated comedy "Family Guy," but apparently butter on a Pop-Tart really is frickin' good (and lots of people declared on social media that they were singing its praises long before Peter Griffin). Similar to the way adding butter significantly amplifies pie crust, it does the same for the dough shell of a toaster pastry, deliciously combating dryness, softening the outer layer, and generally adding butter's magical goodness to the sweet pastry. Whatever type of tart you're toasting, butter's fat content, again, enhances the included flavors, and it gives a freshly baked quality to the definitely not fresh treats. As one Redditor put it, "Butter is pure fat; there's no way it's not gonna taste amazing on [Pop-Tarts]." We concur.

Is anything better than chocolate? That pretty much sums it up — chocolate is widely considered the world's ultimate indulgence. Yet, apparently, even this iconic snack of the grocery gods can be improved with a little butter. In an Instagram reel, a private chef with more than a million Instagram followers shared that a sweet treat of perfect proportions is achieved by placing a pat of cold butter on a square of dark chocolate and then topping it with a little sprinkling of flaky salt. Nothing more to do after that but sink your teeth in, and the melt-in-your-mouth (literally) results are a bit reminiscent of chocolate truffles.

#163. Spiderweb Cookies

Preheat the oven to 350°F. Cream the butter, shortening and sugar until light and fluffy, five to seven minutes. Beat in the egg and vanilla until well combined.

In a separate bowl, whisk together the flour, cocoa powder, baking powder and baking soda. Gradually add the dry ingredients into the creamed mixture, beating until a soft dough forms.

In a large microwave-safe bowl, combine the marshmallows and 1 tablespoon of butter. Microwave until melted, 30 to 45 seconds, then stir until smooth. Let the mixture cool slightly so it’s warm but comfortable to handle.

Editor’s Tip: If the marshmallows aren’t completely melted after 45 seconds, continue microwaving in 10-second intervals, stirring after each, until smooth.

​Editor’s Tip: If the marshmallow mixture becomes too firm to stretch, reheat it in the microwave in 10-second bursts. You want it warm and stretchy, but not too hot and overly soft.

Marshmallow creme isn’t a good substitute for whole marshmallows, as it won’t make fully-formed spiderwebs. Spreadable marshmallow cream has a softer consistency and usually doesn’t contain gelatin, so it won’t stretch into the thin, web-like strands that are created by melting marshmallows.
