For a fall-forward cheesecake, turn to this seasonal recipe. The texture of the filling is ultra-smooth and creamy, and the maple flavor is apparent, yet subtle — the secret is natural maple flavor paired with maple syrup. The pecan crust, meanwhile, is a nutty, salty counterbalance to the filling.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Maple Syrup and Natural Maple Flavor

If you’re looking for a celebratory yet unexpected dessert for your table, we recommend this recipe. A heavy pour of Irish whiskey cream liqueur (save some for your after-dinner coffee!) flavors the smooth, light filling, while silky chocolate ganache adorns the top. Oven space at a premium while you prep Thanksgiving dinner? This dessert is no-bake, so you can save some room in the cooking schedule.

With its burnished top and custardy interior, this cheesecake reimagines the classic with bold autumnal flair, thanks to golden pumpkin purée and warm spices.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This flourless cake is incredibly rich — like sliceable fudge sauce. A thick icing of chocolate ganache glaze takes it over the top, but if you want something a touch lighter after a heavy Thanksgiving feast, top it instead with a dusting of confectioners’ sugar and a spoonful of barely sweetened whipped cream.

Baker's tip: Make your whipped cream in a Mason jar, especially helpful if you're bringing dessert to someone else's home.

Shop the recipe: Callebaut Semisweet Chocolate Chips

This chocolate pie, with its flaky pastry crust and glistening, ruby-colored cranberry topping, is a non-traditional twist on Thanksgiving flavors. With a semisweet chocolate ganache, nutty whole-grain flour in the crust, and tangy fruit, it delivers a novel and enticing new holiday pie.

This pecan tart recipe is the more lavish, decadent cousin of a classic pecan pie. The pecans are enveloped in a rich, chewy caramel filling, and a blanket of velvety smooth chocolate ganache covers the top of the tart, lending it major candy bar vibes with a touch of sophistication.

Shop the recipe: Guittard Semisweet Chocolate Wafers

This nostalgic pie is the perfect combination of crispy crust, dense chocolatey filling, and ethereal whipped cream. The crust is prebaked, then filled with a generous amount of cooked, cooled chocolate filling. You can customize the chocolate flavor to your taste by using bittersweet, semisweet, milk chocolate, or any combination of these that you like.

Based on chess pie, an old Southern favorite, this pie’s texture hits the sweet spot between cheesecake and custard. As it bakes, it also makes its own crackly chocolate-sugar topping, which yields to the dense, fudgy filling beneath.

Watch as Kye shares 4 tips for failproof pie dough.

For years, bakers asked us for a vegan pumpkin pie recipe: This one’s for you! For this dairy-free pie, sweetened condensed coconut milk takes the place of cream, and a cornstarch slurry acts as an egg-like binder. But worry not: Despite being vegan, it has the fragrant spiced flavor of classic pumpkin pie.

Instead of eggs, this pie relies on cornstarch to bind the gooey filling; coconut cream, meanwhile, stands in for butter. With tons of toasty pecans bound together in a rich, sweet syrup and cradled in a flaky crust, it’s hard to believe this pie is vegan.

Shop the recipe: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Guittard Bittersweet Onyx Chocolate Wafers

How do you make a cream pie without dairy or eggs? The secret is coconut: The pudding-like filling is made with both coconut cream and evaporated coconut milk for a rich texture that’s the perfect balance of set but still soft. The sheer amount of chocolate means that it, and not coconut, is still the predominant flavor in this vegan chocolate pie.

Get the recipe: No-Bake Vegan Chocolate Pie

Shop the recipe: Guittard Bittersweet Onyx Chocolate Wafers

A cake so easy that you can mix it in its pan, this reliable recipe is also free of dairy or eggs. And you won’t miss them: This simple chocolate cake is dark and moist, with a slightly coarse crumb. If you’re worried about getting overwhelmed with all the cooking and baking Thanksgiving morning, we recommend this stress-free recipe.

Get the recipe: King Arthur’s Original Cake Pan Cake

Shop the recipe: Triple Cocoa Blend and Espresso Powder

A simple dump-and-stir batter bakes up into this sweet and spicy vegan cake, which has a moist, tender crumb from the inclusion of pumpkin purée and vegetable oil. Add raisins, walnuts, or dried cranberries to the batter for additional texture and flavor.

Our secret to capturing fall in a dessert? Fragrant, uber-flavorful pumpkin pie spice.

A flaky pie crust can be difficult to achieve with gluten-free flour, but our Gluten-Free All-Purpose Flour — along with xanthan gum and Instant ClearJel to help with binding and structure — is up to the task. The pumpkin filling, meanwhile, is classic: smooth, mildly sweet, and just spicy enough.

Shop the recipe: Gluten-Free All-Purpose Flour, Xanthan Gum, and Instant ClearJel

Rich, dark, and dense, this chocolate cake is the perfect finish to a celebratory meal. The almond flour ensures moist, tender texture, while our Triple Cocoa Blend, espresso powder, and bittersweet chocolate all contribute to an extra-indulgent chocolate experience — without any gluten.

Get the recipe: Chocolate Almond Flour Torte

Shop the recipe: Almond Flour and Belcolade Bittersweet Chocolate Wafers

This perfectly tender cake — made with our Measure for Measure Flour for a seamless gluten-free baking experience — incorporates cinnamon, ginger, cardamom, allspice, and black pepper to mimic the flavors in a steaming cup of chai. Lightly sweetened with both brown sugar and honey, it's an ideal autumnal dessert.

Get the recipe: Gluten-Free Chai-Spiced Pound Cake

Shop the recipe: Gluten-Free Measure for Measure Flour

This one-bowl cake belies its simplicity with moist texture and out-of-this-world flavor. The combination of mildly spiced cake, chopped fresh apples, and fudge-like brown sugar frosting is guaranteed to be a hit at the end of your Thanksgiving feast.

Get the recipe: Gluten-Free Old-Fashioned Apple Cake

Shop the recipe: Gluten-Free Measure for Measure Flour

New to gluten-free baking? Read our beginner's guide for everything you need to know.

Looking to skip the pie but still want pumpkin? These soft bars are your solution — they’re also great for feeding a crowd, as they’re baked in an 18” x 13” half-sheet pan. Crowned with tangy cream-cheese frosting and packed with walnuts and raisins, these gluten-free bars are like a bar version of carrot cake.

Get the recipe: Gluten-Free Pumpkin Cake Bars

Shop the recipe: Gluten-Free All-Purpose Flour and Xanthan Gum

A rich, luscious chocolate filling and tender, flaky pie crust are the hallmarks of this gluten-free version of one of our most popular pies. Use high-quality chocolate for the best filling flavor — in such a chocolate-forward recipe, it really does make a difference.

#165. An Insider’s Guide to the Best Coffee Shops in Bogotá

As the world’s third-largest coffee producer, Colombia generated 1.81 billion pounds of green coffee in 2025. Although most visitors to the country associate its bean production with the Eje Cafetero—the departments Caldas, Quindío, and Risaralda—the growing regions here extend far beyond it. Ironically, for decades, the best beans largely went abroad. To this day, Colombia exports more than 90 percent of its coffee crop.

As a result, what’s traditionally consumed within the country is largely the beloved tinto, so named for the dark undertones in red wine (vino tinto). Don’t get me wrong: I love a tinto. Typically made with commodity-quality beans, this potent cup is brewed in a metal pot or filtered through cloth and sweetened with panela (unrefined cane sugar). A tinto evokes a sense of nostalgia and the camaraderie of gathering at the street corner with friends on a leisurely Sunday afternoon. You can never go wrong, because they all taste the same.

In recent years, there has been a movement to drink locally, thanks to a new generation of roasters who are paving the way to showcase the diversity of Colombia’s coffee beans. One of the unique aspects of the country's terrain is its dramatic elevation changes—coffee is cultivated from roughly 4,000 to more than 6,500 feet above sea level. This includes the volcanic mountains of Nariño near the Ecuadorian border, all the way to the misty slopes of Huila, where coffee farms climb the foothills of the Central and Eastern Andes.

The same terrain also allows for an extraordinary range of fruit to flourish, from the tangy lulo and citrusy-sweet passion fruit to the juicy guava and the tart tomate de árbol. All that fruit grown alongside coffee plants, in addition to topography ranging from snowcapped peaks to Caribbean coastline, brings out distinct flavor profiles.

Although I have always loved the taste of coffee, I never quite appreciated the nuances of what I was drinking until I moved to Colombia three years ago. Bogotá has been a large part of that education. The high-altitude capital has become a hub for specialty cafés. Roasters here find distinct ways to serve beans from around the country, from carefully prepared pour-overs to cold brews infused with orange or tamarind. Visiting the city’s cafés can often feel like traveling through Colombia one cup at a time, with single-origin brews offering inspiration on what regions to explore next.

Earthy interiors with terra-cotta tones and smooth concrete open onto a welcoming sun-filled, plant-lined courtyard in this design-forward oasis. With locations in two of the city’s trendiest neighborhoods, El Nogal and Quinta Camacho, Tropicália works with small Colombian producers and rotates its coffees every three months or so. What makes its coffee particularly interesting is the supplier list, which ranges from small producers and women-led farms to competition-grade selections and, more recently, experimental, wild-processed coffees that push flavor in new directions. Each filter coffee comes with tasting notes that help you understand the flavors in your cup. Don’t leave without trying the cold brew tamarindo, where the fruit’s tartness plays against the bitterness of the coffee. Pair your drinks with Tropicália’s popular avocado toast, served with a tangy mango pico de gallo and a poached egg.

One of my favorite things about Bogotá? When I ask for a coffee recommendation, I know I’ll always get a good one. That’s how I stumbled upon Lohas Café by specialty exporter Lohas Beans, a company that has worked with Colombian producers for over a decade. Tucked inside a colonial redbrick house, this minimalist coffee bar offers the intimacy of stopping by someone’s home for a cup. The café specializes in competition-level coffees, including limited lots sourced from producers in southern Colombia’s Huila region. Filter coffees are a highlight, but order a cappuccino or latte to experience one of Lohas’s curious signatures: milk that is frozen to remove much of its water, resulting in a richer cup that pairs beautifully with the selection of coffees.

Cl 93b #13–91Cra. 9 #79A–23 Primer Piso, Chapinero+57 317 720 5538

With locations in Chicó and El Nogal, Azahar Café is a great place to visit when you can’t decide on just one coffee. Order the Cata de Café, a tasting of three coffees from its current rotation. One of the unique aspects of Azahar is its close long-term relationships with producers, ensuring that farmers are consistently paid above-market prices. Pair the top-notch cold brew with one of the delicious flaky almond croissants made in-house. The café also has an outpost at Bogotá’s El Dorado airport for one last cup before leaving the city.

Cl. 119b #5–43, Usaquén, Bogotá+57 3225112476

Libertario Coffee Roasters is the kind of coffee shop that feels effortlessly cool, with elegant interiors and an extensive menu for curious drinkers. With multiple locations across the city, it has a range of coffees in its rotation at any given moment, from balanced and fruit-forward to experimental and rare. I’m generally partial to the filter coffees, but for something more unexpected, order the Bruma, which pairs the cold brew with citrusy yuzu, rose petals, and rosemary. They have an all-day menu spanning pastries and brunch to sandwiches and bowls. Try the torta de almojábana, a play on the beloved cheese bread.

Varietale takes its name seriously, with an impressive collection of coffees ranging from familiar chocolatey and caramel-forward varieties to limited auction lots. The fun is figuring out how you want to drink them: Choose from nine filter methods, including V60, Chemex, and French press, and let the enthusiastic baristas guide you toward the one that best suits your beans. Despite all that geekery, Varietale feels refreshingly unpretentious at all its locations throughout the city. It has the spirit of an old-school cantina, where meeting a friend for a tinto was reason enough to get together.

Cra. 11B #96–54Carrera 5 # 71–45 Local 104Carrera 9 # 78–31+57 3202973150

If you like having options, Café 18 is the place to linger. Between its Chicó, El Nogal, and Rosales locations, the café typically offers around 15 Colombian coffees, with at least five varieties available at any given time. Some of the beans are sourced through Colombian coffee auctions held across the country, giving the café access to distinctive lots from producers. One of my favorite parts of visiting is ordering a filter coffee and watching it being prepared in front of me.

Cra. 6a #117–26, Usaquén, Bogotá, Cundinamarca

Colo Coffee has several locations across Bogotá, but I’d make a point of visiting its sprawling Usaquén café. The space unfolds around trees far older than its walls, with trunks cutting through the floors and coffee planters surrounding the interior. It’s the kind of place where you can easily lose track of time, especially since the coffee shop doubles as a roastery and serves a full menu. Grab a table near the roasting area and pair your coffee with carimañolas, crisp yuca fritters filled with cheese and served with spicy suero costeño, a tangy fermented cream from Colombia’s Caribbean coast. Before leaving, pick up one of Colo’s canned cold brews to go.

Calle 120 A # 3A–47Calle 70a # 5–71+57 321938 4156

Catación Pública is as much a classroom as it is a café. Founder Jaime Duque spent 17 years at Colombia’s National Federation of Coffee Growers before opening a space devoted to understanding what happens between farm and cup. At its original Usaquén café and newer Rosales outpost, you can taste Colombian coffees spanning different varieties and filter brewing methods. Alternatively, you can go deeper through hands-on experiences. The Rosales space mirrors that approach, with a sleek, laboratory-like interior centered around a deep-green coffee bar. I’d book the recently launched 75-minute roasting workshop, where you start with green coffee and watch the beans transform every two minutes as you roast them yourself. At the end, brew your coffee in a French press and leave with a 12-ounce bag of your own roast.

Cl. 12b #2–85, La Candelaria+57 3157307016

Located in La Candelaria, Bogotá’s oldest neighborhood, Jaguar Coffee sits inside a remodeled 200-year-old home. The café unfolds like a maze, with intimate lounge spaces and a bar where you can learn about the coffee cupping process or watch your order being prepared. Founder Mario Patiño has spent more than a decade building Jaguar and now works with some 170 coffee growers across the country. Beyond the café, Jaguar extends the experience to its farm in Silvania, about 30 miles outside Bogotá. Opt for a day trip or stay the night, and you can follow the journey from plant to cup and learn about the cultivation process.

#166. No-Knead Pumpkin Focaccia

For those who fall into the pumpkin-should-be-savory camp, let us offer up a new recipe primed to become a seasonal staple: Pumpkin Focaccia. The iconic bread we know and love is ripe for the pumpkin treatment, lending it a golden hue and earthy sweetness. This version doesn’t require any kneading, making it straightforward enough to pull off in a single afternoon. You’ll perform a series of folds as it rises, simply pulling and stretching the dough to help it develop gluten. A showering of fresh rosemary and flaky salt on top is optional, but it takes crisp, plush focaccia from good to great. Serve it with a bowl of olive oil for dipping or a schmear of cream cheese to lean into the seasonal profile.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Mix one ¼-oz. envelope active dry yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), 5 cups (625 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1½ cups warm water in a large bowl until a dry, shaggy dough forms. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot 15 minutes.

Place a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough and moisten hands in water, shaking off excess. Stretch 1 side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat process 3 more times, turning bowl after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Remoisten your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat entire process 2 more times (folding and resting), about 1 hour more. By the last full fold, the dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Pour ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil into a 13x9" metal baking pan. Lightly oil your hands and punch down dough, then transfer to prepared pan. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Turn dough salted side down to coat both sides in oil. Press into an even layer with your fingers. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 450°. Unwrap focaccia and scatter rosemary leaves and more sea salt over if desired; drizzle with oil. Oil your hands and press fingers into focaccia several times to create dimples across surface, making sure to press fingers all the way down to the bottom of the pan. Bake focaccia, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until deep golden brown, 23–28 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let focaccia cool slightly in pan. Using a metal spatula, turn out focaccia onto rack and let cool completely.

Do Ahead: Focaccia can be made 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

#167. Roasted Brussels Sprouts

Crispy, caramelized edges and tender centers are the hallmarks of perfectly roasted brussels sprouts—and you don’t need much more than olive oil, salt, and pepper to get there. This simple recipe relies on a hot oven and a rimmed baking sheet to turn the humble vegetable into a side dish worthy of both weeknight dinners and the Thanksgiving table.

The key is to halve the brussels sprouts (quarter any especially large ones), then spread them in a single layer so they roast instead of steam. Toss them occasionally as they cook, letting the outer leaves turn crisp and the cut sides develop a deep golden brown color. Serve them straight from the oven, or dress them up with a squeeze of lemon juice, a shower of grated Parmesan, or a drizzle of balsamic vinegar.

How do you make roasted brussels sprouts crispy?

Use high heat (450°F) and spread the sprouts in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet. Overcrowding traps moisture, causing them to steam rather than roast. Use two baking sheets if necessary.

How long should you roast brussels sprouts?

At 450°F, brussels sprouts typically take 15–25 minutes, depending on their size. Start checking around the 15-minute mark, especially if using a convection oven. They’re ready when the centers are tender and the edges are deeply browned.

Can you make roasted brussels sprouts ahead of time?

They’re best served hot from the oven, when the edges are crispiest. To get a head start, trim and halve the sprouts up to a day ahead and refrigerate in an airtight container. Reheat leftovers in a 350°F oven until warmed through, though they won’t be quite as crisp.

Preheat oven to 450°. Toss 3 lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, quartered if large, ¼ cup plus 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground black pepper on a rimmed baking sheet to coat. Arrange in a single layer and roast, tossing occasionally, until tender and browned, 15–25 minutes.

Once you’ve mastered the basics, there are plenty of ways to change things up. Try frico’ed brussels sprouts with a crispy Parmesan crust; brussels sprouts with warm honey glaze or garlicky balsamic brussels sprouts for a savory-sweet finish; or, for a little heat, make roasted brussels sprouts with gochujang brown butter.

Editor’s note: This brussels sprouts recipe was first published in November 2015; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more of our best brussels sprout recipes →

#168. Add This Spicy Ingredient To Ground Beef For Juicier Burgers (Hint: It's Not Chipotle In Adobo)

Whether you're an accomplished griller or just an amateur, you've likely heard many different schools of thought when it comes to how to mix and grill the perfect hamburger. Renowned chef Bobby Flay goes with just salt and pepper. However, you can branch out and can add a little onion powder and Worcestershire sauce. You can even go with one single sauce to season your burger that has tons of flavor built into a single bottle (yes, we're talking A1). But beyond the powders and sauces and other ingredients, you might want to try adding a whole other meat to your burger for some Mexican spice that will make you rethink the common cooked ground beef. Try mixing chorizo into your next blend for a slight hit of heat and extra juiciness that doesn't require a lot of prep.

Okay, so there's Spanish chorizo, and there's Mexican chorizo. You want the Mexican stuff. Spanish chorizo is a cured meat, like a small and firm salami, full of paprika flavor, hard, and generally cut into slices to eat a piece at a time. A Mexican chorizo, on the other hand, is a raw sausage, also usually flavored with paprika, vinegar, and often spices (including a variety of chiles). Sometimes it's made in casings to cook on the grill; sometimes it's packaged in a tube, much like American-style breakfast sausage. Either way, if you want a bit of extra spice, flavor, and juiciness, Mexican chorizo is the perfect addition to your burgers.

Generally, equal parts ground beef and chorizo should get your flavor dialed in. While you'd normally want to go with about an 80/20 ratio for a perfectly juicy all-beef burger (meaning 80% lean and 20% fat), because chorizo is sometimes fattier, you may want to go with a leaner ground beef. About 10% fat should be good. That said, some chorizos have close to an 80/20 fat percentage (or even a leaner blend than that), so you should check out the packaging before selecting your ground beef. To determine the fat percentage, simply divide the total grams of fat by the serving size. For example, if the fat is 16 grams and the serving size is 70 grams, that's roughly 23% fat — pretty close to 80/20.

Depending on where you live, there's likely a Mexican grocery store that can help you with the mixture, and you won't even have to remove the sausages from the casings — if they have a good meat department, and you ask politely, they may even blend it with the beef for you. Depending on how much spice you want (and how spicy the chorizo comes from the counter), you may want to go with a smaller proportion of chorizo to ground beef. While it's not always extremely spicy, it often has added chiles or chili powder, so it can bring a serious kick if you're not sure about the proportions. Chorizo is almost always pork-based, so just like with other burger blend alternatives, you may need to change up your cooking technique a bit. With a full beef burger, you can cook it to whatever doneness you want. With pork, you don't want any pink inside to ensure it's done.

#169. 6 Foods & Drinks You Should Stop Buying After 30, According To A Dietitian

Despite the paralyzing fear I had about turning 30 for years leading up to it, I was pretty relieved once I actually hit the milestone. I felt older, wiser, and more settled. The only downside to the new decade (other than the quarterly Botox bills)? Realizing my metabolism wasn’t quite as speedy as it once was.

Let’s face it: As much as I’d love to still eat as I did in high school, my body feels it differently now. When I drink too much, I feel the hangover for days; overly processed foods make my joints ache; and dairy just doesn’t sit right the way it did at 21 when I was pounding pizza slices at 2 a.m. And those are just the immediate effects. There are a lot of long-term consequences related to diet, too!

So, I tapped an expert on the subject, registered dietitian Lauren Manaker, to help me round up the food and drinks that no one (not me, you, your parents, your besties, anyone!) should be eating after the age of 30—minus, of course, a few caveats and the understanding that most things in moderation are OK* from time to time!

*You can pry the Diet Coke from my cold, dead hands!

Here are six things you should stop buying, eating, and drinking once you hit the big 3-0.

I’m not saying you have to bow out of happy hours the second you turn 30 (I mean that as someone just a year away from that milestone), but you might want to invest in higher-quality bottles—if only to ward off worse hangovers.

Manaker also points out that it's a good age to start reevaluating your relationship with alcohol and potentially cutting back. “Sure, a glass of wine or a cocktail here and there can be part of a balanced lifestyle, but as we age, our bodies process alcohol less efficiently,” she tells Delish. “This means those hangovers hit harder and last longer (ugh). Alcohol can also negatively impact sleep, which can impact mood, focus, and more. Moderation is key if you choose to drink alcohol. Your liver (and your morning self) will thank you.”

Even if you’ve graduated from late-night study sessions fueled by Red Bull to workouts motivated by Alani, as Manaker points out, “your 30-something body isn't as forgiving” when it comes to processing these ingredients. These drinks are packed with caffeine and sugar, and aren't nearly as beneficial as they might seem.

They can “spike your energy temporarily but leave you crashing hard later. Over time, they can mess with your heart health, blood pressure, and even your sleep quality,” she explains. “If you need a pick-me-up, try a cup of tea instead; it’s gentler on your system. Or if you like the idea of a canned energy drink sans the loads of added sugar, plus some extra benefits, an option like Bloom Nutrition Sparkling Energy is a nice choice.”

Like with alcohol, moderation is key when it comes to sweets, but candies like gummy bears are just a bad idea in general. As Manaker puts it, they’re “pure sugar.”

“While gummy bears might have been a fun snack in your teens, they’re not doing your 30-something self any favors. Excess sugar can lead to energy crashes, weight gain, and more,” she says. “Plus, gummy bears don’t offer any real nutrients, so they’re just taking up space that could be filled with something more nourishing.”

A dietitian-approved alternative? Fresh fruit or a square of dark chocolate. If you really can't shake the gummy bear craving, try something with less added sugar and gut-health-supporting fiber, like Smartsweets.

While what I'm about to say isn't a free pass to go wild on actual sugar, artificial sweeteners aren’t the holy grail solution you probably thought once upon a time—in fact, you should steer clear as best you can. They can impact your gut health and more!

According to a study presented at Nutrition 2025, an annual meeting of the American Society for Nutrition, there is a significant link between drinking artificially sweetened beverages and an increased risk of diabetes. The whole study took place over a 30-year time period and found that those who consumed diet bevvys and drinks sweetened by saccharin were more than twice as likely to develop type 2. Since you probably haven't been throwing back diet sodas and eating sugar-free pudding since birth, now is the perfect time to reevaluate your relationship with artificial sweeteners—ya know, before you hit that 30-year mark yourself.

As a Diet Coke stan, this one hurts. “Don't hate me,” Manaker jokes. “But if you're focused on bone health, drinking tons of [Diet Coke] might not be doing you any favors.” She explains that sodas, in particular, contain phosphoric acid, which can interfere with calcium absorption and might even weaken your bones. It also has zero nutritional value.

“To tame my Diet Coke cravings, I drink OLIPOP Vintage Cola,” she says. “It is free from phosphoric acid and contains nothing artificial. Plus, it contains prebiotic fiber to help support gut health—OG Diet Coke could never!”

Frozen meals are the GOAT in college and right out of school because they’re easy and cheap, but let’s face it: they’re not the healthiest—even if the packaging tries to convince you otherwise. While there are some decent frozen options out there, a lot of the frozen aisle contains products with high sodium and little nutritional value. If you're really craving pizza rolls that badly, it might be time to go all Nara Smith and make your own from scratch.

#170. Rice Krispies Treats

Perhaps the most nostalgic of all recipes, a classic Rice Krispies treat is hard to beat. There’s just something about the crisp yet gooey texture that can’t be replicated. While the classic back-of-box recipe is a guaranteed winner, we thought it was high time to give the original a run for its money. Introducing our new favorite way to make Rice Krispies treats, with a few small (but dramatic) tweaks to the original formula. For starters, this version increases the butter and browns it, adding a subtle nutty flavor. From there, the marshmallows are split in two: The first set gets fully melted into the butter along with salt and vanilla, while the remaining set gets folded in along with the cereal so you get pockets of stretchy marshmallow throughout. While seemingly insignificant, these small changes make for a Rice Krispies treat that’s perfectly pullable, delightfully sweet yet salty, and just a touch more exciting than the classic.

Read More: The Only Type of Marshmallows I’ll Use for Rice Krispies Treats

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Lightly coat a 13x9" baking pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray and line with parchment paper, leaving overhang on long sides. Cook ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat, stirring constantly, until butter foams, then darkens to a light amber, about 4 minutes. Remove from heat and immediately add one 10-oz. bag mini marshmallows, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and quickly stir until marshmallows are melted.

Add remaining one 10-oz. bag mini marshmallows and 9 cups Rice Krispies or other puffed rice cereal to pot and mix until cereal is completely coated in melted marshmallow mixture and last addition of marshmallows is melted slightly. Working quickly, transfer mixture to prepared pan and spread into an even layer. (Don’t press too hard.) Let sit at least 1 hour before cutting into squares.

Do Ahead: Rice Krispies treats can be made 2 days ahead. Store tightly covered at room temperature.

#171. How long does pie last in the fridge? : Because we're all wondering what to do with our apple and pumpkin pies.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions. Today: How long does pie last in the fridge?

The season of plentiful pies is upon us. When preparing several pies for a holiday meal, you may be wondering about the imminent leftovers. Should apple pie be stored differently than pumpkin pie? David from our Baker’s Hotline is here with his expert advice to help.

“Baked apple or other fruit pies can be kept covered, at room temperature, for one to two days. After that, they’ll keep in the fridge for one to two more days,” David advises. A 15-minute reheat in a 350°F oven can help revive some of that freshly baked flavor. Tent the pie with foil so it doesn’t brown further.

Interested in prepping ahead? David says that storing an assembled, ready-to-bake apple pie is a bad idea; the fruity filling will release moisture, which will make your crust soggy. Instead, roll out your pie crusts and prep your apples, but keep them separate. And wait to add the sugar and spices to the apples until you’re ready to bake the pie. This way, you can pour off any liquid that’s accumulated from the fruit without draining off your thickener, sugar, and spices.

Sliced apples turn brown, so you don’t want to keep your prepared apples in the fridge very long before baking. Aim for under 24 hours, but a squeeze of lemon juice could help them last another day or so.

And if you want to use your freezer to prep ahead, here’s how to freeze and bake fruit pies.

David advises, “Baked pumpkin pie or other pies containing eggs and/or dairy such as pecan pie, custard pie, or chiffon pie should be stored refrigerated; they’ll keep in the fridge for three to four days. I like to transfer the pie to a shallow, lidded storage container, but plastic wrap or a storage top can be used as well.”

As with apple, if you’re making your pumpkin (and other custard) pie ahead, it’s best to keep filling and crust separate. Pumpkin pie filling can be made ahead; it’ll keep, refrigerated, overnight. In fact, that's actually what we recommend doing; the custard develops incredible flavor and aroma as it sits.

If you can, serve pies the day they were made instead of refrigerating them.

Reheat refrigerated pies in a 350°F oven for about 15 minutes prior to serving.

Apple and other fruit pies will last at room temperature for up to two days, then in the fridge for two more.

Pumpkin, custard, or other egg/dairy-based pies can be stored in the fridge for up to four days.

If you’re making the crust and the filling ahead, keep them separated until it’s time to bake your pie.

#174. Upgrade Your Next Reuben Sandwich With A Sweet, Caramelized Ingredient

When it comes to 1950s throwback sandwiches, Reubens seem to have it all. Hot seasoned meat, creamy dressing, and tangy sauerkraut, all layered between slices of aromatically earthy bread. But if you want to add a little something extra that complements all these ingredients, caramelized onions are the way to go, offering a touch of sweetness, subtle texture, and great vegetable flavor.

The perfect caramelized onions seem to go on just about everything, but they're especially great on Reubens. The fats used to caramelize them boost the richness of the corned beef or pastrami and add another layer of flavor. Those caramelized sugars help mitigate the bite of sauerkraut, but not so much that your sandwich won't have that touch of tang that's vital to cutting through the other heavy ingredients. If you opt for Russian dressing over Thousand Island, those same sugars blend with the horseradish to create a complex web of flavors, ranging from decadently rich onions to sinus-searing heat, all without having to adjust your condiment recipe.

Still, there's something homey and comforting about caramelized onions, just like swirled rye bread that's both rustic and fresh. While they can take a bit of time to cook, they keep for about four days in the fridge and represent a holistic approach to upgrading each individual ingredient on your sandwich. If you love Reubens but are tired of the same old, they offer one of the highest returns on investment and are dead easy to incorporate.

While raw onions can be enjoyed cold or warm, caramelized ones are typically best when consumed hot. Fortunately, their moisture and fat content make them easy to reheat, whether you just pop them in the microwave or get a bit creative and work them into your other ingredient prep.

For the meltiest cheese on such a thick sandwich, you might get better results by layering a slice over your bread and popping the whole thing under the broiler. This not only gives you great texture but also presents a chance to enhance your caramelized onions. A short burst of high heat should warm them all the way through, while the cheese can also act like glue that keeps your onions from shooting out the back of the bread when you take a bite. Compared to warming each side of a fully assembled sandwich, this method offers far better heat penetration and a more consistent result while still toasting your bread a bit.

Cold caramelized onions typically have some congealed juices, and letting those go to waste is a missed flavor opportunity. Warming your meat in a pan before layering it on not only gives it a bit of a toasted flavor, but doing so with a scattering of onions on top lets all that flavor drip directly into the meat. This has the added benefit of helping prevent your meat from drying out, as the onions release additional moisture to compensate for some of what the meat loses during heating.

#175. Chicken Marsala Casserole

When you’re hungry for something that’s comforting, cozy, and a little luxe feeling too, chicken Marsala is a truly excellent option. The pan sauce has plenty of mushrooms, fortified Marsala wine, and a splash of cream, because why not? It’s a fantastic dinner, easy enough for a weeknight and special enough for date night. This Italian-American recipe is such a crowd-pleaser that we have reimagined it with orzo, as a slow-cooker meal, and as a gnocchi and chicken soup too. Now it’s time for chicken Marsala’s casserole moment. There's still a rich mushroom-Marsala sauce and plenty of chicken, but now there’s al dente pasta and lots of melty Swiss cheese, creating a rich, shareable dinner that everyone will reach for.

The cheese:Melted Swiss gives this casserole an almost French onion soup-like flavor. If you can’t buy a block of Swiss cheese, pick up 8 ounces of sliced Swiss cheese from your deli counter and coarsely chop it. A mix of low-moisture mozzarella and white cheddar would work here too.

The chicken:A rotisserie chicken will usually yield 3 ½ to 4 ½ cups of cooked meat. Picking up a whole cooked chicken is a great option here, but definitely not the only one. If you cook chicken for another meal–roasting a whole chicken or chicken thighs or breasts—cooking an extra 1 1⁄2 to 2 pounds of chicken will yield enough cooked meat for this recipe. If you have 4 cups of cooked penne or rigatoni, you can add the cooled cooked pasta to the baking dish in step 2 along with the chicken.

The garnish:Now, a casserole as delicious as this doesn’t need a garnish per se, but some chopped parsley adds a fresh finish, and a little bit of freshly grated Parmesan would add more cheesy, umami notes.

Storage:This casserole can be prepared through step 5. Cover with foil and refrigerate for up to 24 hours. Take the casserole out of the fridge while the oven is preheating. Bake, covered, for 25 to 30 minutes, until the sauce is bubbling, then bake uncovered for 10 to 15 minutes, until the cheese has melted and is browning in spots. You can cook the casserole 4 days ahead; store in an airtight container and refrigerate. Any leftovers should last about the same time.

#176. Salt Bread (Shio Pan)

Welcome to the Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep into why it works. This month we welcome deputy food editor Hana Asbrink to be our guest baker. Come bake and learn with us—and don’t forget to join the Bake Club group chat over on Substack.

The version of this recipe that appeared in our November 2026 print issue has the incorrect bake time listed. The recipe that follows features the correct total bake times of 15–18 minutes (please see step 8).

Salt bread is a wondrous buttery roll known as shio pan in Japanese or sogeum ppang in Korean. It originated in Japan in 2014 and quickly became popularized in Korea soon thereafter, taking off in the post-Covid era around 2021. It’s formed by rolling each ball of dough around a nub of salted butter. As it bakes, the butter melts and oozes out of the bun, “frying” and crisping up the bottom. If you can imagine a warm dinner roll meeting a flaky croissant, you’re getting closer.

You’ll often find a range of salt bread, some leaning closer to sturdy bread with a tighter crumb and others resembling a softer milk bread. In all salt bread cases, there are a few key identifiers: (1) a deeply golden exterior, with the aforementioned crisp bottom; (2) the signature hollow in the middle (where the pat of butter once stood) when you tear the bun in half; and (3) a sprinkle of flaky or coarse salt atop the bun.

In this riff, I use an enriched dough, bringing in qualities of a soft milk bread into the mix. With the bread flour, the end result is a lovely, crowd-pleasing bun that’s great for snacking on its own or enjoying alongside a special holiday meal. If there’s one note to highlight: Ensure you are starting with a fresh pack of instant (or “rapid-rise”) yeast. This will make all the difference in the rise and the eventual yield.

Read More: BA Bake Club’s October Recipe Is the Best Dinner Roll We’ve Ever Made

1 hour 30 minutes (plus 3 hours 30 minutes for resting)

Stir 2 Tbsp. (16 g) flour and ½ cup water in a small skillet, preferably nonstick, over medium heat with a heatproof rubber spatula to combine and cook, stirring constantly, until thickened to the texture of mayonnaise, about 2 minutes; remove from heat. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into small pieces and stir until melted. Transfer tangzhong to the bowl of a stand mixer.

Add 2 large eggs, ½ cup whole milk, ¼ cup (50 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) to tangzhong; stir vigorously by hand with rubber spatula until incorporated. Add remaining 4 cups (500 g) flour, attach bowl to stand mixer fitted with a dough hook or paddle, and mix on low speed until dough is smooth and soft (it may stick to bottom of bowl but should mostly clear sides), 20–25 minutes. Pinch off a small piece of dough and stretch it between your thumbs and index fingers on both hands. The dough should be able to stretch thin enough to let light through without breaking. If it tears, the gluten is not yet developed enough. Keep mixing until it can stretch; it may take up to 30 minutes.

Transfer dough to a work surface (no need to flour) and shape into a ball. Lightly grease stand mixer bowl with vegetable oil. Return dough to bowl, cover tightly with a plate or plastic wrap, and let rise in a warm, draft-free spot until nearly doubled in size, about 2 hours. (For optimal flavor, let dough sit at room temperature 30 minutes, then cover tightly or transfer to an airtight container and chill at least 8 hours and up to 2 days to proof slowly.)

Meanwhile, cut 1 cup (2 sticks) salted butter into 1-Tbsp. pieces and arrange in a single layer on a large plate or small baking sheet. Chill in freezer until ready to use.

Transfer dough to a surface (no need to bring to room temperature before shaping if you chilled it). Using a bench scraper or paring knife, cut dough into 70–75 g portions (you’ll get 12–16 portions depending on how much your dough has risen). Working with 1 portion at a time, cup your hand over dough and drag across surface, moving your hand in a rapid circular motion to form into a tight ball (cold dough is easier to work with; rolling into balls on an unfloured, ungreased counter creates friction and helps the shaping process). Place on a baking sheet and cover with plastic wrap; let sit 15 minutes.

Uncover dough (save plastic wrap) and, working one at a time, carefully roll each ball into a cone shape with your hands (you want them about 4" on the wider end). Return to baking sheet and re-cover with reserved plastic wrap. Let dough rest 15 minutes.

Place a cone in front of you on surface with wider end facing toward you (keep remaining cones covered in plastic wrap). Lightly flatten with your palm, then roll out dough lengthwise to make an isosceles triangle about 12" long with a 3½"–4"-wide base (short side of triangle). Place 1 Tbsp. frozen salted butter at base of dough and roll up (not too tightly) like a croissant. Arrange, seam side down, back on baking sheet. Repeat with remaining cones and salted butter (you may not need all of the butter; save it for another use). Let rolls sit at room temperature until slightly puffed, about 1 hour.

Place a rack in lowest position in oven; preheat to 425°. Remove plastic from rolls. Lightly mist rolls with water from spray bottle; sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Bake 10 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back and continue baking rolls until golden brown on top and bottom, 5–8 minutes more (keep an eye that they don’t burn). Remove from oven (there will be melted butter on baking sheet, so be careful) and, using a heatproof pastry brush, brush butter on baking sheet over rolls. Let rolls cool at least 10 minutes before serving.

Do Ahead: Rolls can be baked 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

In a separate bowl, whisk together the all-purpose flour, cocoa powder, instant espresso powder, baking soda and flaked sea salt. Gradually add the flour mixture to the creamed mixture.

#178. The 10 Best Ground Meat Shopping Tips

Whether it's beef, pork, or poultry, ground meat is a staple in kitchens across the United States, uniquely suited for dozens of dishes and cuisines. You can form it into patties, shape it into kebabs, pile it into lettuce wraps, sprinkle it over tofu, or mold it into meatloaves. But unlike steak, pork chops, or chicken breast, there's an underlying mysteriousness surrounding ground meat that can prevent shoppers from getting exactly what they want or need. While it may seem as straightforward as food can get, there's actually a lot to know about this ubiquitous source of protein.

When shopping for ground meat, you have to come prepared with a little knowledge and know-how. These featured tips will help you select the right meat for the right occasions. Most shoppers are probably familiar with the idea of lean-to-fat ratios, but does everyone know about grind size, modified atmospheric packaging, shrinkage, or a great short rib blend? These insights will not only allow you to get more bang for your buck, but they'll help you develop a greater appreciation for the product itself. So much thought, time, and planning go into each package of ground meat, and the more you know, the better your cooking will become.

At first glance, ground meat may look the same, but those squiggly lines of extruded meat come in a variety of circumferences, primarily determined by grind size. At the end of a commercial meat grinder is a stationary plate with holes of various sizes through which the meat is extruded. Larger holes create a coarser grind; smaller holes make for finer, thinner strands of meat. This isn't just for aesthetics — grind size can affect the texture and durability of your final dish.

A finer grind breaks down completely, making it better for recipes that benefit from a smoother consistency, like meat sauce or lasagna. Finely ground meat also develops more myosin, a protein that serves as a natural binder and helps keep dishes like meatballs, dumpling filling, and meatloaf more or less glued together. This is best when density and structure, not juiciness, are the ultimate goal. Coarser grinds don't bind as easily, resulting in a heartier texture and more rustic appearance — think chunky Bolognese, stuffed peppers, or a meaty Sloppy Joe. If you want some bite to your chili or extra chew to your burger, go for a medium or coarse grind. Unlike lean-to-fat ratios or specific cuts, grind size is typically left off the package, so to identify a finer grind with just your eyeballs, look for meat that appears smooth and densely packed, with more uniform fat distribution.

This is the most important detail to consider when purchasing ground meat. Presented as a two-number fraction, the lean-to-fat ratio tells you how much fat is in your meat relative to lean muscle. A meat's lean-to-fat ratio falls into three general categories: extra lean (10% to 15% fat), lean (15% to 20% fat), and high-fat (25%+); however, in packages of ground poultry, you can find meat containing as little as 1% fat. No ratio is necessarily superior to another; each combination has its own culinary advantages and drawbacks.

The ratio you choose should depend on the dish you're cooking. Lean meat is drier, chewier, and less greasy, making it better for sauces or chili where extra fat can be an issue, and for dishes that require tight cohesion, like meatballs or meatloaf. Since leaner blends often lack flavor and fat, cooks often blend in a proportion of fattier cuts to balance it out. Meat with a higher fat content (20% to 30%) is optimal for a grill or dry skillet — think taco meat, burgers, or a Cuban picadillo. As the fat renders, it coats the protein, giving you more time before the meat dries out completely and overcooks. Most professional cooks recommend an 80/20 blend for your standard backyard burger, but you should always experiment to find a ratio that works for you.

It's normal for ground meat to have a little extra moisture floating around, but too much liquid can indicate a quality issue. The meat industry has a word for this watery byproduct: meat-purge. So what is it exactly? It may look convincingly like blood, but the liquid you see emanating from your steak or ground beef is actually a mix of water and myoglobin, a protein that gives meat its reddish-purple hue. There are a few potential sources of excess liquid, most of them totally natural, while others — not so much.

Meat, like most of the body, is mostly water, which is what gives it its structure, texture, and juiciness. Over time, as the muscle fibers are cut, processed, and packaged, the water held within the cells is released and may pool toward the bottom of the package. Although this may be unappetizing to look at, it's not necessarily a quality issue. The bigger problem is when this moisture results from fluctuations in storage temperature. Continuous freezing, thawing, and temperature changes can increase purge and indicate a lack of freshness or over-handling. Another downside is that if too much moisture escapes the meat, it may dry out faster during cooking. That said, purveyors expect some purge, also known as drip or weep, which is why some ground meat includes a moisture-absorbent pad at the bottom of the package. Still, if deciding between two packages, buy the one that's drier.

Sell-by and use-by dates cause a lot of confusion. And rightfully so; this system of categorization is far from intuitive. What you need to know, especially for meat, is that these dates measure food quality rather than food safety. That means, in most cases, you can eat meat a day or two past its use-by date, as long as you cook it to the proper internal temperature. Think of it more as a message from the manufacturer stating that they can't guarantee quality — taste, texture, color — past the date listed on the package.

Equally important as the sell-by date is the type of container it's stamped on. If you look through the refrigerated meat aisle in your supermarket, you'll see all different packaging options. These aren't just for display; they have a real purpose in preserving the quality and freshness of the ground meat inside. If a supermarket has an in-house butcher, it'll likely display its meat in foam trays covered with plastic wrap. Although the meat might be freshly ground, this packaging lets in the most oxygen, accelerating spoilage. Ground meat packaged by a central supplier is often sold in a plastic container covered with a plastic film called modified atmosphere packaging (MAP), which replaces the air inside the package with other gases to preserve the food more efficiently.

Besides a use-by date, color is one of the only indicators of freshness you can actually visualize. When buying ground beef, aim for a package that's bright red. As the meat ages, the red color will dull, eventually turning brown or gray-brown. Unfortunately, you can't rely on brightness alone. Suppliers can add a puff of gas, such as nitrogen or carbon dioxide, to help the meat maintain its color. Complicating matters further, beef that looks slightly discolored in the package may be fine after all. Oxygen exposure can cause meat to brown on the outside, while its interior may remain perfectly red or pink.

However, a meat's color communicates more than just freshness. A general rule is that beef that's pinker typically has a higher fat content. And speaking of fat, the tiny pellets should be either a clean white (if the cow is grain-fed) or a pale yellow (if its diet was mostly grass). These color tips also apply to poultry and pork. If you're buying ground chicken, lighter meat means a higher proportion of lean breast meat, while a darker or reddish color implies more dark meat. The most important color to watch out for is green, which implies the meat is moldy or spoiled.

Maybe you're in a hurry; maybe you don't like the texture of raw meat; maybe you just got your nails done — whatever the reason, sometimes people simply don't want to go through the effort of flattening ground beef or chicken into a patty. But you'll be rewarded for the effort. Now, pre-formed patties aren't necessarily lower quality, but their very nature goes against much of the criteria that makes a good hamburger.

The first reason, and the most obvious, is that you can't control the size or thickness of your meat. Second, you don't always know the meat's blend or lean-to-fat ratio. But the main issue is how the patty is shaped and pressed. Many pre-formed patties are made by machine, not the soft, gentle touch of a human hand. The result is a densely compressed circle of ground meat, almost always beef, with a slightly chewy bite; far from the luscious, juicy burger we all expect. Much of this has to do with the juices or moisture being literally squeezed from the meat as it's flattened into a denser puck-like patty. However, pre-formed patties are easier to prepare and a definite time-saver, so if you go that route, just check the ingredient label to make sure there aren't added binders, seasonings, or any additional ingredients that will affect your final product.

Sometimes when we're roaming the brightly lit aisles of the supermarket, our eyes are a little bigger than our stomachs. In these cases, it's common to freeze perishable proteins, like ground meat, to use later. But not all packaging is created equal. Your typical foam tray and plastic wrap are less competent at protecting your meat from moisture and subsequent freezer burn. Enter vacuum sealing. Although this technology is nothing new, it has only recently been applied to ground meat. The process removes excess oxygen — the primary source of spoilage — and creates an airtight seal that keeps the meat inside fresh.

Ground meat that's vacuum-sealed can last up to two weeks in the refrigerator and over a year in the freezer while maintaining its original taste, interior moisture, texture, and overall quality. And even if you don't plan on freezing it, vacuum-sealed meat retains more juiciness because none of the moisture can escape. And with convenient package sizes, this is a good option if you can find a price that's comparable to other conventionally packed ground meats.

Buying meat from the butcher counter has several advantages, the most important being the expert knowledge of the person standing behind the display case. But beyond the service, a local butcher can deliver the exact meat, cut, or blend you want, a service that's especially important for ground meat. Unlike steaks or chops, ground meat is more ambiguous. For the reasons listed above — freshness, lean-to-fat ratios, grind size — you want to be as specific with your ground meat order as possible. Otherwise, you might end up with a product that doesn't fit your intended purpose.

And a butcher's expertise extends beyond the realm of the raw into the kingdom of the cooked. Even if you don't know exactly what grind you need for meatballs, Scotch eggs, stuffed cabbage, or a smoky Texas chili, an experienced butcher can point you in the right direction. And the more information you provide, the more they can help. Another obvious benefit is that your butcher can help you customize your blend based on many of the criteria described above. If you want a medium-coarse grind of sirloin, short rib, and chuck, your butcher can likely deliver, especially if you place your order ahead of time. Now, if you walk into your butcher completely clueless, you can't go wrong asking for an 80/20, medium grind of chuck for a reliable balance of fat and flavor.

Supermarkets use all sorts of methods to shape your purchasing decisions. Ground meat is no different. It seems simple enough: The cheaper package is typically the better deal. Well, not quite. What matters most when buying any meat — ground beef, chicken breast, lamb chops — is the price per pound, not the price per package. Price differences can vary by geography or supermarket chain, but they mostly depend on the type of meat, cut, or lean-to-fat ratio. For example, ground meat with a higher lean-to-fat ratio, like beef sirloin or round, typically costs more per pound.

On the flip side, packages labeled simply "ground hamburger" are usually the cheapest option, often made from trimmings or leftover meat scraps. Another point to consider when buying ground meat is cook yield, or "shrinkage." This number refers to the post-cook weight of your meat. Ground meat with higher fat ratios tends to have lower cook yields as the fat renders during cooking, which can negate or at least reduce the initial price advantage of this lower-quality meat. Before purchasing, also consider the final application of your product. Ground chicken is a less expensive option with a neutral flavor, making it ideal for dishes like chili or a bright and herbaceous Thai larb salad. Burgers, on the other hand, are all about the meat, so you'll want a more precise lean-to-fat ratio, cut, and grind size.

In this case, "multi-meat" refers to both a blend of meats from different animals (pork, veal, beef) as well as a mixture of different cuts of beef (sirloin, brisket, chuck) — sorry, poultry; there's not enough variety of cuts at your typical meat market, so the focus is on beef. Look for blends that combine both lean and fat cuts. Sirloin and brisket are firmer with more chew, while short rib, chuck, and oxtail are more decadent, with deep savory flavors and lingering notes of nuttiness. This creates a balanced texture and flavor profile that's ideal for burgers and grilled kebabs.

But sometimes you need meat from three different animals for a truly balanced bite. In most grocery stores and meat markets, you can find packages that combine pork, beef, and veal. These mixes are especially well-suited for dishes that need both a firm, cohesive texture and a smooth interior, like meatballs, meatloaf, or Salisbury steak. In this scenario, the beef provides taste and structure; the pork contributes fat and flavor; and the veal adds moisture and collagen, a natural binder that holds everything together.

#179. I Ate My Way Through Edinburgh For A Weekend & Had One Of The Best Meals Of My Life

I found plenty to love before I even made it to the Michelin star.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

I love traveling, but I usually like having someone there to experience everything with me. Every once in a while, though, I need a few days where I can move completely at my own pace.

I have some Scottish roots, and when I got the opportunity to take myself to Edinburgh for a long weekend, the answer was pretty easy. I wanted to walk as much of the city as possible, get a little lost, see the sights, and, most importantly, eat extremely well along the way.

With only a few days to work with, I squeezed in everything from Scottish classics I’d never tried before to an old favorite and, for my final dinner, a Michelin-starred tasting menu that I’ll never forget.

Here’s everything I ate and drank along the way.

Nothing says “welcome to Scotland” like getting off a plane and immediately finding an almond croissant of epic proportions.

Cobbled Roastery was my first food stop, and I wasn’t looking for anything complicated. The croissant had a flaky shell that shattered everywhere the second I tore into it. It was aggressively almond-y in the best way, covered with powdered sugar, and after an overnight flight, it did exactly what I needed.

Dishoom and I already had history. I first went in London and loved it enough to return for breakfast on the same trip, so in Edinburgh I did what any adventurous food writer would do and ordered basically the exact same things again.

That consisted of their vegetable samosas and some Chicken Ruby with a healthy side of jasmine rice. The samosas were crisp and packed with warmly spiced peas and potatoes, while the Chicken Ruby was exactly as rich and silky as I remembered it. I had zero regrets about repeating myself.

Later that day, I joined Eating Europe’s Old Town Food & Drinks Tour, which was my crash course in some of the Scottish foods I probably wouldn’t have known to order on my own.

First up was Cullen skink at The Doric, a Scottish soup made with smoked haddock, potatoes, and cream. I’ll admit, a bowl of creamy fish soup didn’t immediately sound like something I needed in my life, but this won me over. The smoke came through first, then the creaminess, while the haddock was much subtler than I expected. It tasted more like a really good potato soup that happened to have smoked fish in it than a bowl screaming “SEAFOOD!” at me.

I knew what haggis was in the broadest sense, but then I actually Googled the ingredients and briefly wished I hadn’t.

Thankfully, eating it was a much better experience than reading about it. Arcade serves theirs as little fried bon bons with whisky marmalade and crispy kale, and the texture immediately reminded me of arancini with that crunchy outside and soft, savory inside. The filling was super meaty without tasting remotely as intimidating as the ingredient list sounds, and my skepticism quickly turned into borderline plate-licking.

By dinner at BABA inside the Kimpton Charlotte Square Hotel, I had reached the part of the trip where ordering one thing felt unnecessarily restrictive, so I went with the Best of BABA and let the table fill up.

This was also where I remembered how aggressively I love a good dip. I kept going back to the muhammara with the warm pita, and somehow haggis made another appearance on one of the skewers (we’re dating now). And I couldn’t remember the last time I’d deliberately ordered pork neck, if ever, but it was gone very quickly.

Then there was the mandarin crème brulée. The top had that satisfying crack, with smooth, citrusy custard underneath, and photographic proof of a completely scraped-clean dish was 100 percent necessary.

A brief interruption from all the eating for one of my favorite moments of the trip.

I grabbed a Cold Town lager, sat outside at Kick Ass, and looked straight out at Edinburgh Castle right there in the distance. Just me, my Scottish beer, and a lot of people watching. Not every moment needs to be more complicated than that.

By my second night, I wanted to go classic: fish and chips.

Herbie More’s did it with panko-crusted haddock, tartare sauce, fries, and mushy peas. The fish had that ideal contrast of a super-crisp outside and flaky interior, and I was embarrassingly happy about the mushy peas. I love peas enough that I regularly put them in pasta at home, although admittedly I usually stop short of mushing them first.

I only meant to stop for coffee until I saw a sausage roll sitting in the bakery case—which is generally how these things happen.

The pastry was buttery and flaky enough to leave evidence all over the plate, while the pork filling had leeks and potato worked through it. It tasted like something somebody had actually made that morning rather than something pulled from a plastic package and reheated.

87-91A Henderson Street, Leith, Edinburgh EH6 6ED

I saved my most ambitious meal for last. Heron in Leith has a Michelin star, and for roughly three hours—longer than some Avengers movies—I was taken through course after course, each paired with wine and presented with such precision that I almost felt guilty disturbing the plate.

The squid was one of my early favorites, but the venison was probably the course I kept thinking about afterward. It was rich, really well cooked, and one of those dishes I was genuinely bummed to finish.

And I will always find room for dessert. One of the final bowls got the same treatment as that crème brulée at BABA: spoon around the edges, spoon across the bottom, and leave nothing to investigate.

It was probably one of the best meals I’ve ever eaten, and as a final dinner, I couldn’t have planned much better.

More than anything, I loved that I got to experience the city through food without feeling like I was eating the same version of “Scottish food” for three straight days. And for someone who doesn’t usually seek out solo travel, eating my way through Edinburgh turned out to be a pretty convincing argument for doing it more often.

#180. Cottage Cheese Meatballs

Adding cottage cheese to a meatball might sound like an attempt to cram extra protein into a recipe, but it’s not the only valid reason. Something magical happens with the addition of cottage cheese: It practically disappears in the baking process, lending the meatballs juiciness and a subtle savory-salty flavor. As a bonus, the cottage cheese helps to stretch the recipe and you’ll end up with almost twice as many meatballs from one pound of ground beef.

Think of this recipe as a bit of a blank canvas, allowing you to use the meatballs however you please. You can bake them and pop them in your mouth as is, drop them into simmering tomato sauce, or stuff them between slices of bread for a hearty sandwich. They, like most meatballs, are also very meal-prep-friendly and take to freezing well.

More great cottage cheese recipes this way: Cottage Cheese Lasagna; Cottage Cheese Caramelized Onion Dip; and Roasted Honeynut Squash With Cottage Cheese and Chili Crisp.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Mix together 1 large egg, 4 garlic cloves, finely chopped, one 16-oz. container cottage cheese, 1 lb. ground beef, 1 cup Italian breadcrumbs, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large bowl to combine. Scoop out into 2-Tbsp. (heaping) portions and roll into smooth balls between your hands (you should have about 30).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large nonstick skillet over high heat. Working in batches and adding more oil between batches as needed, cook meatballs in a single layer, turning halfway through, until browned on 2 sides, about 3 minutes per batch. Transfer to a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet and bake in oven until cooked through, 12–14 minutes.

Do Ahead: Meatballs can be made 3 days ahead. Let cool; transfer to an airtight container and chill, or freeze up to 1 month.

#181. How to prebake pie crust — and why you should: The key to flaky — not flabby — pie crust.

A soggy bottom. Not something you want for your baby. Or your pie crust. And while we can’t help you with your baby, there’s a simple solution to pies with soggy bottoms: prebake (also known as blind bake) the crust.

There are a number of reasons your pie can end up with a soft, pale, underbaked crust — and steps you can take to help prevent that unfortunate result.

But the one surefire way to make certain your pie’s crust will be golden brown, crisp, and delicious — just as appealing as its filling — is to prebake it. That’s right: bake the bottom crust first, before adding the filling.

Most commonly, it's smart to prebake pie crust when:

But some fillings might instead cook fully on the stovetop, like the rich, thick filling for chocolate cream pie. When it’s done, you simply pour it into its crust — and said crust had better be prebaked to perfection, since the pie’s not going anywhere near an oven.

Other pies, typically those with a more delicate, egg- and cream-based filling (think custard pie or quiche) require at least some baking — but don’t spend long enough in the oven (at a high enough temperature) to guarantee a fully baked, brown and crispy crust.

In these cases, you need to prebake your crust.

The recipe you're following may explain explicitly how to prebake your crust. But if it doesn't, follow this process:

First, roll your bottom crust and place it in the pan. Crimp or flatten the edge. Chill it for 30 minutes, to relax the gluten and firm up the fat(s); this will help prevent shrinkage, so don't skip!

Line the crust with foil, parchment, or a paper coffee filter. Fill it about two-thirds full with dried beans, uncooked rice (or other uncooked grain berries), pie weights, or granulated sugar.

Bake the crust in a preheated 375°F oven for 20 minutes, set on a baking stone or steel if you have one. Remove the crust from the oven and lift out the liner and weights. (If you’ve used sugar, save it for your future baking; it’ll be lightly toasted and yummy!)

At this point your crust is partially prebaked, and good for any of your pies that tend to exhibit a wan, flabby bottom crust when done. Think pumpkin pie: You don’t want to bake the filling so long that it’s stiff and dry, but you may pull your pie out of the oven to find your perfectly baked filling is resting in a partially baked crust. Prebaking your crust partway is a sensible solution for this scenario.

To fully prebake the crust, prick the bottom all over with a fork to prevent bubbles. Return the crust to the oven and bake for an additional 20 to 25 minutes, until it’s golden all over.

If, despite your best efforts, the lined, weighted crust still slips down the inside of the pan while it prebakes, try this: Bake the crust upside down.

To start, you’ll need two identical (or nicely nestable) pie pans with flat rims.

Place your rolled-out crust in one of the pans, anchoring it to the rim of the pan with a fork-tine crimp. Place a liner of some kind (same as above: parchment, foil, coffee filter) into the pan. Nest the second pan into the first.

Pick up both pans, turn them over, and set them on a baking sheet. Place the baking sheet and pie pans in the oven, and bake as directed above. As the crust bakes, gravity will pull it down toward its rim — rather than into a puddle at the bottom of the pan. Magic!

After 20 minutes remove the baking sheet from the oven, carefully turn the pans over, lift out the empty pan, and remove the liner. At this point, your crust is partially prebaked. To prebake it fully, place the crust back in the oven, right side up, and bake until it's golden.

If you struggle with a pale, pasty bottom crust in your fruit pie, then yes, you can prebake it — with a couple of caveats:

So, soggy bottoms begone! From now on I expect every pie you bake will have a deep golden brown, flaky, crispy crust on the bottom — all because of the prebake.

And if you have any other questions about pie — from creating tender, flaky crust to thickening fruit filling to assessing when your pie is perfectly baked — please check out our Pie Baking Guide.

#182. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.
