#183. Lowe’s Christmas Tree Review: The Retro, Colorful Lights Are Pure Nostalgia

Forget minimalist holiday decor—this tree brings back the old-fashioned holiday magic we remember from childhood.

Forget minimalist holiday decor—this tree brings back the old-fashioned holiday magic we remember from childhood.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

I’ve always had a soft spot for colorful Christmas lights. Some of my favorite childhood holiday memories involve the big, bright bulbs on Christmas trees and the colorful lights decorating houses around the neighborhood. For me, the bigger the bulb, the better! There’s something about that old-fashioned glow that instantly makes the holidays feel magical.

So when I had the chance to test a prelit Christmas tree from Lowe’s featuring oversized, multicolored bulbs, I was ecstatic. Our team is no stranger to finding the best artificial Christmas trees, but this one caught my eye for a more personal reason: It reminded me of the holiday decor I grew up loving.

Holiday trends have a way of coming full circle, and I have a feeling these nostalgic lights are about to have their moment again. If you love the charm of old-fashioned Christmas decor as much as I do, this is one tree I’d keep an eye on before it sells out.

This prelit Christmas tree features oversized, multicolored bulbs that bring a nostalgic, old-fashioned feel to your home.

The Holiday Living 7.5-foot prelit Christmas tree from Lowe’s puts a nostalgic spin on traditional holiday decor. It features 450 large, multicolored C7 LED lights, giving it a big, colorful look that makes it stand out. With 2,969 lifelike branch tips, a full shape and a 52-inch width, it offers plenty of room for ornaments while making a festive statement on its own.

The tree also features Quick Set technology, which connects the lights automatically when you slide the tree sections together, so there’s no need to connect separate light strands. It comes with a folding metal stand, an on/off foot pedal and replacement lights and parts, plus a two-year limited warranty. Shoppers can also purchase the 5-foot version, as well as an optional Lowe’s Protection Plan, which offers two- or three-year coverage on all their trees.

Shipping was incredibly fast and seamless. My tree arrived less than 24 hours after I placed my order, and Lowe’s provided detailed tracking updates, so I knew exactly when to expect the delivery down to the minute (which was extremely convenient, as I was able to direct the driver to place the box in my garage). The boxed tree arrived in good condition and even had two handles, making it easy for me to lift and carry into my house on my own.

Unboxing was just as simple. Inside, I found the assembly instructions, a few replacement lights and parts, the folding metal stand and the tree itself, which came in three sections. The bottom section also had the power cord and an on/off foot pedal, a convenient feature for turning the lights on and off without bending down to reach the plug.

The tree comes with assembly instructions, though I found setup fairly intuitive without them. I’d still recommend holding on to them for future troubleshooting. The metal stand was easy to unfold and lock into place, and each tree section fit together smoothly, thanks to arrows that indicate how the pieces should align.

The branches feature two needle styles, which add texture and help give the tree a fuller, more natural appearance. Fluffing the branches was straightforward, too, although I learned one helpful lesson along the way: Fluff the top section before attaching it to the rest of the tree. Reaching the highest branches once the tree is fully assembled can be tricky! I ended up removing the top section to finish fluffing it, which was easy enough and gave me confidence that taking the tree down at the end of the season should be just as manageable.

With the press of a button, the tree came to life—and the lights are easily my favorite part. Truthfully, they’re even better in person. Sometimes multicolored LED lights can look a little too uniform or modern, but these have that big, bright, old-fashioned charm I remember from childhood. The oversized bulbs give the tree a cheerful, nostalgic glow that instantly makes the whole room feel more festive.

One thing to know is that the lights have just one setting: a constant pattern with no customization or flashing effects. Personally, I don’t mind this at all, since the classic, steady glow is exactly what I want from this style of tree.

This tree far exceeded my expectations, and I’m genuinely excited to share it with others who love this style of holiday decor as much as I do. Part of what makes the holidays so special is revisiting the traditions we loved as kids, whether that’s admiring colorful lights or counting down to the big day with one of the best Advent calendars. Add in the easy setup and convenient foot pedal for switching the lights on and off, and this tree will be a keepsake for years to come. If you’ve been looking for a tree that brings back the magic of childhood holidays, this one is worth a look.

With its large, multicolored lights, this prelit Christmas tree brings back the cheerful charm of childhood holiday memories.

The Holiday Living Prelit Christmas Tree is available exclusively at Lowe’s in a 7.5-foot size, with a smaller 5-foot version also available. Both options feature the oversized, multicolored lights that give this tree its nostalgic charm.

#184. The McDonald's Breakfast Dupe You Can Find At Trader Joe's

McDonald's breakfast has a long and storied history, starting in the 1970s, when morning meal items first appeared on the menu. Since then, it has become a beloved Saturday treat or pre-work stop — but despite the drive-thru's ease, it's not always the most convenient option, as the breakfast hours can get busy. So you might opt instead to make breakfast sandwiches at home, but there's something missing — aha! A crispy side in the form of a hash brown. And rather than make them from scratch (because seriously, who has time for that?), you can buy a solid dupe for these potato patties from Trader Joe's.

Yes, that's right, the store with the iconic canvas totes and beloved frozen food aisle carries fully cooked frozen hash browns (stylized as "Hashbrowns" by the chain) in packages of 10 for $2.99. Even better, they're a store staple, so you don't have to worry about seasonality, just their constant popularity, which can cause sellouts. Customers adore these breakfast patties, often comparing them to McDonald's version, which they tend to rate favorably in terms of taste, but especially price. After all, you can get these hash browns for about 30 cents each, whereas a McDonald's hash brown costs around $2.70 for just one (though prices may vary).

One of the best parts about making these Trader Joe's Hashbrowns at home versus ordering from McDonald's is that you can control how crispy and dark they get, instead of having to order them "well-done" at the restaurant. And happy customers on the internet are pretty much unanimous: The absolute best way to cook the patties is not in a skillet or the oven, as the packaging suggests, but rather in an air fryer — just make sure to flip them over at the halfway point so they get nice and golden on both sides. However, if you don't have an air fryer, they'll also cook well in a toaster!

As for ways to use them (beyond just squirting them with ketchup and eating them, which is fantastic in its own right), you can get pretty creative. Substitute one of these crisp potato patties for bread in a super crunchy and satisfying avocado toast, piled high with avocado (of course), bacon, an over-easy fried egg, and a drizzle of something yummy, like chili oil or sriracha. Or you can lay them down in a baking dish as the base for a breakfast casserole, or flatten them out in a pie pan and use them as the crust for a quiche.

Come for the hockey, stay for the sandwich stuffed with pierogies, mozzarella sticks, and waffle fries.

#186. The best apples for apple pie: Here's how to choose.: We put six varieties to the test.

Which are the best pie apples? With apple-picking season hard upon us, it's time to dust off your favorite apple pie recipe, sharpen your crust-rolling skills, and get ready to enjoy fall's favorite dessert: apple pie.

You may be tempted to make your pie from one of the six apple varieties that dominate the domestic market year-round: Red Delicious, Golden Delicious, Gala, Fuji, Granny Smith, and McIntosh.

But when fall rolls around, farmers' markets and orchard farm stands offer an abundance of apple choices.

You've probably identified your favorite eating apple. But what about the best pie apples? They're not necessarily the same. Red and Golden Delicious, for instance, are reliably crisp, sweet-eating apples. But when you bake them into a pie, they can become mushy and lose some of their sweetness. So what are the best apples for pie?

We'll put six different pie apples to the test.

The pie apples: I decide to put two of my favorites, Golden Russet and Northern Spy, up against a couple of classic pie apples: McIntosh and Cortland. I also add Granny Smith because, if there's one ubiquitous, year-round apple, Granny Smith is it. Ginger Gold — a Golden Delicious cross with Albemarle Pippin — is another variety that's often available in fall, and a worthy representative of the Delicious family.

And yes, there are plenty of other apple varieties to choose from: Fuji, Gala, Honey Crisp, and so many more. But with limited time and resources — and a pan with space for just six pies — I'm not able to test every apple out there. But if you want to choose the best pie apples among your personal favorites, you can have fun doing this same test at home.

I use a muffin tin to bake apples sweetened with a bit of sugar. To mimic apple pie (sans crust), I pile sliced apples high in the pan. Then I bake them in a preheated 425°F oven for 20 minutes, lower the oven temperature to 375°F, and continue to bake the apples until they're bubbly, about 40 minutes.

I had no idea there'd be such significant differences in both texture and flavor. For example, Russets and Macs are sweetened with the same amount of sugar, bake at the same temperature, for the same amount of time —  and offer way different results.

So, Granny Smith looks like the best combination of both taste and texture. Does it make the very best apple pie?

Not necessarily. I've baked many pies with this all-purpose apple, especially during the winter when other apples are scarce or pricey. A pie made 100% with Granny Smith apples is a mighty fine pie. But in fall, when every apple variety in the world is seemingly at your fingertips, why not take advantage of one or two (or more) of your own local favorites?

At the end of the day, choosing the best pie apples is a personal decision. My best apple pie would include a combination of these three: Cortland, for flavor; Russet, for texture; and Granny Smith, for its combination of the two.

What apples would fill your best pie? Bake your favorite varieties side by side and see what happens; the results may surprise you.

#187. Egg Salad Reaches Peak Flavor When You Add 1.5 Tablespoons Of This Ingredient (Thanks, Ina Garten)

Despite the fact that she almost left her TV career behind, Ina Garten has a way of reaching out to her audience and inviting them to bring small, luxurious touches into their everyday cooking. She's got a secret ingredient for every dish, it seems, and while these are often low-key and no-fuss, sometimes they can be indulgent and more high-end. Case in point? Over on Instagram, the Barefoot Contessa shared her recipe for egg salad, but with an indulgent twist. You see, she adds 1½ tablespoons of white truffle butter to the mix, taking the dish from ho-hum to high-class and helping it reach peak flavor.

The brand Garten uses is Urbani, and it is indeed an indulgence — $16 for a 3-ounce tub (and $74 for a pound). But if you can swing the price, it will certainly elevate your everyday egg salad by adding a rich depth of flavor that is at once earthy and lightly garlicky, while lending a creamy, silky texture to the salad.

Garten manages to elevate her meal to the height of elegance by serving it on focaccia instead of regular sandwich bread. You can further channel your inner Ina by adding luxurious touches to this simple preparation, like a bit of truffle oil. White or black varieties would work with the delicate egg flavors, though the latter generally has an earthier, more robust profile than its white counterpart.

Another way to infuse your egg salad with the flavor and aroma of truffles is to use them in mayo form. While you can definitely buy truffle mayonnaise ready-made from any number of gourmet shops (both brick-and-mortar and online), you could also try your hand at making it yourself using truffle oil. All you need is a food processor or immersion blender, and you can adjust everything as you go so that your upgraded, bougie mayo suits your personal taste.

Finally, while it's more of a garnish, if you're going to be eating your egg salad on crackers or crostini, you might consider topping each bite with a bit of caviar. The mild brininess of this most famous of all luxury foods pairs well with the richness of egg salad, cutting through the thick mayo and adding a pop of oceanic flavor. For the ultimate in decadence, you might try topping a truffle-infused egg salad with caviar, combining the two elements.

#188. Dutch Apple Snacking Cake

Every autumn the siren song of baking calls bakers home until the volume becomes too much to bear. And at that moment, the only thing that can silence it is a warm-spiced apple cake—the kind that hugs you closer than a knit sweater. This recipe, which keeps things simple, relies on the winning combination of cinnamon and apples to perfume a vanilla cake with pockets of tender fruit. A blanket of cinnamon streusel crowns the cake, giving it a contrasting crunch and a coffee-cake-like character. Feel free to stash the cake on your counter, slicing it throughout the week, enjoying its plush interior as it magically gets better with time.

More cozy bakes this way: Caramel Apple Snacking Cake; Chocolate Olive Oil Cake; and Lemon Poppy Seed Loaf.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lightly coat an 8x8" metal baking pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line with parchment paper, leaving overhang on all sides. Lightly coat parchment with nonstick spray. Place 1¼ cups (156 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (packed; 200 g) light brown sugar, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1½ tsp. ground cinnamon, ½ tsp. baking powder, and ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, melted, in a large bowl and mix with your hands, squeezing together as needed, until marble-size clumps form. Set streusel aside.

Toss 1 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 2 large), peeled, cored, thinly sliced, slices halved crosswise, and 2 Tbsp. (16 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl to coat.

Whisk 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1½ tsp. baking powder, ¼ tsp. baking soda, and remaining 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl to combine. Add ½ cup (1 stick) chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until no visible pieces remain. (Mixture should look like lightly moistened sand. Don’t worry about overworking it.) Add 2 large eggs, ⅔ cup buttermilk, 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil, and 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract and stir until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Mix in about two thirds of apples.

Scrape batter into prepared pan and spread into an even layer; smooth surface. Scatter reserved streusel and remaining apples over, letting them organically intermix. Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out clean, 65–75 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan. Using parchment overhang, lift cake out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Dust with powdered sugar and cut into 12 pieces if serving immediately.

Do Ahead: Cake can be made 5 days ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

#189. Cauliflower Piccata

Recipe by Susan Bronson, Rhinelander, Wisconsin

Oven-roasted cauliflower steaks take the place of chicken in this vegetarian riff on chicken piccata.

Back in my vegetarian days, I used to joke to my friends that I was more of a “pastatarian,” as I tended to nosh on pasta dishes rather than elaborate vegetarian entrees. If only I had more recipes like this cauliflower piccata in my repertoire at the time. I would have eaten it all the time! Turns out roasting veggies and adding a flavorful sauce is incredibly easy and flavorful.

This particular cauliflower recipe features a head cut into thick steaks, roasted in the oven until crispy and caramelized before being doused in a bright and buttery lemon-caper sauce. You can serve this dish as a side dish alongside a vegetarian entree, or serve it as a main alongside a quinoa salad or protein-rich dense bean salad.

Preheat the oven to 400ºF. Slice the head of cauliflower through the core into four 1-inch-thick steaks. Place them on greased, foil-lined baking pans. Brush both sides of the steaks with olive oil.

In a small bowl, combine the salt, garlic powder and pepper, then sprinkle them over both sides of the cauliflower. Roast the cauliflower until it’s tender and the edges are browned, 40 to 45 minutes, turning once halfway through the cook time.

Editor’s Tip: Some of the florets may crumble when you slice the cauliflower head into steaks. Don’t worry! Toss extra florets with olive oil and any leftover seasoning. Spread them onto the same baking sheet with the steaks and roast them for the same amount of time.

Heat 1 tablespoon of olive oil in a medium skillet or sauce pot over medium-high heat. Add the shallot and saute it until it’s lightly golden, about one minute. Add the minced garlic and saute it with the shallot for another 30 to 60 seconds. Stir in the vegetable stock, then season the sauce with salt and pepper.

Bring the sauce to a boil, then reduce the heat to medium and simmer it until it’s reduced by half, about 8 to 10 minutes. Add the capers, lemon juice and lemon zest. Remove the sauce from the heat and stir in the butter, 1 tablespoon at a time, until it’s creamy.

To serve, place a cauliflower steak on a plate and top it with the piccata sauce. Garnish it with chopped parsley.

Leftover cauliflower steaks should be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Store any leftover lemon-caper sauce in a separate airtight container.

Cauliflower piccata lasts for up to five days when stored properly in the refrigerator.

The best way to reheat the cauliflower steaks is in the oven. Place the steaks on a rimmed baking sheet and reheat them in a 350º oven for 8 to 10 minutes, or until they’re heated through and crispy around the edges.

You can also reheat the steaks in the microwave, but you won’t get the same crispness. Reheat any leftover lemon-caper sauce in a saucepan on the stovetop until it’s heated through, stirring frequently to reincorporate the butter.

You’ll need a sharp knife and a cutting board to cut cauliflower steaks. Begin by slicing off the bottom stem and removing any remaining green leaves. Stand the cauliflower upright on its flattened stem and use long, steady strokes to slice into the cauliflower. I find it works best to first slice the head into two halves, then cut those halves into half to make four evenly sized steaks.

Once cut, be gentle with the steaks; they can easily fall apart. Gently brush them with oil and use a thin spatula to flip them rather than using your hands. Don’t worry if some of the florets crumble as you cut the steaks—you can always roast them alongside the steaks.

If you prefer a thicker lemon-caper sauce, the best way to thicken it is to use cornstarch. Before adding the butter, carefully remove 1 tablespoon from the liquid and stir in 1 tablespoon of cornstarch. Return the cornstarch slurry to the sauce and stir until the sauce is thickened. Add the butter when the pan is off the heat.

Roasting the cauliflower in the oven gives the steaks a perfectly caramelized and crispy texture. If you prefer even more browning and crispiness, pop them under the broiler for a few minutes. Just keep an eye on them—the steaks can go from crispy to charred in a blink of an eye!

#190. 'Changed My Life' Lentil Soup and More Recipes We Made This Week

It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

A fried fish sandwich has no season. Also, I’m currently in Tennessee, where it’s hit 90° this week, so it’s basically still summer. I used my colleague Shilpa Uskokovic’s excellent Fritto Misto batter to coat some flounder. After frying, I slid a couple small fillets into top-split hot dog buns with juicy slices of tomato and a quick tartar sauce. It was pure summer satisfaction, even this deep into October. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO and cooking

The days when my husband and I both commute are, to put it lightly, b-a-n-a-n-a-s. That’s when my deep freezer fulfills its destiny. Case in point: this superlative basil pesto, thawed overnight, tossed with hot rigatoni, plus frozen peas thrown in with the pasta for the last few minutes of boiling. It is nourishing and feels purposeful, even if it took less than 10 minutes of effort. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

Andy Baraghani’s Honey-Chipotle Shrimp Tacos are one of my most-made recipes of all time. Last week I decided to change things up and eat the shrimp over some homemade Mexican rice and beans instead of wrapping them in a tortilla. The shrimp are so easy to make (just toss in a two-ingredient marinade and pan-fry) that I ended up cooking fresh batches for lunch on the following days to pair with the leftover rice and beans. The canned chipotles in adobo lend a smoky complexity, and I love how the honey helps the shrimp take on just enough char. A luxurious WFH lunch if there ever was one! —Alaina Chou, commerce writer

Soup on a weeknight? It’s a foreign concept to me. If I’m making soup, I’m committing hours to the cause. But this week I couldn’t quell my craving for a sippable bowl, so I scoured the archive for a quick hit and landed on this Curried Lentil, Tomato, and Coconut Soup. Red lentils break down and create a substantial body, while golden Japanese S&B curry powder adds a mellow earthy kick. After mixing in crushed tomatoes and coconut milk, I went rogue and followed up with a couple dashes of fish sauce for extra umami. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

The ever adaptable rotisserie chicken is one of my favorite emergency dinners. When crunched for time, I’ll grab one on my way home and transform the bird into something unrecognizable. Most recently, I used it to make Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser’s Nuoc Cham Chicken Salad. The pulled meat is tossed with the quickest mayo-lime dressing, then stuffed into lettuce leaves. I like to finish the cups with sliced cucumber, fried shallots, and a flurry of fresh herbs. Don’t bother bringing out plates. I eat this with my hands straight from the platter like nachos. —Carly Westerfield, manager, audience strategy

Whenever I want something more for breakfast, but I don’t want to work for it, it’s a Dutch baby all the way. Heat a skillet with butter, dump a couple of always-on-hand ingredients—eggs, flour, milk, sugar—into a blender, and 20 minutes later, it isn’t breakfast: It’s brunch. Last weekend I tossed the reserved browned butter from Epi’s Take It Easy Dutch Baby into a bowl of sliced Italian plums. I added a glug of maple syrup and a pinch of salt, then let the fruit soak in the flavors while I fiddled over my coffee. Puffed bébé out of the oven, the plums and all their juices went on top, and I sat down to enjoy my morning. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, cooking and SEO

I make lentil soup pretty frequently once the “feels like” temperature dips below 50 degrees. And I was just about to mince up my mirepoix when I stumbled upon senior Test Kitchen editor Shilpa Uskokovic’s Soy-Braised Black Lentils. The promise of salty, tender-but-toothsome legumes on a bed of rice was good enough to shake up my routine. I hauled out my rice cooker, set it to steam, and started a dead-simple simmer of a pack of shiny black Beluga lentils with glugs of soy sauce and thin slices of garlic. Once the liquid was mostly gone, I stirred in glossy agave nectar plus added sugar until they formed a loose, syrupy glaze. We ate half the pot tucked into sheets of toasted seaweed snack along with generous spoonfuls of rice. The next morning, the rest was eaten with crusty bread and fried eggs. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

Ever since I started working at BA, I’ve seen this single recipe for Bolognese top the charts time and time again. An oldie but a baddie, it’s received over 500 comments that would taunt me on a daily basis, with one overall glaring thesis: Make this! Now! So I decided to hunker down, put on a killer album (Once in a Lifetime), and get comfortable in the kitchen. Yes, this Bolognese takes time—cough cough, three hours—but so do all good things. For those who need immediate gratification, your kitchen will be awash in the savory, primal smells of browned beef and pancetta in just 10 minutes. After adding a good amount of liquid from wine, stock, and milk (in stages), then stirring, dancing, and stirring, it was finally time to serve my meaty sauce tangled with fat pappardelle and a charitable shower of Parmesan. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

When I saw a bunch of bright-eyed leeks at the farmers market from my favorite vendor, I knew just what to do with them: my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s cheesy baked pasta. It was one of those love-at-first-sight recipes for me in the Test Kitchen—somehow minimalist and dramatic at the same time. Save this one for a chilly night when you’re having friends over. The sauce uses a cup of white wine, so there’s most of a bottle left to enjoy with dinner. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

I’ve been making a lot of solo dinners lately, and nine times out of ten that means I’m cooking an omelet. My version with fried shallot, apple, and Fontina cheese is a go-to—I wrote all about it for our series, Me, Myself, and Dinner—but if I haven’t gone grocery shopping, I’ll just cobble together fun stuff from my fridge. Some recent wins: chopped kimchi and yellow cheddar; spinach, feta, and dill; black beans, avocado, and salsa macha. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor

This week I did something I haven’t done in years. I roasted a chicken. And it was revelatory. Not fussy. Easy! Rewarding. Inspired by the method in Kitty Cowles’s cookbook, I sprinkled the bird with salt and let it hang out in the fridge for a few hours. Then I rubbed it with olive oil, threw some lemon and garlic in the cavity, and roasted it as high as my oven would go, convection on. While the chicken was resting, its skin a golden crackle, I deglazed the pan juices with white wine, and let those simmer into a tangy gravy. Served with a salad, it was the coziest supper, even romantic if you ignore my toddler cooing. The next day, the carcass simmered in a pot of water with onion and ginger for a broth I’ll sip for days. The surplus meat has morphed into a rice bowl, towering sandwich, day care lunch box, 3 p.m. snack. And the joy from it all? Incalculable. —E.L.

I’m always on the hunt for a protein-rich, not-too-finicky dinner that I can pull together in a blip. It’s gotta taste good because I’ll probably cook it for five consecutive days, at which point I will tire of it and resume my hunt anew. Like sands through the hourglass, these are the recipes of our lives. This week I settled on customizable Soy-Glazed Salmon Bowls. Cook the salmon in that salty-sweet soy and honey sauce, throw it atop rice, and add whatever vegetables you have. This time, I went with shreddy carrots and cukes, plus some of those crispy sheets of nori that I used to scoop up bite after bite. —Sam Stone, senior editor

My very talented colleague Shilpa Uskokovic forever changed the way I cook ground chicken. She mixes the chicken with baking soda—yes, baking soda—for clusters of bouncy nubbins. Now, anytime a recipe calls for ground meat, I use this hack. This week’s victim: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps. It has a sweet, fiery sauce made from sriracha, brown sugar, soy, and fish sauce that deliberately clings to the juicy meat. I piled the chicken into butter lettuce with a squeeze of lime, and a handful of torn mint for freshness. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

#191. ‘GBBO’ Fans Are Rallying Behind The Bakers After A Brutal Technical: ‘If The Whole Class Fails…’

Paul Hollywood called it the worst one he’d seen in 17 years.

I’ve watched enough Bake Off Technicals to know they’re supposed to make the bakers sweat. But in this week’s Bread Week episode, when Paul Hollywood asked the remaining contestants to make eight flatbreads stuffed with roasted grapes and blue cheese in one hour, I already had a feeling this one was going to get ugly.

For one thing, the concept itself threw several bakers, and speaking as an American, I understood the confusion. When I hear flatbread, I’m picturing something thin and pizza-adjacent, not dough wrapped around roasted grapes and blue cheese and somehow rolled flat afterward.

By the time judging rolled around, the challenge had gone about as badly as everyone feared. Some of the flatbreads were too large or thick, some had grapes sitting on top instead of tucked inside, and several were raw or undercooked in the middle.

Paul said he couldn’t remember a worse Technical in the show’s 17-year run, and fellow judge Nigella Lawson suggested they “eat them” as punishment for their baking crimes. But viewers quickly started wondering whether the bakers were really the problem.

“If the whole class fails, there was something wrong with the teacher,” one person wrote. Another asked, “If 10 bakers can’t get it right, the problem isn’t the bakers, It’s the method, surely?”

Others had less sympathy for the challenge itself. “This was one of the worst bread weeks ever. And usually bread week is my favorite,” one viewer wrote, while another viewer just wasn’t sold on the flavor combination: “ROASTED GRAPES???? And BLUE CHEESE???? Stuffed in a flatbread???? Horrifying, really.”

Even some former bakers were willing to push back on Paul, too. 2025 finalist Aaron Mountford-Myles wrote, “Some of those were blatantly flat. I will die on this hill,” disputing at least one part of the judging and refusing to let him erase their flatness entirely.

And 2023 contestant Saku Chandrasekara recognized the situation immediately, commenting, “Paul said the same for our steam puddings 😳,” a callback to another Technical where undercooked puddings caused trouble across the tent.

Because apparently nothing bonds generations of Bake Off contestants quite like being collectively roasted by Paul Hollywood.

#192. Bobby Flay And Martha Stewart Agree: Pork Chops Are So Much Juicier When You Buy This Cut

Pork chops make for a reliable protein source. The meat is easy to cook, flavorful, and shines in a wide array of pork chop dinner recipes, like Sichuan salt and pepper pork chops or even a one-skillet French onion pork chop. The one downside, though, is that the cut is predisposed to dryness. Chops can come low on fat, making moisture loss a prevalent issue. In addition to marinating pork chops in lemon to make them juicier, one of the best ways of curtailing dry meat is selecting an optimal cut. From shoulder to sirloin, the pork meat comes in a wide variety of compositions. And an especially well-regarded option is a boneless center cut.

Noted by both Bobby Flay (per Today) and Martha Stewart, this pork chop cut is prized for its juiciness. Also called a loin chop, the center cut piece consists of loin and tenderloin, two distinct pork regions. A center-cut chop comes with a T-shaped bone, which separates both sides. Meanwhile, a boneless center cut removes this dividing structure, yielding a tender piece of meat that cooks evenly.

A boneless center cut is low in fat and not too porky in flavor. As a result, it's terrific for both high-heat cooking and braising. Cooked for too long and too hot, the meat can still turn tough. However, with a careful application of heat, it makes for a balanced and juicy experience.

When choosing how to prepare the meat, think of center-cut boneless pork chops like a nice steak. The meat typically comes in over an inch thick. And like with beef, the worst you could do is overcook the cut at high heat. This pork chop is best built for either a rapid sear or a braise, not a cooking amalgamation of the two.

To achieve optimal texture, it's best to quick brine the meat, letting salt work its tenderizing magic. With no fat or bone, the center cut offers limited moisture protection. So if you go with a high-heat method — whether on a grill, pan or broiler — keep it to a brisk two or three minutes per side. Have a thermometer in hand to verify the temperature you need. Cooked to proper doneness, you'll get a flavorful chop, which will turn out even better with a paprika-based dry rub for added flavor.

The braise method showcases the same cut in a completely different light. Start by browning the pork a few minutes per side, as when searing. Then, cover the cut in water and vinegar, plus various aromatics (think Worcestershire sauce, alliums, or sugar). An hour of braising will result in a tender yet meaty piece of pork, showcasing the center cut in another delicious light.

#195. Chickpea Saag

This take-out staple is easy enough to recreate at home and fantastic for family dinners. If you’re looking for a comforting vegetarian weeknight meal, this stripped-down version is the ticket—it takes little time to prep, is both budget- and pantry-friendly (thanks to frozen spinach and canned chickpeas), and always goes down a treat. If you have kasuri methi or dried fenugreek leaves, crumble a healthy pinch into the spinach when you’re blending the mixture. It’ll make the saag even more fragrant and delicious. Leftover saag, if any, tastes even better the next day.

Find more delicious vegetarian dinner ideas here: Gochujang-Butter-Braised Tofu; Crispy Tofu With Peanut Sauce; and Sheet-Pan Gnocchi With Soy-Dressed Mushrooms.

Melt 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium skillet with a lid over medium heat. Add 1 large white onion, thinly sliced, 8 garlic cloves, coarsely chopped, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, coarsely chopped, 2 tsp. cumin seeds, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and tender, 8–10 minutes.

Uncover pan and add ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ½ tsp. ground turmeric. Cook, stirring often, until yogurt is slightly thickened (it will split into tiny curds), about 2 minutes. Let cool a few minutes, then transfer to a blender; reserve skillet.

Add ½–1 serrano chile (depending on the spiciness of your chile and your heat preference), one 10-oz. package frozen spinach, thawed, and ½ tsp. garam masala to blender; blend until mixture is very smooth, about 3 minutes.

Return purée to reserved skillet and add one 15-oz. can chickpeas, rinsed. Cook saag over medium-low heat, stirring often, until heated through (do not bring to a simmer or saag may split).

Transfer saag to a medium bowl. Serve with steamed rice and/or warm naan, lime wedges, and more yogurt alongside.

Do Ahead: Saag can be made 1 day ahead. Let cool. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Reheat over medium-low heat before serving.

#196. This Cookbook Author Explores Cemeteries for Recipes To Die For

A recipe quite literally taken to the grave?

That’s the foundation for creator Rosie Grant’s ongoing archival project turned cookbook To Die For. And it’s exactly how it sounds.

Apropos for Spooky Season, the book collects “gravestone recipes” so synonymous with departed loved ones they’re immortalized on their headstones. It celebrates the legacies of ordinary folks who did extraordinary things. They were teachers or coaches, the local dentist, the neighbor everybody knew, and they all showed love through cooking for their communities.

What began as a light curiosity turned into a larger, more emotional realization around identity, place, and what we leave behind.

Over the past five and a half years since starting her TikTok and Instagram accounts under the username ghostly.archive during a digital archives internship at the Congressional Cemetery in Washington, DC, Grant’s travels have taken her across the United States—as far as Nome, Alaska—as well as Nova Scotia, to visit their final resting places and families to learn their stories.

It’s an almost feel-good way to get into the topics of mortality and death, Grant assesses, as sitting around the table to share a meal or stepping into a memory-filled kitchen disintegrates conversational barriers. Though she was raised by parents who gave ghost tours at local cemeteries in Alexandria, Virginia, she says her family was much more comfortable with the idea of hauntings than discussing and planning for the inevitable themselves.

“Something like a recipe feels so life-giving,” Grant expresses, adding that these conversations could also encompass music or travel. “Talking about these many life-filling moments might be an easier way to talk about tough topics.”

The 40 recipes were all approved by family members of the deceased, whom Grant tracked down mostly through internet sleuthing (obituaries and social media) to ask permission to publish.

Initially Grant tried to separate the recipe from its provider and solely focus on the food itself, but the process didn’t feel quite right.

Grant has since cooked with seven families highlighted in To Die For, and has shared her pilgrimages to the gravesites with the goods themselves to pay respect. With her years of research and immersion, Grant notes that burials and grave markers have become so much more personal over the course of time. Granite headstones have allowed for almost any customization after mass-industrialization made the tools to work on it more accessible, and are much more durable compared to the formerly used wood, slate, or marble, making for lasting memorials. Proof cemeteries are beautiful grounds still vibrating with life and knowledge, if you’re open to it.

Her approach to keeping such individual histories alive has deeply resonated, furthering her relationship to the Death Positive Movement: formed by hospice workers, death doulas and other care workers who advocate that discussions around mortality and afterlife planning make for a healthier society; and establishing a more intimate sense of collectivity amongst strangers across the globe.

While she’s gotten her share of detractors for various reasons (mainly self-identified Mediums claiming the deceased, and in one case–one participant still living, didn’t appreciate their culinary secrets being shared), many folks have found inspiration as they consider their own gravestone recipe. Some commenters, meanwhile, express regret around not asking their own loved ones for recipes or helpful tips that most instructions don’t leave nuance for when they had the chance.

“I thought I could just have this on socials and do a PDF format online,” Grant says. “[The families] were like ‘We like the idea of a physical book. Something that’s precious.’ Even the visual style of it is meant to be something you’d inherit from a grandparent.”

The most underrated section of her book offers a thoughtful list of questions to begin documenting one’s own familial food legacies.

“It can feel really morbid to be like ‘Hey mom, can you write down your recipe because you’re gonna die someday?’” Grant says jokingly. “That can look like a lot things. Take pictures of the recipe box and text it to all the cousins or the family group chat and save it to a drive somewhere. Cook with your family member. Teach me how to do it, let’s cook it together. Passing down that knowledge, there’s something very powerful about that shared experience.”

Sentiments from both participants in the book and Grant’s audience echo how revisiting these recipes offers sensory catharsis in addition to talking about their grief. What started as a nerdy food adventure manifested into an exploration of what it means to be remembered for how people made us feel when we were with them; highlighting turn-of-the-century attitudes toward heritage, family and home life, and serving as a “rite of passage” or way to pass the torch to the next generation.

Grant reminds us of observing and maintaining such rituals. “If we don’t do it, nobody else will.”

#197. Chipotle’s Latest Drop Is A Massive 170-Liter Takeout Bag You Can Actually Win—Here’s How

Chipotle has been making a surprising number of moves into fashion and accessories lately. There was its Béis travel collection, and earlier this year, even hockey jerseys got involved. But apparently none of that was big enough—and I mean that quite literally.

Chipotle has created the Big Ass Chipotle Bag, a comically oversized take on the brown paper bag that usually carries your lunch. It measures 36 inches wide, 24 inches tall, and 12 inches deep, with a 170-liter capacity. To put that into perspective, there’s enough room in there for things like a trumpet, a traffic cone, and even a desk chair.

At three feet wide, you could also probably lose your actual Chipotle order inside it. But there is, technically, a reason the brand decided its usual bag needed this kind of growth spurt.

The stunt is really a very large advertisement for Chipotle’s Family Meals. Previously called Build-Your-Own Chipotle, the online-only order is meant for four to six people, with enough ingredients for everyone to turn dinner into whatever they want—bowls, tacos, salads, nachos, or some combination of the above.

Naturally, Chipotle decided all that food required packaging with roughly the subtlety of a moving van.

“A Big Ass Meal deserves a Big Ass Bag,” Fernando Machado, Chipotle’s Chief Brand Officer, said in a statement. “We took one of the most recognizable parts of the Chipotle experience, gave it an outsized upgrade, and created something that's impossible to miss. It's fun, it's ridiculous and it's exactly the kind of thing we knew our fans would want to get their hands on.”

Unfortunately, you can’t just stroll into Chipotle and ask them to supersize your paper bag. To have a shot at taking one home, U.S. Rewards members need to order a Family Meal through Chipotle’s app or website. That purchase puts them into the giveaway, with more winners picked throughout the promotion.

The Family Meals come in at less than $10 per person, which is a perfectly reasonable price point being used to promote a deeply unreasonable bag.

I just hope whoever wins one has somewhere to put it.

The Halloween tradition returns to McDonald’s this October with Disney villain Boo Buckets.

As someone who knows her way around a musical theater score, I’ve always argued that Disney villains get the best songs. “Poor Unfortunate Souls,” “Be Prepared,” “Gaston”—I’ll take a theatrical villain plotting someone’s downfall over a lovesick hero singing about their dreams any day. The villains have better lyrics, better entrances and considerably more interesting things to say.

Five of Disney’s most notorious characters are getting their own collectible buckets, just in time for trick-or-treating.

The Disney Villains Boo Buckets Happy Meal arrives at participating McDonald’s restaurants nationwide on October 20, 2026.

This year’s collection features five characters who have caused their fair share of trouble: Jafar from Aladdin, Ursula from The Little Mermaid, Scar from The Lion King, Cruella de Vil from 101 Dalmations and Maleficent from Sleeping Beauty. It’s a formidable lineup, though I do wonder what Captain Hook did to get himself excluded.

Each collectible bucket features a design inspired by its villain, along with a character-themed lid and stickers depicting familiar faces and details from the films. It’s a departure from the classic pumpkins, ghosts and other Halloween creatures that have appeared on McDonald’s Boo Buckets over the years, but the concept remains the same. Enjoy your Happy Meal, hang on to the bucket, and put it to work collecting the best new candy on Halloween night.

The original Boo Buckets debuted in 1986, so there’s a good chance some parents will be nearly as excited about this promotion as their kids. And with five designs to choose from—or at least hope for—McDonald’s has given collectors another reason to make a few extra trips through the drive-thru.

I don’t approve of her methods, but I respect the commitment. And if I can get a Halloween candy bucket out of the deal without signing away my voice, even better.

#199. Why does my challah have stretch marks?: How to stop your challah from tearing.

Recently, our Community Development Coordinator Kat Mayerovitch shared a very important update from the King Arthur Baking subreddit: a surprising amount of people were wondering why their challah has “stretch marks.”

If you’re not one of those people and don’t know exactly what that means, you may still be familiar with the problem: Sometimes, challah loaves come out of the oven with stretches or tears along the braided strands. It doesn’t affect the quality of the bread, but it does affect the appearance.

To address this issue, I asked our Baking School Curriculum Developer Jack Tissiere for their thoughts on this problem, and they identified two potential causes.

Challah dough rises twice: Once after it’s mixed (known as bulk fermentation) and a second time after the loaf is shaped or braided. Cutting short that second rise can lead to a challah that develops tears as it bakes. As Jack explains, “When we underproof our challah loaves (in other words, don't give them enough time to rise), the bread is still super active and energetic. When it hits the heat of the oven it expands energetically, and that sudden burst of volume before the dough sets can cause the bread to stretch or rip.”

How to fix: Give your braided challah loaf a little more time to rise before baking. Push the proof until the loaf is puffy and marshmallow-y; when you press it with a floured finger, the indent should slowly fill in, which is a sign that it’s ready to be baked. Sometimes, depending on the temperature of both your dough and your environment, this can take longer than the recipe says; trust your instincts rather than relying on the clock. If you fully proof the bread, when you put the loaf into the oven it’s less energetic, which means there isn’t as much oven spring (and subsequent tearing) while baking.

The other reason your challah may have stretch marks is because the loaves are shaped or braided too tightly. As Jack explains “When loaves are braided very tightly, they don’t have a lot of room to grow during the rising and baking process, causing stretches or tears as they expand.”

How to fix: Give your challah dough some slack when shaping: Braid loosely, allowing extra space for the dough to expand as it undergoes its final proof before baking. And for a pretty, even braid, start braiding from the middle; this video shows you how.

Ready to tackle your next braided loaf? Check out our Braided Challah recipe from The Big Book of Bread.

#200. Soaking Chicken In Vinegar: What It's For And Why It's Recommended

If you've ever scrolled deep into TikTok or Instagram looking for inspiration on what to do with the chicken sitting in your fridge, you've more than likely stumbled upon a home cook soaking their chicken in a vinegar solution before deep frying, roasting, or grilling it. It might seem like a harmless step, but it has proven to be divisive. For some, it's a non-negotiable. To others, it's completely unnecessary. So why do some people choose to go through the effort?

It all comes down to smell. Raw chicken can sometimes carry a distinctly gamey odor, and if you suffer from the chicken ick, it can be pretty off-putting. Just to be clear, this is very different from the rancid smell of spoilage, which means the chicken should be thrown away immediately. With perfectly good chicken, however, vinegar's acetic acid can help neutralize those natural odors, making it far more agreeable to work with. Lemon or lime juice is often added to the mix for a clean, refreshing aroma, and some people go a step further and rub the cut fruit directly over the surface. In some cases, people skip vinegar altogether and use lemon juice instead.

This step is by no means mandatory, and skipping it poses no food safety risk if your chicken is in good shape. But one common misconception is that the soak can stand in for a marinade, with the acidic vinegar tenderizing the outer layer of meat. Unfortunately, that isn't really the case. The vinegar is usually very diluted in water, so there's not nearly enough vinegar or time for it to do much beyond tackling odors. Anyway, you can also marinate the chicken afterward.

One common, potentially dangerous misconception among home cooks is that soaking chicken in vinegar will sanitize it. Look, it's not an entirely out-there assumption. Vinegar is a popular DIY cleaning staple thanks to its acidic properties, and it's often used around the kitchen to help tackle grime and grease. Mix it with baking soda, and you'll even get that satisfying fizz that can help loosen stubborn dirt. But while vinegar has its uses as a household cleaner, that doesn't mean it can reliably eliminate harmful bacteria from raw chicken.

One of the biggest concerns when handling raw chicken is Salmonella, a bacterium responsible for numerous foodborne illness outbreaks and some of the biggest recalls in food history. Unfortunately, soaking chicken in vinegar won't reliably remove or kill Salmonella, so it shouldn't be treated as a food safety measure. The only dependable way to kill harmful bacteria is to cook chicken to an internal temperature of 165 degrees Fahrenheit, checking the thickest part with a meat thermometer.

In certain cases, a vinegar soak can also create another opportunity for cross-contamination. Any liquid that comes into contact with raw chicken can carry bacteria onto your hands, countertops, utensils, and other kitchen surfaces. Even picking the chicken up out of the bowl and washing it under the tap can cause contaminated liquid to drip or splash. If you do choose to soak the chicken in vinegar, handle it carefully and keep the liquid contained. Once you're finished, wash your hands and thoroughly clean the bowl, utensils, and any surfaces that came or could have come into contact with the raw chicken using hot, soapy water. There's no need to rinse the chicken itself.

#201. Lemon Poppy Seed Loaf Cake

Something about having a loaf of lemon poppy seed cake on the counter makes you feel like the star of a sitcom. As if you might drink your coffee from a thick-walled mug and scratch your cat under the chin just before you leave for work, a slice of said cake in your hand as you dash to the bus stop. Whether that rings true or not, know that this is a main character cake, worthy of its own show. Tall and hefty with a gentle tang and the crunchy burst of poppy seeds in every bite, it is completely unfussy yet still elegant. The bright loaf cake sings of sunny lemons thanks to the zest as well as juice. With the addition of oil and the insulating cap of snow-white glaze, it keeps nicely for a couple of days.

Find more cheerful bakes here: Chocolate Guinness Cake; Apple Cider Doughnut Loaf Cake; and Preserved Lemon Tea Cake.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Generously coat a 9x5" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray or unsalted butter, room temperature; line with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Whisk 2¼ cups (281 g) all-purpose flour, 1½ tsp. baking powder, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine.

Beat zest of 3 large lemons, ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, 5 Tbsp. vegetable oil, 2 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, and 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract on medium speed in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with paddle attachment until light and creamy, about 5 minutes.

Add 3 large eggs, one at a time, beating after each addition to combine before adding the next one (batter may look curdled at this point). Scrape down sides of bowl with a rubber spatula, add half of dry ingredients, and beat on low speed just to combine. Add ¾ cup whole milk and remaining dry ingredients and mix until batter is smooth and creamy, about 1 minute. Add ¼ cup poppy seeds; scrape down bottom and sides of bowl and fold batter with spatula a few times to ensure it’s evenly mixed.

Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. (If your pan looks more than three quarters full, transfer excess batter to a greased small ovenproof container and bake alongside cake as a cook’s treat). Generously coat the blade of a small paring knife with nonstick spray; run knife lengthwise through center of batter to make a shallow cut (this will help cake split cleanly along line as it bakes rather than cracking randomly).

Bake cake until golden brown all over, it springs back when gently pressed, and a tester inserted into the center comes out with only a few moist crumbs attached, 60–65 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet and let cake cool slightly in pan, about 15 minutes.

Run a small offset spatula around edges of cake to loosen, then invert out onto rack. Turn cake right side up and let cool completely.

Stir 1 cup (110 g) powdered sugar, 1 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, and a pinch of kosher salt in small bowl, adding up to 1 Tbsp. additional lemon juice as needed, until thick but pourable. Pour glaze over cake, letting it drip down sides. Top with poppy seeds and thin strips of lemon zest if using while glaze is still wet; let sit until glaze is set, at least 45 minutes.

Do Ahead: Cake can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

Tested by Paul Rankin, Mary Henn and Daria Smith

Cheese, whiskey and pickles—oh, my! We tested nearly 100 options to find the best Advent calendars for men in 2026.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

If you’ve ever found yourself stumped while looking for the perfect gift for the men in your life, you’re not alone. Shopping for someone we love is often even harder than buying for a stranger. Finding the right Advent calendar for the man in your life is like giving them a whole bunch of gifts that span the season, and it takes surprisingly little effort! The hardest part? With the perfect mix of elegance and flavor, the Flaviar whiskey Advent calendar is our top pick for folks who frequently enjoy a nightcap. And, as if that’s not enough of a reason to preorder, you also get a tasting journal and two high-quality Glencairn glasses you can keep for future flight sampling.

We tried Flaviar’s whiskey Advent calendar in 2023, 2024 and 2025—and can confirm it’s still a stellar deal for serious spirit lovers. While we have yet to taste this year’s pick (it’s currently en route!), we expect it will be equally memorable.

Contents span spicy instant noodles, Fly by Jing’s original chili crisp and the brand’s signature Sweet & Spicy Zhong sauce. Inclusions hit every tastebud that matters: spicy, swicy and savory. #205. 15 Of The Oldest Candy Stores In America

From sugar wafers to chocolate bars to conversation hearts and licorice, candies' rush of sweetness has enamored Americans for centuries. They've even become a symbol of love and care, exchanged during holidays like Valentine's Day and Easter. And nostalgic candy can bring back childhood memories and carefree times like nothing else.

But candy is a robust cornerstone of American business, too. As the National Confectioners Association points out, confectionery retail sales rake in $54 billion per year and create almost 700,000 jobs in the United States. While some of these stats can be attributed to large manufacturers, there are also plenty of small family-run businesses that still make candy the old-fashioned way — and have been doing so for decades.

These candy stores scattered across the United States are perfect examples. They effortlessly transport visitors into the past — because they are all more than 100 years old. As early pioneers, they changed the face of American candy stores, and they're still thriving today.

In business since 1806, Ye Olde Pepper Candy Companie is now owned by its fourth generation of candy makers. Its flagship location in Salem, Massachusetts, cranks out classics like Black Jacks and the famous Gibralters (available in lemon and peppermint flavors, they're touted as the first commercially sold candies in America), all still made by hand.

According to company history, Mary Spencer sold her Salem Gibralters back in the early 1800s, peddling her candies from a local church's steps in Salem. Black Jacks, on the other hand, were created by John Pepper, a friend of the family who wanted to make a "more masculine" candy to counter the "ladylike" options of the time. Both of these classic recipes were purchased with the store (then called the George W. Pepper Companie) around the turn of the 20th century by George Burkinshaw. He'd worked at the establishment from boyhood, sweeping the floors and helping out with other odd jobs, eventually assisting with candy making and then finally purchasing the business. His family has now passed it down for three generations. Today, the business has branched out into a second location, in North Andover, Massachusetts, as well as a wholesale operation and an online retail store.

Established in 1863, this Philadelphia candy store's claim to fame is that it's America's oldest continuously operating confectionery, still making "artisanal candy and ethical chocolate" in the style of its original founders. Shane Confectionery owners emphasize that they strive to keep tradition alive with products like its beloved buttercreams, made using the same Shane family recipe for 100-plus years, and on the same machine that has been used for more than century. The business also incorporates seasonal and local ingredients, makes products in small batches by hand, and even produces its own chocolate from raw, responsibly sourced cacao beans. In other words, this legendary candy company proves that old-time techniques can go hand in hand with meeting modern-day demands like environmental sustainability.

The owners are clearly evolving with the times and having fun, too — in recent years, Philadelphia Magazine reports, the business has offered Halloween-themed boxes based on hauntings and other ghoulish lore around the City of Brotherly Love. And it offers private workshops and tastings for groups, as well as private parties in a memorable setting, the "Cacao Pod," where the bean roasting takes place in a historic four-story brick building that has hosted confectionery operations since the 1850s.

Schimpff's roots stretch back to 1871, when Charles Schimpff opened the first Schimpff confectionery in Jeffersonville, Indiana, in 1871. But it was Gustav "Gus" Schimpff Sr. and his son Gus Jr. who opened the confectionery at 347 Spring Street in Jeffersonville — the same location the store operates in today, since 1891. After moving through multiple generations, the owners of this Midwestern candy mecca passed the torch to current sixth-generation owners Steve Shepherd and Beth Shepherd, who carry on its time-honored traditions.

Located in historic downtown Jeffersonville, the candy store is known for its 1950s soda fountain vibe (think old-school tin ceiling, candy jars, glass cases, and turn-of-the-century candy equipment). Meanwhile, Schimpff's is so entrenched in American history that it's featured as part of the Lewis & Clark Trail Experience, which calls out its most notable confections: Red Hots, hard candy fish, Modjeskas (marshmallow dipped in caramel), and turtle candies (pecan caramels topped with chocolate).

Wittich's Candy Shop claims to be the nation's oldest family owned and operated confectionery, as founder G.F. Wittich established this candy wonderland in 1840. Today, the business is now more than 185 years old and has been run by four generations of Wittich family members. It's known for goodies like hand-dipped chocolate candy, molded candies, and nut brittles, but Wittich's especially touts its Ohio specialty, Buckeyes. They're an indulgent favorite across the Buckeye state, but Wittich's notes it's the only candy maker to completely coat the peanut butter center in chocolate (choose from milk, dark, or white) for added freshness.

However, this historic store wasn't always just a candy peddler. The company actually started as a general store, selling items like flea powder, but Wittich soon started making hard stick candies before branching out into chocolates. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the sweets ended up being more in demand than anti-flea remedies. The store now features a historic soda fountain and even sells DIY candy making supplies for those who want to attempt their own candy craftsmanship at home.

Orne's Candy Store lore explains that it started as a female-run business when it opened on July 4, 1885, in downtown Boothbay Harbor, on the coast of Maine. Owner Addie Orne stocked her shop with ice cream, bananas, and a variety of candies. In 1960, Wollcott Webster purchased the store, intending to "preserve the atmosphere of an old-fashioned 19th century candy shop" while making now-popular additions like handmade fudge and chocolates displayed in the store's antique glass and wooden cases.

Today, Orne's is now run by the Webster family (who took over in 1978), and it's known as the "sweetest tradition in the Harbor," according to the Boothbay Register, even hosting an annual rock skipping competition. Fittingly, this sweets shop takes plenty of inspiration from the area's coastal locale, with candy specialties like Gravel (also called Magic Rocks — milk chocolate inside a small candy "stone"), Pebbles (a hard candy coating around a "softer surprise"), and Rock Candy, sold on a stick or a string, in every color of the rainbow.

11 Commercial St, Boothbay Harbor, ME 04538

While the exact original invention of candy canes is up for debate, Claus Doscher, founder of Doscher's Candy, claims to have created Cincinnati's first handcrafted candy cane back in 1871, when the shop opened. His proprietary handmade process — still used today — incorporated real peppermint oil, and he cooked the treats in small batches in copper kettles, creating an end result that the company calls "perfectly chewy and airy" and "a one-of-a-kind piece of confectionery art."

Today, this longstanding candy shop is also known for its Handmade Peppermint Pieces, Butter Mints, Candy Buttons, and, of course, candy canes in a rainbow of colors, including a Hanukkah collection. In addition to its online shop, the physical store in Cincinnati now hosts a curated collection of seasonal goods designed to bring a fun and festive vibe home, from candy-themed items to children's gifts. The store focuses on featuring handcrafted, locally-made, and Cincinnati artists' products, so customers can pick up gifts that give back to the community, along with some sweet treats.

Opened in the late 1800s and still going strong, Littleton, New Hampshire's Chutter General Store is now a bona fide piece of American candy store history, in more ways than one. That's because it's not just one of the oldest candy stores, but the largest — at least in terms of the length of its candy counter. At 111 feet, 11 inches, it nabbed a Guinness World Record for this feat, which draws in candy lovers as well as World Record enthusiasts.

This New England institution has been a mainstay on Littleton's charming historic Main Street for over 100 years, and it's still considered a destination for its famous fudge, plus must-have goodie bags and party favors for gatherings. The store is named after its original owner, Frederick George Chutter.

Today, the counter promises more than 500 types of candy to choose from, ensuring that customers of all ages can feel like a literal kid in a candy store again as they browse Chutter General Store's mega-size selection of sweets. Need more? Check out Chutters' second location in Lincoln, New Hampshire, just south of the original.

A true Texas original, Lammes Candies has been serving up goodies since 1885. First known for selling ice cream and the Gem, a frozen fruit dessert made from whole milk (similar to sherbet), it really made waves in 1892 when it introduced the Texas Chewie Pecan Praline, still a best seller today. Its outpost on Congress Avenue in Austin, Texas, was a hot spot for these iconic goodies for decades.

Sadly, the historic company made headlines (and broke hearts) when it announced it was closing in April 2026. But People magazine reported just a few months later, in September 2026, that new owners announced plans to revive it. For now, the owners are taking orders through the company's website and plans to re-emerge in Texas retailers as it figures out whether to offer a dedicated brick-and-mortar outlet again.

Interestingly, Lammes Candies is no stranger to close calls. It was once famously lost in a poker game by the original founder, William Wirt Lamme (the shop was then called Red Front Candy Factory, opened in 1878). But it was quickly rescued by his son, David Turner Lamme, Sr., and reopened as Lammes Candies in 1885.

Made in Santa Cruz, California, since 1915, Marini's Candies is widely regarded as one of the best candy stores in the nation. Follow this guide to chocolate tasting to start your own competition.

Marini's original claim to fame was its saltwater taffy, still sold today along with hand dipped nut clusters and caramels, caramel pecan patties, homemade fudge, caramel apples, and a variety of candies from around the world. Its founder, Victor Marini, was a barbershop owner who turned his purchase of a popcorn stand into a four-generation candy business, and his descendants carry on those traditions today.

Marini's has two locations to serve customers in Santa Cruz, including one on the Municipal Wharf, which has its own claim to fame as the longest wooden pier in the United States — an ideal spot for eating sweets while attempting a sighting of whales, dolphins, sea lions, or sea otters.

With the tagline "Making life a little bit sweeter since 1919," Claeys Candy had humble beginnings: Its founder, Jerome C. Claeys, started his candy making business in a garage in South Bend, Indiana. Today, it's still run by the same family — his grandson, Gregg Claeys, is the current president. But the Indianapolis Business Journal notes that the business has grown significantly over the years from those modest roots: Its latest facility, opened in 2022, is a 50,000-square-foot building that is twice as large as its previous factory.

Claeys has contributed several innovations to the candy landscape. Its first item made was the Etabar, a caramel nut bar covered with icing (originally sold for $0.05). Later, a popular Christmastime treat emerged, and it's still sold today: the Chocolate Charlie (originally called Charlie Chaplin), which is made of marshmallow and peanuts covered with chocolate. The candy manufacturer also sells beloved classics such as old-fashioned fudge, peanut brittle, and hard candies.

Open since 1905, Canelake's Candies in Virginia, Minnesota, was the brainchild of brothers Christ, Gust, Tom, and Nick Canelake, and today the third generation of family members is overseeing operations. This family-run business has been hailed by local radio station WJON as "one of Minnesota's top artisanal candy boutiques." It sells sweets through its brick-and-mortar location and also ships nationwide, but only during the winter months (because no one likes a melted chocolate mess arriving in the mail).

But, as Canelake's owners point out, this outpost is more than just Minnesota's oldest candy store—it offers up an old-fashioned soda fountain, local and handcrafted American goods like Minnetonka Moccasins and Folkmanis Puppets, a candy museum, and memorabilia from the Iron Range of Minnesota. Unique hard candies — think Root Beer Fish and Pickle Hard Candy — are available alongside its beloved chocolates, candy apples, and licorice.

Candy corn's name hearkens back to America's agricultural history, but the beloved Halloween candy takes a fun gummy form at this Northeast Pennsylvania institution, in business since 1904. Dunmore Candy Kitchen also offers chocolates and a bevy of other sweet treats at its two in-person locations in Dunmore (the original, hence the name), and Moosic, Pennsylvania, as well as on its online shop. One of the many standouts of the business is its impressive selection of molded and figures candies, from text-stamped squares sharing holiday wishes to chocolate alligators and army tanks. You can find almost any candy here.

For customers who want to try their hand at making their own designs, the company even provides custom candy wrappers and mold designs. And the old-time company even started an entire fundraising arm to give back to the local community through its now-legendary candies.

Now with two locations in Bethlehem and Allentown, Pennsylvania, the history of Josh Early Candies reaches back to 1904, when founder J. Mark Early (known as Josh Early III) started a wholesale candy business with a partner. A retail business followed. Later, his son, Josh Early IV, with wife Millie, opened Early's Old Fashioned Chocolates in Reading, Pennsylvania, in 1938.

CBS News Philadelphia grabbed a behind-the-scenes look at this fifth-generation business, owned today by a sister-brother duo, calling it a "Lehigh Valley staple." Customer favorites include Peanut Rolled Eggs (vanilla butter cream wrapped in milk and dark chocolate, rolled in ground peanuts), Caramel Marshmallow Bars, and Assorted Chocolates boxes stuffed with a variety of Creams, Caramels, Nougats, and Chews. The candies have been crafted by-hand for five generations now using the same recipes from the early 1900s.

Laura's Candies has been churning out sweets since 1913 in New Orleans' French Quarter and now has a second outpost in Metairie, Louisiana, west of The Big Easy. While the original owner sold only fudge and pies when it opened, the company has now branched out into selling gourmet products like pralines, chocolates, truffles, and even spicier selections, like Louisiana Hot Sauce and Chocolate Body Frosting.

Owner Brian Boehm took the reins of the company in 2008, but he still carries on the made-by-hand process that started more than 100 years ago. He favors down-home Southern traditions like preparing pralines fresh daily. The tried-and-true approach seems to be working well, as Laura's Candies' fudge and other classics are still a hit with customers today. Plus, purchasing premade is a much easier option than making your own homemade fudge.

In Wilton, Iowa, The Candy Kitchen was established in 1860 as a confectionery but was later upgraded to encompass a restaurant, soda fountain, and ice cream parlor before the turn of the century. In 1990, the Nopoulos family bought the business and ran it until 2015, when sisters Lynn and Brenda Ochiltree took over. Through multiple generations, The Candy Kitchen still serves up food, drinks, and ice cream in an old-school soda fountain setting.

But this store offers sweets with a side of history. For those who can't make the in-person trip, the candy depot hosts a virtual museum where visitors can browse historic memorabilia from the archives (also displayed onsite in the shop). The collections of the Candy Kitchen and Lynn Ochiltree are estimated to include more than 100,000 artifacts and documents from the surrounding Muscatine County, focusing on the Moscow and Wilton, Iowa, communities. The Candy Kitchen also offers a store stocked with unique items, antiques, and soy candles locally made by hand, making it a one-stop shop for gifts and goodies.

#206. Delta Is Seriously Upgrading Its Airplane Food & I Got A First Taste—Here’s What’s On The New Menu

We’ve come a long way from peanuts and a snack box.

On a long-haul flight, I care about two things: Can I get comfortable enough, and what exactly am I going to eat while I’m up there? We’ve come a long way from sad snack boxes and over-salted peanuts, and if an airline is charging premium-cabin money, I want the meal to feel like part of the splurge instead of something I politely move around with a fork.

Delta apparently agrees, as the airline has begun rolling out a major refresh of its Delta One experience, with food and drinks getting a particularly serious upgrade. The new setup launches first on transoceanic Delta One flights leaving Los Angeles this fall before expanding across the global network in early 2027.

I recently got to try a handful of dishes from the new menu, which moves between familiar comfort food and much more restaurant-y territory. My tasting included everything from a soup-and-salad starter, risotto, and lamb to a Wagyu burger and upgraded dessert, giving me a pretty good sense of what Delta is going for before any of it reaches a tray table.

The starter was a nice kickoff, and the meats were tender, but the risotto was probably the biggest pleasant surprise. And if you’ve watched enough Top Chef, you know putting risotto on the menu can feel like tempting fate. The lamb was flavorful, though a little harder to cut than I would’ve liked, especially when the dining surface is approximately the size of a laptop.

I’m also personally not rushing to order fish on an airplane, but the sea bass felt far more upscale than most meals I’ve encountered in the sky.

The meal could’ve ended there and I would’ve been perfectly satisfied, but I have a sweet tooth and Delta is keeping its dessert cart. I didn’t even particularly want a sundae until I spotted the soft doughnut sitting on top of one, alongside chocolate sauce, Amarena cherries, and pecan praline crumble. There’s also a dairy-free sorbet that can get a Champagne Taittinger float, plus a cheese plate featuring Northern California cheeses and crackers.

The drinks are getting an upgrade, too. Blanton’s bourbon joins the menu in December, while the wine list is being refreshed with new bottles and an expanded Champagne Taittinger partnership. And starting in 2027, passengers will also be able to order both boozy and non-alcoholic versions of Hugo Spritzes and Palomas.

It’s tough for any airline meal to make me forget I’m eating somewhere over the Atlantic, but if I’m paying to sit up front, this gets much closer to what I want waiting on the tray table.

#209. Lasagna-Vibes Zucchini Skillet

For years, one of my go-to dinners in the summer was zucchini lasagna, where zucchini is used in place of noodles. It’s delightful, but it’s also very labor-intensive, requiring you to slice the zucchini into long, thin planks, salt each individual plank, wipe each individual plank, and then layer the zucchini “noodles” with ricotta, sauce, and mozzarella. Now I have far too many children to be salting individual planks of zucchini—so I make this. It’s a dump-and-go skillet meal that has all of those favorite flavors in a way, way quicker and easier format.

Read More: Finding My Way Back to the Kitchen After Giving Birth

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground turkey and cook, breaking up into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until mostly cooked through with only a little pink remaining, about 4 minutes. Add 3 medium zucchini (about 20 oz.), halved lengthwise, sliced crosswise ⅛" thick, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt; season with freshly ground black pepper. Increase heat to high and cook, stirring often, until meat is cooked through and no longer pink and zucchini is tender, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium and stir in one 14.5-oz. can tomato sauce, 2 tsp. Italian seasoning, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. onion powder, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and half of 1 cup thinly sliced basil leaves. Taste zucchini mixture and season with more salt and pepper if needed. Swirl in spoonfuls of 4 oz. whole-milk ricotta (about ½ cup), then sprinkle 4 oz. mozzarella, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup), over. Reduce heat to low, cover pan, and cook until mozzarella is melted, about 4 minutes.

Top zucchini mixture with remaining basil and crushed red pepper flakes (if using) to serve.
