#210. I Indulged in Rare, 135-Year-Old Wine at This Sonoma Resort

In Hotels With Great Taste, we’re pulling back the curtain for a peek at the “special sauce” that hotels use to create memorable, meaningful culinary experiences for their guests.

Look closely at the lodgings that make up Dawn Ranch and you’ll notice they’re actually a patchwork of historic structures in different shapes and sizes. Each building at the luxe 15-acre Russian River resort, which is nestled amongst the towering redwoods in the petite town of Guerneville, California, is linked to a different era of the property’s past.

Built in 1905, it was originally Murphy’s Ranch, a getaway for well-to-do families that operated for seven decades. Later it served for more than 20 years as the pioneering gay resort Fife’s. Today, it’s a refined wine country escape that exists at the crossroads of nature and high-end luxury. The hotel is situated in a floodway, which limits construction for safety purposes, so since 1993 the site’s various owners haven’t been able to build anew; renovating ad infinitum has proven to be just dandy though.

In fact, this limitation turns out to be central to Dawn Ranch’s retro, summer camp-adjacent charm, which feels like a happy throwback even with its modernized facilities and amenities. Spectacularly refurbished in 2023, the current upscale iteration features 81 California-cool rooms, a tremendous spa, a fine-dining restaurant that may very well become impossible to book once word gets out, and a thoughtful, dynamic wine program that highlights some of the world’s most unique bottles.

When it comes to bunking, you have choices that span a hodgepodge of rustic-chic cabins, chalets, cottages, bungalows, and glamping tents. On the main campus, cabins are cozy and compact, while the cottages and chalets offer more space. Most include private outdoor decks, equally ideal for taking in a morning cuppa or an evening tipple. The bungalows are the roomiest accommodation, outfitted for families and large groups with two bedrooms, two baths, a full kitchen, and gas fireplaces. Across the street, the resort’s Grove campus offers more options, which range from snug single-room affairs to spacious two bedrooms.

They’re all scattered amongst the tree-filled property’s sycamores and redwoods, so traipsing to your room feels like a walk in the forest. Inside, the aesthetic is a study in NorCal quiet luxury, with plenty of smooth blonde wood, layered textiles, and eclectic furniture pieces, plus Parachute linens and Le Labo bath goodies.

More adventurous guests will appreciate the smartly furnished glamping tents, situated in Dawn Ranch’s 120-year-old apple tree orchard. The walls may be canvas, but the beds feature the same Bear hybrid mattresses as those in Dawn Ranch’s more conventional rooms. You will, however, have to share a bathhouse—albeit an extremely nice one—with your fellower glampers.

No matter where you sleep, make sure you lay eyes on the resort’s namesake, a 70-year-old pair of rare dawn redwoods located near the pool on the main campus.

The Lodge at Dawn Ranch, which houses the hotel’s main dining, bar, and lounge areas, manages a laid-back vibe that nonetheless feels rarefied and celebratory, with plush mauve-colored banquettes and dim romantic lighting.

But food is the real draw: Co-executive chefs (and husband-and-wife team) Ignacio “Nacho” Zuzulich and Juliana Thorpe center a nine-course, $155 tasting menu informed both by their respective Argentinian and Brazilian backgrounds and their experience cooking in lauded kitchens from Mugaritz in Spain to Napa Valley’s Meadowood resort. A truncated version of the tasting menu is served at the bar for $90.

Seasonal Golden State ingredients take top billing. On a recent visit, corn was a standout, taking the form of a delicate tostada set atop a fire-roasted corn custard. Festooned with the marigold-like flowering herb huacatay, it conveyed an impossibly large, flawless lobe of Santa Barbara uni.

In the morning, don’t skip breakfast at the Lodge, which is best taken on the sprawling outside deck. Soft scrambled eggs with avocado and furikake on homemade brioche are straightforward but deeply effective, while the cinnamon rolls glossed in cream cheese frosting are the perfect excuse to eat dessert before noon.

When drinking, whether in the dining room or bar, vino is the move. This is wine country, after all. The handwritten “Sommelier’s Notebook” dispenses with formality, breaking wines into playful categories like “The Wild Ones,” “Extrovert Whites,” and “Quiet Elegance.” You’ll have plenty of fun ordering by the bottle or glass; if you’re after just a taste, some offerings are available in one-ounce pours.

But for the deep-pocketed, the $400 Decades Wine Pairing is a voyage through time and space, guiding you through wines bottled across generations. The offerings frequently shift, but this past summer, the oldest pour was an intensely molasses-forward D'Oliveiras Verdelho Madeira, first put under cork in 1891.

With its decadent syrup-like texture and vibrant acidity, the Madeira made for a complex complement to the tasting menu’s show-stopping dessert course, which presented local peaches in three manners: a quenelle of peach sorbet; a crystal cupful of peach nectar; and a tart of roasted peach jam and white chocolate ganache, topped with intricately woven, paper-thin peach slivers and served alongside a peach sabayon.

Best of all, returning to my cottage after dinner required only a brief, tipsy walk through the redwoods, the stars lighting my way.

#211. McDonald's French Fries Aren't Dairy-Free

Up there with the Big Mac and McNuggets, McDonald's gloriously greasy fries have achieved legendary status within the fast food world. Their signature slender shape, generous sprinkling of salt, and crisp exterior give way to a soft, fluffy center that has people, quite literally, lining up around the block. Plenty of fans swear they're the best any fast food chain has to offer, and they owe their signature flavor to one rather unexpected ingredient: milk.

That's right, McDonald's fries in the U.S. aren't dairy-free — our condolences to all the vegans out there! Potatoes and vegetable oils make up the bulk of the recipe, but the ingredient list also includes something called "natural beef flavor." Here's where things get interesting — this flavoring contains hydrolyzed wheat and milk. Hydrolysis is a process that uses water to break proteins down into smaller compounds, including peptides and amino acids, which can contribute to flavor. The result is a distinctly savory, beefy note, despite the fries being cooked only in vegetable oil, with no beef fat in sight. The recipe differs across certain locations, too. In the U.K., for example, McDonald's fries contain no animal-derived ingredients and are officially suitable for vegans.

Milk-derived flavoring wasn't always part of the picture. Back in the day, McDonald's cooked its fries in beef tallow, a rendered fat prized for its rich, savory flavor. Tallow can be used in several ways — from baking flaky pie crusts to frying potatoes until they're extra crispy — lending dishes a rich depth that's hard to replicate with vegetable oil alone. But in 1990, amid growing scrutiny over saturated fat, McDonald's made the decision to abandon beef tallow in favor of vegetable oil.

McDonald's fries have been around for a long, long time. The chain was founded in 1940, and fries joined the menu in 1949, less than a decade later. In fact, the cheeseburger is one of the few original menu items that predates them, having been available since the restaurant first opened.

The story of McDonald's fries starts on the potato farm. The chain doesn't rely on a single variety, although Russet Burbank makes up a significant portion of its supply, alongside varieties such as Shepody, Ranger Russet, and Umatilla Russet. An important trait all these potatoes share is their starchiness, characterized by a relatively low moisture content. This combination helps create the fries' signature contrast between a crisp exterior and a fluffy center.

Once harvested, the potatoes head to processing facilities, where the real magic happens. They're cleaned, inspected, peeled, and sliced before being blanched and treated with ingredients that help maintain their familiar appearance. Dextrose helps the fries develop that signature golden hue, while sodium acid pyrophosphate keeps them from turning gray. After drying, the fries are partially fried in oil containing the natural beef flavoring. They're then frozen and shipped to McDonald's restaurants, where they get their final fry before being salted and served hot.

#212. This Unexpected Fruit Will Show Up All Over Coffee Menus In 2027—Here’s Why

Its presence on café menus has nearly doubled in just one year.

Long gone are the days when a cup of black coffee was the only way to get through the day—not because it doesn’t provide energy, but because innovative lattes are being served in cafés around the world.

More and more consumers are looking for ways to dress up their everyday drink, experimenting with everything from classic vanilla to lavender and even banana bread coffee. Fruit used to be a background character in your cup of coffee; now it’s primed to be the main event. And according to Nestlé’s 2027 Food and Beverage Trend Forecast, the future of coffee is looking very fruit-forward.

While these flavors may sound a little out there, fruit pairs well with coffee because the beans themselves can carry subtle fruity notes. And one flavor in particular that’s poised to show up on a lot more menus next year is none other than fig.

Linh Phillips, Director of Consumer Insights & Foresight at Nestlé USA, explains that fruit is moving from a supporting note to a much bigger part of the coffee experience. “In 2027, fruit is showing up in new combinations, formats, and textures, turning coffee and matcha into a source of discovery, customization, and flavor exploration,” she says.

According to Datassential, mentions of fig on coffee menus have grown 98.5 percent over the past year. “As younger consumers look to their coffee cup as a place for new experiences, ingredients like dates and figs will add new complexity to drinks,” Phillips explains. “Date caramel, figs and dark stone fruits bring caramel-like, jammy and toffee notes, while cherries, plums and prunes add a rich, slightly tart sweetness. We’re already seeing this shift on menus.”

Steadfast Coffee, a local shop in Nashville, Tennessee, has seen success with its “Fig Season” drink. And the inspiration came from somewhere unexpected: the charcuterie board.

“We wanted to see how we could highlight our obsession with cheese and jam, minus the salami. So we crafted a housemade fig syrup, topped it with cream cheese cold foam, and sprinkled some pistachios on top and hoped for the best!” shares Sydnie Neumann, the café’s General Manager.

“Fortunately, we can’t keep it in stock!” she continues. “It’s so awesome to see people branch out and try something new. Figs are pricier than other fruits, so making it accessible in an affordable way makes people feel like they get to really treat themselves while enjoying the familiarity of a great cup of coffee.”

Phillips says fruit can also add more than flavor. Cold foam, jellies, and freeze-dried fruit can bring extra texture and visual appeal to a drink, making it feel more premium—and more social-media friendly.

Move over figgy pudding, I’m here for figgy drinks!

#213. This Is the Only Gluten-Free Flour I’ll Bake With

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

About half of my large family is gluten free, so at holidays and gatherings, almost everything is prepared without gluten. It’s easier and safer that way, preventing confusion or cross-contamination. Dessert is often served with the claim, “You’d never know it’s gluten free.” Perhaps it’s my background as a professional recipe developer, but I can always tell. Sometimes it’s yummy with only a slight textural difference; other times … I just smile politely. Gluten-free recipes—even ones made with the best gluten-free flour blends—can be hit or miss. And that’s frustrating.

My own results using gluten-free flour blends aren’t always great. I’ve tried a bunch, and usually end up with gritty, dense, gummy or crumbly bakes—and sometimes all of those at once. Most of the time, I skip the GF blends entirely and stick with a crowd-pleasing flourless chocolate cake. But recently I saw something new on the shelf from Bob’s Red Mill, a well-known brand I love that sells tons of gluten-free products. The product—Bob’s Red Mill Gluten-Free 1-To-1 Baking Flour—is only kinda new, I should say, because it’s actually an update, with fresh packaging and a new formulation. I decided to put it to the test. And I’m so glad I did!

Gluten-free flour blends are made with a combination of starches, gums, and grain or rice flours. The goal is to have a mixture that absorbs liquid and holds together when baked, mimicking the effect of the gluten in all-purpose flour. Every brand has its own ratios and ingredients, but there are a lot of similarities and overlap between them. White and/or brown rice flour is commonly used as the base. It has a lovely neutral flavor, but the trade-off is that it can be gritty, creating a coarse texture and crumbly interior.

When reformulating, Bob’s Red Mill stuck with its previous base of sweet white rice flour and whole grain brown rice flour, but it adjusted the starch proportions to improve the texture. It also changed one key ingredient. The new formula replaced whole grain sorghum flour with pearled white sorghum flour. Pearled sorghum flour doesn’t include the outer hull of the grain, which gives it a lighter color, finer texture and milder taste. It seems like a small change, but it made a huge difference in my bakes.

One category of recipes to avoid, however, is yeasted recipes. The package specifies this blend is best for recipes without yeast, meaning it won’t work for pizza dough, cinnamon rolls or bread.

One of the best things about Bob’s Red Mill is how widely available it is. My go-to large grocery store, ShopRite, has an entire section just for various Bob’s Red Mill products, including this gluten-free baking flour. #214. 3-Ingredient Curry Pumpkin Soup

This dead simple three-ingredient soup houses a wealth of flavor with a shockingly trim ingredient list. Made by sizzling curry paste in oil, then adding a can of pumpkin purée and coconut milk, this cozy soup is a celebration of simplicity, creating something that tastes far more complex than it was to make. For the best flavor, I like to use the Maesri brand curry paste, leaning on its warm intensity to lend the soup its depth, but the ubiquitous Thai Kitchen, sold in almost all grocery stores, is also nice, producing a gentle heat.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: The 3-Ingredient Pumpkin Soup You’ll Fall For.

Transfer a couple of spoonfuls or so of one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, stirred well, to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Heat 1 Tbsp. unrefined coconut oil or other oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 2 Tbsp. red curry paste and cook, stirring constantly, until fragrant, 2–3 minutes. Add one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, remaining coconut milk in can, and 1½ cups water. Increase heat to high and bring soup to a simmer. Remove pot from heat. Taste soup and season with kosher salt if needed. Ladle into bowls and drizzle some reserved coconut milk into each bowl.

#215. Nara Smith Regrets Trying to Make Twizzlers

Nara Smith’s internet persona is built on a specific kind of perfection: extravagant gowns, immaculate kitchens, and from-scratch recipes that make artisanal homemade cereal feel entirely reasonable. A true modern renaissance woman, she seamlessly balances cooking, influencing, and motherhood, and is even set to star alongside Charlize Theron and Demi Moore in the upcoming thriller Tyrant, a film delving into NYC’s elite fine dining scene. Her new book, Homemade, balances her campy approach to cooking—the cover features Smith in a dress that doubles as a table—with recipes for homemade cinnamon toast squares alongside more practical, kid-friendly dishes like pork schnitzel and Coconut Cassava Waffles.

In person, she’s far less precious and much funnier. During Smith’s visit to the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen, her relentless pace was on full display. When I ran down a couple of floors to return a pen her producer had left behind, I found her completely transformed, glam fully retouched, already posing for her next shoot for Vanity Fair.

We spoke to Smith about the kitchen slippers hiding beneath her camera frame, the failed homemade Twizzlers that still haunt her, the sudden onset of her egg ick, and the oddly specific way her dad taught her to cut pancakes into tiny squares.

What’s the first thing people get wrong about you?

People think I’m wearing heels. I’m actually wearing slippers. I’m very tall, and if I wear heels the counter is too low and nothing looks proportionate. Also, I’m standing all day and my lower back would never forgive me. So it’s always a really good cushioned house slipper. Comfort first.

You spend so much time making food on camera. Are there recipes that feel especially personal to you?

These German pancakes. My dad made them before school when I was growing up. He’d always make the first one before he woke us up because the first pancake is always bad. When I was writing the recipe for my cookbook, I asked him for measurements, and he was like, “A little bit of this, a little bit of that, maybe two, maybe three eggs.” That's not exactly cookbook language.

Your cookbook is full of from-scratch recipes. Is there anything you’d never make yourself?

Never say never. I tried making Twizzlers once, and they were terrible. Absolutely terrible. I still think about trying again because I love a challenge, but candy is one of those things that can really humble you.

What’s been your biggest kitchen disaster?

The Twizzlers were bad, but sourdough was probably worse. My first few attempts were a complete mess. The funny thing is I often make recipes for the first time on camera, so if something goes wrong, everyone gets to watch it happen in real time.

The Test Kitchen wanted to know: What’s your favorite way to eat eggs?

This is controversial because I have 20 chickens, but I got the egg ick while I was pregnant, and it never fully went away. If I’m eating eggs, I want a fried egg with crispy edges and a runny yolk on top of fried rice. Just don’t give it to me first thing in the morning.

Honestly? My garden is dying. The zucchini is struggling. The cucumbers are gone. All my lettuce died. Between the heat and the rain, everything has kind of given up. It’s my first year, though, so I’m trying to be kind to myself. Next year will be better.

What’s the most specific food habit you have?

I cut these pancakes into tiny squares. My dad used to do it for me, and now it’s the only way I like eating them. I put applesauce on top, dust them with powdered sugar, cut them into little squares, and eat them one by one. Everyone else in my family thinks it’s weird.

Weigh your ingredients. Especially flour. A cup of flour means something different to everyone. Good ingredients matter, too, but if you’re baking, a scale will save you a lot of heartbreak.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

I’m as susceptible to Reese’s as the next person, no matter what shape they put it in. But staring at 3.25 pounds of peanut butter and chocolate may finally be where my devotion starts to feel overly ambitious.

A 52-ounce Reese’s Milk Chocolate Peanut Butter Pie has been spotted in the wild, and calling it a “pie” feels almost too polite. It’s essentially one absolutely enormous peanut butter cup, with a milk chocolate exterior and peanut butter center, weighing 3.25 pounds and selling for about $40.

Food account @snackolator shared the find on Instagram, noting that Reese’s sold a similar giant version online five years ago and it disappeared almost immediately. This time around, shoppers are actually finding the massive dessert in warehouse stores, and listings have also popped up on DoorDash and Instacart.

The nutrition label really puts the scale of this thing into perspective. Reese’s considers it approximately 48 servings, with each 31-gram serving clocking in at 160 calories. Do that math and the whole thing comes to roughly 7,680 calories.

Forty-eight servings also means whoever is cutting this at Thanksgiving better have the precision of a surgeon. Between its size, the price, and the sheer amount of Reese’s involved, people had plenty to react to on social media once photos started circulating.

“I’ve been imagining this for years. I want this so bad,” one person wrote. Another added, “I neeeeeeeeed this!!!!”

One commenter who bought the earlier version offered some firsthand perspective: “I got the one years ago lasted me a month ate a quarter of it every Saturday.”

Others were more skeptical, particularly about whether it would taste like the Reese’s they remember. “If it isn’t the old recipe they can throw this right in the trash…,” one commenter wrote. Another agreed, writing, “If it tastes like Reese's used to taste, I'd buy it.”

Then there was the one person already thinking about how to get the thing to the holiday table: “I wonder if the TSA would let me bring this with me to Thanksgiving.”

My mouth is already sticking shut just thinking about it.

#218. I Made 3-Ingredient Pumpkin Cake Balls, and I Finally Get the Pumpkin Spice Hype

These easy pumpkin cake balls have me second-guessing my ambivalence toward pumpkin spice. I used store-bought products to save prep time, and you'd never know they were only half-homemade.

Pumpkin spice season is taken very seriously in my house. My husband is fairly reasonable about it, but my kids spend most of fall acting as though cinnamon, nutmeg and cloves are a food group. I’m the outlier. Sure, I like a slice of pumpkin pie at Thanksgiving, but I’ve never understood the annual rush to make everything taste like it.

I do, however, have a soft spot for the pumpkin loaves that start appearing in coffee shops and grocery-store bakeries this time of year. So when I came across an Instagram video from @thefoodarrondissement making cake balls out of banana bread, I wondered what would happen if I gave the idea a more autumnal twist. Instead of baking anything, I picked up a package of frosted pumpkin loaf slices from Walmart, a can of vanilla frosting and chocolate candy melts.

The ingredients and very little work later, I had one of the best pumpkin desserts I’ve made in a while. Unfortunately for my longstanding position as the household pumpkin-spice skeptic, I may have to give this one to the fanatics.

They’re essentially cake pops without sticks, though there’s no reason at all you couldn’t serve them as cake pops as well. They’re made by crumbling cake, mixing it with frosting, rolling the mixture into balls and coating them in chocolate.

The version that inspired me used banana bread in place of regular cake, and pumpkin seemed like a natural swap for the season. You could certainly bake a loaf of pumpkin bread for the purpose, but I was interested in the shortcut version. Walmart sells frosted pumpkin cake slices in its bakery section, which meant most of the work—and even some of the frosting—was already taken care of.

I crumbled the entire package of pumpkin slices into a large bowl, including the frosting on top of each slice. Because the cake was already moist and frosted, I only needed about 1/3 cup of canned vanilla frosting to bring everything together. If you’re using an unfrosted pumpkin loaf, you’ll likely need more, so add it a little at a time until the mixture holds together easily when you squeeze it.

Vanilla worked well because it didn’t compete with the pumpkin and spices, but cream cheese frosting would be a delicious choice here too. Salted caramel or coffee frosting could take them in a slightly less sweet direction.

Once the mixture held together, I rolled it into balls, dipped each one in melted chocolate and sprinkled with a pinch of sea salt. I transferred the cake balls to the fridge to let the coating set. It took about 10 minutes. That’s it!

These pumpkin cake balls have no business being so delicious for how easy they are to make. Pumpkin cake is dense and moist to begin with, so the centers had a richer, softer texture than the standard cake balls I’ve made with regular cake and frosting. More importantly, they weren’t too sweet. The pumpkin and spices were beautifully balanced beneath the vanilla frosting and chocolate shell, and that little bit of warmth kept the whole thing from becoming cloying.

There’s also something particularly wonderful in the contrast between the firm chocolate shell and the almost truffle-like pumpkin center. I may never completely share my family’s enthusiasm for pumpkin spice, but these easy cake balls just got me a lot closer.

If you test these out, let us know what you think in the comments below!

#219. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#220. Gochujang Yogurt Chicken

Don’t be surprised if this becomes your new go-to weeknight chicken dish. The marinade features a host of winning pantry ingredients you likely already have on hand: yogurt, gochujang, soy sauce, and maple syrup. A smack of freshly grated garlic joins in to make a delicious spicy-savory-sweet marinade you’ll find yourself using on everything. (Yes, in fact, you can reserve a small portion to thin out later to become a nice drizzling sauce over the cooked chicken. More on that below in the recipe instructions.)

Yogurt is a powerful tenderizer, so even just 20 minutes of marinating time while you prep the rest of dinner is enough to imbue flavor into the meat. The yogurt also helps to temper the heat from smoky-spicy gochujang, the assertive and versatile Korean hot pepper paste. If you have the time, an overnight rest in the fridge is even better. Lean on my favorite go-to broiler for a quick cook with minimal cleanup. These chicken thighs take very well to batch-cooking at the start of the week and enjoying in the ensuing days. They are great with rice, over salad, in a wrap, or even just cold out of the fridge (who, me?).

Save more weeknight dinner winners: Gorgeous Green Shrimp; Spicy Salmon Bowl; and Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry

Whisk 4–6 garlic cloves, finely grated (about 1 Tbsp.), ½ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt, ¼ cup gochujang (Korean hot pepper paste), 3 Tbsp. pure maple syrup, 3 Tbsp. soy sauce, 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a small bowl until salt is mostly dissolved. (If you’d like to reserve ¼ cup marinade for dressing, now is the time; chill until ready to use.)

Pour marinade into a large resealable plastic bag and add 2½–3 lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs. Close bag and turn chicken to coat. Let sit at room temperature at least 20 minutes, or chill, turning occasionally, up to 12 hours.

Heat broiler. Place a wire rack inside a foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Coat or brush rack with nonstick vegetable oil spray or vegetable oil. Remove chicken from marinade, letting excess drip back into bag, and arrange, smoother side up, on rack. Broil, turning halfway through, until golden brown with some edges getting a deeper char, 15–18 minutes. Let chicken rest about 5 minutes, then slice if desired.

If using reserved marinade as a sauce, add 1–2 Tbsp. water to reserved marinade to thin to desired consistency. Serve chicken with sauce drizzled over.

#222. Ina Garten’s Biggest Cookbook Lesson Started With A Roast Chicken Nobody Wanted

Before Ina Garten became the person I trust to make everything from a fall salad to a very large Cosmopolitan look effortless, she was figuring out the food business one roast chicken at a time. And apparently, even Ina had to serve a few flops before figuring out what people actually wanted.

On a recent episode of The Mel Robbins Podcast, Garten looked back on the earliest days of Barefoot Contessa, the tiny Westhampton specialty food store she bought at 30 despite having zero experience running one. She’d come from working on nuclear energy policy in Washington, D.C., but Garten doesn’t actually see the career pivot as quite as random as it sounds.

“If you’re cooking, you’re testing things,” she told Robbins. “But instead of ending up with, like, gibberellic acid, you end up with roast chicken. So which would you rather have?”

The learning curve was immediate. Garten said she didn’t know how to cash out a register, slice smoked salmon, or scale the 12 brownies she could make for friends into 1,000 for customers. After her first week, she even told Jeffrey, “This is the stupidest thing I’ve ever done in my life.”

Her first day as owner didn’t exactly scream future food empire, either. The register had just $87 in it, prompting Jeffrey to do the math and tell her, “I don’t think you’re gonna make it here.” By the end of the very next day, a busy Friday before Memorial Day weekend, the store was completely cleaned out. Garten and the previous owner stayed up through the night making chocolate cake and chicken salad so they could do it all again. But one of the most important lessons came from food that wasn’t selling.

Garten initially assumed a Hamptons specialty shop called for fancy food, so she made dishes like veal with morels and displayed roast chickens on a huge white platter surrounded by fresh herbs. Nobody wanted them. She eventually moved those same chickens into little red-and-white checkered baskets—and they sold in 10 minutes.

Her takeaway? “People have elegant taste, but they don’t want fancy food at home.” Garten said the realization “totally informed all of my cookbooks.”

That philosophy feels pretty familiar if you’ve ever made her Honey White Bread or Crispy Chicken With Lemon Orzo. When Garten eventually did start writing cookbooks, she said her formula was simple: dependable recipes, beautiful photography, and ingredients you could actually find at the grocery store.

And, fittingly, when Robbins asked Garten for her favorite recipe at the end of the conversation, she didn’t name anything particularly elaborate. She picked a French apple tart with a thin buttery crust, sliced apples, butter, and sugar.

“It’s a very simple recipe,” Garten said. “I just think it’s just gorgeous.”

#223. We Tried Home Depot’s Viral Grand Duchess Christmas Tree—Is It Worth It?

Can a $349 artificial Christmas tree really compete with premium models? After a month of testing Home Depot's Smart Grand Duchess, I was surprised by just how much it delivers for the price.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

A realistic (but still artificial) Christmas tree with customizable lighting, smart controls and easy assembly usually comes with a pretty hefty price tag. That’s why I was interested in trying Home Depot’s 7.5-foot Smart Grand Duchess Twinkling Balsam Fir, which promises all of those features for around $350.

I’ve tested plenty of home products and holiday decorations over the years, including artificial Christmas trees costing significantly more than this one. I wanted to see whether Home Depot’s relatively affordable smart tree could really compete with the premium options.

After a full month of testing, decorating, experimenting with the lighting and eventually packing it away, I came away thoroughly impressed. In fact, it held its own against a much more expensive King of Christmas tree I already own.

A smart artificial Christmas tree with app and remote controls and a surprisingly lush look for the price.

The Smart Grand Duchess Twinkling Balsam Fir is a pre-lit artificial Christmas tree from Home Depot’s Home Decorators Collection, available in 7.5-, 9-, 12- or 15-foot size options. It uses both realistic molded branches with 2,250 color-changing micro LED lights and smart controls through the Hubspace app.

At first glance, its biggest selling point is how realistic it looks. The outer branches are made from molded plastic designed to replicate the appearance and texture of natural evergreen foliage. Unlike the flat, papery needles found on cheaper artificial trees, these branches have convincing dimension and structure.

Look a little deeper into the tree, though, and you’ll discover something interesting. The interior uses less expensive, traditional artificial foliage to fill out the branches. It’s a clever cost-saving approach that works really well. The premium-looking tips are what you see from the outside, while the cheaper foliage provides fullness without drawing attention to itself.

The tree also features “Quick Set” technology, which connects the lighting through the trunk as you assemble the sections, along with memory-wire branches that require less shaping. Its integrated lighting can be controlled using the included remote or the Hubspace smartphone app, with adjustable brightness, various lighting effects and customizable schedules.

I set up the Smart Grand Duchess in my home and tested it for one month, evaluating everything from assembly and branch realism to smart features, everyday usability and storage.

Throughout the testing period, I experimented with different lighting modes, decorated the tree, used both the remote and smartphone app, and paid attention to how well the branches maintained their shape. I also compared its appearance and overall quality with my considerably more expensive artificial tree I’ve had for a few years already.

One of the first things I appreciated about the Smart Grand Duchess was how straightforward it was to assemble. From opening the box to getting the tree standing with its lights connected, the process took around 20 minutes. That’s not including any additional time spent fluffing and shaping the branches (which can take hours if you’re anything like me).

The Quick Set design eliminates much of the frustration that can come with assembling a pre-lit tree. Instead of hunting for electrical connections between sections, the lighting connects through the trunk as the pieces fit together. This seems to be a pretty standard feature in modern artificial trees, so I was glad to see it included in this model.

Once assembled, I spent some time arranging the branches to achieve a natural shape and fill any obvious gaps. Thanks to the memory-wire construction, this was relatively easy, and the tree quickly started to look full and balanced.

The metal stand is fairly basic, but it does its job well. I didn’t experience any stability issues during the month I had the tree displayed.

For me, the appearance is where this tree really shines. I’ve seen plenty of artificial Christmas trees that look convincing from across the room but noticeably cheap when you get closer. That wasn’t the case here.

The molded outer branches have an impressively realistic appearance, especially considering the price. They provide the shape and texture you’d expect from a more premium artificial tree, and there’s enough variation in the foliage to keep it from looking overly uniform.

What impressed me most was how effectively Home Depot disguises the less expensive materials inside the tree. The traditional foliage toward the center adds density and prevents the tree from looking sparse, but it’s largely hidden behind the realistic outer branches.

It’s a smart design decision. You’re not paying for premium molded foliage in areas that nobody is likely to see, yet the finished tree still looks full and convincing.

According to Kristin Ilgunas, founder and designer at A Merry Little Kristmas, a luxury holiday design studio, this combination of materials is actually something to look for in a quality artificial Christmas tree. “Then there are trees that are a mix: realistic PE on the outer edges and the PVC on the inside. This makes them full and is generally what a lot of ‘nicer’ artificial trees are now,” she explains. “This is actually what I prefer to use because the inner PVC is easy to manipulate and attach ribbon and other items to.”

The construction on our tested tree also appears to help minimize shedding. Since much of the visible foliage consists of molded plastic pieces rather than individual loose needles, I noticed very little debris during assembly, decorating or disassembly.

I decorated the tree with relatively lightweight ornaments, and the branches held their shape without noticeable sagging. I can’t speak to how well they’d support particularly heavy decorations, but they handled my everyday ornaments without trouble.

Another thoughtful detail is the long, upright section at the very top of the tree. It’s ideal for securing a tree topper and helps keep it standing straight.

Perhaps the strongest endorsement of the tree’s appearance came from friends and family. Several people commented on how good it looked and were surprised when I told them how much it cost.

While the realistic branches were my favorite part of the design, the lighting came a very close second.

The Smart Grand Duchess includes 2,250 micro LED lights, with settings that range from traditional white lighting to colorful displays and animated effects.

I’ve tested trees with multicolored lighting that looks overly bright and almost cartoonish. This one is different. The colors are slightly more subdued and sophisticated, giving the tree a polished appearance rather than an overwhelming display.

My favorite setting was the steady multicolored mode. I loved the way the different colors illuminated the branches without constantly changing or distracting from the decorations. I also found myself returning to the slow-fade version, which adds a little movement while maintaining that more understated look.

Connecting the tree to Home Depot’s Hubspace app was quick and painless. The interface is clean and straightforward, with easy access to lighting modes, timers, schedules and brightness adjustments.

One of the most useful features was the ability to schedule the lights. Rather than switching them on and off manually each day, I could set the tree to light up automatically when I wanted it.

The brightness controls have three settings: low, medium and high. I’d ordinarily prefer a more precise slider, but in practice, these three levels were enough for my needs.

Even with the app working reliably throughout testing, I still found myself reaching for the physical remote quite frequently. It’s simply more convenient when you’re sitting nearby and want to flick through a few lighting options without opening your phone.

I particularly appreciate that the tree doesn’t force you to use its smart features. The app adds some useful functionality, but you can still enjoy the lights without making every adjustment through your smartphone.

Ilgunas says convenience is one of the biggest reasons to invest in a smart Christmas tree. “We don’t need to crawl under the tree to unplug it or switch it off, and we don’t need to worry about resetting the timer after a short power outage. A remote control and/or phone app gives you total control at the tip of your finger.”

Over the course of a month, the Smart Grand Duchess continued to impress. The branches maintained their shape, the stand remained stable and the lighting and smart controls worked without any noticeable issues.

I also didn’t experience the sort of excessive needle shedding that you might find with cheaper artificial trees.

When it came time to pack everything away, the process was as straightforward as it gets.

One detail worth knowing before you open the packaging is that the original shipping box doubles as a storage box. I’d recommend taking a little extra care when unboxing so you have a decent container to use when the holidays are over.

Personally, I actually preferred storing this tree in its original box rather than using a dedicated Christmas tree bag. I’ve dealt with large, floppy storage bags in the past, and they can be awkward to carry, move around and organize in a storage area.

The rigid cardboard box was much easier to handle and fit neatly into my storage space. Of course, you’ll want to keep it somewhere dry, and a dedicated storage bag may be preferable for more demanding storage conditions.

Still, having a usable storage option included with the tree is a welcome bonus, especially considering its price.

I’ve owned and tested artificial Christmas trees across a fairly wide range of prices, including a much more expensive model from King of Christmas.

That’s what made the Smart Grand Duchess such a pleasant surprise. Looking at the two trees, the price difference isn’t nearly as obvious as I expected.

My King of Christmas tree is undeniably a premium product, but the Home Depot model manages to achieve a similarly attractive overall appearance for considerably less money. The realistic outer foliage does much of the heavy lifting, while the interior filling provides the density needed to create a convincing finished tree.

Where the Grand Duchess stands out most is in its combination of price and technology. You get integrated multicolored lighting, app-based schedules, a physical remote and easy assembly without paying the premium that often comes with higher-end artificial trees.

That doesn’t necessarily mean it’s better than every more expensive option. If you prioritize premium materials throughout the entire tree or specialized construction, you may still find a reason to spend more.

But for most people who want a full, realistic-looking Christmas tree with plenty of lighting options, I think the Grand Duchess gives you an excellent balance of quality, features and price.

After a month of testing, I can confidently say that the Home Depot Smart Grand Duchess Christmas tree is one of the better-value artificial trees I’ve found.

Its biggest achievement is making a relatively affordable tree look considerably more expensive than it is. The molded outer branches are convincing, the less expensive interior foliage is cleverly concealed, and the finished result is full and attractive.

The lighting is another highlight. Rather than offering flashy effects simply for the sake of having them, the tree gives you a few beautiful settings that complement its appearance. The Hubspace app is easy to navigate, and the included remote makes everyday adjustments even simpler.

There are a few compromises, including the basic stand and limited brightness controls, but none meaningfully detracted from my experience. Even better, the tree was reliable throughout my testing, drew plenty of compliments from visitors and was easy to pack away afterward.

If you’re looking for a realistic, pre-lit Christmas tree with smart features but don’t want to spend a small fortune, the Smart Grand Duchess would be very high on my list.

A smart artificial Christmas tree with app and remote controls and a surprisingly lush look for the price.

The 7.5-foot Smart Grand Duchess Twinkling Balsam Fir is available at The Home Depot for around $350, and up to around $1,500 for the 15-foot version.

Home Depot also offers other sizes and configurations within the Grand Duchess collection, including slim and flocked versions, so it’s worth comparing the options to find the right fit for your space.

Yes. Based on our testing, realism is one of its greatest strengths. Molded plastic foliage on the outer branches provides a convincing appearance, while less expensive artificial needles toward the center fill out the tree without being particularly noticeable.

Yes. The tree includes a physical remote that lets you to change lighting effects without using your smartphone. The Hubspace app adds features such as customizable schedules and convenient smart controls.

In our testing, assembly took about 20 minutes, not including additional fluffing and branch shaping. The Quick Set design helps simplify installation by connecting the electrical components through the trunk.

We noticed very little shedding during our month of testing. Its molded outer foliage consists largely of solid plastic pieces, which helps reduce the number of loose needles compared with some artificial trees that rely more heavily on traditional PVC foliage.

Yes. We successfully packed the tree back into its original shipping box and found it convenient for storage. Take care when unboxing to preserve the cardboard, and keep the box in a dry location to protect it from moisture.

For this review, product tester and editor Paul Rankin spent approximately one month evaluating the Home Decorators Collection Smart Grand Duchess Christmas tree in his own home. He assembled, decorated and displayed the tree, tested its lighting and smart controls, monitored its performance over time and evaluated how easily it could be packed away.

Paul has years of experience testing and reviewing home products for publications including Family Handyman, Bob Vila and Reader’s Digest. His experience with other artificial Christmas trees, including higher-end models from King of Christmas, provided additional context for evaluating the Grand Duchess’s realism, features and value.

We also consulted Kristin Ilgunas, founder and designer at A Merry Little Kristmas, a luxury holiday design studio specializing in high-end residential and boutique commercial holiday décor. Ilgunas provided expert insight into artificial Christmas tree construction, the differences between PE and PVC foliage, and the practical benefits of smart lighting features.

#224. Can You Make Stuffing Ahead of Time? Yes—Here’s How

The key to a breezy Thanksgiving is the same as for any dinner party: Do absolutely everything you can ahead of time. I don’t just mean getting a jump on cranberry sauce, pie dough, or overnight-brining the bird—you should cross every single item, big and small, off your to-do list as far in advance as possible, to free up the big day for last-minute mishaps and (this is going to sound crazy) to enjoy yourself.

Can you make stuffing ahead of time? Absolutely. Many Thanksgiving stuffing recipes can be prepared at least partially in advance. Our make-ahead stuffing recipe uses a two-stage baking process: cook the stuffing through the day before Thanksgiving, then refrigerate it overnight. The next day, all that’s left is to reheat it and crisp up the top while your turkey rests.

If you’re used to throwing together a dish of stuffing from a store-bought mix, this make-ahead stuffing recipe is a very easy, very delicious upgrade. Instead of coating a bag of brittle dried bread cubes with unidentified poultry seasoning, this homemade stuffing recipe builds big flavor with hearty torn sourdough bread, hot Italian sausage, fresh herbs, and a boatload of caramelized onions. It requires minimal day-of labor (without sacrificing taste) by relying on the prep time you’ll carve out on Thanksgiving Eve. The result is a stuffing that’s ready when you are—and plenty of time on T-Day to focus on your turkey recipe and all those other Thanksgiving side dishes.

If you want to make stuffing ahead of time, the type of bread matters. Some classic stuffing recipes call for plain white bread, which will likely absorb too much moisture and disintegrate. A sturdier loaf, like sourdough bread, is more likely to retain its structure as it soaks in the chicken broth, making it the ideal choice for this make-ahead stuffing recipe.

Drying the bread on two baking sheets gives you room to spread the bread cubes into a single layer for even toasting. You’ll dry them in an oven on low heat (250°). Don’t skip this part, even if you’re using a stale loaf (since stale bread isn’t actually dried out), as it helps the sourdough maintain its integrity once submerged into its custardy bath. Transfer the dried bread chunks to a large bowl and prep the rest of the mixture.

True caramelized onions take a long time to break down and become the melty, sweet-savory magic you want them to be. On Thanksgiving dinners past, you would not find a caramelized onion within 100 feet of my table because I absolutely did not have that kind of time. But if I’m assembling the entire stuffing the day before, I can cook spicy sausage, caramelize onions, and create a sage-scented base for torn bread without worrying about the clock.

Sweet, jammy, and totally worth the wait.

Build layers of flavor by sautéing the onions in the same skillet you used to render the sausage fat. Season the onions with kosher salt, add a little extra olive oil, and cook over medium heat until they’re a deep golden brown. If anything starts to stick, add a little water and scrape up the bottom of the pan. Don’t stop cooking the onions until they are certified jammy. Then add in the rest of the aromatics: celery, garlic, and black pepper, plus finely chopped herbs and unsalted butter. Deglaze the pan with white wine and let it simmer before adding it to the bowl with the bread; add the eggs and chicken stock or broth, then transfer the whole mixture to a casserole dish. (Don’t have one? Use a large skillet instead—ovensafe, please.)

Bake the stuffing through its first stage a day or two before Thanksgiving, then let it cool briefly before refrigerating it within two hours of cooking.

On Thanksgiving Day, when your roast turkey is resting, remove the foil and return the stuffing to the oven for its second bake. The recipe calls for another 10 to 15 minutes to warm through and crisp up the top, but go by temperature, not just the clock: The center should reach 165°F before serving.

Yes. Many stuffing recipes can be frozen ahead of Thanksgiving. Our Simple-Is-Best Stuffing, for example, can be baked through its first stage, then frozen for up to six months before the final bake. Let the stuffing cool briefly, wrap tightly, and freeze.

Thaw it in the refrigerator before reheating, allowing at least 24 hours for a large dish. Reheat until the center reaches 165°F, uncovering toward the end to crisp up the top.

How do you reheat stuffing without drying it out?

If your stuffing seems dry, add a splash of chicken or vegetable broth before reheating. Cover the baking dish with foil to help retain moisture, then reheat in an oven set to at least 325°F until the center reaches 165°F. Remove the foil toward the end to crisp up the top.

How long can you keep stuffing in the refrigerator?

According to the USDA, stuffing can be refrigerated for 3–4 days, as long as it’s cooked through and refrigerated promptly. Store it in a covered container, ideally shallow enough to cool quickly, and reheat it thoroughly before serving.

Additional reporting contributed by Zoe Denenberg.

#225. Magical Midnight Margarita

Fans of the cult classic film Practical Magic may recognize some version of this cocktail. The “Midnight Margarita” is inspired by a scene in which two characters blend up a witchy brew to the soundtrack of Harry Nilsson’s “Coconut.” Some fans even start the movie at exactly 11:12 p.m., so the pivotal moment arrives at the stroke of midnight.

While the movie’s cocktail appears to be a standard standard frozen margarita—no eye of newt or toe of frog, (maybe hair of the dog if you prefer tequila and lime in the morning)—but our version leans into the magic. Blackberries give the drink its deep purple color, while coconut water adds a subtle sweetness and makes the frozen version especially refreshing. Serve it on the rocks or blended. If serving on the rocks, garnish with a torched rosemary sprig for a smoky, spellbinding flourish.

More tequila drinks to cheers to at midnight: Paloma; Citrus Slushy; Aperol-Kombucha Cocktail

Because freezing can dull flavors, adding a little extra lime juice perks this version up. We’ve also increased the coconut water so you won’t have to dilute the drink with plain ice.

| Yield: Makes 1 | Total time: 10 minutes plus chilling |

Pour some flaky sea salt on a small plate. Halve 2 limes and rub a cut side of 1 half around rim of a rocks glass; dip rim into salt to coat. Squeeze juice from limes into a small measuring glass or bowl (you should have about 2 oz).

Place 5 blackberries in glass and muddle berries just to break up.

Combine lime juice, 2 oz. coconut water, 2 oz. tequila blanco, 1 oz. orange liqueur (such as Cointreau or Triple Sec), and ½ tsp. sugar in a cocktail shaker filled with ice. Cover and shake until outside of shaker is very cold, about 30 seconds.

Fill glass with blackberries with ice cubes. Strain cocktail over and garnish with a rosemary sprig, briefly singed over a flame, if desired.

#226. Beware the sourdough starter fake out: Don’t fall for this classic sourdough starter trick.

We think of baking as a wholesome hobby, but certain threats stalk our kitchens. Our Test Kitchen is terrified of cake cleaching. Soggy bottoms haunt our nightmares. And in our bread baking, nothing is more dispiriting (and mystifying) that the sourdough starter fake out.

The sourdough starter fake out can occur when you’re making a brand-new starter from scratch or if you’re reviving a dormant one. In both cases, you start by giving your starter regular feedings of flour and water until it’s reliably active. Directions typically tell you to feed a starter consistently, once or twice a day, until it doubles or triples in volume 6 to 8 hours after feeding — that is when it is healthy and active enough to start making bread. If you’re making a new starter, this can often take up to a week.

Sometimes, however, you'll find that after the first few days, your culture is way ahead of schedule, doubling in volume and seeming very active in very little time. It must be ready!, you think. Then, suddenly, it stops.

Is it dead? No. The rising you see in those first days is caused by a sudden rush of activity as all the wild yeasts and bacteria in the mix start to feed voraciously. This burst of activity may make you think your starter is healthy and ready to go (and its subsequent screeching halt may trick you into thinking it’s immediately dead). In actuality, however, this is just a brief feeding frenzy. As your culture begins to ripen, it becomes more acidic, and a whole complex battle takes place, as microbes throw different molecules at one another, meant to kill their competitors and leave more food for themselves. A portion of these microorganisms just can’t hang on. As they die off, the culture takes on the sudden appearance of inactivity. That’s what makes it seem dead when it’s really just fine.

But with more time and regular feeding, a robust yeast colony will become established (only the strong survive!), which is when you’ll begin to see predictable rising and falling again after each feeding, along with bubbles. At this point, your starter is ready to bake — which means you can make Rustic Sourdough Bread, Sourdough Focaccia, Chocolate Sourdough Babka, and more. So if your culture rises dramatically and then seems to fall dormant, don’t be discouraged: It's just a sign that your starter needs more time.

#227. TIME’s 2026 Best Inventions List Includes 3 Game-Changing Baking Tools

Your sourdough hobby just got a lot easier.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Baking at home is a labor of love. From tending a sourdough starter to meticulously crimping pie crust, each recipe takes finesse and precision. Thankfully, new technological innovations make home baking easier—and many of them appear on TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026.

Each year, the publication rounds up the latest groundbreaking products that make life easier. The 2026 edition spans almost every industry, from tech to healthcare to household goods. But some of the most notable inclusions target home bakers. Here’s what made the list:

Sourdough gets its signature tang from a starter, which needs regular feeding and maintenance to keep the yeast and healthy bacteria alive. And anybody who had a sourdough phase during the pandemic knows how tedious that process can be. That’s where the Sourdough Sidekick comes in.

This compact countertop appliance, made in partnership with King Arthur Baking Company and FirstBuild, automates the process of maintaining sourdough starter. It features a water tank, flour hopper, and mixing paddle that can manage the feeding process for up to a week. The digital display and connected mobile app let you fine-tune settings or choose a preset mode that does the hard work for you.

Since the Sourdough Sidekick debuted in June of this year, home bakers have given it rave reviews, calling it “revolutionary” and “a dream come true.” You can buy it from King Arthur Baking for $179.95.

If you like the idea of baking fresh sourdough but aren’t committed to maintaining a starter long term, Leaven offers a new shortcut. Most store-bought yeast helps your dough rise, but doesn’t bring any unique flavors to the table. Leaven’s Instant Sourdough, on the other hand, offers similar lift with the same live cultures you’d find in a real sourdough starter.

The creators used DNA sequencing to isolate the exact microbes you’d find in a starter and replicated them as a shelf-stable powder—no feeding required. Each pouch can be used for up to eight recipes. While it’s not a 1:1 substitute for store-bought yeast, Leaven offers a detailed guide with conversion charts and a lineup of beginner-friendly recipes for convenient sourdough treats.

Leaven currently sells a three-pack of its Instant Sourdough for $19.99.

After using all of your elbow grease to knead a loaf of bread, the last thing you want to do is spend more time scrubbing bits of dough from the sides of your mixing bowl. Instead of just leaving it to soak overnight (aka procrastinate), you can use this new cleaning product called Dough Dissolve.

Most dish soap is designed to tackle grease and other fat-based residue on dishes. Dough Dissolve is a cleansing gel that instead uses the enzyme amylase to specifically target starches. A few pumps of Dough Dissolve on your dirty dishes, plus a quick 10-minute soak, will dissolve stuck-on stains with little to no scrubbing.

You can get your hands on a bottle directly from Dough Dissolve for $23.39.

#228. Caroline Chambers on Why Cooking Can Feel Like 'An Absolute Hellscape'

What does Caroline Chambers cook when she doesn’t feel like cooking? That’s what I wanted to ask her after reading her brutally honest and heartwarming essay from our series The Fourth Trimester, all about postpartum meals. In it, Caroline writes about finding herself as a cook after giving birth to her first son. Now she has added three more kids to the mix and is navigating a wild blend of family, work, and life, yet showing up with incredible authenticity and humor. Read our conversation below—and make it to the end for the cover recipe from Caroline’s latest book.

Chris Morocco: Our team loved your first book (for readers who don’t know, we named it one of our favorites of 2024) and eagerly awaited your second. How did you decide on time as the theme for your next title, Make It Fast?

Caroline Chambers: I think that a huge, huge part of why cooking dinner can feel like such an absolute hellscape is that we simply do not have the time. We’re overbooked, overworked, we’re trying to make time to be good parents and good friends and somehow get in a few minutes of exercise in. At the end of the day, cooking yet another meal usually feels like the absolute last thing on earth that you want to do. So knowing exactly how much of a time investment you are going to have to make feels really good. Being able to flip through the 15-minute chapter and think, Okay, I can freaking do this! Or the “walk away” chapter and know that, with under 30 minutes of prep time, you can throw something in a pot to simmer away, or in the oven to slow roast, while you go about your day.

You made the bold choice to incorporate all ingredient prep in your recipe instructions, so your active times actually include how long it takes to chop every onion and shred every carrot. Very few recipes do this! How did you arrive at this practice?

Like Bon Appétit, I have years of hearing directly from my readers via my Substack, What to Cook When You Don’t Feel Like Cooking. When something takes longer to chop than I thought it would take them, I hear about it. And this is a wonderful thing! I can adjust, learn what their pain points are, and help educate them about ways to do it with more ease the next time. But I’ve definitely learned that people do not like to be bamboozled by the prep step being included in the ingredient list. They want to be told exactly when to do it. Plus, when I lay out exactly when they should prep each ingredient, I can help maximize their efficiency in the oven. Mince the garlic while the chicken sears. Chop the herbs while the pasta cooks. Without spelling it out for them in this way, a novice home cook might mise-en-place it all out at the beginning, and that adds a lot of time. And time is of the essence with this book, we ain’t got time to spare!

What are the ingredients you can’t live without that save you time in the kitchen?

I freaking love a bagged salad. I had this series on Instagram once all about how to make bagged salads taste better. I need to bring that back. Taylor Farms Caesar is a regular staple in my household—it’s just an honest-to-God delightful Caesar salad. We’ll have that and steaks for dinner at least a couple of times a month. I know that isn’t really an ingredient, but it sort of is? Other staples: lemons, rice (I cook a huge batch and freeze it in individual portions), those frozen garlic and ginger cubes, Better Than Bouillon (I’m a low-sodium chicken gal but I dabble in the fun ones, too, like “sofrito” and “sautéed onion”). I always have a jar of Trader Joe’s salsa verde (poach chicken thighs in it, shred, dinner is served). I love many types of chili crisp for instant flavor, but Red Clay’s southern chili crisp with peanuts and shallots is king.

During my time in food media, I have seen a trend of the most popular recipes in the zeitgeist getting simpler and easier. Is there any hope for people wanting to roast a chicken again, or has the prevalence of rotisserie chickens in supermarkets made such recipes obsolete?

I have a theory that cooking is really hard for everyone right now, not only because none of us have the time to do it, but also because none of us were taught how to do it. Our mothers and fathers were the first generation of parents where it was really widespread for both parents to be in the workforce. Mom wasn’t home cooking and teaching her daughters how to cook. She was at work! So a lot of people simply never were taught fundamental cooking skills. Like how to cut an onion! If you don’t know how to cut an onion, or mince a garlic clove, you’re instantly pissed. The second you start cooking a recipe, and it tells you to cut an onion, you instantly feel like you suck at cooking and it takes forever.

So…I don’t know, Chris! The irony of my entire brand, What to Cook When You Don’t Feel Like Cooking, is, of course, that my readers do feel like cooking. Instead of ordering DoorDash, they’re willing to give my newsletter and cookbooks a try. They want to want to cook!

I know, and you know, that people feel so proud of themselves when they cook a delicious meal. So I do think that the more people can nail really simple, easy recipes, and learn to cook from those simpler recipes, the more incentivized they are to try things that intimidate them—like roasting a whole bird.

On that note…favorite thing to do with a rotisserie bird?

I have an entire section in What to Cook about what to do with a rotisserie chicken, but the honest answer is that I mostly just eat it straight up! Chop it up for the kids, throw a leg to the baby in his high chair, slice up the breasts and serve them with a salad. I had some leftover rotisserie tonight, in fact, and fed it to the boys with baby broccoli, and made a version of the kale and quinoa salad for my husband and brother and his girlfriend (they live with us!). It’s so good—from the new book!

My other favorite thing to do with a rotisserie chicken is to keep it in the front seat for the drive home from the store and tear it apart with my hands like an absolute animal. If anyone ever sees me eating a chicken leg while cruising on the 1, no you didn’t.

I have two kids with such different tastes in food. Sometimes I think they exaggerate their preferences just to show the world how different they are, which is fine when it comes to hairstyles and shoes, but a bummer with dinner. Is it challenging for you to find meals that all your kids will eat?

Chris. Yes. These kids kill me. I have four boys—7, 6, 4, and 14 months. Those little turds will tell me ribs are their favorite meal, that they dreamed about ribs (!), and then I’ll make the exact same ribs recipe I cooked the last time, and half of them will tell me they’re too spicy. I’m with you—I think kids use food preferences as power. It allows them to have their own opinions and their own say. It absolutely kills me. I recently instigated a very strict and probably absolutely not child-therapist-approved two-bite rule. They have to try at least two bites of dinner, and if they truly do not like it, I’ll make them a PB&J or hummus and veggies. Most of the time, my 7- and 4-year-olds wind up eating the entire thing. My 6-year-old very, very rarely does. That guy is eating a lot of PB&Js right now. And just FYI, the PB&J is: Dave’s Killer Bread 21 Whole Grains, Ground Up Honey Sea Salt peanut butter, Bonne Maman Strawberry Jam. I can’t really blame him, it’s delicious.

After a day working on recipe development, when you have been elbow-deep in pasta and dishes since 9 a.m., do you ever think to yourself when dinner time rolls around, Oh heck no! Is that just me? What do you cook when you don’t feel like cooking? And what’s your go-to takeout?

HELL YES. The cobbler’s kids get no shoes, as they say!!! We live kinda in the country, so our take-out options absolutely suck. My take-out option is steaming frozen dumplings and broccoli florets at the same time in a steamer basket and making a peanut sauce while they’re steaming. Everyone absolutely devours this meal. Except for my six-year-old, of course. But the good news is that the peanut butter is already out for his dinner.

You have two pieces of advice in Make It Fast that I absolutely adore: “Lay corn flat on its side to cut it,” and “salt and pepper are not married.” I guess that isn’t really a question, just wanted to say thank you! And if you have any other sage advice like this, I want to hear it.

Oh my gosh, thanks for noticing those! I’m a self-taught cook, meaning that America’s Test Kitchen and the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen are responsible for so much of my early learning. So that means a lot to hear from you. I read this book called Eight Flavors about the eight major flavors in American cuisine many, many years ago. One of the chapters is about black pepper and to absolutely butcher her beautifully done research and writing—the common use of salt and pepper together, in every single freaking recipe, basically boils down to really good marketing when spice traders first introduced black pepper to America. Salt and pepper are not married!

A few other pieces of advice from the book, for people who do not feel like cooking:

#229. Blueberry Protein Pancakes (No Protein Powder)

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week.

Tofu in blueberry pancakes?! Your eyes do not deceive you. Here, silken tofu acts as a binding agent in these protein-packed vegan blueberry pancakes. As there are no eggs in this recipe, you’ll need as much help with leavening as possible to cut through the density of the tofu. This means adding both baking powder and soda—and a lot of it. Baking powder (make sure to use the aluminum-free kind to mitigate any unpleasant flavor) will activate with the water and again when the batter hits the heat; baking soda will react with the water and the acid in the brown sugar. The result is a fluffy, crisp-edged pancake with a slightly chewy, almost mochi-like interior. Small wild blueberries are best, but whatever kind you find at the store will work.

As is the case with most baked goods—even those that technically don’t go into the oven—these pancakes are most successful when the ingredients are measured by weight with a scale. If measuring by volume with measuring cups, it can be easy to pack in a little extra flour. If so, you may need to add about a tablespoon or so more water; you want the batter to be the approximate consistency of pourable whole-milk yogurt (not thick Greek-style).

Discover more Good for You recipes here: Veggie Club Sandwich; Berry Protein Smoothie; Chopped Salad With Sardines and Preserved Lemon

Read More: How I Make Protein Pancakes Without Protein Powder

Whisk 1½ cups (188 g) all-purpose flour, ½ cup (62 g) whole wheat flour, 3 Tbsp. light brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. aluminum-free baking powder, 1 tsp. baking soda, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine.

Blend tofu and liquid from one 16–17-oz. package silken tofu in a blender until very smooth. Scrape down sides and add 1 Tbsp. avocado oil or vegetable oil and 1½ cups water; blend until mixture is very smooth. Scrape into bowl with dry ingredients and gently fold in with a whisk.

Heat a dry large nonstick skillet over medium for 3 minutes. Drizzle in 1½ tsp. avocado oil or vegetable oil. Pour 2 scant ⅓-cupfuls of batter into skillet, leaving space around each. Top each pancake with about 1½ tsp. fresh or frozen wild blueberries. Cook pancakes until tops start to look matte, about 4 minutes. Gently flip and cook until golden underneath, about 4 minutes. Transfer pancakes to a plate or wire rack. (Alternatively, transfer to a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet and keep warm in a 300° oven while you make the rest). Working in 7 more batches, repeat process with remaining oil, batter, and blueberries, adjusting heat as needed to keep pancakes from absorbing too much oil or burning.

Do Ahead: Pancakes can be made 3 months ahead. Let cool, then stack between sheets of parchment paper and place in an airtight container or resealable plastic bag and freeze. Reheat in a toaster or toaster oven until warmed through.

#230. Tom Colicchio Just Joined The Growing Backlash Against The Michelin Guide

A new report has chefs and diners questioning the iconic restaurant guide.

Pop into any food-related Reddit thread these days, and you’ll find people questioning the relevance of the Michelin Guide. What was once considered the Mount Everest of restaurant accolades seems to be losing its luster in recent years—and it’s now under even greater attack after a report accused the prestigious awards of using AI to write its latest Dallas guide.

For background, Michelin updated its Texas guide last week, adding new restaurants in the Dallas area. D Magazine reportedly conducted an investigation with academic experts and AI detection software and concluded that most of the Dallas additions were written with AI.

While Michelin has denied the allegations, the accusation has reignited the conversation about the guide's relevance today.

“The guide was how you found out about the best of the best back in the day, now you can easily figure out what’s going on in the culinary world...Now we have Instagram and YouTube,” wrote one person on Reddit.

“It’s still relevant. But it’s no longer the Oscars for food,” another person agreed.

“It’s lost some credibility as more people started to find out that it’s a “pay-to-play” marketing process in the cities that are reviewed. As travel [influencer] content has increased over time, people are realizing that Michelin leaves out a lot of great restaurants in cities that don’t participate,” one person said, referring to the fact that tourism boards and destination marketing groups sometimes pay Michelin to bring the Guide to their region. Michelin says those partners don’t control the restaurant selections, though the arrangement has raised questions about independence.

And this was all before the big AI of it all. Even celebrity chef Tom Colicchio thinks the Michelin Guide should be relegated to the past. “It’s time to start ignoring this guide,” he commented on D Magazine’s social media post.

While many people echo Colicchio’s sentiments, others still defend the guide.

“AI detection software is anything but bulletproof...Making accusations based on those is quite literally like calling someone a witch because she floats in water,” one person said on Reddit.

“WHO CARES??? It’s a writing aide…not a controversy. Nothing about the use of AI makes the inspection notes any less real or accurate,” another person commented.

The consensus: People are divided. Many will still consult the Michelin Guide before traveling, whether the AI allegation is true or not, while others look to more modern sources like social media. Time will tell how well the prestigious guide holds up.
